j-r-jayewardene: Junius Richard Jayewardene was born on 17 September 1906 in Colombo, the eldest of twelve children of the lawyer Eugene Wilfred Jayewardene, in a family with a strong association with the legal profession. He was educated at Royal College, Colombo, where he played cricket and captained the rugby team, and at Ceylon Law College, and passed his advocates' examinations in 1931.

He converted from Anglicanism to Buddhism and in 1943 gave up full-time practice to become an activist in the Ceylon National Congress. In 1943 he was elected to the State Council, and in 1944 he moved a motion that Sinhala alone should replace English as the official language. He was a founder member of the United National Party in 1946 and became finance minister in the island's first cabinet in 1947.

After the UNP's defeat in 1956 he lost his seat, and he pushed the party to endorse the Sinhala Only Act, which the island's minorities bitterly opposed. He succeeded Dudley Senanayake as party leader in 1973. The UNP won the election of 21 July 1977 with five-sixths of the seats, and he was sworn in as prime minister on 23 July. A constitutional amendment made the presidency an executive post, and he became the first executive president on 4 February 1978. A new constitution of 31 August 1978 granted the president sweeping powers, almost dictatorial according to some critics. He opened the state-controlled economy to market forces and moved the legislative capital to Sri Jayawardanapura Kotte.

He passed the Prevention of Terrorism Act in 1979 against Tamil militant groups. After the ambush of Four Four Bravo, the Black July riots of 1983 transformed the militancy into a civil war that lasted from 1983 to 2009. In 1987 he and the Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi concluded the Indo-Sri Lanka Accord, which provided for devolution to Tamil-dominated regions and an Indian peacekeeping force in the north. The LTTE rejected it, Sinhala nationalists were outraged, and an attempt was made on his life. A revolt by the Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna was put down by 1989, when he retired from politics.

Jayewardene died of colon cancer on 1 November 1996, aged 90, in Colombo. His economic policies are often credited with transforming a stagnant economy, while his response to the Black July riots has been heavily criticised and accused of heightening ethnic tensions. He is respected in Japan for his call for peace and reconciliation with Japan at the San Francisco Peace Conference in 1951, and a statue of him stands at the Kamakura Temple in Kanagawa Prefecture. The J. R. Jayewardene Centre, established by an act of Parliament in 1988, holds his library and papers.
ja-vi-elsker-dette-landet: Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson wrote the words between 1859 and 1868, and his cousin Rikard Nordraak wrote the melody during the winter of 1863 to 1864. The song was first performed in public on 17 May 1864, in connection with the 50th anniversary of the constitution. Bjørnson wrote in a modified version of the Danish used in Norway at the time, and the text sung today keeps his words with modernised spelling and punctuation. Usually only the first and the last two verses are sung, the first by far the most often. In each verse the last two lines are sung twice, with one or two words repeated a further time.

Until the mid-1860s the songs Sønner av Norge and Norges Skaal were commonly regarded as national anthems, Sønner av Norge being the better known. Ja, vi elsker dette landet gradually came to be recognised as an anthem from the mid-1860s, and until the early 20th century both were used, with Sønner av Norge preferred in official situations. Norway had no official anthem until 11 December 2019.

The original version contained a verse that hailed the king, who had succeeded his father in July 1859. It described the king as a strong and open border guard whose best weapon was the brethren pact, a military treaty by which Norway, Sweden and Denmark were to help one another if any was attacked. When German troops invaded South Jutland in February 1864, none of the partners came to Denmark's rescue, and the failure shattered hopes of a united Scandinavia. Bjørnson went from monarchist to republican, and the tribute to the sovereign was struck from the song.

In 1905 the Norwegian Storting declared the union with Sweden dissolved on 7 June, which brought the two nations to the brink of war in the autumn. Swedish Social Democrats, whose leaders Hjalmar Branting and Zeth Höglund spoke for a peaceful settlement, sang the song to support the Norwegian right to leave the union. During the Second World War it was used both by the Norwegian resistance and by Nazi collaborators, mainly for propaganda, and the German occupiers eventually forbade any use of it.
Norway also has an unofficial royal anthem, Kongesangen, based on God Save the King, and the psalm Gud signe vårt dyre fedreland, by Elias Blix, which is often called the national psalm.
jabal-al-druze: Jabal al-Druze, Arabic for Mountain of the Druze, is also known as Jabal al-Arab or Jabal Hauran. It is an elevated volcanic region in Hauran, in the Suwayda Governorate of southern Syria. Its volcanic field, the southernmost in Syria, lies on the Haurun-Druze Plateau near the border with Jordan and forms the northern part of the large Harrat al-Sham field, which extends to Saudi Arabia. It consists of 118 basaltic volcanoes active from the lower Pleistocene to the Holocene, and its highest feature rises to 1,800 metres. In Jabal al-Druze the Arabic word tell, mound or hill, refers to a volcanic cone: Tell Qeni, at 1,803 metres, is the highest peak.

Safaitic inscriptions were first found in this area. In the past the name Jabal al-Druze was used for a different area, in Mount Lebanon. From 1921 to 1936 the Jabal Druze State was an autonomous area within the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon, and it had 42 of the roughly 180 towns of the Hauran.

Most of the inhabitants of the region are Druze, and there are also significant Christian communities. Suwayda Governorate takes in almost all of Jabal al-Druze and is the only governorate in Syria with a Druze majority. In the 1980s Druze made up 87.6 per cent of its population, Christians, mostly Greek Orthodox, 11 per cent and Sunni Muslims 2 per cent. In 2010 the governorate had about 375,000 inhabitants, 90 per cent of them Druze, 7 per cent Christians and 3 per cent Sunni Muslims. The proportion of Christians has declined because of low birth rates and high emigration.
jabalpur: Jabalpur lies on the banks of the Narmada River and is the administrative headquarters of the Jabalpur district and division. Its name is traditionally derived from a sage named Jabali who meditated on the river's banks, though another theory takes it from the Arabic jabal, meaning boulders. The city is known for the Marble Rocks at Bhedaghat, a gorge of marble cut by the Narmada below the Dhuandhar Falls. In 1828 the British officer William Henry Sleeman found a dinosaur fossil near Bara Simla Hill, the first such find in Asia.

Ashokan relics from about 300 BCE at Rupnath, north of the city, indicate Mauryan presence. Later the region came under the Satavahana dynasty and then became a vassal state of the Gupta Empire. The Kalachuri dynasty conquered it in 875. Under the Gond kings of Garha-Mandla the city was an important centre of power: Madan Shah built a watchtower and small fort at Madan Mahal, and Rani Durgavati built more than 85 ponds. A Maratha invasion in 1742 made the kingdom a tributary, and the Maratha rulers of Sagar annexed it in 1781. The Bhonsle kings of Nagpur held the Narmada valley until 1818, when the East India Company seized it after the Battle of Sitabuldi.

The British made Jabalpur the headquarters of the Narmada territories, set up a cantonment and made it the capital of the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories, which joined the Central Provinces in 1861. The Congress session at nearby Tripuri in 1939 re-elected Subhas Chandra Bose as president against Mahatma Gandhi's candidate, and he resigned in April of that year. After independence in 1947 the Central Provinces and Berar became Madhya Pradesh.

Jabalpur is the seat of the Madhya Pradesh High Court and the zonal headquarters of the West Central Railway. Its municipal population was 1,081,677 at the 2011 census, and Hindi is the predominant language. Its cantonment is one of the largest in India, and ordnance factories, including the Gun Carriage Factory begun in 1904, make it a centre of defence industry. It is generally accepted that snooker originated here, devised in 1875 by Colonel Neville Chamberlain. The Hanumantal Bada Jain Mandir, a seventeenth-century temple with 22 shrines, is the largest independent Jain temple in India. The name Jubbulpore was replaced by Jabalpur in 2006.
jablonec-nad-nisou: Jablonec nad Nisou lies about 7 km south-east of Liberec and 83 km north-east of Prague, at the confluence of the Lusatian Neisse and the Bílá Nisa in the eastern tip of the Zittau Basin, ringed by the Jizera Mountains. The Czech name means little apple tree, because the village was founded where an apple tree grew. German-speaking settlers of the 16th century turned it into Gablonz, and in 1904 the suffix nad Nisou, or an der Neisse, was made official in both languages.

The first written mention is in a Latin document of 1356, which treats the village as founded in the 14th century. Troops of rebelling Lusatians burned it in August 1469 during their war with King George of Poděbrady, and it was resettled in the 1530s and 1540s by mostly German-speaking colonists. In the first half of the 17th century it belonged to Albrecht von Wallenstein, who sold it to the Desfours family, and it was burned again in 1643 during the Thirty Years' War.

Glass production began to flourish in the second half of the 17th century. The first bijou was made in the 18th century, and the exporter J. F. Schwann spread the village's name through Europe. Emperor Francis II made it a market town on 21 April 1808, and Emperor Franz Joseph I made it a town on 28 March 1866. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 to 1871 damaged competitors, its traders took over foreign markets. By the turn of the 20th century Bohemian garnet jewellery sold in Chicago came from Gablonz. The crash of 1929 hit the glass and jewellery trade, and foreign competition and changing fashion added to the crisis of the 1930s.

After the Munich Agreement the town was annexed to Nazi Germany in October 1938 and administered as part of Reichsgau Sudetenland until 1945. Between 1945 and 1949 most of the Germans were expelled under the Beneš decrees. Some of them founded a new settlement in Bavaria and named it Neugablonz, new Jablonec. It is now a district of Kaufbeuren.

Jablonec nad Nisou is a city of about 46,000 inhabitants, the second largest in the Liberec Region, and it forms a conurbation with Liberec. Its historic centre is protected as an urban monument zone. The New Town Hall, built in the functionalist style in 1930 to 1933, is a national cultural monument. The Church of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross of 1900 to 1902 is counted among the most important Art Nouveau churches in Europe. The Museum of Glass and Costume Jewellery, founded in 1904, presents the local tradition of costume jewellery and beads.
jaca: Jaca stands on the Aragón River near the Pyrenees and the border with France, at a height of 820 metres. It lies at the crossing of two great early medieval routes, one from Toulouse to Santiago de Compostela and one from Pau to Zaragoza. The County and Kingdom of Aragon developed out of the city, and it was the capital of the district of Jacetania.

The origins of the city are obscure, but its name apparently derives from the Iacetani, whom Strabo lists among the small tribes of the Ebro basin. Jaca minted coins from the second half of the 2nd century BCE, showing a horseman with a spear and the Iberian inscription iaka. The Roman consul Cato the Elder began the conquest of the city in 195 BCE and finished it in the spring of 194 BCE. Huesca fell to the Muslims in 720, and the region of Jacetania then served as a buffer zone for the Carolingian Empire; by 799 Aureolo had stabilised an independent county.

Ramiro I of Aragon, who reigned from 1035 to 1063, gave it the title of city and capital of the Kingdom of Aragon, and in 1063 it was the site of the Synod of Jaca. As the Aragonese conquered land to the south from Muslim rule, the capital was moved to Huesca in 1096, though Jaca remained a market city for its region. It was home to Aragon's oldest Jewish community until the expulsion of 1492. In 1592 Philip II ordered the pentagonal citadel, designed by the Italian engineer Tibúrcio Spannocchi, to defend the Pyrenees against a possible French invasion. A mutiny there on 12 and 13 December 1930, whose leaders demanded the abolition of the monarchy, was suppressed with some difficulty.

Jaca has medieval walls and towers around the 11th-century Romanesque cathedral, and the citadel of the late 16th century. The Diocesan Museum of Jaca keeps Romanesque and Gothic frescoes from the district. From the early 1970s the town changed from a small garrison town into the gateway to winter resorts such as Astún and Candanchú.
jachymov: Jáchymov, in German Sankt Joachimsthal or Joachimsthal, lies in the Ore Mountains in the Karlovy Vary District, about 15 kilometres north of Karlovy Vary on the border with Germany. The town stands in a valley at 733 metres, and its territory includes Klínovec, the highest mountain of the range at 1,244 metres. It was founded in a valley called in German simply Thal and was named after Saint Joachim, so that the name means Saint Joachim's Valley.

The village of Joachimsthal was founded by Steffan Schlick in 1516. The silver caused the population to grow rapidly and made the Counts of Schlick one of the richest families in Bohemia. From 1520 they minted silver coins, the Joachimsthalers, called Thaler in German and tolar in Czech, from which, through the Dutch daalder, the word dollar derives. In 1528 Ferdinand I seized the right of mining. Georgius Agricola based his metallurgical studies on observations made here in the late 1520s. In 1534, with about 20,000 people, Jáchymov was the second most populous town in the Kingdom of Bohemia, behind Prague.

The Church of Saint Joachim, built in 1534 to 1540, was the first Lutheran church in the Kingdom of Bohemia; after the Counter-Reformation took effect in 1621 many Lutheran citizens migrated to nearby Saxon territory. The war and the lack of pumps to drain deep mines left the town unable to compete with cheap Spanish silver from the American colonies. Later Martin Heinrich Klaproth found that pitchblende could colour glass yellow, and discovered a new element in 1781, naming it uranium. The Austrian government sent 100 kilograms of waste from the uranium pigment factory to Marie Skłodowska-Curie and Pierre Curie, who found radium in it. Until the First World War this was the foremost source of radium in the world.

Jáchymov was annexed by Nazi Germany after the Munich Agreement in 1938, and most of its German population was expelled in 1945 and 1946. After the Second World War uranium mining began on a large scale, and almost all the uranium was exported to the Soviet Union. Prison camps held prisoners of war, forcibly recruited citizens, political prisoners and opponents of the communist regime. At the peak in 1955 over 46,000 people worked there, 20 per cent of them involuntarily. Mining ceased in 1964.

Jáchymov has about 2,200 inhabitants. The first radon spa in the world was founded there in 1906. The town is part of the Ore Mountain Mining Region, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and its historic centre is protected as an urban monument zone. The Royal Mint, built in 1533 to 1536, houses a museum of mining.
jacmel: Jacmel is a commune on the south coast of Haiti, the capital of the department of Sud-Est, 24 miles (39 kilometres) southwest of Port-au-Prince across the Tiburon Peninsula. Its name comes from the Taíno name Yaquimel. The area was Taíno territory, part of the Xaragua chiefdom ruled by the cacique Bohechio, before the French renamed it Jacmel.

The Compagnie de Saint-Domingue founded the town in 1698 as the capital of the southeastern part of the French colony of Saint-Domingue. It was developed to boost sugar production and trade but soon became a centre of the coffee trade. A fire in 1896 destroyed most of its buildings. The city was rebuilt, often with prefabricated cast-iron pillars and balconies shipped from France, and the mansions of wealthy coffee merchants from this period survive with little change. In 1925 Jacmel was the first town in the Caribbean to have electricity.

During the Haitian Revolution, in 1791 and 1792, Romaine-la-Prophétesse led thirteen thousand rebels in besieging, occupying and later burning Jacmel, and in attacking the plantations around it and freeing their slaves. In the War of the South, which began in June 1799, Toussaint Louverture fought André Rigaud for the city. By November the rebels had been pushed back to this strategic port, defended by Alexandre Pétion, and Jacmel fell to Toussaint's troops in February 1800. Pétion and other leaders went into exile in France.

In 1806 Francisco de Miranda raised the first flag of Gran Colombia from the corvette Leander, anchored in the Bay of Jacmel, on 12 March, a day still kept as Venezuelan Flag Day. The flag was the model for those of Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador. In 1870 the Puerto Rican independence leader Ramón Emeterio Betances spent a short time in Jacmel gathering support for an uprising in the Dominican Republic, which the Haitian president Nissage Saget backed.

Jacmel is known for its well-preserved gingerbread houses of the early 19th century, which are said to have influenced the houses of New Orleans. It is also known for its papier-mâché masks and handicrafts, a month-long carnival and a film school, the Ciné Institute. It was heavily damaged in the Haiti earthquake of 12 January 2010. The town has been tentatively accepted as a World Heritage Site, and its main square is named for Toussaint Louverture.
jacob-roggeveen: Jacob Roggeveen was born in Middelburg, the capital of the province of Zeeland, on 1 February 1659. His father, Arend Roggeveen, was a mathematician learned in astronomy, geography and the theory of navigation, who studied the supposed southern continent Terra Australis and obtained a patent for an exploring voyage that he never made. Jacob became a notary of Middelburg and took a doctorate in law at the University of Harderwijk on 12 August 1690.

In 1706 he joined the Dutch East Indies Company and worked from 1707 to 1714 as a councillor of justice at Batavia. He married twice and was widowed twice, and returned to Middelburg alone in 1714. There he became involved in religious controversy by publishing a leaflet of the liberal preacher Pontiaan van Hattem, The Fall of the World's Idol. The city council confiscated and burned the first part in 1718, and Roggeveen moved to Flushing and then to Arnemuiden, where he published two further parts.

On 1 August 1721 Roggeveen, aged 62, set out at the head of an expedition paid for by the Dutch West India Company, rival of the East Indies Company. His brother Jan helped plan it. The aims were to find Terra Australis and to open a western trade route to the Spice Islands. He had three ships, the Arend, the Thienhoven and the Afrikaansche Galey, with 223 men. He sailed to the Falkland Islands, which he renamed Belgia Australis, passed through the Strait of Le Maire and went beyond 60 degrees south before entering the Pacific. He landed near Valdivia in Chile and spent from 24 February to 17 March 1722 at the Juan Fernandez Islands.

On Easter Sunday, 5 April 1722, the ships reached Easter Island, where he reported seeing between 2,000 and 3,000 inhabitants. He then charted six islands in the Tuamotu Archipelago, two in the Society Islands and four in Samoa, and was the first European to find Bora Bora, Maupiti and Samoa. He lost the Afrikaansche Galey at Takapoto atoll. At Makatea he fired on a crowded beach after a violent encounter, and the islanders ambushed a shore party and killed ten of his crew.

The two remaining ships passed New Guinea and reached Batavia in 1722. There the East Indies Company arrested Roggeveen for violating its monopoly and confiscated the ships. After a long lawsuit in the Netherlands the company was forced to compensate him for his losses and to pay his crew. After his return he published a fourth part of his religious work. He died on 31 January 1729.
jacobin-club: The club began in 1789 as the Club Breton, a group of Breton deputies at the Estates General at Versailles, and deputies from other regions soon joined. Early members included the comte de Mirabeau, the Abbé Sieyès, Antoine Barnave and Robespierre. It was re-founded in November 1789 and rented the refectory of the Dominican monastery of the Jacobins in the Rue Saint-Honoré, next to the Assembly. In January 1790 it took the name Société des amis de la Constitution, though its opponents had already dubbed it the Jacobins.

Once in Paris the club admitted citizens besides deputies. There were one hundred and fifty-two affiliated clubs by August 1790 and, at the peak, at least 7,000 chapters with a membership estimated at half a million or more. Women were not members but could follow debates from the balconies, and the high subscription confined membership to well-off men.

The club supported the monarchy until the eve of the Republic on 20 September 1792. In late 1791 a group around Brissot, later called Girondins, urged war with Prussia and Austria, which Robespierre opposed in the club; the war was decided in April 1792, and the two groups then polarised. On 2 June 1793 a crowd of armed men besieged the Convention, which expelled 22 leading Girondins. Robespierre and the Mountain then dominated the government until July 1794. In October 1793 twenty-one Girondins were sentenced to death, and between September 1793 and July 1794 there were 17,000 death sentences across France.

On 28 July 1794 the Convention had Robespierre and 21 associates guillotined. The club's membership fell to about 600, and gangs of the jeunesse dorée attacked it. On 12 November 1794 the National Convention decreed its permanent closure by a nearly unanimous vote, and within a year 93 percent of the Jacobin clubs had closed. An attempt to revive it in July 1799, the Club du Manège, was suppressed after about a month.

In power the Jacobins completed the abolition of feudalism, decided in principle on 4 August 1789 but held back by a clause requiring compensation. They set up the Cult of Reason and the Cult of the Supreme Being in place of Catholicism. They consolidated republicanism in France, while their unjudicial methods discredited the Revolution in many eyes. The term Jacobin was later applied to radicals of similar views.
jacobitism: Jacobite ideology originated with James VI and I, who in 1603 became the first monarch to rule England, Scotland and Ireland together. Its basis was divine right, which emphasised the crown's descent by hereditary right. His concept of personal rule, and his wish for political and religious union, were widely unpopular in all three kingdoms, above all in England. His son Charles I continued the policy, and his Personal Rule from 1629 led to a crisis that ended in the First English Civil War in 1642. In November 1688 the Glorious Revolution replaced James II with his daughter Mary II and her husband William III. Jacobites held that, since kings held office through divine right, the whole post-1688 regime was illegitimate.

Jacobitism drew on a political theology shared by mostly non-juring Tories in the Church of England and members of the Scottish Episcopal Church. It held that kings ruled by divine right and were accountable to God, not to Parliament, that the crown descended by dynastic right that could not be annulled, and that subjects owed passive obedience. Frank McLynn noted that the movement contained sincere men who aimed solely to restore the Stuarts but also gave legitimacy to political dissent of all kinds.

Support differed in the three kingdoms. Irish Catholic backing rested on James's religion and his supposed willingness to support Irish autonomy, while most Irish Protestants opposed his policies. In England Jacobitism was often associated with the Tories, but the Church of England's supremacy and the doctrine of non-resistance held most back. In Scotland about 20,000 men fought for the Jacobites in 1715, against 11,000 in the government army. Many Jacobites were Protestant Lowlanders, not the Catholic Highlanders of legend, and many Highland clansmen were raised through feudal obligation to their landlords.

Besides the Williamite War in Ireland of 1689 to 1691 and the Scottish rising of 1689, there were serious revolts in 1715, 1719 and 1745, and French invasion attempts in 1708 and 1744. The defeat of the 1745 Rising ended Jacobitism as a serious political movement. The Heritable Jurisdictions Act then removed the feudal controls of Highland chiefs, and the Act of Proscription outlawed Highland dress unless worn in military service, though its impact is debated and it was repealed in 1782.

Later the movement became a romantic symbol of the past. A brief neo-Jacobite revival began in the late 1880s with the Order of the White Rose, founded in 1886, and largely ended with the First World War. Jacobitism also inspired the Irish Aisling poems, among them Mo Ghile Mear by Seán Clárach Mac Domhnaill, and the Scottish Gaelic poetry of Iain Lom and Alasdair Mac Mhaighstir Alasdair.
jacobo-arbenz: Juan Jacobo Árbenz Guzmán was born on 14 September 1913 in Quetzaltenango, the son of a Swiss German pharmacist who had emigrated in 1901 and a Guatemalan schoolteacher. His father's morphine addiction ruined the family business, and since the family could not afford a university, Árbenz took a scholarship at the Polytechnic School as a military cadet in 1932. He graduated in 1935 and was the school's first sergeant, an honour given to only six cadets from 1924 to 1944. As a junior officer he had to lead squads escorting chain gangs of prisoners under the dictator Jorge Ubico, an experience that traumatised him and shaped his views.

Ubico fell in 1944 after protests that included students, workers and junior officers, and a successor junta under Federico Ponce Vaides took over. Árbenz, who had been living in El Salvador, was one of the leaders of the plot within the army, and insisted that civilians take part. After the October revolution he served as Minister of National Defense from 1944 to 1950 under President Juan José Arévalo and helped put down a military coup in 1949. He resigned on 20 February 1950 to run for the presidency, and he easily defeated Miguel Ydígoras Fuentes, taking office on 15 March 1951.

The centrepiece of his programme was the agrarian reform law, passed by the National Assembly on 17 June 1952, which transferred uncultivated land from large estates to poor labourers, with compensation. When he took office, 2% of the population owned 70% of the land. About 500,000 people benefited, most of them indigenous. The United Fruit Company, the country's largest landowner and employer, lobbied the United States government against him, and Washington also feared communist influence. President Eisenhower authorised the CIA's Operation PBSuccess in August 1953, led by Carlos Castillo Armas with about 150 mercenaries, and the coup of 1954 ousted Árbenz.

Árbenz and his family spent 73 days in the Mexican embassy before leaving the country, then lived in Paris, Prague, Moscow, Uruguay from May 1957 and Cuba from July 1960. His daughter Arabella died by suicide in Bogotá in 1965, and he settled in Mexico, where he died on 27 January 1971. In October 2011 Guatemala's president Álvaro Colom apologised for the government's role in his overthrow. Historians dispute his legacy, which they say the CIA's media campaign shaped. Greg Grandin wrote that the land reform decree represented a fundamental shift in the power relations governing Guatemala, though the United States-backed military governments that followed reversed much of the reforms of Árbenz and Arévalo.
jacopo-peri: Jacopo Peri was born in either Rome or Florence to a middle-class family. He himself claimed to be from Rome. The reigning Fernando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, held pro-Roman sentiments, and it may have been a disadvantage to be known as a Florentine, which may have led Peri to misstate his birthplace. He was employed to sing at the Servite monastery of Santissima Annunziata in Florence, and probably received an education at its school. Because the Medici court attended mass there each week, the monastery was a route by which musical students developed their careers and found patrons. Peri studied with Cristofano Malvezzi and worked in several Florentine churches as an organist and singer.

Around September 1588 Peri began work at the Medici court, first as a tenor and keyboard player and later as a composer. His earliest works were incidental music for plays, intermedi and madrigals. In the 1590s he became associated with Jacopo Corsi, the leading patron of music in Florence. They believed contemporary art inferior to that of classical Greece and Rome and set out to recreate Greek tragedy as they understood it. Their work added to that of the Florentine Camerata of the previous decade, which produced the first experiments in monody, solo song over a continuo bass that eventually developed into recitative and aria.

Peri and Corsi brought in the poet Ottavio Rinuccini to write a text. The result, Dafne, is seen as the first work in a new form, opera. Rinuccini and Peri next collaborated on Euridice, first performed on 6 October 1600 at the Palazzo Pitti for the wedding of Marie de' Medici and Henry IV. Unlike Dafne it survives, though it is hardly ever staged. It used recitatives between the arias and choruses to move the action along. Peri wrote further operas, among them La Flora with Marco da Gagliano, and pieces for court entertainments.

Few of Peri's pieces are still performed. By the time of his death on 12 August 1633 his operatic style was considered old-fashioned beside the work of younger reformers such as Claudio Monteverdi. His influence on those composers, however, was considerable. He was sometimes known by the byname Il Zazzerino, the blond one.
jacques-callot: Callot was born and died in Nancy, the capital of the Duchy of Lorraine, then an independent state on the north-eastern border of France. He came from an important family; his father was master of ceremonies at the ducal court, and he often described himself as noble in the inscriptions to his prints. At fifteen he was apprenticed to a goldsmith but soon travelled to Rome, where he learned engraving from the expatriate Frenchman Philippe Thomassin. He probably then studied etching with Antonio Tempesta in Florence, where he lived from 1612 to 1621. More than 2,000 preparatory drawings survive, but no paintings by him are known.

In Florence Callot became an independent master and often worked for the Medici court. After the death of Cosimo II de' Medici in 1621 he returned to Nancy, where he lived for the rest of his life, visiting Paris and the Netherlands later in the decade. The courts of Lorraine, France and Spain commissioned work from him, as did publishers, mostly in Paris. His prints were distributed widely through Europe, and Rembrandt was a keen collector. He made more than 1,400 etchings of soldiers, clowns, drunkards, Romani, beggars and court life, as well as religious and military subjects, and most were small, at most about 15 centimetres on their longest dimension.

Callot developed the échoppe, an etching needle with a slanting oval end that let etchers make a swelling line like an engraver's. He also seems to have introduced an etching ground of lute-makers' varnish in place of a wax-based one, so that lines could be etched more deeply and the risk of foul-biting was reduced, allowing detailed work that had been the monopoly of engravers. He used multiple stoppings-out more extensively than earlier etchers, achieving subtle effects of distance and light and shade. Abraham Bosse spread his innovations with the first published manual of etching.

His best known prints are two series on the Miseries and Misfortunes of War: 18 prints published in 1633 and the earlier, incomplete Les Petites Misères. They show soldiers pillaging and burning through towns, country and convents, before being arrested and executed by their superiors, lynched by peasants or surviving as crippled beggars. In 1633 Lorraine was invaded by the French during the Thirty Years' War. The series is still ranked with Francisco Goya's Disasters of War, which it influenced, among the most powerful artistic statements of the inhumanity of war.
jacques-cartier: Jacques Cartier was born on 31 December 1491 in Saint-Malo, the port on the north-east coast of Brittany. A respected mariner, he improved his social standing in 1520 by marrying Mary Catherine des Granches, a member of a leading aristocratic family. In 1534 Jean Le Veneur, bishop of Saint-Malo, introduced him to King Francis I, citing voyages to Newfoundland and Brazil as proof of his ability to lead ships to new lands.

Cartier sailed on 20 April 1534 under a royal commission, hoping to find a western passage to the East Indies. He explored the coasts of Newfoundland, the Gaspé and the Gulf of St. Lawrence, and on 24 July planted a 10-metre cross in Gaspé Bay to claim the land for France. There he kidnapped the two sons of the St. Lawrence Iroquoian chief Donnacona, who agreed on condition that they return with European goods.

On a second voyage in 1535 he sailed up the St. Lawrence with three ships and 110 men to Stadacona, and on 2 October reached Hochelaga, now Montreal, where over a thousand people greeted the French. The rapids blocked his way; convinced that the river was the Northwest Passage, he named them the Lachine Rapids after the French word for China. The fleet wintered frozen at the mouth of the St. Charles River, and scurvy killed about 50 Iroquoians. A remedy from the tree annedda, learned from Domagaya, saved 85 of the French. Cartier then took Donnacona to France to tell of the Kingdom of Saguenay, said to hold gold and rubies.

In 1541 Jean-François de La Rocque de Roberval was named lieutenant general of the colonisation project, with Cartier as chief navigator. Cartier sailed ahead with five ships and settled at Cap-Rouge, founding the fortified Charlesbourg-Royal. The minerals he took to be diamonds and gold proved to be quartz and iron pyrites. Iroquoians reportedly killed about 35 settlers during the winter, and he returned to France in 1542; the settlement was abandoned in 1543.

Cartier spent his last years in Saint-Malo and on his nearby estate, and died on 1 September 1557 at the age of 65 during an epidemic, possibly of typhus, and was buried in Saint-Malo Cathedral. He was the first European to describe and map the Gulf of St. Lawrence and the St. Lawrence River, and the first to document the name Canada, which comes from the Iroquoian word kanata, meaning village. Eastern parts of the continent had been visited before him by the Norse and by Basque, Galician and Breton fishermen, and no permanent European settlement followed before 1605.
jacques-necker: Jacques Necker was born on 30 September 1732 in Geneva, the son of Karl Friedrich Necker, a lawyer from Küstrin in Prussia who became professor of public law at the Academy of Geneva. Necker moved to Paris in 1748 and became a clerk in the bank of Isaac Vernet and Peter Thellusson. A series of trades on the stock exchange brought him a quick profit of half a million livres, and in 1762 he became a partner in the bank. In 1764 he married Suzanne Curchod, a Swiss governess once engaged to Edward Gibbon; their daughter became the author Madame de Staël.

In his first term Necker refused a salary. He tried to divide the taille and the capitation more equally, abolished more than five hundred sinecures and financed the French debt by loans at high interest rather than by new taxes. In April 1778 he paid 2.4 million livres from his own fortune into the treasury. His provincial assemblies, with equal numbers from the Third Estate, succeeded only in Berry and Haute-Guyenne.

The Compte rendu au roi of 1781 summarised income and expenditure and was the first record of royal finances made public; some 200,000 copies were sold. Critics accused him of brightening the picture by leaving out military outlays and the national debt. When Necker demanded a seat on the royal council, Maurepas and Vergennes threatened to resign, and he was dismissed on 19 May 1781.

On 25 or 26 August 1788 he was called back to office, this time insisting on the title of Controller-General and a place on the royal council. In the winter of 1788–89 he arranged grain for France through the Amsterdam bank Hope & Co., using the 2.4 million livres in the treasury as collateral.

At the Estates-General on 5 May 1789 Necker spoke for three hours, though a secretary read most of the address; he urged moderation and a constitutional monarchy of the English type. By September 1789 the treasury was empty, and in December the Constituent Assembly voted the first issue of assignats secured on confiscated church lands. He resigned in September 1790 to general indifference and was allowed to leave France on 11 September.

He spent his last years at Coppet Castle writing on political economy and law. His house and two million livres were confiscated after he was placed on the list of émigrés. He died on 9 April 1804. Necker Hospital for Children in Paris is named after him.
jadidism: The Jadids were a Turco-Islamic modernist movement in the Russian Empire. They usually called themselves Taraqqiparvarlar, progressives, Ziyalilar, intellectuals, or Yäşlär, youth. They held that the Muslim peoples of Tsarist Russia had fallen into moral and social decay that only a new kind of knowledge and cultural reform on a European model could cure, while reviving what they saw as pristine Islamic belief. Telegraph, railways, the postal system and above all print spread their ideas. A leading figure was the Crimean Tatar educator and publisher Ismail Gasprinsky (1851 to 1914), whose newspaper Tercüman was widely read among the empire's Turkic peoples. In 1884 he founded the first new-method school in Crimea.

The name comes from the Usul-i Jadid, the new method of teaching. Jadids criticised the traditional maktab for its stress on memorising religious texts: the writer Sadriddin Ayni recalled learning the Arabic alphabet in the 1890s without being able to read a text he had not memorised. New-method schools taught reading by phonetic methods and added geography, history, mathematics and science, with benches, desks, blackboards and maps. They taught in native languages, forbade corporal punishment and encouraged girls to attend, though few parents sent daughters. Mahmud Khoja Behbudiy founded one of Turkestan's first such schools, and Munawwar Qari the first in Tashkent. By 1916 over 5,000 schools ran on Jadid lines, by one count.

Jadids also wrote plays, textbooks and newspapers. In Turkestan their papers appeared after the 1905 revolution until the authorities banned them in 1908, and they usually had small circulations. Many clergy called the Jadids' programmes un-Islamic innovations, while Jadids called these Qadimists corrupt defenders of local custom. Adeeb Khalid sees both sides as contending over the values of Central Asian culture.

After 1917 many Jadids worked with the Bolsheviks, who wanted separate ethnic states, while the Jadids hoped for a Turkic nation. Their provisional government at Kokand, in 1917 to 1918, was crushed by the Tashkent Soviet, and around 14,000 people were killed, many of them leading Jadids. By 1926 the Communist Party no longer needed them. Throughout the 1920s and 1930s virtually the whole Central Asian intelligentsia, including writers such as Cholpan and Abdurrauf Fitrat, was purged. After the Soviet Union dissolved, Uzbekistan honoured the Jadids as national heroes.
jadwiga-of-poland: Jadwiga was born in Buda, the youngest of three daughters of Louis I of Hungary and Elizabeth of Bosnia, probably between 3 October 1373 and 18 February 1374. Both her grandmothers were Polish princesses, which linked her to the Piast dynasty. Louis had no sons, and in 1374 the Polish nobles accepted that one of his daughters would succeed him in Poland after he confirmed their liberties in the Privilege of Koszyce. She was symbolically married to William of Austria in 1378. When Louis died in 1382 her sister Mary was crowned king of Hungary, while the Polish nobles resolved to obey only a daughter of Louis who would settle in Poland.

Jadwiga was crowned king, not queen, in Kraków on 16 October 1384 by Archbishop Bodzanta. Scholars suggest the title marked her as a sovereign rather than a consort. The Polish lords refused to accept the fourteen-year-old William of Habsburg, thinking he could not guard Poland against its neighbours, above all the House of Luxembourg. The lords of Lesser Poland proposed Jogaila, the pagan grand duke of Lithuania, whose envoys asked for her hand in January 1385. In August 1385 he signed the Union of Krewo, promising to convert with his kinsmen and subjects and to pay 200,000 florins to William. Polish legend says she agreed only after long prayer before a crucifix in Wawel Cathedral.

Jogaila was baptised Władysław in Kraków in February 1386, and Jadwiga declared her union with William void. He was crowned as her co-ruler. Her real political power was limited, but after her mother was murdered in 1387 she went into Galicia–Volhynia and persuaded most of its people to accept the Polish crown. She mediated between Poland and the Teutonic Order. In 1397 she issued a charter for a college for Lithuanian students in Prague.

Jadwiga became pregnant in September 1398 and gave birth to a daughter at Wawel Castle on 22 June 1399. She died on 17 July 1399 of postpartum complications, and her daughter predeceased her. As the last hereditary monarch of Poland, her death made the throne elective. Six days after her funeral Władysław left for Ruthenia, and the lords sent envoys to renew their oaths to him; Jadwiga founded hospitals, schools and churches and encouraged hymns in Polish. The historians Oscar Halecki and S. Harrison Thomson rank her among the great rulers of Poland. The Catholic Church canonised her in 1997.
jaffa: Ancient Jaffa stood on a ridge of kurkar sandstone 40 metres high with a broad view of the coastline, which gave it strategic importance. The tell formed by the debris of centuries made the hill higher still. The name appears in Egyptian sources and the Amarna letters as Yapu. A tradition says it was named for Japheth, son of Noah, and Greek tradition links it with Andromeda's mother Iopeia; an outcrop of rocks near the harbour is said to be where Perseus rescued Andromeda.

Pottery shows that Jaffa was settled as early as the 4th millennium BCE, and its earliest settlement remains date to the 18th century BCE, when it was a small fortified site of about three hectares on the sea routes linking the Levant, Egypt and Cyprus. In the 15th century BCE it came under Egypt's New Kingdom and is listed among the cities conquered by Thutmose III. The Hebrew Bible calls it the northernmost Philistine city, the port through which cedars of Lebanon reached the Temple, and the place where the prophet Jonah embarked. Under Persian rule it was awarded to Sidon, as an inscription on the Sarcophagus of Eshmunazar II attests.

In the Hellenistic period Antigonus Monophthalmus captured it in 315 BCE and Ptolemy I Soter destroyed it in 312 BCE, but it was resettled and became a Ptolemaic mint. It passed to Seleucid control after the Battle of Paneas in 198 BCE. In the Roman period Pompey annexed it to Syria, Julius Caesar restored it to Judaea, and Herod captured it in 39 BCE, though the harbour Herod built at Caesarea reduced its importance. In the New Testament it is the town where Saint Peter raised the widow Dorcas and had the vision that led him to preach to the gentiles.

In the Crusades Jaffa was the centre of the County of Jaffa and Ascalon. The Battle of Jaffa of 1192 was followed by a truce between Richard the Lionheart and Saladin. Napoleon sacked the town in 1799, and the British took it in 1917. In the 19th century it became known for its orchards and the Jaffa orange.

Jaffa is the southern part of Tel Aviv-Yafo, to which it was united as a single municipality in 1950. Most of its Arab population fled or was expelled after the 1948 Palestine War, and it is one of the mixed cities of Israel. Before 1948 it had been a centre of Palestinian journalism, where the newspapers Falastin and Al-Difa' were founded.
jaffna: Excavations point to early settlement on the peninsula. A bronze seal from Anaikoddai carries Tamil-Brahmi and Indus script, and urn burials and inscribed potsherds have been found at Kandarodai, Poonakari and Anaikoddai. Finds at the fort show trade with South Asia, Arabia and the Far East. The region was part of the chiefdom of Naga Nadu, named in the Tamil epic Manimekalai and the Pali Mahavamsa, whose Naga people scholars think were assimilated to Tamil language and culture by the 9th century CE.

The name is Tamil, Yazhpanam, earlier Yazhpanapattinam, with a suffix meaning seaport. A legend tells that a king presented a sandy plain to a blind musician who played the yal, a stringed instrument.

In the 13th century the Kingdom of Aryacakravarti arose as an ally of the Pandyan Empire, with its capital at Nallur, now a suburb of Jaffna. Its rulers made it independent, and other regional kingdoms paid it tribute in the 13th and 14th centuries. It lost its independence to the Kotte Kingdom from 1450 to 1467 but was re-established.

In 1619 a Portuguese expedition led by Filipe de Oliveira captured Cankili II, the last native king, and moved control from Nallur to Jaffnapatao, a fortified town. The Dutch East India Company took it in 1658 after a three-month siege, rebuilt the fort and most of the Hindu temples the Portuguese had destroyed. Britain took over from 1796 and built roads and a railway to Colombo, while missionary societies founded the schools behind the town's high literacy.

After independence in 1948 relations between Sinhalese and Tamils worsened, and Jaffna became a centre of Tamil nationalism. The Jaffna library was burnt in 1981 and civil war began in 1983. The Sri Lankan Army regained the city in 1995, and the war ended in 2009. Jaffna is the capital of the Northern Province, about 396 kilometres from Colombo, on a flat limestone peninsula; most of its people are Sri Lankan Tamils, mainly Shaivite Hindus.
jagannath: Within Odia Hinduism, Jagannath is held to be the supreme god, Purushottama and the Para Brahman. Most Vaishnava Hindus see him as a regional form of Krishna, sometimes of Vishnu, and some Shaiva and Shakta Hindus regard him as a tantric form of Bhairava. His icon in the temples is a brightly painted, rough-hewn log of neem wood with a square flat head, a large circular face and two big round eyes without eyelids, one said to symbolise the sun and the other the moon. It has no neck, ears or limbs. The wooden images are replaced with new ones at regular intervals, about every 12 years according to one account.

At the annual Ratha Yatra, held in June or July, the three images are brought out of the sanctum of the Puri temple, placed in temple cars and pulled by volunteers to the Gundicha Temple, about 3 km away. They stay there eight days and return on the ninth. About a million devotees come to Puri to see Jagannath in his chariot, and similar processions are held at Jagannath temples elsewhere in the world.

Accounts of origin differ. The Skanda Purana tells how King Indradyumna of Avanti sought the sapphire deity Nilamadhava and how a neem log floated ashore, from which Vishnu, disguised as an old carpenter, began to carve the images; the king opened the sealed pavilion early and the figures stayed unfinished and without hands or feet. Scholars have proposed Vedic, Buddhist, Jain, Vaishnava and tribal sources, and others call the deity syncretic. The Daitas, hereditary non-Brahmin servitors believed to descend from the Sabara tribe, have the first view of each new image.

The early inscriptions and texts name only a single deity, Purushottama Jagannath. A copper-plate inscription of 1198 says the Puri temple was built by the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga (1078-1147), originally for Vishnu and Lakshmi, which has led to arguments that Balabhadra and Subhadra were added later to form a triad. The Vaishnava reformer Ramanuja is said to have visited Puri between 1107 and 1111.

Chaitanya Mahaprabhu, who spent the last 20 years of his life in Puri, encouraged the identification of Jagannath with Krishna, and the deity is widely revered in Bengal. Guru Nanak made a pilgrimage to Puri in 1506 or 1508. Court historians record that Firuz Shah Tughlaq raided Odisha and desecrated the temple, and attacks on the Puri temple became serious after the death of Akbar, under whom the tradition had flourished. A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada selected Jagannath for ISKCON temples, which now hold the Ratha Yatra in many Western cities. Early British observers rendered the name as juggernaut, a word that came to mean a very large and unstoppable force.
jagiellonian-dynasty: The dynasty was a cadet branch of the Gediminids, the ruling house of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and takes its name from Jogaila, whose name means strong rider in Lithuanian. The Piast rulers of Poland had ended with the death of King Casimir III the Great. In the Union of Krewo, Jogaila agreed to be baptised and to marry the young Queen Jadwiga of Poland, and as Władysław II Jagiełło he became king as her co-ruler. Jadwiga died in 1399, and as their only daughter had died as an infant, Jogaila's descendants had no inherited right to the Polish crown. He remained king as an elected ruler, and later had four more children.

Members of the dynasty were Kings of Poland from 1386 to 1572, Grand Dukes of Lithuania in 1377–1392 and 1440–1572, Kings of Hungary in 1440–1444 and 1490–1526, and Kings of Bohemia and imperial electors from 1471 to 1526. The union strengthened Poland and Lithuania in their shared opposition to the Teutonic Knights and the growing power of Moscow, and linked states on the two sides of the divide between the Latin and Byzantine worlds. Władysław III briefly ruled both Poland and Hungary from 1440 to 1444, and Vladislaus II, son of Casimir IV, ruled Bohemia and Hungary from 1490, moving his court to Hungary.

In 1515 a congress in Vienna arranged a succession agreement and marriages between the Jagiellons and the Habsburgs of Maximilian I. The Ottoman expansion damaged the last Jagiellon monarchies: Suleiman I took Belgrade in 1521, and in 1526 the Hungarian army was defeated at the Battle of Mohács, where Louis II Jagiellon was killed. Hungary was afterwards partitioned between the Habsburgs and the Ottomans. In Poland the dynasty ended with Sigismund II Augustus, whose heirs were his sisters; Catherine's son Sigismund III Vasa joined the Polish branch to the House of Vasa.

The sixteenth century, especially the reigns of Sigismund I and Sigismund II, the last two Jagiellonian kings, is most often identified with the Polish Golden Age and the rise of Polish Renaissance culture, built on the prosperity of the landed nobility and the townspeople of Kraków and Gdańsk. The Jagiellons were polyglots, and Sigismund II Augustus kept separate Lithuanian-speaking and Polish-speaking courts in Vilnius. The Jagiellonian University and its library in Kraków preserve the name.
jagiellonian-university: Casimir III the Great concluded that Poland needed an educated class, above all lawyers who could arrange the country's laws and run its courts and offices. Pope Urban V allowed him to set up a university in Kraków, and a royal charter of foundation was issued on 12 May 1364, with a matching document from the city council granting privileges to the Studium Generale. After Casimir's death development stalled.

The university was restored in the 1390s. Queen Jadwiga and her husband Władysław II Jagiełło chose to buy an existing building rather than build, and in 1399 acquired a house on Żydowska Street that had belonged to the Pęcherz family. The queen gave all her personal jewellery to the university, which allowed it to enrol 203 students. On 26 July 1400 Jagiełło reformed it on the model of the Sorbonne, and a Faculty of Theology was established.

For several centuries almost the whole intellectual elite of Poland studied there. Its astronomers, lawyers and theologians attracted eminent scholars, among them Albert Brudzewski, who from 1491 to 1495 was one of Nicolaus Copernicus's teachers. It was the first university in Europe to set up independent chairs in mathematics and astronomy. Its golden age fell in the Polish Renaissance, between 1500 and 1535, when 3,215 students attended in the first decade of the 16th century. That record was not passed until the late 18th century.

After the third partition of Poland in 1795 Kraków became a free city under Austrian protection, and in 1846, after the Kraków Uprising, it passed to the Austrian Empire. The Austrians were in many ways hostile to the university but Ferdinand I of Austria decreed that it be kept. On 6 November 1939, after the German invasion, 184 professors were arrested and deported to Sachsenhausen concentration camp, and the university was closed for the rest of the war. It reopened in 1945, but was suppressed by the Communist government in 1954.

The Jagiellonian Library, which holds Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, has almost 6.5 million volumes.  The university's alumni include Copernicus, King John III Sobieski and Pope John Paul II,. Today it is a public research university whose grounds form part of the Kraków Old Town, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
jahanara-begum: Jahanara Begum was born on 23 March 1614, the second and eldest surviving child of Shah Jahan and Mumtaz Mahal. Her first teacher was Sati al-Nisa Khanam, sister of the poet laureate Talib Amuli, who was known for her knowledge of the Qur'an, Persian literature and medicine.

When Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, Jahanara, aged 17, took her place as first lady of the empire, though her father had three other wives. She was given charge of the imperial seal, with the right to issue farmans and nishans, and was granted the title Padshah Begum. She lived in her own palace outside Agra Fort, where she held a court, and nobles and foreign ambassadors sought her intervention with the emperor.

In March 1644 Jahanara suffered serious burns, and accounts differ on how: either her perfumed garments caught fire, or she was burned while helping a dancing woman whose dress had ignited. Shah Jahan ordered alms for the poor and the release of prisoners, and she recovered after about a year. She then received the revenues of the port of Surat. She owned ships and kept up trade with the English and the Dutch.

When Shah Jahan fell seriously ill in 1657, war broke out among his four sons. Jahanara backed Dara Shikoh, the eldest. After Aurangzeb defeated Dara at Samugarh on 29 May 1658, she proposed a partition of the empire, which Aurangzeb refused. Aurangzeb besieged Agra Fort and held his father prisoner there, and Jahanara joined him and cared for him until his death in 1666. After this she reconciled with Aurangzeb, who restored her titles and made her first lady of the court again. She is recorded as arguing against his austerity measures and his restoration of the poll tax on non-Muslims in 1679.

With Dara Shikoh she became a disciple of Mullah Shah Badakhshi, who initiated her into the Qadiriyya Sufi order in 1641. She wrote Mu'nis al-Arwāḥ, a biography of Moinuddin Chishti, the founder of the Chishti Order in India, whom she regarded as her spiritual guide, and a biography of Mullah Shah. In Agra she paid for the Jami Masjid, built in 1648, and a madrasa attached to it. She died in 1681 and was buried in the Nizamuddin Dargah complex in Delhi, in a marble tomb she had built during her lifetime, open to the sky and covered only with grass.
jahangir: Prince Salim was born at Fatehpur Sikri on 31 August 1569, the third and only surviving son of Akbar and Maryam uz-Zamani. His two elder brothers, the twins Hassan Mirza and Hussain Mirza, had died in infancy, and Akbar sought the blessing of the religious leader Salim Chishti, who lived at Fatehpur Sikri. Salim studied Chagatai, Persian and Hindustani as well as military tactics.

In 1594 he led an army against a revolt of the Bundela at Orchha, and after their leader Vir Singh Deo surrendered, Orchha became a vassal state. In 1599, while Akbar was campaigning in the Deccan, Salim declared himself emperor at Allahabad and issued coins in his own name. The rebellion ended without a decisive battle, and by 1604 peace was restored through the mediation of nobles such as Man Singh of Amber.

Jahangir succeeded to the throne on 3 November 1605. In April 1606 his son Khusrau rebelled, left Agra with 350 horsemen and besieged Lahore, but Jahangir relieved the city and defeated him at Bhairowal. Khusrau was captured while crossing the Chenab, and Jahangir had his young aristocratic supporters tortured and impaled as a warning. Khusrau was later blinded and imprisoned until 1619.

From his marriage to Mehr-un-Nissa, later Empress Nur Jahan, Jahangir left the reins of government largely in her hands and appointed her relatives to high positions, which displeased courtiers and foreigners. He was famed for his Chain of Justice, by which subjects denied justice could appeal to the emperor, and he ordered the foundation of free hospitals in the cities of his empire. He recorded his reign and the natural world in his memoir, and commissioned painters such as Ustad Mansur to illustrate it. The editor Henry Beveridge, however, judged him a weak ruler who lost Qandahar to the Persians.

A lifelong user of opium and wine, Jahangir was frequently ill in the 1620s. He died in October 1627 near Bhimber, on the journey from Kashmir to Lahore. His entrails were buried at Baghsar Fort, and his body was taken to Lahore and buried at Shahdara Bagh, where his son Shah Jahan commissioned his tomb. Shah Jahan succeeded him after a brief succession crisis. The tomb site was placed on the tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage status in 1993.
jainism: Jainism is an ancient Indian religion rooted in the independent Śramaṇa tradition of ascetics, which developed alongside but distinct from the orthodox Vedic religion. Jains maintain that their faith is eternal and that in the present cosmic time cycle it has been guided by 24 tirthankaras, beginning with Rishabhanatha. Historians date the 23rd, Pārśvanātha, to about the eighth or seventh century BCE. The 24th, Mahavira, was a contemporary of the Buddha and a central figure in the Śramaṇa movement of Greater Magadha, which rejected the authority of the Vedas.

Some scholars have proposed that seals from the Indus Valley Civilization show early forms of Jain asceticism, but because the Indus script is undeciphered, mainstream historians treat this as a hypothesis. The Hathigumpha Inscription of King Kharavela of Kalinga at the Udayagiri Caves in Odisha, from the second century BCE, records his patronage of Jain monks.

Jainism teaches a path to spiritual purity through disciplined nonviolence, ahimsa, to all living creatures. It is transtheistic: the universe was not created and has no creator, governor, judge or destroyer. Its philosophy rests on three ethical pillars, ahimsa, anekantavada, the doctrine that reality has many sides and no single viewpoint is completely true, and aparigraha, non-possession. Purification of the soul and liberation, moksha, are held to be achievable through the three jewels of right vision, right knowledge and right conduct. Laypersons keep five small vows and mendicants five great vows. Nonviolence led the community to avoid agriculture and warfare, and many Jains became merchants and bankers.

Devout Jains practise lacto-vegetarianism, and monks and nuns and some followers avoid root vegetables, since tiny organisms are injured when the plant is pulled up. The most fundamental invocation, accepted by all sects, is the Namokar Mantra. The most important annual festival is Paryushana among the Śvētāmbaras and Dasa lakshana parva among the Digambaras, a time of fasting and prayer.

The community is divided into the Digambara (sky-clad) and Śvētāmbara (white-clad) traditions, which differ on monastic discipline, canonical texts and the liberation of women. The Digambara account places the origin of the schism around the fourth century BCE, when Bhadrabahu predicted a twelve-year famine in Magadha and led monks to Karnataka. Most modern scholars, such as Padmanabh Jaini and Paul Dundas, conclude that it was a gradual hardening of differences over several centuries.

Royal patronage helped Jainism grow and decline. Rashtrakuta kings sponsored major Jain cave temples, and the Yadava dynasty built many temples at the Ellora Caves between 700 and 1000 CE. The Pallava king Mahendravarman I converted from Jainism to Shaivism. Virchand Gandhi, a Gujarati Jain scholar, represented Jainism at the first World Parliament of Religions in 1893 in Chicago. Jainism has between four and five million followers, mostly in India.
jaipur: Jaipur lies in eastern Rajasthan, 268 km from New Delhi, and covers 467 km2. Fertile alluvial plains lie to the east and south, while the northern and western margins have hill chains and arid areas; the Aravalli range bounds the city, with the Nahargarh hills to the north and the Jhalana hills to the east. The Dravyavati River serves as the main drainage channel. The climate is hot and semi-arid, with rain falling mostly in July and August with the southwest monsoon.

Jai Singh II, the Kachhwaha Rajput ruler of Amer, who ruled from 1699 to 1743, founded Jaipur on 18 November 1727 and gave it his name. He planned to move his capital 11 km from Amer because of a growing population and increasing water scarcity, and the city was planned on the principles of Vastu Shastra and Shilpa Shastra under the guidance of Vidyadhar Bhattacharya. Construction began in 1726. The city had gates facing east, west and north, and its architecture was heavily influenced by the 17th-century architectural renaissance under Mughal rule.

In 1876 the city was painted pink to welcome Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, which gave it the epithet Pink City. In the British period it was the capital of the princely state of Jaipur. In the 19th century it grew rapidly, reaching 160,000 people by 1900, and after independence in 1947 it became the capital of the new state of Rajasthan in 1949.

Jaipur is the capital and largest city of Rajasthan, with 3,046,163 people at the 2011 census, and Hindi is the official language. The earlier rulers invited skilled artisans from India and abroad, and the city remains known for block printing, stone carving, jewellery, gems, blue pottery and hand-knotted rugs. Its sites include the City Palace, Hawa Mahal, Amer Fort and the Jantar Mantar observatory, a collection of 19 astronomical instruments. The Jantar Mantar was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2010, and the historic city centre on 6 July 2019.
jajce: Jajce lies in the region of Bosanska Krajina, at the crossroads between Banja Luka, Mrkonjić Grad and Donji Vakuf, where the rivers Pliva and Vrbas meet. At the confluence stands a waterfall 22 metres high. Beneath the town is the Jajce Mithraeum, a temple of the sun god Mithra dated to the 2nd century CE and renovated in the 4th. It is regarded as one of the best preserved in Europe, was found by accident during the building of a private house and is a National Monument of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Hrvoje Vukčić Hrvatinić, at the height of his power, is credited with founding the town and building a fortress on the site of an earlier fort. Jajce was first built in the 14th century and served as capital of the independent Kingdom of Bosnia; its name first appears in written sources in 1396. Its last king, Stjepan Tomašević, received his crown there from Pope Pius II. The Ottomans besieged the town and executed him in 1463, but held it for only six months before Matthias Corvinus of Hungary took it, which derailed Ottoman plans for nearly half a century.

Later in 1463 Matthias Corvinus established the Banate of Jajce. Queen Catherine restored Saint Mary's Church before her death in 1478, and it is now the oldest church in the town. A siege by Skenderbeg Mihajlović in 1501 failed, though it foreshadowed the end of Hungarian rule. Jajce fell to the Ottomans in 1527 and lost its strategic importance as the border moved north. Austria-Hungary administered it with the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1878 to 1918, and the Franciscan monastery of Saint Luke was completed in 1885.

From 1929 to 1941 Jajce belonged to the Vrbas Banovina of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia. During the Second World War it became the centre of a large area of free territory. On 29 November 1943 the second convention of the Anti-Fascist Council of National Liberation of Yugoslavia (AVNOJ) met in the Sokol building, built in 1934 by Momir Korunović. Its delegates decided to establish a federal Yugoslavia with equality between its ethnic groups and made Bosnia and Herzegovina one of its republics.

Jajce is a town and municipality in the Central Bosnia Canton of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 7,172 inhabitants in the town at the 2013 census. Its walled old core, the waterfall and sites such as the Mithraeum are designated as the Natural and Architectural Ensemble of Jajce and proposed for inscription on UNESCO's World Heritage list. Tourism, which flourished in Yugoslav times because of the AVNOJ session, has since returned.
jakarta: Jakarta lies on the north-western coast of Java at the mouth of the Ciliwung river, facing Jakarta Bay. It covers about 664 square kilometres of land. Apart from some hills in the south, the city spreads across low, flat terrain, much of it an alluvial plain with elevations from below sea level to about 50 metres. Thirteen rivers run through it toward the bay. The plain was historically swampy, and seasonal flooding remains common.

The Buni culture, a prehistoric pottery culture of the northern and western coast of Java, is dated to roughly 400 BCE to 100 CE. The mid-5th-century Tugu inscription, found near Tanjung Priok, records the excavation of two waterways and attributes one of them to King Purnawarman. By the 10th century the Sunda Kingdom ruled the area, and by the early 16th century Kalapa was one of its leading ports. The Portuguese writer Tomé Pires called it Sunda's most important trading port, drawing ships from Sumatra, Malacca and Java. A treaty of 21 August 1522 allowed the Portuguese to build a fortress at Kalapa.

In 1527 Islamic forces captured Kalapa, and sources differ over whether Fatahillah or Sunan Gunung Jati led them. The settlement became a dependency of the Banten Sultanate under the name Jayakarta. The Dutch East India Company seized and destroyed Jayakarta in 1619 and rebuilt it as Batavia, its main administrative centre in Asia and an important trading port. In the early 19th century the Dutch colonial administration moved south to Weltevreden.

Indonesian independence was proclaimed in Jakarta in 1945, and after the Indonesian National Revolution it became the capital of the unitary republic in 1950. It became a first-level region in 1957 and a Special Capital Region in 1961. In 2022 the Indonesian government began the legal process of moving the capital to Nusantara in East Kalimantan.

Jakarta is the capital and largest city of Indonesia, with the status of a province, and had about 11 million registered residents in 2025. No ethnic group forms a majority; Javanese, Betawi, Sundanese and Chinese Indonesians are the largest. The Betawi people formed in colonial Batavia from people of varied origins. Indonesian is the official language, and the city hosts the headquarters of ASEAN. Its Old Town keeps the historic core.
jakob-bohme: Jakob Böhme was born on 24 April 1575 at Alt Seidenberg, a village near Görlitz in Upper Lusatia, a territory of the Bohemian Crown. His father, George Wissen, was a Lutheran and a reasonably wealthy peasant. Böhme was the fourth of five children and began as a herd boy. At fourteen he was sent to Seidenberg to learn shoemaking, and although he had no formal education he prayed regularly and read the Bible and works by visionaries such as Paracelsus, Weigel and Schwenckfeld.

By 1599 he was a master of his craft with premises in Görlitz, and he married Katharina, daughter of the butcher Hans Kuntzschmann. They had four sons and two daughters. He joined a study group organised by Martin Moller. In 1600, as he looked at a beam of sunlight reflected in a pewter dish, he had a vision which he believed revealed the spiritual structure of the world and the relation between God and man, and good and evil. A second inner vision in 1610 led him to feel a special vocation from God.

Twelve years after the first vision Böhme began to write Morgenröte im Aufgang, which a friend named Aurora. It was never finished. A nobleman, Karl von Ender, had copies made and circulated them, and one reached Gregorius Richter, the chief pastor of Görlitz, who denounced it as heretical from the pulpit and threatened Böhme with exile. Böhme wrote nothing for several years. He began again in 1618, at the insistence of friends, and in 1619 wrote De Tribus Principiis, followed by many treatises, copied by hand and passed among friends.

His first published book, Weg zu Christo, or The Way to Christ, appeared on New Year's Day 1624 and caused another scandal. The Town Council summoned him on 26 March 1624 and warned him to leave. He went to Dresden in May 1624, where nobles, clergy and professors received him favourably. He returned home and began the 177 Theosophic Questions, but fell ill and died on 17 November 1624, after the new clergy had made him answer a long list of questions before he could receive the sacrament.

The chief concern of his writing was the nature of sin, evil and redemption. Böhme held that humanity had fallen from grace into sin and suffering and that God's aim was to restore the world to grace. He departed from Lutheran theology in rejecting justification by faith alone. He described the Fall as perhaps a necessary stage in the evolution of the universe, though his obscure, oracular style leaves this open to question. His followers were called Behmenists. Hegel described him as the first German philosopher, and he influenced German idealism and Romanticism.
jakob-fugger: Jakob Fugger was born in Augsburg on 6 March 1459, the tenth of eleven children of Jakob Fugger the Elder and Barbara Bäsinger. His grandfather Hans Fugger had settled in Augsburg in 1367 and acquired wealth by trading textiles with Italy. Jakob's older brothers Ulrich and Georg created the basis for the firm's rise, founding manufactories in Venice and Nuremberg around 1470. Jakob began his education at fourteen in Venice, which remained his main residence until 1487. After 1487 he was the de facto head of the business, though Ulrich still formally led it.

Fugger laid the foundation of his mining business in Salzburg, lending to silver mine owners and demanding shares, called Kuxe, instead of the usual acknowledgments of debt, so that more mine operators had to sell their silver directly to the Fuggers. From 1493 the firm extracted silver and copper in Bohemia and Hungary and gained an almost monopolistic hold on the European copper market. He met Maximilian I in 1489 and supported the Habsburgs as a banker. The Fuggers were the first German trading house in direct business with the Roman Curia; Fugger financed the recruitment of the Swiss Guard for Pope Julius II in 1505 and 1506.

After Maximilian died in January 1519, Fugger supported the election of his 19-year-old grandson Charles, to secure his investments in the Habsburgs. Francis I had already offered 300,000 guilders in election money, and Henry VIII and Frederick III of Saxony also announced candidacies. Fugger was a lifelong Roman Catholic. In 1513 he lent 20,000 guilders to Albert of Brandenburg for a dispensation; the indulgence granted in 1515 was to repay him in part, and Luther's protest against its preaching led to the Ninety-five Theses. After the Diet of Augsburg of 1518, Luther answered Cardinal Cajetan in the Fugger House.

In 1498 Fugger married Sybille Arzt, and the couple had no children. He died on 30 December 1525 and left his nephew Anton Fugger company assets of 2,032,652 guilders. He founded the Fugger chapel in the St Anna church in Augsburg, built from 1509 to 1512 as Germany's first Renaissance building. From 1516 he funded the Fuggerei, a settlement for craftsmen and day labourers in need, of which 52 houses stood by 1523. The yearly rent was one symbolic guilder, with three daily prayers for the Fugger family. About 150 people live there today, and it is described as the oldest social housing complex still in use.
jalal-al-din-mangburni: Jalal al-Din was the eldest son of the Khwarazmshah Ala ad-Din Muhammad II and was brought up at Gurganj, the wealthy capital of the Khwarazmian homeland. His mother, Ay-Chichek, was a concubine of Turkmen origin. Because of her low status, his grandmother Terken Khatun, a Kipchak princess, refused to support him as heir and favoured his half-brother Uzlagh-Shah. He first appears in the records in 1215, when his father divided the empire among his sons and gave him the south-western part, formerly Ghurid land. He proved an able general, and was the one commander his father trusted.

When the Mongols overran Khwarazmia and his father died destitute on an island in the Caspian Sea, Jalal al-Din gained the loyalty of most Khwarazmian loyalists. At Gurganj the nobility planned a coup in favour of Uzlaq, so he left with 300 cavalry and gathered some 50,000 loyalists at Ghazni, joined by his uncle Temur Malik with 30,000 veterans. In autumn 1221 he defeated a Mongol force under Shigi Qutuqu at the Battle of Parwan, but then lost half his army in a dispute over booty. Genghis Khan caught him on the Indus in November 1221. Jalal al-Din escaped by leaping into the river fully armed, which is said to have won Genghis Khan's admiration.

He spent about three years in India and returned to Persia in late 1223. There he took Tabriz from the Eldiguzids on 25 July 1225, defeated the Georgians at the Battle of Garni and captured Tbilisi, where a hundred thousand citizens are said to have been put to death for refusing to renounce Christianity. He repelled a Mongol army at Dameghan in 1227 and fought another near Isfahan in August 1228. The Seljuq sultan Kayqubad I defeated him at the Battle of Yassıçemen in 1230, and he fled to Diyarbakır.

After the Nizari Ismaili Assassins proposed joint action, Ögedei Khan sent an army of 30,000 to 50,000 under Chormagan, which swept away the remaining Khwarazmians. Jalal al-Din took refuge in the Silvan mountains and in August 1231 was killed by a Kurd who said he was avenging a brother killed by Jalal al-Din's forces at Ahlat. His kingdom collapsed at once. Contemporary writers praised his courage, while modern historians judge him a gifted general but a poor ruler, whose isolation against the Mongols owed much to his enmity with neighbours.
jalayirid-sultanate: The Jalayirids came from the Jalayir tribe, a prominent Mongol tribe from the area of the River Onon in eastern Mongolia. In the 14th century in West Asia they became largely Turkish-speaking, and they are credited with strengthening Turkic influence in Arabic-speaking Iraq. The dynasty was also called the Ilka dynasty or Ilkanids, after Ilka Noyan, great-grandfather of Hasan Buzurg. Ilge Noyan accompanied Hulegu to West Asia in the 1250s, took part in the siege of the Assassins' strongholds in Qohestan in 1256 and oversaw the rebuilding of Baghdad after its siege in 1258. After the death of Abu Sa'id in 1335, his family emerged as inheritors of the governors of the Ilkhanate's south-western lands.

Hasan Buzurg, cousin of Abu Sa'id, installed Muhammad Khan on the throne at Tabriz and married Abu Sa'id's widow Dilshad Khatun. For a short time in 1337 and 1338 his authority was recognised across the Ilkhanate except Khorasan, but expelled from Azerbaijan he held only Iraq. He died in July 1356 and was buried in Najaf. His son Shaykh Uways (1356 to 1374) took Azerbaijan after the Golden Horde withdrew, and marks the peak of the dynasty. A weakening followed. Sultan Ahmad Jalayir executed his brother Shaikh Hussain after seizing Tabriz.

Timur attacked in 1384 and took Tabriz in 1386. He captured Baghdad in 1393, and Sultan Ahmad fled to the Mamluks and returned with their army. When Timur took Baghdad again in 1401 after a siege of forty days, the city was sacked and its people massacred. After Timur died in 1405, Ahmad recovered Baghdad with the help of Qara Yusuf of the Qara Qoyunlu and held Tabriz from 1406 to 1410. Qara Yusuf defeated and killed him in 1410. The remnants were pushed into lower Iraq, around Hillah, Wasit and Basra, and the last ruler, Hosayn II, was pursued and killed after the Qara Qoyunlu prince Aspan captured Hillah.

The administration was modelled on that of the Ilkhanate, with documents in Persian and Mongolian, and diplomatic correspondence in the Ilkhanid style with a red square seal bearing Arabic Islamic phrases. The Jalayirids were great patrons of Persianate culture, and their patronage marks an important period in the evolution of Persian art, where major aspects of later Persian painting developed. Their art was marked by increased naturalism, with parallels noted to contemporary Late Gothic trends and to Chinese art. Among illustrated manuscripts, Ahmad Jalayir is known for the Khosrow and Shirin, made at Tabriz.
jalisco: The name comes from the Nahuatl xalisco, meaning over a sandy surface, and until about 1836 it was spelled Xalisco. Nomadic peoples moving south arrived in the area around 15,000 years ago, and some of the oldest evidence of human occupation is found around Lake Zacoalco and Lake Chapala. When the Spanish arrived the main ethnic groups were the Cazcanes in the north, the Huichols in the north-west, the Guachichil in the Los Altos area, the Cuyutecos, who spoke Nahuatl, in the west, and the Tecuexes and Cocas near what is now Guadalajara.

At the start of the 19th century the Intendencia of Guadalajara still included Colima, parts of Zacatecas and the San Blas region. The area had relative freedom from Spanish colonial authorities and prospered with fewer trade restrictions, which, together with indigenous resentment of Spanish rule dating from the 16th century, made it sympathetic to the insurgent movements of the early 19th century.
