Jalisco is a state in western Mexico with 342 kilometres of Pacific coastline, bordered by Nayarit, Zacatecas, Aguascalientes, Guanajuato, Michoacán and Colima. The saying Jalisco es México reflects how many things typically associated with Mexico originated there, among them mariachi, charreadas, the Mexican Hat Dance, tequila and the wide-brimmed sombrero. Mariachi is thought to have originated in the town of Cocula, and the music became most developed around Guadalajara.

Jalisco has 125 municipalities, and its capital and largest city is Guadalajara. The 2020 census counted 8,348,151 people, over half of them in the Guadalajara metropolitan area. The Huichols and the Nahuas are its two significant indigenous populations. Tequila is made from the blue agave of a small region of the state, and José Antonio Cuervo received the first official permission to make and sell it in 1758. San Juan de los Lagos, where an image of the Virgin Mary made in the 16th century is venerated, is one of the most visited pilgrimage sites in Mexico.
jallianwala-bagh-massacre: During the First World War British India supplied millions of soldiers and labourers and large quantities of food, money and ammunition. The war's costs, inflation, heavy taxation and the 1918 flu pandemic increased suffering, and nationalist feeling revived as moderate and extremist groups of the Indian National Congress ended their differences. The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1917 were judged insufficient, and Mahatma Gandhi emerged as a leader of growing civil disobedience. In April 1919, especially in Punjab, rail, telegraph and communications were disrupted, and Lieutenant-Governor Michael O'Dwyer is said to have believed that a coordinated revolt was planned for May.

On Sunday 13 April 1919 Dyer banned all meetings. At 09:00 he proclaimed a pass system, a curfew from 20:00 and a ban on gatherings of four or more, read in English, Urdu, Hindi and Punjabi, though many paid no heed or learned of it later. Many villagers gathered in the Bagh to celebrate the Baisakhi festival and to protest peacefully against the arrest and deportation of Satyapal and Saifuddin Kitchlew. Dyer was told of the meeting at 12:40.

He surrounded the crowd with Gurkha and Sikh troops of the British Indian Army. The garden could be left only on one side, since buildings enclosed the other three, and Dyer blocked that exit and ordered his troops to fire. They continued even as people tried to flee, until their ammunition ran low. Estimates of the dead range from 379 to 1,500 or more, and over 1,200 others were injured, 192 of them seriously. Many people jumped into a well to escape the bullets and drowned. Dyer reported that he had faced a revolutionary army, and O'Dwyer obtained martial law. At least 115 people were killed by security forces in the following days, by one historian's count.

The Hunter Commission was set up on 14 October 1919 to inquire into the disturbances. Winston Churchill, then Secretary of State for War, called the massacre unutterably monstrous, and on 8 July 1920 the House of Commons voted 247 to 37 against Dyer. Many moderate Indians abandoned their loyalty to the British, and the anger fed the non-cooperation movement of 1920-22. Sikh clergy at the Golden Temple gave Dyer a saropa, which shocked Sikhs and contributed to the founding of the Shiromani Gurudwara Prabandhak Committee in 1920. In 1940 Udham Singh, who had been wounded at the Bagh, shot O'Dwyer in London.

A memorial designed by Benjamin Polk was inaugurated on 13 April 1961. Bullet marks remain on the walls, and the well is a protected monument. The British Army was retrained in less violent crowd control, with the principle of minimal force.
jamaica: Jamaica covers 10,991 square kilometres and is the third-largest island in the Greater Antilles and the Caribbean, after Cuba and Hispaniola. It lies about 145 km south of Cuba and 191 km west of Hispaniola. Mountains dominate the interior, among them the Blue Mountains in the east, where Blue Mountain Peak rises to 2,256 metres, and a narrow coastal plain surrounds them. The island lies within the main development region for Atlantic tropical cyclones and sometimes suffers heavy storm damage. When the Spanish arrived in 1494 the country was deeply forested, and European settlers later cleared much of it for timber and cultivation.

There is no archaeological evidence of human presence until about 500 CE. A group known as the Redware people, after their pottery, arrived around 600 CE, followed by the Taíno around 800 CE, who most likely came from South America. The Taíno lived by farming and fishing, and at their height are thought to have numbered some 60,000 people in around 200 villages headed by caciques. Christopher Columbus claimed the island for Spain after landing in 1494 on his second voyage. The first Spanish settlement, Sevilla, was founded in 1509 by Juan de Esquivel and abandoned around 1524; the capital moved to Spanish Town, then St. Jago de la Vega, around 1534.

The Taíno died in large numbers from introduced diseases and from enslavement by the Spanish, who then imported enslaved Africans. Many escaped and formed autonomous communities in the remote interior, mixing with the remaining Taíno; these became the Jamaican Maroons, who kept their freedom for generations under leaders such as Juan de Serras. By the early 17th century an estimated 2,500 to 3,000 people lived on the island.

England conquered Jamaica from Spain in 1655. Under British rule it became a leading sugar exporter, with a plantation economy that depended on importing enslaved Africans. The British emancipated all slaves in 1838, and many freedmen chose subsistence farms over plantation work. From the 1840s the British brought Chinese and Indian indentured labourers. Independence from the United Kingdom came on 6 August 1962.

Jamaica is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a Commonwealth realm, with a bicameral Parliament, and its constitution dates from 1962. The capital and largest city is Kingston. Most Jamaicans are of African or partly African descent, with minorities of European, Indian, Chinese and Lebanese origin. The Maroon communities of Accompong and elsewhere continue to keep their own traditions. The island is the birthplace of the Rastafari religion and of reggae, ska, dub and dancehall music, and its national motto is Out of Many One People.
jamal-al-din-al-afghani: His name al-Afghani claims an Afghan origin, and by his own account he was born in Asadabad near Kabul. Nikki Keddie and several other scholars hold that he was raised in a Shia family in Asadabad near Hamadan in Iran, and that he claimed Afghan birth to win influence among Sunni Muslims or to escape the Shah. His rivals Shaykh Yusuf al-Nabhani and Shaykh Abu al-Huda al-Sayyadi called him Mutaʾafghin, meaning the one who claims to be Afghan. He was educated at home, then in Qazvin, Tehran and the Twelver shrine cities of Ottoman Iraq.

In 1856–57 he travelled to British India and spent some years studying religions. In 1866 he is recorded in Afghanistan, where he advised Mohammad Afzal Khan and urged a turn to Russia; Sher Ali Khan expelled him in 1868. In Istanbul he joined the Council of Education and spoke at the opening of Istanbul University, but conservative clerics found his views too radical and he was expelled in 1871. In Egypt he met the young Muhammad Abduh, preached political reform, and sought the removal of Isma'il Pasha. He was exiled to India in August 1879.

In 1884 he and Abduh published the Arabic newspaper al-Urwah al-Wuthqa in Paris, calling for a return to the principles of Islam and for unity among Muslims. After Russia and Munich he returned to Iran in 1889, took sanctuary in the Shah Abdol-Azim Shrine, and was expelled in 1891. His agitation is thought to be one source of the Tobacco Protest of 1891. Sultan Abdul Hamid II then invited him to Istanbul.

He joined a critique of Western imperialism to an appeal for Muslim unity, urging the adoption of Western science and institutions, and held that Islam was compatible with reason. He wanted Hindus and Muslims to cooperate against British rule in India. In 1881 he published Refutation of the Materialists, which included an early Islamic argument against Darwin; in later work he accepted evolution for animals but rejected it for humans, because humans have souls.

In Istanbul in 1895 he met his former disciple Mirza Reza Kermani, and the two planned the assassination of Naser al-Din Shah. Kermani shot the Shah on 1 May 1896 and was hanged in August 1897. Iran failed to obtain al-Afghani's extradition. He died of cancer of the jaw in Istanbul on 9 March 1897. In 1944 his remains were taken to Afghanistan and laid in a mausoleum at Kabul University.
jameh-mosque-of-isfahan: The mosque results from continual construction, reconstruction and renovation on one site from about 771 CE to the end of the 20th century. The first mosque was built around 771 in the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur. It was relatively small, about 52 by 90 metres, made of mud-brick with stucco decoration in the Syro-Mesopotamian style. Excavations in the 1970s showed it stood over earlier structures from the Sasanian or early Islamic period, part of the ancient town of Yahūdiyya.

In 840, under al-Mu'tasim, a larger mosque of about 88 by 128 metres replaced it, with a different qibla orientation. It had a large central courtyard surrounded by an arcade and a hypostyle hall of baked brick pillars, six bays deep on the qibla side. Under the Buyid dynasty another arcade of polylobed brick piers was added around the courtyard, decorated with patterned brickwork, together with two minarets at the entrance, the first recorded instance of the double minaret arrangement that later became common in Iran.

The Seljuks made the next great changes. Isfahan became their first capital after its conquest in 1050. In 1086, under the patronage of the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, columns in front of the mihrab gave way to a large domed space, the largest masonry dome in the Islamic world at the time, with eight ribs and a new type of squinch. In 1088 his rival Taj al-Mulk had another dome built on the north side, whose interlacing ribs form pentagons and five-pointed stars. It is considered a masterpiece of medieval Iranian architecture.

By the early 12th century, probably after a fire in 1121, a large iwan replaced the columned space between the dome and the courtyard, and three more monumental iwans were built, giving the mosque the four-iwan form that became prevalent in Iran and elsewhere. Around 200 smaller cross-ribbed vaults, each with a different design, renovated the old hypostyle halls.

Nearly every later period saw work on the mosque. Under the Ilkhanid sultan Uljaytu a winter hall was added with a stucco mihrab dated to 1310, signed by the calligrapher Haydar. The Muzaffarids added a madrasa, and the tilework of the southern iwan was first added under the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan in 1475. Most Safavid rulers worked on the mosque, and its present minarets, either side of the southern iwan, were erected in the 17th century.

The mosque today combines styles and periods that cannot always be easily dated, and its perimeter is enmeshed with the surrounding bazaar and old city, so that it presents few clear exterior façades. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2012, and the Grand Bazaar of Isfahan lies towards its south-western wing.
james-bond: Ian Fleming began writing the first Bond novel, Casino Royale, on 17 February 1952 at his Goldeneye estate in Oracabessa, Jamaica, where he wrote all his Bond books during the months of January and February each year. Jonathan Cape, who did not like the manuscript as much as Fleming's friend William Plomer did, published it in 1953 on the recommendation of Fleming's older brother Peter, an established travel writer. Between 1953 and 1966 twelve novels and two short-story collections appeared, the last two books posthumously.

Bond is an officer of the Secret Intelligence Service, commonly known as MI6, and a Royal Naval Reserve Commander, known by his code number 007. Fleming said he was a compound of all the secret agents and commando types met during the war, among them his brother Peter. For the first five novels Bond carried a Beretta, until the gun expert Geoffrey Boothroyd wrote to Fleming that it was a lady's gun and suggested a Walther PPK; Fleming then named the armourer of MI6 Major Boothroyd. The films added gadgets from Q Branch, which became one of the motifs of the series.

After Fleming's death in 1964 other authors wrote authorised Bond novels, among them Kingsley Amis, John Gardner and Sebastian Faulks. The character has also been adapted for television, radio, comic strips and video games. CBS aired a live one-hour adaptation of Casino Royale on 21 October 1954, in which Barry Nelson played an American Bond.

Eon Productions, owned by Harry Saltzman and Albert R. Broccoli, released Dr. No in 1962 with Sean Connery as 007. The role passed to George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan and, from Casino Royale in 2006, Daniel Craig, whose fifth and final film, No Time to Die, appeared in 2021. After Dr. No other studios rushed out imitations, 22 secret agent films in 1966 alone, and Bond was parodied in Carry On Spying (1964) and later the Austin Powers series. The Harry Palmer films, beginning with The Ipcress File (1965), were seen as an anti-Bond. Critics have accused the series of sexism and imperial nostalgia.
james-bruce: James Bruce of Kinnaird was born on 14 December 1730 at Kinnaird, Stirlingshire, and was educated at Harrow School and Edinburgh University. He began to study for the bar but entered the wine trade through his marriage to a merchant's daughter, who died in October 1754, within nine months of the marriage. Examining oriental manuscripts at the Escorial led him to the study of Arabic and Geʽez. In 1763 he reached Algiers as British consul, and from August 1765 he explored Roman ruins in Barbary, then travelled to Crete, Syria, Palmyra and Baalbek, making careful drawings and acquiring enough medicine to pass in the East as a physician.

In June 1768 Bruce arrived at Alexandria, resolved to discover the source of the Nile. He gained the support of the Mamluk ruler Ali Bey at Cairo, reached Massawa on 19 September 1769 and Gondar, then the capital of Ethiopia, on 14 February 1770. He was well received by Emperor Tekle Haymanot II and Ras Mikael Sehul, and received court appointments, including command of the Koccob Horse, the emperor's household cavalry. Setting out again in October 1770, he reached Gish Abay, the source of the Lesser Abay, on 14 November 1770. He admitted that the White Nile was the longer stream but argued that the Blue Nile was the Nile of the ancients.

The Jesuit Pedro Páez had reached the source of the Blue Nile in 1618, and Jerónimo Lobo had visited it in 1629. Bruce disputed Páez's visit and suggested that Athanasius Kircher had fabricated the passage, though later research showed that Lobo's description was correct in its details. Leaving Gondar in December 1771, Bruce went by Sennar to Nubia, the first European to trace the Blue Nile to its confluence with the White Nile. At Sennar his house was attacked by thieves, whom he suspected of acting with the knowledge of the king. He reached Aswan on 29 November 1772, Cairo in January 1773 and France in March.

Bruce came to London in June 1774 and was interviewed by James Boswell; offended by the incredulity with which his story was received, he retired to Kinnaird. His Travels to Discover the Source of the Nile, in five quarto volumes, appeared in 1790 and sold well but was assailed by other travellers as unworthy of credence; the substantial accuracy of his Ethiopian travels has since been demonstrated. He brought back Ethiopian manuscripts, including three copies of the Book of Enoch, a text lost in Europe since the Middle Ages, whose arrival marks the beginning of modern studies of it. He died on 27 April 1794 of injuries from a fall down stairs at Kinnaird House the day before.
james-clerk-maxwell: James Clerk Maxwell was born on 13 June 1831 at 14 India Street, Edinburgh, the son of John Clerk Maxwell of Middlebie, an advocate, and Frances Cay. His mother took charge of his early education, and at eight he could recite long passages of John Milton and the whole of the 119th psalm. She died of abdominal cancer in December 1839. On 12 February 1842 his father took him to Robert Davidson's demonstration of electric propulsion and magnetic force. He studied at the University of Edinburgh from 1847 and discovered photoelasticity there. In October 1850 he went to Cambridge and graduated in 1854 from Trinity.

In 1856 Maxwell became head of the department of natural philosophy at Marischal College in Aberdeen. He studied the rings of Saturn and correctly proposed that they were made of numerous small particles, for which he won the Adams Prize in 1859. At King's College London, from 1860 to 1865, he did what was probably the most productive work of his career: he won the Rumford Medal in 1860 for his work on colour, was elected to the Royal Society in 1861. Around 1862 he calculated that an electromagnetic field travels at about the speed of light, and his paper A Dynamical Theory of the Electromagnetic Field of 1865 showed that electric and magnetic fields travel through space as waves.

He also worked on the kinetic theory of gases, first deriving the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution. In 1871 he came back to Cambridge as the first Cavendish Professor of Physics and oversaw the construction of the Cavendish Laboratory.

In April 1879 Maxwell began to have difficulty swallowing, the first symptom of his fatal illness. He died in Cambridge of abdominal cancer on 5 November 1879, aged 48, the same age and of the same type of cancer as his mother. Albert Einstein described his work on the centenary of Maxwell's birth as the most profound and fruitful that physics had experienced since the time of Newton, and when told in 1922 that he stood on Newton's shoulders he replied that he stood on those of Maxwell.
james-cook: James Cook was born on 7 November 1728 in the village of Marton in the North Riding of Yorkshire, the second of eight children of a Scottish farm labourer. His father's employer paid for him to attend a school run by a charitable foundation, and after five years of schooling he began working for his father, by then a farm manager. On 17 June 1755 he enlisted in the Royal Navy at Wapping. In the Seven Years' War he took part in the capture of the Fortress of Louisbourg in 1758 and surveyed the entrance to the St. Lawrence River, then spent five seasons charting the coast of Newfoundland. This work brought him to the attention of the Admiralty and the Royal Society.

Cook's first voyage, in HMS Endeavour from 1768 to 1771, was sponsored jointly by the Royal Navy and the Royal Society. Its stated purpose was to observe the 1769 transit of Venus from Tahiti, and secret orders told him to search for the supposed southern continent, Terra Australis, and to claim lands for Britain. In October 1769 he landed at Poverty Bay in New Zealand and, with the aid of the Tahitian priest Tupaia, was the first European to communicate with the Māori, though early encounters turned violent and several Māori were shot dead. On 19 April 1770 the crew sighted Point Hicks, the first European encounter with Australia's eastern coast.

On the second voyage, from 1772 to 1775, his crews became on 17 January 1773 the first recorded Europeans to cross the Antarctic Circle, though Cook never sighted Antarctica. He concluded that no polar landmass reached beyond about 50°S. The third voyage, from 1776, sought a North-West Passage; Cook visited Kerguelen Island and Hawaii and explored the coast of North America to the Bering Strait. He is credited with early work on preventing scurvy, and the Royal Society awarded him the Copley Medal.

Cook returned to Hawaii in late November 1778 and landed at Kealakekua Bay on Hawaiʻi Island, where King Kalaniʻōpuʻu received him with respect. Many Hawaiians appear to have thought him an embodiment of the god Lono. After the ships left, a gale broke Resolution's foremast and they returned for repairs. Relations had worsened, and on 13 February 1779 Hawaiians stole one of his cutters. Cook was killed the next day. His voyages greatly expanded European knowledge of the Pacific. Historians debate his responsibility for violent encounters with Indigenous peoples, for the spread of infectious diseases and for claiming lands without consent.
james-ensor: James Sidney Edouard Ensor was born on 13 April 1860. His father, James Frederic Ensor, was born in Brussels to English parents, and his mother, Maria Catherina Haegheman, was Belgian. He spent his childhood in a souvenir shop run by his parents and was fascinated by the carnival masks sold there, which became a source of inspiration. He left school at fifteen to train with two local painters, and from 1877 to 1880 he attended the Académie Royale des Beaux-Arts in Brussels. He first exhibited in 1881. From 1880 until 1917 he had his studio in the attic of his parents' house, and he travelled very little.

His early works, such as Russian Music of 1881 and The Drunkards of 1883, show realistic scenes in a sombre style. His palette then brightened and his subjects became increasingly bizarre. Paintings such as The Scandalized Masks of 1883 and Skeletons Fighting over a Hanged Man of 1891 show figures in grotesque masks, and he dressed skeletons up in his studio. The years from 1888 to 1892 were a turning point, when he turned to religious themes, often the torments of Christ. Although he was an atheist, he identified with Christ as a victim of mockery.

In Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889 a vast carnival mob in grotesque masks advances toward the viewer, with Belgian politicians and members of Ensor's family among them and Christ on his donkey nearly lost in the throng. Les XX rejected it, and it was not publicly shown until 1929. Ensor also made 133 etchings and drypoints, 86 of them between 1886 and 1891. Late 19th-century critics often rejected his work as scandalous.

Recognition came slowly. In 1895 the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium acquired his painting The Lamp Boy, and he had his first solo exhibition in Brussels. He was named a baron by King Albert in 1929 and received the Légion d'honneur in 1933. His output fell after the first decade of the 20th century, and historians have generally seen his last forty or fifty years as a period of decline. He turned increasingly to music and played the harmonium for visitors. He died in Ostend on 19 November 1949, aged 89.

He influenced expressionist and surrealist artists such as Paul Klee, Emil Nolde, George Grosz and Alfred Kubin. His work is in the Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium, the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Musée d'Orsay, among others.
james-francis-edward-stuart: James Francis Edward Stuart was born on 10 June 1688 at St. James's Palace, the only surviving son of James II of England and his second wife, Mary of Modena, and was created Prince of Wales in July 1688. His birth was unexpected, coming five years after his mother's tenth pregnancy, and it revived disputes over religion. Rumours spread among Anglicans that the child was an impostor smuggled into the birth chamber in a warming pan, and James II published the testimony of over seventy witnesses in October 1688.

On 9 December Mary of Modena, disguised as a laundress, escaped to France with the infant. He grew up at the Château de Saint-Germain-en-Laye, which Louis XIV had given to the exiled king, and received a military education. When James II was dying in 1701 he urged his son never to give up his Catholic faith.

On his father's death in September 1701 Louis XIV proclaimed him rightful king, and Spain, the Papal States and Modena also recognised him; he was attainted for treason in London on 2 March 1702. A French attempt to land him at the Firth of Forth on 23 March 1708 was intercepted by the fleet of Admiral Sir George Byng. He served as a volunteer in the French army in the War of the Spanish Succession and was noted for his valour at Oudenarde.

In 1714 Robert Harley and Lord Bolingbroke hinted that his conversion to Protestantism would ease his accession, but he refused, writing that he had chosen his own course. After the Hanoverian accession he reached Scotland on 22 December 1715, set up court at Scone Palace in January 1716 and sailed back to France from Montrose on 5 February, leaving his allies ill-disposed towards him. A further expedition from Spain in 1719 ended at the Battle of Glen Shiel.

James settled in papal territory and from 1718 lived in Rome, in the Palazzo Muti offered by Pope Clement XI, where he held a Jacobite court and received English visitors on the Grand Tour. On 3 September 1719 he married Maria Clementina Sobieska, a granddaughter of King John III Sobieski of Poland; their sons were Charles Edward Stuart and Henry Benedict Stuart, later a cardinal. The 1745 rising was led by Charles, and the two quarrelled bitterly.

James died on 1 January 1766 at the Palazzo Muti and was buried in the crypt of St. Peter's Basilica. The pope then declined to recognise Charles, and over the following decade Rome accepted the Hanoverian dynasty as rulers of Britain and Ireland.
james-frazer: Frazer was born on 1 January 1854 in Glasgow, the son of Katherine Brown and Daniel F. Frazer, a chemist. He studied at the University of Glasgow and at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he graduated with honours in classics and remained a Classics Fellow all his life. He went on to study law at the Middle Temple but never practised. He was knighted in 1914. In 1896 he married Elizabeth Grove, known as Lilly, a writer who became his manager and publicist and arranged translations of his work into French.

Frazer's interest in social anthropology was aroused by E. B. Tylor's Primitive Culture of 1871 and encouraged by his friend, the biblical scholar William Robertson Smith. Except for visits to Italy and Greece he did not travel widely; his data came from ancient histories and from questionnaires mailed to missionaries and imperial officials around the world. He was the first scholar to describe in detail the relations between myths and rituals.

The Golden Bough appeared in two volumes in 1890, in three in 1900, and in a third edition of twelve volumes finished in 1915, with a thirteenth added in 1936. Lilly Frazer compiled an abridgement in 1922. In the third edition Frazer proposed that cultures pass from magic to religion to science. He saw magic and science as alike in their stress on experiment, and religion as belief in personal supernatural forces that are to be appeased. He also wrote a six-volume commentary on Pausanias's description of Greece, which scholars still value.

The Golden Bough reached beyond academia. Sigmund Freud cited Frazer's Totemism and Exogamy in Totem and Taboo, and the cycle of life, death and rebirth that Frazer saw behind many peoples' myths captivated artists and poets; the most notable product was T. S. Eliot's poem The Waste Land of 1922. Frazer's vision of the annual sacrifice of a Year-King has not been borne out by field studies.

Late-20th-century scholars criticised the work. Edmund Leach objected to its comparisons between widely separated cultures, and the historian Timothy Larsen argued that Frazer applied Christian terms such as baptism to non-Christian cultures. More recently the book has been criticised for assuming that European peasants, Aboriginal Australians and Africans represented earlier stages of cultural evolution. Frazer and his wife died in Cambridge within a few hours of each other on 7 May 1941.
james-i-of-aragon: James was born at Montpellier on 2 February 1208, the only son of Peter II of Aragon and Marie of Montpellier. His father tried to placate the crusaders of the Albigensian Crusade by arranging a marriage between the two-year-old James and Amicie, daughter of Simon IV de Montfort, and in 1211 entrusted the boy to Montfort's care. Peter was killed at the Battle of Muret on 12 September 1213, and Pope Innocent III insisted that Montfort give James up.

James was raised at Monzón by Guillem de Montredó, head of the Knights Templar in Aragon and Provence. In 1217 the Templars and some loyal nobles brought him to Zaragoza. In 1221 he married Eleanor, daughter of Alfonso VIII of Castile, and rebellions by nobles filled the next six years until the Peace of Alcalá of 31 March 1227.

After a scheme to inherit Navarre came to nothing, James turned south and east. On 5 September 1229 a fleet of 155 ships carrying 1,500 horsemen and 15,000 soldiers sailed for Majorca, which fell on 31 December 1229; Menorca followed in 1232 and Ibiza in 1235. Valencia capitulated on 28 September 1238. By the Treaty of Almizra of 26 March 1244 James and Alfonso X of Castile fixed the border of the new Kingdom of Valencia.

In May 1258 the Treaty of Corbeil ended his conflict with Louis IX of France: France renounced claims of sovereignty over Catalonia, and James gave up his rights in Provence. Catalonia's ties with Languedoc faded as a result. In 1269 he assembled a fleet for a crusade, but a storm drove him to Aigues-Mortes and he abandoned the voyage.

James compiled the Llibre del Consolat de Mar, which governed maritime trade, and sponsored the University of Montpellier. In 1263 he presided over the Barcelona Disputation between the rabbi Nahmanides and the convert Pablo Christiani. He wrote or dictated the Llibre dels fets, the first autobiography by a Christian king and an early work of Catalan prose. At the urging of his confessor Ramon de Penyafort he brought the Inquisition into his realm in 1233.

In his will he divided his lands between his sons by Yolanda of Hungary: Peter received the mainland kingdoms and James the Kingdom of Majorca, a division that led to conflict between the brothers. James died at Valencia on 27 July 1276.
james-ii-of-aragon: James II, called the Just, was born at Valencia, the second son of Peter III of Aragon and Constance II of Sicily. He succeeded his father in Sicily and, on the death of his elder brother Alfonso III in 1291, in Aragon and the rest of the Spanish territories, including Majorca. He was also Count of Barcelona and King of Valencia. His full title for the last three decades of his reign was James, by the grace of God, king of Aragon, Valencia, Sardinia and Corsica, and count of Barcelona.

In Sicily James was crowned at Palermo and was excommunicated by Pope Honorius IV in response. By a peace treaty with King Charles II of Naples he agreed to give up Sicily, but the Sicilians installed his younger brother Frederick on the throne, and Frederick reigned there until his death in 1337. Pope Boniface VIII then asked James, with Charles II, to remove Frederick, and enticed him by investing him with the title to Sardinia and Corsica and appointing him papal gonfalonier. James could not disguise his apathy and returned to Aragon. By the Treaty of Anagni in 1295 he returned the Balearic Islands to his uncle James II of Majorca, who recognised his suzerainty by the Treaty of Argilers in 1298.

Back in Aragon, James sought access to the Muslim south, from which Castile restricted his kingdom. With his admiral Bernat de Sarrià he allied with the enemies of the young Ferdinand IV of Castile, wanting Murcia for access to Granada; his allies entered it from all directions in 1296, and he held Murcia until 1304. In 1313 he granted administrative and political autonomy to the Aran Valley, described in a Latin manuscript called the Querimonia. He was nominally king of Sardinia and Corsica from 1297 but acquired Sardinia only by conquest in 1324. In 1321 he ordered the arrest and torture of French lepers seeking shelter in his realm.

James composed one surviving piece of Occitan poetry, a religious dansa to the Virgin Mary titled Mayre de Deu, probably during his time in Sicily. Arnau de Vilanova wrote a verse-by-verse Latin commentary on it in 1305. It compares the Church to a ship in a storm, poorly guided by its pilot, the Pope, and its final verses ask Mary to protect the king from sin. It seems to have been written when James was in conflict with the papacy, perhaps to show his piety and fidelity to the Church.

James married four times: Isabella of Castile, a marriage never consummated and annulled; Blanche of Anjou, daughter of Charles II of Naples, with whom he had several children, among them his successor Alfonso IV; Marie of Lusignan; and Elisenda de Montcada.
james-ii-of-england: James was born on 14 October 1633 at St James's Palace, the second surviving son of Charles I and Henrietta Maria of France, and was designated Duke of York at birth. At the age of three he was appointed Lord High Admiral, an honorary post that became a substantive office after the Restoration. He was present at the Battle of Edgehill in October 1642 and spent most of the next four years in the Royalist capital of Oxford.

After the Restoration of 1660 he was created Duke of Albany in Scotland and was confirmed as Lord High Admiral. In October 1660 Charles II made him Governor of the Royal Adventurers into Africa, the company later reformed as the Royal African Company, which over its lifetime carried more enslaved Africans across the Atlantic than any other single institution.

The Exclusion Crisis of 1679–81, when the Whigs tried to bar him from the succession, failed because the memory of the Commonwealth made the public reluctant to undermine hereditary succession. Charles II died on 6 February 1685, and James succeeded with widespread support, many believing that a Catholic monarchy would be temporary. He was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 23 April 1685.

He enlarged the standing army and used his dispensing power to let Roman Catholics command regiments without taking the oath required by the Test Act. When Parliament objected he prorogued it in November 1685, and it never met again in his reign. In April 1688 he re-issued the Declaration of Indulgence and ordered the clergy to read it. Seven bishops who petitioned against it were tried for seditious libel and acquitted on 30 June, and the birth of his son James Francis Edward on 10 June raised the prospect of a Catholic dynasty.

Leading English figures invited William of Orange, James's nephew and son-in-law, who landed at Brixham on 5 November 1688. James's army deserted and he went into exile in France on 23 December. In February 1689 a Convention Parliament held that he had vacated the throne and installed William and Mary. James landed in Ireland in March 1689 with French help, but William defeated him at the Battle of the Boyne on 1 July 1690 (Old Style), and James fled to France, never to return. He lived at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, under Louis XIV's protection, until his death on 16 September 1701.

His son was recognised as James III and VIII by his supporters, later called Jacobites, and led a rising in 1715. Historians have disagreed on James: Macaulay cast him as a cruel absolutist, while some 20th-century writers praised his advocacy of religious tolerance, and more recent scholarship takes a middle course.
james-ii-of-scotland: James was born at Holyrood Palace on 16 October 1430, the younger twin son of James I and Joan Beaufort. His brother Alexander died within months, leaving him the only surviving son. The Auchinleck chronicle called his birthmark, which covered one side of his face, the fyre mark in his face. He was crowned at Holyrood Abbey on 26 March 1437, aged six. The regency was marked by disorder, famine and plague. On 24 November 1440 the regents Crichton and Avandale invited the young William, 6th Earl of Douglas, to Edinburgh Castle, where he was beheaded in the event known as the Black Dinner.

The Douglas family dominated Scottish politics in the 1440s under William, 8th Earl of Douglas, who in 1443 used the twelve-year-old king's banner to take a Crichton tower. James began his personal rule in 1449, and married Mary of Guelders at Holyrood Abbey on 3 July 1449. In September 1449 he attacked the Livingston family, and the comptroller Robert Livingston was executed. In 1451 John, Earl of Ross, attacked royal castles, and Douglas, allied with Ross and the Earl of Crawford, refused to support the king.

On 22 February 1452 the king and Douglas dined at Stirling. James asked him to dissolve the alliance, Douglas refused, and James stabbed him twice before his attendants joined in. The killing of a man under royal protection damaged James's standing.

The new earl, James, 9th Earl of Douglas, burned Stirling in March 1452. A parliament cleared the king of the murder. In August 1455 parliament disinherited the Douglases for treason, and James distributed their lands, creating new earldoms after 1457. He attacked English Berwick in 1455, exploiting the Wars of the Roses, and renounced the truce with England in May 1456.

James was killed at Roxburgh on 3 August 1460 when a bombard near him exploded, probably during a salute for the queen's arrival at the siege. The historian John Major blamed him for being over-curious in the matter of engines of war. The castle fell on 8 August, and James III was crowned at Kelso Abbey on 10 August. James II was buried at Holyrood Abbey. His widow Mary of Guelders became the leading figure in Scottish politics and was formally appointed regent in 1461. James has been described as a largely successful king who strengthened the Scottish monarchy.
james-iii-of-scotland: James was the first surviving son of King James II and Mary of Guelders, daughter of Arnold, Duke of Guelders. The exact date and place of his birth are debated. He became king when his father was killed at the siege of Roxburgh Castle on 3 August 1460, and he was crowned at Kelso Abbey a week later. His minority lasted almost a decade. At first his mother governed as regent, and in April 1461 the Lancastrians she had sheltered, Henry VI of England and Margaret of Anjou, gave up Berwick to the Scots in return for refuge and loans.

In July 1466 Robert, Lord Boyd, and his son Thomas seized the king while he was hunting at Linlithgow Palace and took control of the government. The Boyds arranged a marriage to Margaret, only daughter of Christian I of Denmark and Norway, whose dowry was 60,000 Rhenish guilders. When her fleet reached Leith in 1469 the Boyds fled and were convicted of treason, and James married the 13-year-old Margaret at Holyrood Abbey in July 1469. Orkney and Shetland came to Scotland through the marriage, and the reign saw Scotland reach its widest extent.

James began his personal rule in 1469. He planned costly schemes on the continent, among them a claim to Brittany that he gave up after clerical protests. In 1475 he moved against John MacDonald, Lord of the Isles, who had agreed in 1462 to the Treaty of Westminster with Edward IV of England. The Lord of the Isles was declared forfeit in December 1475, but he appeared before the king in July 1476 and the forfeiture was lifted. He lost the earldom of Ross and was reduced to a Lord of Parliament.

James faced growing criticism. Parliament complained that he did not hold the Justice Ayres in person and drew money from remissions for serious crimes, and he favoured men of low birth such as William Scheves, who became Archbishop of St Andrews. His brother John, Earl of Mar, died in prison in 1479. In 1482 his brother Alexander, Duke of Albany, tried to take the throne with an English army, which cost Scotland Berwick, and nobles imprisoned the king for a time before he regained power.

In February 1488 the fifteen-year-old heir, James, Duke of Rothesay, left Stirling Castle and became the figurehead of a rebellion led by the Earls of Angus and Argyll and the Home and Hepburn families. It ended at the Battle of Sauchieburn on 11 June 1488, where the king died, and the prince succeeded him as James IV. His reputation as Scotland's first Renaissance monarch has sometimes been exaggerated.
james-iv-of-scotland: James was born on 17 March 1473 at Stirling Castle, the eldest son of King James III and Margaret of Denmark, and was Duke of Rothesay from birth. He was educated by Archibald Whitelaw and the theologian John Ireland. Besides Scots he became fluent in Latin and Spanish, learned French, German, Flemish and Italian, and was the last Scottish monarch known to have spoken Gaelic. He became king at fifteen on 11 June 1488, when his father died at the Battle of Sauchieburn, after a rebellion in which he had been the figurehead of the rebels, and he was crowned at Scone Abbey on 24 June.

In 1491 Alexander MacDonald of Lochalsh raided Ross-shire in an attempt to recover the earldom of Ross. In consequence, a parliament in Edinburgh in May 1493 declared the title and possessions of John MacDonald, Lord of the Isles, forfeit to the Crown. James then made an expedition to the western Highlands, where local chiefs submitted, and John of Islay was brought to court with an annual pension. Parliaments met ten times from 1488 to 1496 but only three times in the remaining seventeen years, and royal income doubled over the reign. The Treaty of Ayton of 30 September 1497 agreed a seven-year truce with England, and the Treaty of Perpetual Peace followed in 1502, with James's marriage to Margaret Tudor in 1503.

He took a close interest in the navy, commissioning or acquiring at least thirty-eight ships, and naval spending became the largest single item of royal expenditure. He was a patron of the Scots poets William Dunbar, Walter Kennedy and Gavin Douglas, backed the foundation of King's College, Aberdeen, and passed the education act of 1496, which required the eldest sons of barons and substantial freeholders to attend grammar school. His court was cosmopolitan and included Africans, among them two women mentioned in the treasurer's accounts in 1504. In 1507 Pope Julius II granted him the title Protector and Defender of the Christian Faith.

When Henry VIII invaded France in 1513 as part of the Holy League, James chose the Auld Alliance with France over the Perpetual Peace and led an army of some 42,000 across the Tweed around 22 August. He took Norham, Etal and Ford castles, and on 8 September faced the English under Thomas Howard, Earl of Surrey, on Branxton Hill. James and many of his nobles were killed at the Battle of Flodden on 9 September 1513. His body was identified the next day, taken to Berwick-upon-Tweed and embalmed. He was the last monarch in Great Britain to be killed in battle and was succeeded by his son James V.
james-joyce: James Joyce was born on 2 February 1882 in Rathgar, Dublin, the eldest of ten surviving siblings. His father, John Stanislaus Joyce, was appointed rate collector by Dublin Corporation in 1887, but his unpredictable finances made family life chaotic. Joyce attended Clongowes Wood College and Belvedere College, and in 1898 enrolled at University College, Dublin, to study English, French and Italian, graduating in 1902. There he met the scholasticism of Thomas Aquinas, which influenced his thought for the rest of his life. He lapsed from the Catholic Church early, though his work is deeply influenced by Catholicism.

In October 1904 Joyce and Nora Barnacle went into self-imposed exile. He taught English in Pola and then Trieste, then part of Austria-Hungary, worked for eight months as a correspondence clerk in a Roman bank, and lived in Trieste until 1915, publishing Chamber Music and Dubliners there. He spent most of the First World War in Zurich, supported by a stipend that Pound and Yeats helped arrange and by regular sums from the editor Harriet Shaw Weaver, who supported him for the rest of his life.

In 1920 he moved to Paris, his main home for twenty years. Sylvia Beach, who ran the bookshop Shakespeare and Company, became one of his publishers. Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922; its publication in the United Kingdom and the United States was prohibited as obscene, and copies were smuggled in and pirated until the mid-1930s, when publication became legal. He began Finnegans Wake in 1923, and suffered increasingly severe eye problems.

When Germany occupied France in 1940, Joyce moved back to Zurich. He underwent surgery for a perforated duodenal ulcer on 11 January 1941 and died on 13 January, aged 58. Though he spent most of his adult life abroad, his fiction centres on Dublin. Ulysses is a model for fiction writers, and Finnegans Wake has become one of the key texts for French post-structuralism. His work and life are marked each year on 16 June, known as Bloomsday, in Dublin and in a growing number of other cities.
james-madison: James Madison Jr. was born on 16 March 1751 (5 March 1750 in the Old Style calendar) at the Belle Grove plantation near Port Conway in the Colony of Virginia. His father was a tobacco planter who, with an estimated 100 slaves and a 5,000-acre plantation, was among the largest landowners in Virginia's Piedmont. Madison joined the Patriots in 1774, believing that Parliament had overstepped its bounds in taxing the colonies,. With Thomas Jefferson he drafted the Virginia Statute for Religious Freedom, passed in 1786, which guaranteed freedom of religion and disestablished the Church of England.

Troubled in the 1780s by the weakness of the central government and the disunity of the states, Madison helped organise the Constitutional Convention, and his Virginia Plan was the basis of its deliberations. He became a leader of the movement to ratify the Constitution and wrote essays of The Federalist Papers with Alexander Hamilton and John Jay. Elected to the House of Representatives in 1789 after a hard contest against James Monroe, he introduced the Bill of Rights on 8 June 1789 after studying more than two hundred amendments proposed at the state ratifying conventions.

In the 1790s he opposed Hamilton's economic programme, including the First Bank of the United States, arguing that the Constitution gave Congress no power to create it, and with Jefferson he organised the Democratic–Republican Party. He served as Jefferson's Secretary of State from 1801 to 1809 and was elected president in 1808.

As president he tried to play Britain and France against each other over attacks on American shipping, and when this failed he led the country into the War of 1812. Madison was re-elected in 1812. The war ended inconclusively in 1815, but many Americans saw it as a second war of independence, and he presided over the creation of the Second Bank of the United States and the Tariff of 1816. During his presidency the United States acquired 26,000,000 acres from Native American tribes through treaties or war.

Madison retired to his plantation, Montpelier, in 1817,. Madison owned over one hundred slaves, and his views on slavery were conflicted throughout his life; his will freed none of them. He died of congestive heart failure at Montpelier on 28 June 1836, aged 85, and was one of the last prominent members of the Revolutionary generation to die. Historians regard him as one of the most significant of the Founding Fathers.
james-monroe: James Monroe was born on 28 April 1758 in Westmoreland County in the Colony of Virginia, the son of Andrew Spence Monroe, a craftsman who took part in protests against the Stamp Act, and Elizabeth Jones. In early 1776 he left college and joined the 3rd Virginia Regiment of the Continental Army as a lieutenant. At the Battle of Trenton he suffered a severed artery and nearly died; George Washington cited him for bravery and promoted him to captain. From 1780 to 1783 he studied law under Thomas Jefferson.

Monroe sat in the Congress of the Confederation from November 1783, where he helped to write the Northwest Ordinance. He opposed the ratification of the Constitution, and in 1790 was elected to the Senate. Washington appointed him minister to France in 1794 but recalled him in 1796. He was governor of Virginia from 1799 to 1802, and as Jefferson's envoy he helped to negotiate the Louisiana Purchase. He fell out with James Madison over the Monroe–Pinkney Treaty, but in April 1811 became Madison's Secretary of State, and in the War of 1812 also served as Secretary of War.

He defeated the Federalist Rufus King in 1816, and his inauguration on 4 March 1817 opened what was called the Era of Good Feelings, as the Federalists collapsed; in 1820 he was re-elected unopposed. He signed the Missouri Compromise, and in the Adams–Onís Treaty of 1819 the United States secured Florida and a border across the continent.

After his term ended in 1825 Monroe lived at Oak Hill in Aldie, Virginia, and was beset by financial difficulties. His wife Elizabeth died in 1830, and he moved to New York City, where he died on 4 July 1831. Monroe owned dozens of enslaved people, and sold property, including enslaved people, to pay debts. Polls of historians tend to rank him as an above-average president. He was a member of the American Colonization Society, and Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, is named after him. He was the last president to wear the powdered wig and knee-breeches of the late 18th century.
james-river: The James River begins in the Appalachian Mountains, at the confluence of the Cowpasture and Jackson Rivers in Botetourt County, and flows 348 miles (560 km) to Chesapeake Bay; counting the Jackson River it is 444 miles (715 km) long. It is the longest river in Virginia, and its catchment covers 10,432 square miles (27,020 km2). Tidal waters extend west to Richmond at the fall line, the head of navigation, where the coastal plain gives way to the piedmont. At its mouth the Elizabeth and Nansemond Rivers join it to form the harbour of Hampton Roads.

The Native Americans east of the fall line called the river the Powhatan River, after the Powhatans. The colonists who arrived in 1607 named it after James I of England and built the first permanent English settlement in the Americas about 35 miles (56 km) upstream from the bay. For its first fifteen years the river was the major highway of colonial Virginia. In 1612 John Rolfe cultivated a non-native strain of tobacco that proved popular in England, and the river became the main route for exporting it from plantations with wharfs along its banks, which made the Virginia Company's efforts financially successful.

The James River and Kanawha Canal was meant to link the river to the Ohio Valley through the Kanawha River, but railroads eclipsed canals, and the canal stopped at Eagle Rock; the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway reached the Ohio River by 1873. In the 1960s and 1970s mishandling of the insecticide Kepone contaminated large stretches of the estuary downstream of plants in Hopewell. In December 1975 Governor Mills Godwin Jr. closed 100 miles of the river to fishing, and the ban lasted 13 years. The Chesapeake Bay Agreement of 1983 set baseline protections for the river's clean-up.

Jamestown and Williamsburg, Virginia's first colonial capitals, and Richmond, its present capital, lie on the river. It is a major source of drinking water, and a two-mile stretch of rapids ends in downtown Richmond where the river goes over the fall line. The James River Reserve Fleet, an anchorage of mothballed ships of the National Defense Reserve Fleet, lies on its lower course.
james-scullin: James Henry Scullin was born at Trawalla, Victoria, on 18 September 1876, the fourth of eight children of Irish Catholic parents from County Londonderry. His father was a railway labourer. The family moved to Ballarat in 1887, and after leaving school at 12 he did manual odd jobs until about 1900, then ran a grocer's shop for ten years. He read widely, belonged to the Catholic Young Men's Society and was a skilled debater. He remained a devout Catholic, a non-drinker and a non-smoker.

He was a foundation member of his local Political Labor Council in 1903 and an organiser for the Australian Workers' Union. He won Corangamite in 1910, lost it in 1913, and returned to the House of Representatives in 1922 for Yarra. In March 1928 he replaced Matthew Charlton as Labor leader.

Scullin came to Canberra with the largest majority Labor had won to that time. His cabinet was sworn in on 22 October 1929, and two days later news of Black Thursday on Wall Street reached Australia. Unemployment was just over 13 per cent at the end of 1929, and prices for wool and wheat, the chief exports, had fallen by almost a third. With his treasurer Ted Theodore he proposed plans for debt repayment, relief for farmers and stimulus by deficit spending, but the Senate and the Commonwealth Bank repeatedly blocked them. Theodore resigned in June 1930 after a Royal Commission criticised him over the Mungana affair.

Scullin's party split. Jack Lang, Premier of New South Wales, urged repudiation of interest on debts to Britain, and when Scullin reappointed Theodore as treasurer in January 1931, Joseph Lyons and James Fenton resigned from the cabinet. In May, with unemployment at 27.6 per cent, Scullin agreed with the premiers to the Premiers' Plan, which cut spending by 20 per cent, including social welfare. Core Labor supporters felt betrayed, and the government was defeated at the 1931 election by the newly formed United Australia Party.

Scullin remained Labor leader for four more years and lost the 1934 election. He then became a respected authority on public finance and taxation, advised John Curtin closely and remained member for Yarra until 1949. Disappointed with his own term, he lived to see the Curtin and Chifley governments carry out many of his ideas, and died in January 1953 at the age of 76.
james-the-great: James was born into a family of Jewish fishermen on the Sea of Galilee. His parents were Zebedee and Salome, and Salome was a sister of Mary, the mother of Jesus, which made James a cousin of Jesus. He was the brother of John the Apostle. He is called the Greater to distinguish him from the other apostle James, the Lesser, the term meaning older or taller rather than more important. The Synoptic Gospels state that James and John were preparing to fish with their father by the shore when Jesus called them to follow him.

James, John and Peter formed an informal triumvirate among the Twelve. They were the only apostles present at three occasions of the ministry of Jesus: the raising of Jairus' daughter, the transfiguration and the agony in the Garden of Gethsemane. The brothers were nicknamed Boanerges, the Sons of Thunder. James and John, or in another tradition their mother, asked Jesus for seats on his right and left in his glory, and Jesus rebuked them.

The Acts of the Apostles records that Herod the king, usually identified with Herod Agrippa, had James executed by the sword. He was the first of the apostles to be martyred. The Armenian Apostolic Cathedral of St. James in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem is the traditional site, and his head is believed to lie under the altar of its Chapel of Saint James the Great.

The Historia Compostelana, commissioned by Diego Gelmírez in the 12th century, sets out the legend as it was believed at Compostela. James preached in Hispania as well as the Holy Land, and after his execution his followers carried his body by sea to Padrón in Galicia and overland to Santiago de Compostela. The Compostela tradition places the discovery of the relics in the 9th century, when Pelayo found them in the Libredon forest in the time of Bishop Theodemir and King Alfonso II. The pilgrimage route known as the Way of St. James began to form from that century.

A later tradition has him appear in battle for the Christian army at Clavijo, as Santiago Matamoros, and Spanish Christian armies took his name as a battle cry. The military Order of Santiago was founded in Spain in the 12th century. His emblem is the scallop shell, which pilgrims wore, and his feast day is 25 July.
james-vi-and-i: James was born on 19 June 1566, the only son of Mary, Queen of Scots, and Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley, both great-grandchildren of Henry VII of England. He was entrusted to the Earl and Countess of Mar at Stirling Castle and crowned at the Church of the Holy Rude on 29 July 1567, at thirteen months, with John Knox preaching the sermon. Although his mother was a Catholic, he was raised as a Protestant. Four regents governed during his minority, which officially ended in 1578, though he did not fully control his government until 1583.

In Scotland James married Anne of Denmark in 1589, after sailing from Leith to fetch her when storms forced her ship to the coast of Norway. His visit to Denmark sparked an interest in witchcraft, and he attended the North Berwick witch trials. In 1597 and 1598 he wrote The True Law of Free Monarchies and Basilikon Doron, which set out the divine right of kings. He is credited with achieving most of his aims in Scotland.

Elizabeth I died early on 24 March 1603, and James was proclaimed king in London the same day. He tried to bring about a closer union of Scotland and England, but they stayed separate states with their own parliaments, judiciaries and laws, and from 20 October 1604 he styled himself King of Great Britain. He faced the Gunpowder Plot, discovered on the night of 4 to 5 November 1605, and quarrels with the English Parliament. After the plot he sanctioned harsh measures against English Catholics, including the Oath of Allegiance, though he was conciliatory to those who took it. He sponsored the translation of the Bible later named for him, and a 1604 revision of the Book of Common Prayer.

In his last years James suffered from arthritis, gout and kidney stones and was often seriously ill. He died on 27 March 1625. His reign in Scotland, of 57 years and 246 days, was the longest of any Scottish monarch. He was widely mourned, and his people had enjoyed peace and comparatively low taxation under him. He had often neglected government for the hunt, and his reliance on favourites at a scandal-ridden court weakened the image of monarchy that Elizabeth I had built. The courtier Anthony Weldon is credited with the epithet the wisest fool in Christendom.
james-watt: James Watt was born in Greenock, Renfrewshire, in January 1736, the eldest of the five surviving children of Agnes Muirhead and James Watt, a shipwright, ship owner and contractor who served as Greenock's chief baillie in 1751. The family's wealth came in part from his father's trading in slaves and slave-produced goods. His parents were Presbyterians and strong Covenanters, but he later became a deist. He was educated at home by his mother and then at Greenock Grammar School, where he showed an aptitude for mathematics while Latin and Greek failed to interest him. After leaving school he worked in his father's workshops, and when his father's ventures failed he left for Glasgow to find employment as a mathematical instrument maker.

In 1759 his friend John Robison called his attention to steam as a source of motive power. The Newcomen engine had been used for almost fifty years to pump water from mines and had hardly changed. Watt began to experiment, though he had never seen an operating steam engine, and came to realise the importance of latent heat, which his friend Joseph Black had discovered years before. His insight was that contemporary engines wasted energy by repeatedly cooling and reheating the cylinder, and he introduced the separate condenser to avoid this. Eventually he adapted the engine to produce rotary motion, which greatly broadened its use beyond pumping water.

Watt had great financial difficulties until he entered a partnership with Matthew Boulton in 1775. The first engines were installed in commercial enterprises in 1776, and for the next five years he installed more, mostly in Cornwall. Boulton and Watt charged an annual payment equal to one-third of the value of the coal saved compared with a Newcomen engine. Mine owners in Cornwall became convinced that his patent could not be enforced and withheld payments, and Watt had to go to court. The Soho Foundry formally opened in 1796, and in 1800 Watt retired, the year his fundamental patent and the partnership expired.

The story that Watt was inspired by a boiling kettle is probably apocryphal, possibly created by his son James Watt Jr.; Watt did not invent the steam engine but improved the existing Newcomen engine. He also devised a letter copying machine and studied chemistry, finding that a solution of chlorine could bleach textiles. In retirement he built machines for copying sculptures, which he never patented. He was a member of the Lunar Society of Birmingham. The chemist Humphry Davy said that those who considered him only a practical mechanic formed an erroneous idea of him, since he was equally distinguished as a natural philosopher and a chemist. He died on 25 August 1819, and the SI unit of power, the watt, is named after him.
james-wolfe: James Wolfe was born on 2 January 1727 (New Style) at the vicarage in Westerham, Kent, the older of two sons of Edward Wolfe, a soldier of Anglo-Irish family who later became a lieutenant general, and Henrietta Thompson. The family moved to Greenwich around 1738. Destined for the army from his earliest years, Wolfe entered his father's 1st Marine regiment as a volunteer at thirteen. Illness kept him from the expedition against Cartagena in 1740, which lost most of its men to disease.

He received his first commission in 1741 and transferred to the 12th Regiment of Foot early in 1742, serving in Flanders as lieutenant and adjutant. Already a brigade major at eighteen, he was a lieutenant-colonel by twenty-three.

In the War of the Austrian Succession Wolfe fought in Flanders and southern Germany, and in the Jacobite rising of 1745 he served under Henry Hawley at Falkirk and under the Duke of Cumberland at Culloden on 16 April 1746. A story that he refused an order to shoot a wounded Jacobite officer has no supporting evidence, and he himself wrote that as few Highlanders as possible should be taken prisoner. At Lauffeld on 2 July 1747 he was badly wounded and received an official commendation.

Peace in 1748 left him on garrison duty in Scotland for about eight years. He commanded the 20th Regiment, wrote military pamphlets, taught himself Latin and mathematics and struggled with ill health suspected to be tuberculosis. In the Seven Years' War he distinguished himself at Rochefort in 1757, was promoted brigadier general on 23 January 1758 and served at the siege of Louisbourg. William Pitt the Elder then chose him to lead the assault on Quebec, with the local rank of major general, while in Europe he remained a full colonel.

Wolfe was known for demanding much of himself and his troops, and for carrying a musket, cartridge box and bayonet like his infantrymen, which was unusual for officers of the time. He was killed at the height of the Battle of the Plains of Abraham by three musket balls, and the French commander Montcalm died the next day.

His death made him a hero in Britain. It inspired Benjamin West's painting The Death of General Wolfe, the folk ballad Brave Wolfe and the opening line of the Canadian song The Maple Leaf Forever. In 1792 John Graves Simcoe named islands at the entrance to the St Lawrence for the victorious generals. In 1832 a column was raised where Wolfe is thought to have fallen; the inscription on Quebec's later obelisk was shortened to Here Died Wolfe so as not to offend French Canadians.
jamestown: Jamestown stood on the north-east bank of the James River, about 4 km south-west of present-day Williamsburg, in what later became James City County. The Virginia Company of London established it as James Fort on 4 May 1607 O.S., which is 14 May 1607 N.S. It followed earlier failed English attempts at colonisation, including the Roanoke Colony of 1585. The colonists chose a river island to avoid Spanish naval patrols, but it was infested with mosquitoes, lacked drinkable water and was used by the Paspahegh people. The fleet, under Captain Christopher Newport, consisted of the Susan Constant, Discovery and Godspeed.

Only 60 of the original 214 settlers survived the winter of 1609–1610, known as the Starving Time. Progress in the first years was uneven, owing to the aristocratic backgrounds of many colonists, a historic drought and the communal organisation of work. In 1612 tobacco from the West Indies was cultivated successfully, which led to an economic boom for the colony and for England. By 1613 Sir Thomas Dale had assigned 3-acre plots to the early planters, and the settlers began to spread onto land belonging to local native peoples.

Jamestown was the colonial capital from 1616 to 1699. In 1619 it saw the first legislative assembly in the New World, a labour strike and the first recorded African slaves in the Virginia colony, who most likely worked in the tobacco fields. A native uprising in 1622 devastated the surrounding settlements, but the capital was warned in time. In 1624 King James revoked the Virginia Company's charter and Virginia became a crown colony. Jamestown was deliberately burned during Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 and rebuilt, and in 1699 the capital moved to Williamsburg. The settlement then declined, and the church was abandoned in the 1750s.

Jamestown is now an archaeological site. The remains of the original 1607 fort, thought to have been lost to the river, were discovered in 1996 by the Jamestown Rediscovery project. Historic Jamestowne, run jointly by the National Park Service and Preservation Virginia, has the fort site, a seventeenth-century church tower and a museum of the artifacts found. Nearby, Jamestown Settlement is a living-history museum with replicas of the three ships. Jamestown, Williamsburg and Yorktown form the Historic Triangle of Colonial Virginia.
jami: Nūr ad-Dīn 'Abd ar-Rahmān Jāmī was born on 7 November 1414 at Kharjerd in Khorasan to a Persian family. His father, Nizām al-Dīn Ahmad, had come from Dasht in the district of Isfahan, so his early pen name was Dashti; he later chose Jami for two reasons he gave in a poem, his birthplace of Jam and the Sufi Sheikh-ul-Islam Ahmad Jam. A few years after his birth the family moved to Herat, where he studied philosophy, mathematics, rhetoric, logic and Arabic and Persian literature at the Nizamiyya, with his father, also a Sufi, as his first teacher. He completed his studies at Samarkand and made a pilgrimage that raised his reputation across the Persian world.

In Herat Jami held an important position at the Timurid court and was a mentor and friend of the Turkic poet Alisher Navoi. He belonged to the Naqshbandi Sufi order and the school of Ibn Arabi, though he did not always follow it: on the dependence of God and creatures he wrote, "We and Thou are not separate from each other, but we need Thee, whereas Thou dost not need us." He became a Sufi shaykh in 1453 and defined terms such as sainthood and the levels of tawhid.

He wrote about eighty-seven books and letters. His major poetical work is the Haft Awrang (Seven Thrones), seven long masnavis, by his own admission influenced by Nizami, among them Salaman va Absal, an allegory of the stages of the Sufi path, and Yusuf and Zulaykha, based on the Quran. He also wrote the Kherad-name in the tradition of the Alexander Romance, three collections of lyric poems, the Nafahat al-Uns, a collection of biographies of Sufi saints, and the Baharestan, modelled on Saadi's Gulestan, for his surviving son Zia-ol-din Yusef. His commentary on the Arabic grammar Al-Kafiya was a staple of Ottoman madrasa curricula.

Jami was living in Herat at the end of his life. Dates for his death vary, but most sources give November 1492. The prince of Herat conducted his funeral, which large numbers attended. His poetry was popular across the Islamic East, Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, and his works were used in schools from Samarqand to Istanbul and in the Mughal Empire. Babur, in the Baburnama, called him the foremost authority of the age in all of the sciences, and later Mughal emperors made versions of Yusuf and Zulaykha. Jami himself politely declined an invitation to settle in the Deccan.
jami-al-tawarikh: Jāmiʿ al-Tawārīkh was written by Rashid al-Din Hamadani (1247 to 1318) at the start of the 14th century and has been called the first world history. The Ilkhan Ghazan commissioned it because he wanted the Mongols, now settled and adopting Persian customs, to remember their nomadic roots. It first set out the history of the Mongols and their predecessors on the steppes, as the Taʾrīkh-ī Ghazānī. To compile it Rashid al-Din set up a precinct at the Rab'-e Rashidi in Tabriz, with a mosque, hospital and library. After Ghazan died in 1304 his successor Öljaitü asked for a history of the whole known world, finished between 1306 and 1311.

Rashid al-Din was born into a Jewish family at Hamadan, became a physician at court, converted to Islam around the age of thirty, was vizier from 1304 and was executed on 13 July 1318, convicted of poisoning Öljaitü.

The work has four main parts. The Taʾrīkh-ī Ghazānī gives the history, genealogies and legends of the Mongol and Turkic tribes and the history of the Mongols from Genghis Khan to Ghazan's death. A second part carries the reign of Öljaitü to 1310, and a universal history following al-Tabari's order from Adam to the pre-Islamic kings of Iran, Muhammad and the caliphs, the Islamic dynasties of Persia, the Turks, China, the Jews, Europe and the Indians. The remaining parts are a set of five genealogies and a geographical compendium, which has not survived.

Rashid al-Din used written and oral sources: Juvayni's history of the Mongols, the Shahnameh, the chronicle of Martin of Opava for Europe, the Altan Debter for the Mongols and translated Chinese works on medicine and administration. Scholars regard the work as collective, and some of it, including the period after Genghis Khan's death, is borrowed directly from Juvayni.

Rashid al-Din ordered one Arabic and one Persian copy each year for distribution across the Ilkhanate. About twenty illustrated copies were made in his lifetime, but only parts survive. The illustrations belong to the Persian miniature tradition and show Chinese influence, in dark outlines and transparent washes, and Byzantine influence in the figures. Surviving portions include an Arabic manuscript split between the Edinburgh University Library and the Khalili Collection, and two Persian copies of 1314 and 1317 in the Topkapı Palace Library, which later belonged to the Timurid ruler Shahrukh. The Arabic copy was in Herat in the 15th century and later passed to the Mughal court, including the emperor Akbar, before the British acquired it in the 19th century.
jammu: Jammu lies on the Tawi river among low ridges in the Shivalik hills, with the Shivalik range to the north, east and southeast and the Trikuta Range to the northwest, at an average elevation of 300 metres. The old city overlooks the river from its north bank, and the newer neighbourhoods spread over the south bank. According to local tradition it was named after its founder Raja Jambulochan, who is believed to have ruled in the 9th century, and the tradition says the city is 3,000 years old, a claim historians do not support.

According to the Tarikh-i-Azmi, Jammu came into existence around 900 CE, and the state of Durgara, from which the names Duggar and Dogra come, is attested from about the same time. Its rulers are repeatedly mentioned in Kalhana's Rajatarangini. Timur's chronicles name Jammu, since he returned to Samarkand through it after invading Delhi in 1398. Babur's chronicles describe it as a powerful state of the Punjab hills ruled by Manhas Rajputs. Akbar brought the hill kingdoms under Mughal suzerainty, though their kings kept considerable autonomy, and the Mughal empire treated them as allies and partners.

After Mughal power declined in the 18th century the Jammu state under Raja Dhruv Dev of the Jamwal family asserted its supremacy among the Dugar states. Its height came under his successor Raja Ranjit Dev, who ruled from 1728 to 1780 and promoted religious freedom and security, which drew craftsmen and traders to settle there. Towards the end of his rule the Sikh misls gained ground; around 1770 the Bhangi misl forced Ranjit Dev to become a tributary, and his successor Brij Lal Dev was defeated by Mahan Singh of the Sukerchakia misl, who sacked Jammu.

In 1808 Ranjit Singh, son of Mahan Singh, annexed it to the Sikh Empire. In 1818 Kishore Singh, father of Gulab Singh, was appointed ruler of the Jammu principality, which began the Jamwal or Dogra dynasty that came to rule the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir under British suzerainty.

Jammu is the winter capital of the union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, to which the offices move from Srinagar from November to April. It was the winter capital of the princely state from 1846 to 1952 and the capital of Jammu Province. The city is the cultural and economic centre of the Jammu division, and is about 600 kilometres from New Delhi.
jamsetji-tata: Jamsetji Nusserwanji Tata was born on 3 March 1839 in Navsari, to a respectable but poor family of Zoroastrian priests. His father, Nusserwanji Ratanji Tata, had broken with the priestly tradition to become the first businessman in the family. Jamsetji's mother tongue was Gujarati. His parents saw that he was gifted in mental arithmetic, and he joined his father in Bombay at the age of 14 and enrolled at Elphinstone College, completing his studies as a Green Scholar. He married Hirabai Daboo while still a student. After graduating in 1858 he joined his father's export-trading firm and helped set up branches in Japan, China, Europe and the United States.

His father sent him to China to learn how business was done there, including the opium trade. Tata saw instead that the cotton industry was booming. He worked in his father's company until he was 29 and then founded a trading company in 1868 with ₹21,000 of capital. In 1869 he bought a bankrupt oil mill at Chinchpokli, converted it to a cotton mill called Alexandra Mill, and sold it two years later at a profit. In 1874 he floated the Central India Spinning, Weaving, and Manufacturing Company in Nagpur, and people in Bombay, the Cottonopolis of India, scorned the unconventional choice of place.

In 1885 a company he floated in Pondicherry to distribute Indian textiles to nearby French colonies free of duty failed for lack of demand. He then bought the Dharamsi Mills at Kurla, resold them, and bought the Advance Mills in Ahmedabad, named for its up-to-date machinery. He supported the principles of Swadeshism before the Swadeshi movement began in 1905, and named a new Bombay mill the Swadeshi Mill, meant to produce cloth to match Manchester's. He tried to improve the cultivation of cotton in India and was the first to introduce the ring spindle into his mills, which replaced the throstle.

Tata set himself four aims: an iron and steel company, a world-class learning institution, a unique hotel and a hydroelectric plant. Only the hotel was completed in his lifetime, when the Taj Mahal Hotel opened on the Colaba waterfront in Mumbai on 3 December 1903. His successors achieved the other three. He gave generously to education and healthcare. He fell seriously ill on a business trip to Germany in 1900 and died at Bad Nauheim on 19 May 1904, and he was buried in the Parsi burial ground in Brookwood Cemetery, Woking, England. His sons Dorab and Ratan continued his work, and Dorab succeeded him as chair of the Tata Group. Jawaharlal Nehru called him a One-Man Planning Commission.
jamshedpur: Jamshedpur lies at the confluence of the Swarnarekha and Kharkai rivers in the south of Jharkhand, bordered by Odisha and West Bengal, and is surrounded by the forested Dalma Hills. It is part of the larger Chota Nagpur Plateau, at an average elevation of 135 metres. The modern city was built over the village of Sakchi. Its central part includes old neighbourhoods such as Sakchi, Bistupur and Golmuri, while the south-east is largely industrial and residential. It is also known as Tatanagar.

At the end of the nineteenth century Jamshedji Tata met steelmakers in Pittsburgh to obtain the most advanced technology for his plant, and at the turn of the twentieth century he asked the geologist Charles Page Perin to find a site for India's first steel plant. The search for a place rich in iron, coal, limestone and water began in April 1904. His son Dorabji Tata chose the location at Sakchi, the project began in 1908 and the plant was operating by 1912. Lord Chelmsford named the city Jamshedpur in 1919, in honour of Jamshedji, whose birthday, 3 March, is marked as Founder's Day.

During the First World War Tata Steel supplied rail and steel to British military campaigns in Mesopotamia, Egypt, Salonica and East Africa. In the Second World War the city was a high-value target, and British and American troops and air bases were stationed in the region. On 1 January 1948 the Orissa Military Police opened fire on a crowd of over 50,000 at Kharsawan, who were protesting against its merger; official records state 35 deaths, while other sources give figures as high as 2,000. After independence the city lay in Bihar until it became part of the new state of Jharkhand on 15 November 2000.

The 2011 census counted 629,659 people in the city and 1,337,131 in the urban agglomeration. Hindi, Bengali, Santali, Bhojpuri, Odia, Urdu and Punjabi are the main languages. Tata Steel, in the centre of the city, occupies about a fifth of its area, and Tata Motors is the second major industry. The city is called India's first planned industrial city, envisioned by an Indian, planned by an American, named by a British Viceroy and landscaped by a German botanist. Jubilee Park, of 225 acres, is decorated with lights for about a week on Founder's Day.
jan-hus: Jan Hus was born at Husinec in southern Bohemia to peasant parents; the exact date is disputed and most of what is known of his early life is unsubstantiated. He took his name from the village, and the word hus means goose in Czech. He began teaching at the University of Prague in 1398, defended propositions of John Wycliffe in public for the first time in 1399, and was ordained as a Catholic priest in 1400. He became dean of the philosophy department in 1401 and a rector of the university a year later, and in 1402 he was appointed preacher at the Bethlehem Chapel.

Hus translated Wycliffe's Trialogus into Czech and helped distribute it, even though Church authorities banned many of Wycliffe's works in 1403. From his pulpit he denounced the moral failings of clergy, bishops and even the papacy. In 1409 King Wenceslaus IV, wishing the university to stay neutral in the Western Schism, decreed that the Czech nation should have three votes and the German nation only one. The German masters and students left for Heidelberg and Leipzig, more than a thousand of them by one estimate, and spread accusations of Bohemian heresy. Hus was excommunicated and spent two years in exile.

King Sigismund arranged a general council at Constance, which opened on 1 November 1414, and Hus agreed to attend under his promise of safe-conduct. At his trial on 8 June 1415 thirty-nine sentences drawn from his books were read to him. He declared himself willing to recant if his errors were proved from the Bible, but refused to confess that he had erred.
