In 1682 he commissioned the project that became the Code Noir of 1685, which sanctioned a brutal system of repression to enforce slavery in the French colonies.

Colbert held that the country was enriched by commerce. Critics have condemned parts of his scheme: by maintaining the corporation system he left each industry in the hands of privileged bourgeois and closed advancement to the lower classes, and France still grew impoverished by the King's spending on wars.

He founded the Academy of Inscriptions and Medals in 1663, the Academy of Sciences in 1666, the Paris Observatory in 1667 and the Academy of Architecture in 1671. In 1665 he brought Gian Lorenzo Bernini to Paris to design the east facade of the Louvre, a design finally rejected. He gave pensions to writers such as Molière, Corneille and Racine. He died on 6 September 1683; a large stone was found in his urinary tract. His son, the Marquis de Seignelay, succeeded him as Navy Secretary.
jean-baptiste-jourdan: Jean-Baptiste Jourdan was born in Limoges on 29 April 1762, the only surviving child of Roch Jourdan, a surgeon. He was orphaned young and raised by an uncle, a parish priest who ran a boarding school in Beaurecueil. After about a year as a clerk for another uncle, a cloth merchant in Lyon, he enlisted in the Royal army in 1778. He served in the American War of Independence, at the Siege of Savannah in October 1779 and in the West Indies, where illness troubled him for the rest of his career. Demobilised in 1784, he returned to Limoges and worked for a cloth merchant.

Jourdan welcomed the Revolution and in 1792 commanded a battalion of volunteers at Jemappes. He became a general of division in 1793 and took command of the Army of the North on 22 September. He defeated Prince Josias of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld at Wattignies and broke the siege of Maubeuge, though Lazare Carnot claimed the credit. Leading the Army of Sambre-et-Meuse he took Charleroi on 25 June 1794 and won the Battle of Fleurus the next day, after which the Austrian Army evacuated Belgium.

In 1796 Archduke Charles defeated him at Amberg and Würzburg; the chief cause was thought to be the plan imposed by the government, but he was made the scapegoat. As a member of the Council of Five Hundred he framed the conscription law of 1798, the Jourdan Law. Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire in 1804. He became military adviser to Joseph Bonaparte, followed him into Spain, and on 21 June 1813 was defeated at the Battle of Vitoria, where the British captured his marshal's baton. The defeat led to the permanent loss of Spain.

After Waterloo Jourdan submitted to the Bourbons and refused to sit on the court that sentenced Marshal Michel Ney to death. He supported the Revolution of 1830, held the foreign affairs portfolio for a few days and then served as governor of the Hôtel des Invalides until his death in Paris on 23 November 1833; he was buried in Les Invalides. On Saint Helena Napoleon said he had used Jourdan very ill and called him a true patriot.
jean-baptiste-kleber: Jean-Baptiste Kléber was born in Strasbourg on 9 March 1753, where his father worked as a master builder. He studied architecture for four years, partly in Paris with Jean-François Chalgrin, and gained a commission in the Imperial Army of the Holy Roman Emperor. He left in 1783 because his humble birth hindered promotion beyond unterleutnant. Back in France he became inspector of public buildings at Belfort and between 1784 and 1792 designed buildings, among them the Hôtel de Ville at Thann.

In 1792 Kléber enlisted in the 4th Battalion of Volunteers of Haut-Rhin and was soon its lieutenant-colonel. He distinguished himself at the defence of Mainz in July 1793 and became a brigade general in August. In western France he took part in suppressing the Revolt in the Vendée, contributed to the victory at Cholet and was made divisional general on 17 October 1793. He was recalled after saying that the Vendéans merited lenient measures, but was reinstated in April 1794 and served at Fleurus on 26 June. In 1796 he was a most active lieutenant of Jean-Baptiste Jourdan and twice declined a permanent post as commander-in-chief. He retired in early 1798 and later joined Napoleon Bonaparte's Army of the Orient.

In Egypt a head wound at Alexandria made him governor of Alexandria. In 1799 he commanded the vanguard in Syria and won the Battle of Mount Tabor on 15 and 16 April. Napoleon left him in command without consulting him. On 24 January 1800 he signed the Convention of El Arish, which would have let the army return to Europe, but the British government refused to accept it, and on 20 March 1800 he defeated an Ottoman army of 60,000 with 10,000 men at Heliopolis. He then returned to Cairo and suppressed another revolt.

On 14 June 1800, in the garden of the palace of Alfi bika in Cairo, Kléber was stabbed to death by Suleiman al-Halabi, a Syrian student living in Egypt, who was caught and later executed. Napoleon, fearing that his tomb would become a symbol of Republicanism, had his embalmed body held at the Château d'If for 18 years. It was buried in Strasbourg Cathedral on 15 December 1838 and from 1840 lay beneath his statue in the Place Kléber. His heart is in an urn at Les Invalides, and his name is inscribed on the Arc de Triomphe.
jean-bodin: Bodin was born near Angers, possibly the son of a master tailor, into a modestly prosperous middle-class family. He was apparently educated in the Carmelite monastery of Angers, where he became a novice friar. He obtained release from his vows in 1549 and went to Paris, where he studied at the university and at the humanist Collège des Quatre Langues, now the Collège de France. In the 1550s he studied Roman law at the University of Toulouse under Arnaud du Ferrier and taught there, his special subject apparently being comparative jurisprudence. His plan for a school on humanist principles in Toulouse failed to win local support, and he left in 1560.

From 1561 Bodin was licensed as an attorney of the Parlement of Paris. When the Wars of Religion broke out in 1562 he affirmed his Catholic faith by oath, like other members of the Parlement, although his convictions at that time cannot be determined.

He joined the discussion circles around Prince François d'Alençon, a leader of the politiques, the faction of political pragmatists, and after the prince's hopes of the throne failed he transferred his allegiance to Henry III. In 1576 and 1577 he lost the king's favour as a delegate of the Third Estate at the Estates-General at Blois, where he led his estate's moves in February 1577 to prevent a new war against the Huguenots and tried to restrict supplemental taxation. He then withdrew from political life and lived as a provincial magistrate at Laon.
During the wars that followed the death of Henry III in 1589 he at first supported the Catholic League, expecting it to win quickly. He died in Laon during one of the plague epidemics of the time.

His Methodus ad facilem historiarum cognitionem of 1566 was an influential manual on writing history, which rejected the biblical model of the Four Monarchies and the classical theory of a Golden Age. His Reply to Malestroit of 1568 offered one of the earliest scholarly analyses of inflation. The Six Books of the Republic, written in 1576, defined sovereignty as the absolute and perpetual power of a Republic and stated that the sovereign prince is accountable only to God. He saw sovereignty as indivisible, but he held that only passive resistance to authority was justified.

On the Demonomania of the Sorcerers, first issued in 1580 and published in ten editions by 1604, developed the concept of pact witchcraft, based on a deal with the Devil. He also argued that a state might contain several religions, an unusual position in his time, and left an unpublished dialogue among different religions, including Judaism, Islam and natural theology, in which all agreed to coexist. His works were placed on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum, all of them in 1628.
jean-claude-duvalier: Jean-Claude Duvalier was born on 3 July 1951 in Port-au-Prince, the son of Simone Ovide, a woman of mixed descent, and François Duvalier, a black nationalist leader who became dictator of Haiti. He was brought up in an isolated environment and later studied law at the University of Haiti. In April 1971 he became president on his father's death, at the age of 19, the youngest president in the world. He had at first resisted the dynastic arrangement and would have preferred that the presidency go to his older sister Marie-Denise.

The constitution gave Duvalier absolute power, but he left substantive matters to his mother and to a committee led by his father's Interior Minister Luckner Cambronne, while he attended ceremonies. He released some political prisoners and eased press censorship, but opposition was not tolerated and the legislature remained a rubber stamp. Thousands of Haitians were tortured and killed during his presidency, and hundreds of thousands fled the country. Much of the family's wealth came from the Régie du Tabac, a tobacco monopoly that he expanded into a slush fund with no balance sheets.

On 27 May 1980 he married Michèle Bennett in a wedding that cost US$2 million, which Haitian dissidents and the international press criticised. In 1982 United States authorities insisted on the eradication of Haiti's pigs after an outbreak of African swine fever, which devastated the peasants who bred them as an investment. Pope John Paul II visited in March 1983 and said that things must change in Haiti.

A revolt began in the provinces in 1985, with demonstrations in Gonaïves, and protests spread to six other cities and then to the south. Duvalier cut staple food prices, closed independent radio stations and ordered a crackdown, without effect. In January 1986 the Reagan administration pressed him to leave, and on 7 February 1986 the Duvaliers left for France on a United States Air Force flight. He separated from his wife in 1990 and divorced her in 1993, losing most of his wealth.

He returned unexpectedly to Haiti on 16 January 2011 and was arrested the next day. On 28 February 2013 he pleaded not guilty to charges of corruption and human rights abuse. He died of a heart attack on 4 October 2014, aged 63.
jean-francois-champollion: Jean-François Champollion was born on 23 December 1790, the last of seven children of a book trader who had settled in Figeac, in the Department of Lot. He was mostly raised by his older brother, Jacques-Joseph, who took him to Grenoble in March 1801, taught him to read and supported his education. At the age of 16 he lectured before the Grenoble Academy, arguing that the language of the ancient Egyptians was closely related to Coptic, a view later confirmed. In 1806 he wrote to his brother of his decision to become the one to decipher the Egyptian script.

He avoided military service in the Napoleonic Wars, with the help of the prefect of Grenoble, Joseph Fourier, by arguing that his work was too important to interrupt. His loyalty to Napoleon during the Hundred Days led to royalist surveillance, internal exile in Figeac and the loss of his university post.

Before Champollion, scholars had speculated about the hieroglyphs without a method, many holding that they were purely ideographic or reserved for sacred matters. The British polymath Thomas Young had made the first advances, and in 1820 Champollion began the project in earnest. In 1822 he published his first breakthrough on the Rosetta hieroglyphs, showing that the system combined phonetic and ideographic signs, and he identified the names of Ramesses and Thutmose in cartouches from Abu Simbel. In 1824 the Précis du système hiéroglyphique, dedicated to and funded by Louis XVIII, set out the values of the signs.

That year he catalogued Bernardino Drovetti's collection of Egyptian antiquities at Turin. With Ippolito Rosellini he led the Franco-Tuscan Expedition to Egypt, travelling in 1829, where he read many hieroglyphic texts never before studied. A chair of Egyptian history and archaeology was created for him at the Collège de France by a decree of 12 March 1831.

Exhausted by the Egyptian journey, Champollion gave only three lectures before illness forced him to stop teaching. He died of a stroke in Paris on 4 March 1832, aged 41, and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. His brother supervised the posthumous publication of his Egyptian grammar. His readings were long disputed, and some faulted him for not crediting Young sufficiently, but later confirmations led to their acceptance, and he is regarded as the founder and father of Egyptology. A museum devoted to him was inaugurated at Figeac in 1986.
jean-froissart: Little is known of Froissart's life, and it comes mainly from his historical writings and from archives that mention him in the service of aristocrats or receiving gifts from them. His poems were once used to reconstruct his biography, but this approach is now said to be flawed, since the I of many poems should not be read as a reliable reference to the author. Froissart came from Valenciennes in the County of Hainaut, at the western tip of the Holy Roman Empire. Earlier scholars suggested that his father painted armorial bearings and that he began as a merchant before becoming a cleric, but the evidence for both is questionable.

At about 24 Froissart left Hainaut and entered the service of Philippa of Hainaut, queen consort of Edward III of England, in 1361 or 1362. This service is often presented as an official post of court poet or historiographer. Croenen, from the surviving English court archives, concluded that it was no official position and was probably more a literary construction, in which a poet dedicated poems to his lady and received occasional gifts. He travelled in England, Scotland, Wales, France, Flanders and Spain gathering material and first-hand accounts for his Chronicles. He went with Lionel, Duke of Clarence, to Milan to attend and chronicle the duke's wedding to Violante, daughter of Galeazzo Visconti, where Chaucer and Petrarch were also present.

After Queen Philippa's death in 1369 he enjoyed the patronage of Joanna, Duchess of Brabant, among others. His rewards included the benefice of Estinnes, near Binche, and later a canonry of Chimay, enough to finance further travels. He returned to England in 1395 but seemed disappointed by changes he saw as the end of chivalry. The date and circumstances of his death are unknown.

Froissart wrote Chronicles, Meliador, a long Arthurian romance, and a large body of poetry, both short lyrical forms and longer narrative poems, among them L'Horloge amoureux. For centuries the Chronicles have been recognised as the chief expression of the chivalric revival of the 14th-century kingdoms of England, France and Scotland, and they are an important source for the first half of the Hundred Years' War. They survive in more than 100 illuminated manuscripts. One of the most lavish was commissioned by the Flemish nobleman Louis de Gruuthuse in the 1470s, and its four volumes hold 112 miniatures by Flemish artists. Froissart is thought to have been among the first to mention the verge escapement in European clockworks, by 1368.
jean-jacques-dessalines: Dessalines was born into slavery, as Jean-Jacques Duclos, on the Cormier plantation near Grande-Rivière-du-Nord in Saint-Domingue. The names of his parents and their region of origin in Africa are not known. He rose to commandeur, or foreman, and worked there until he was about 30. He was then bought by a free man of colour named Dessalines, whose surname he took and kept after he gained his freedom. When the uprising of 1791 began on the Plaine-du-Nord, he joined it,.

Dessalines became a lieutenant in the army of Jean François Papillon and followed him into Spanish service, where he met Toussaint Louverture. After France ended slavery in 1794 Louverture switched to the French, and Dessalines followed, becoming his chief lieutenant and a brigadier general by 1799. He took several towns, and in 1801 quickly ended an insurrection led by Louverture's nephew Moyse, gaining a reputation for taking no prisoners and burning villages. When General Charles Leclerc's expedition arrived in 1802, he defended the fort of Crête-à-Pierrot with 1,300 men against 18,000 attackers on 11 March, and after a 20-day siege broke out with his army largely intact.

He briefly sided with Leclerc afterwards, and several historians hold him partly responsible for Louverture's arrest in June 1802. When the French plan to restore slavery became clear he changed sides again in October 1802. By November he led the alliance with the blessing of Alexandre Pétion, and he became commander of the Indigenous Army on 18 May 1803. Leclerc died of yellow fever, and the harsh methods of his successor Donatien de Rochambeau united the rebels. The decisive battle was Vertières on 18 November 1803.

On 1 January 1804 at Gonaïves Dessalines declared independence and named the country Ayiti, after the Taíno name. He was governor-general for life until the generals proclaimed him Emperor Jacques I on 22 September 1804; he was crowned at Le Cap on 6 October. Between February and April 1804 he ordered the massacre of the remaining French population, killing between 3,000 and 5,000 people. Some historians cite the threat of a French reinvasion and restored slavery. He spared Polish Legionnaires who had defected, and made them citizens. The 1805 constitution confirmed the abolition of slavery and forbade white colonists to own property.

He enforced plantation labour, called agrarian militarism by the historian Michel-Rolph Trouillot, and many newly freed people felt it resembled slavery. He was assassinated at Larnage, north of Port-au-Prince, on 17 October 1806 by members of his own administration, among them Pétion and Étienne-Élie Gérin, while on his way to put down a revolt in the south. A mob then dismembered his body, which a vivandière, Dédée Bazile, buried. Accounts of the killing differ.
jean-jacques-rousseau: Rousseau was born on 28 June 1712 in the Republic of Geneva, a Protestant city-state and associate of the Swiss Confederacy that had been a Calvinist republic since 1536. His family belonged to the middle order of citizens with voting rights, and he generally signed his books Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Citizen of Geneva. In practice a small number of wealthy families ruled the city through its councils. When the reformer Pierre Fatio protested in 1707, he was shot by order of the Small Council, and Rousseau's grandfather, who had supported him, was penalised. His father, Isaac Rousseau, was a watchmaker, a former dance teacher and a lover of music.

Rousseau took formal music instruction at the house of Françoise-Louise de Warens, who housed him on and off for about 13 years. In 1742 he presented to the Académie des Sciences a system of musical notation using numbers, which they rejected while praising his effort. His first opera, Les Muses galantes, was written in 1743 and first performed in 1745. He wrote seven operas in all, the best known being the one-act The Village Soothsayer, composed in 1752. After 1752 he felt he could not go on working for the theatre.

A question set by the Academy of Dijon in 1750, whether the rebirth of the arts and sciences had purified morals, gave Rousseau what he called another universe. His essay in reply began his central argument that social and cultural progress had led to the moral degradation of humanity. In the Discourse on Inequality (1754) he held that private property is the source of social inequality. The Social Contract and Émile appeared in 1762, and Julie, or the New Heloise in 1761. Émile's endorsement of religious toleration led to its condemnation in both Calvinist Geneva and Catholic Paris.

In The Social Contract Rousseau described a legitimate political order resting on the general will, the collective will of a society as a whole, reached through the active involvement of every citizen in discussion and voting. The phrase was not original, since Diderot and Montesquieu had used it. During the French Revolution the Jacobin clubs invoked him in demanding equality, and Robespierre and Saint-Just took inspiration from him. His Confessions, completed in 1770, were published in 1782.
jean-monnet: Jean Omer Marie Gabriel Monnet was born on 9 November 1888 in Cognac, into a family of cognac merchants. His father, Jacques-Gabriel Monnet, ran a mid-sized distiller and distributor renamed J.-G. Monnet & Cie in 1901, and his mother, Marie Demelle, was deeply religious. He did not complete the baccalauréat. He went instead to London to learn business with the firm's agent, and travelled for the family trade to Canada, the United States, Scandinavia and Russia.

In the First World War Monnet argued that victory required combining the British and French war efforts. Joint bodies such as the Wheat Executive (end of 1916) and the Allied Maritime Transport Council (end of 1917) followed. After the Paris Peace Conference he became Deputy Secretary-General of the League of Nations, leaving at the end of 1922 to manage the family firm. In September 1939 he went to London to coordinate Franco-British war supplies, and in 1940 he advocated a Franco-British union, which Churchill, Charles de Gaulle and Paul Reynaud supported and the French cabinet rejected.

In 1946 he negotiated the Blum–Byrnes agreement with the United States, which cleared a debt of $2.8 billion and gave France a loan of $650 million. As first head of the General Planning Commission he was the chief advocate of the plan known by his name, which aimed to exceed France's 1929 production by 25 per cent in 1950. It has been called indicative planning, unlike rigid Soviet-style planning. Although not all goals were met, it is credited with giving direction to the country.

He prepared the Schuman Declaration, made by Robert Schuman on 9 May 1950, which proposed placing French and German coal and steel under a common High Authority open to other countries. The date is now Europe Day. After the failure of the European Defence Community he founded in 1955 the Action Committee for the United States of Europe, which he closed on 9 May 1975.

Monnet, who was never elected to public office, died on 16 March 1979 at his home in Houjarray, aged 90. In 1976 he became the first Honorary Citizen of Europe, and in 1988, on the centenary of his birth, his remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris. His Memoirs were published in 1976, and an English translation in 1978.
jean-moulin: Jean Moulin was born on 20 June 1899 in Béziers, the son of a lay teacher and Freemason, Antoine-Émile Moulin. In 1917 he enrolled at the Faculty of Law of Montpellier, and through his father's influence he was appointed attaché to the cabinet of the prefect of Hérault. He was mobilised on 17 April 1918 in the 2nd Engineer Regiment, and was on his way to the front in the Vosges when the Armistice was signed. He obtained his law degree in July 1921 and became a sous-préfet at Albertville in 1925 and at Châteaulin in 1930.

In 1932 the politician Pierre Cot made Moulin his chef adjoint, and in 1936 Moulin was again chief of cabinet at the Air Ministry. In January 1937 he became France's youngest prefect, in the Aveyron, and in January 1939 prefect of Eure-et-Loir at Chartres. The Germans arrested him on 17 June 1940 when he refused to sign a false declaration that Senegalese soldiers had killed civilians at La Taye, which had in fact been bombed by Germans. The Vichy regime dismissed him on 2 November 1940, and he joined the Resistance.

He went to London in September 1941 and was received by Charles de Gaulle on 24 October. De Gaulle gave him the task of unifying the Resistance groups, and on 1 January 1942 he parachuted into the Alpilles under the codenames Rex and Max. In January 1943 three movements joined as the Mouvements Unis de la Résistance. Back in France from 21 March 1943, he obtained agreement on a joint programme and recognition of de Gaulle as leader. The first meeting of the National Council of the Resistance took place in Paris on 27 May 1943, with representatives of eight resistance movements, two labour unions and six political parties.

On 21 June 1943 the Sicherheitsdienst arrested Moulin at a meeting of Resistance leaders at the house of Dr Frédéric Dugoujon in Caluire-et-Cuire, near Lyon. He was held in Montluc Prison and tortured by Klaus Barbie. His death certificate, drawn up by the occupying force, places his death near or in the railway station of Metz, but reports conflict about when and where he died. Who betrayed him has been much debated; suspicion has fallen on the Resistance member René Hardy, who was acquitted for lack of evidence in two trials after the war.
In 1964 his remains were transferred to the Panthéon, and André Malraux, then Minister of Culture, spoke on the occasion in a speech that became among the best known in French history.
jean-parisot-de-valette: Jean Parisot de Valette was born into the noble La Valette family in Quercy, in south-western France, a family that had been important for many generations, various members having taken part in the Crusades. His grandfather Bernard de La Valette was a knight and king's orderly, and his father Guillot was a Chevalier de France. He joined the Knights Hospitaller in the Langue de Provence at about the age of 20, around 1514, and never returned to France or his family estates. He was present at the Great Siege of Rhodes in 1522 and accompanied Grand Master Philippe Villiers de L'Isle-Adam after the Ottomans under Suleiman expelled the Order from Rhodes.

After the loss of Rhodes the Emperor Charles V granted the Order the Maltese Islands and Tripoli. In 1538 Valette was imprisoned in Gozo for four months after attacking a man. In 1541 he was wounded in a naval battle against Abd-ur-Rahman Kust Aly, and his galley, the San Giovanni, was captured. Barbary pirates under Turgut Reis held him as a galley slave for a year until a prisoner exchange freed him. He became Governor of Tripoli in 1546 and Captain General of the Order's galleys in 1554.

On the death of Grand Master Claude de la Sengle in 1557 the knights, aware that an attack was certain, elected Valette in his place. In 1560 he allied with the Habsburg Empire to reconquer Tripoli, but the expedition ended in a Christian defeat at the Battle of Djerba. Later in his term he greatly strengthened the Order's navy.

In the Great Siege of Malta in 1565, Valette organised the defence against an Ottoman force of no fewer than 30,000 soldiers, including Janissaries, with a fleet of some 193 ships. The vastly outnumbered Christians lost Fort St Elmo after about a month of fierce fighting, though the Ottoman engineers had judged that it would fall in three days. The Order held out in Birgu and Senglea until a relief force arrived, and the Ottomans withdrew with too few men, supplies and too little morale to counterattack. Valette gained great prestige in Europe, and declined the offer of a cardinal's hat to preserve independence from the papacy.

In 1566 he laid with his own hands the first stone of a new city on Mount Sciberras, named Valletta after its founder. He suffered a stroke while praying in a chapel and died on 21 August 1568, exactly eleven years after his election, before the city was complete. He was succeeded by Pierre de Monte, and his tomb lies in the crypt of the Conventual Church, now St John's Co-Cathedral. The form of his surname is disputed: the historian Giovanni Bonello states that he always signed himself de Valette, without the La.
jean-paul-sartre: Jean-Paul Sartre was born on 21 June 1905 in Paris, the only child of Jean-Baptiste Sartre, a French Navy officer who died of an illness, most likely contracted in Indochina, when Sartre was two. He was raised at Meudon by his mother and his grandfather Charles Schweitzer, a teacher of German who introduced him to classical literature very early. As a teenager he was drawn to philosophy by Henri Bergson's Time and Free Will, and at the École Normale Supérieure he met Raymond Aron and Paul Nizan. In 1929 he met Simone de Beauvoir, and the two became lifelong companions in a relationship that was not monogamous.

During the Second World War Sartre was drafted, captured and later released, and then co-founded the resistance group Socialisme et Liberté. He wrote plays including The Flies and No Exit and became an influential voice in occupied France. After the war he co-founded the journal Les Temps modernes. He supported anti-colonial movements, condemned French policies in Algeria and opposed intervention in Vietnam. His friendship with Albert Camus ended after Camus's The Rebel (1951); Sartre believed violence was at times necessary for change. In 1964 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, which he tried to refuse, saying that a writer should not allow himself to be turned into an institution.

Sartre's central claim is that human beings are condemned to be free. Because there is no creator, humans have no essence before their existence: existence precedes essence. They cannot explain their actions by a fixed human nature and are fully responsible for them. Authenticity means facing the indeterminate character of existence in anguish; the inauthentic way flees that anguish by lying to oneself, which he called bad faith.

His principal philosophical work is Being and Nothingness (1943). Existentialism Is a Humanism (1946) began as a lecture, and his other works include the novel Nausea (1938), the play Dirty Hands (1948) and the autobiography The Words (1964). He died on 15 April 1980, and 50,000 mourners attended his funeral.
jean-racine: Racine was born in La Ferté-Milon, in Picardy in northern France. He was orphaned by the age of four, since his mother died in 1641 and his father in 1643, and his grandparents took him in. When his grandfather died in 1649, his grandmother, Marie des Moulins, went to live in the convent of Port-Royal and took the boy with her. He received a classical education at the Petites écoles de Port-Royal, a school run by followers of Jansenism, a theology that the French bishops and the Pope condemned as heretical. The Jansenists influenced him for the rest of his life. He excelled in the classics there, and the themes of Greek and Roman mythology came to play large roles in his plays.

Racine wrote mainly tragedy, with the plays Phèdre, Andromaque and Athalie among the works held up as models of neoclassical perfection. He wrote one comedy, Les Plaideurs, and a muted tragedy for the young, Esther. His plays used the twelve-syllable French alexandrine, and his vocabulary is said to be limited to about 2,500 words. He observed the classical unities strictly, describing only the final stage of a prolonged crisis, with a minimum of characters, all of them royal, and almost no action on stage. The Greek tragedians, from whom he borrowed freely, tended to see humanity as controlled by indifferent gods. In his religious plays he kept closely to his Old Testament sources.

Contemporaries criticised Racine for the lack of historical accuracy in Britannicus of 1669 and Mithridate of 1673, and for the lack of incident in Bérénice of 1670. He replied that his rivals were among the worst offenders and that tragedy need not consist of bloodshed. He was constantly compared with Pierre Corneille, whose ornate intricacy he abandoned. In 1674 the poet and critic Boileau published his Art Poétique, which judged Racine's model of tragedy superior to Corneille's. Later, Friedrich Schiller and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe called his work courtly drama, and some French critics dismissed it as a historical document. Twentieth-century critics reread Phèdre as realist drama with universal characters, and Marcel Proust developed a fondness for Racine at an early age.
jean-sibelius: Johan Christian Julius Sibelius was born on 8 December 1865 in Hämeenlinna, then in the Grand Duchy of Finland, an autonomous state within the Russian Empire. His father, the Swedish-speaking doctor Christian Gustaf Sibelius, died of typhoid in July 1868, leaving heavy debts, and the family moved into the home of his maternal grandmother. His uncle Pehr Ferdinand Sibelius, who gave him a violin at ten, acted as his musical adviser. In 1885 he began to study law but soon moved to the Helsinki Music Institute, where he studied until 1889 under its founder Martin Wegelius, and later with Ferruccio Busoni, a lifelong friend.

Sibelius married Aino Järnefelt on 10 June 1892 and spent his honeymoon in Karelia, the home of the Kalevala, which inspired En saga, the Lemminkäinen legends and the Karelia Suite. His reputation in Finland grew in the 1890s with the choral symphony Kullervo, and the First Symphony was first performed in 1899, at a time when Finnish nationalism was evolving. The family moved into their new home, Ainola, by Lake Tuusula near Järvenpää, on 24 September 1904. In April 1915 he saw sixteen swans fly by, and they inspired the finale of the Fifth Symphony.

After the Seventh Symphony of 1924, the incidental music for The Tempest and the tone poem Tapiola, both of 1926, he produced no further major works for the last thirty years of his life. He said he had simply felt he had written enough. He worked for years on an Eighth Symphony, which he later burned. The so-called silence of Järvenpää was something of a myth, since visitors, colleagues and grandchildren came to Ainola.

His core work is the seven symphonies. His thirteen symphonic poems, the first composed in 1892 and the last in 1926, show his fascination with nature and Finnish mythology, and among them is The Swan of Tuonela. Valse triste began as incidental music for his brother-in-law Arvid Järnefelt's 1903 play Kuolema and became an instant success as a concert piece in 1904. He also wrote a Violin Concerto, over a hundred songs, and the one-act opera The Maiden in the Tower. He died on 20 September 1957. Ainola became a museum in 1974, and Finland keeps 8 December, his birthday, as a flag flying day, the Day of Finnish Music.
jeanne-dalbret: Jeanne was born on 16 November 1528 at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. From the age of two she was raised apart from her parents at the Château de Plessis-lèz-Tours, at the wish of her uncle Francis I of France, and was taught by the humanist Nicolas Bourbon. On 13 June 1541, at the age of twelve, she was forced for political reasons to marry William, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg, and had to be carried to the altar by the Constable of France, Anne de Montmorency, after protesting in writing. The marriage was annulled in 1545. On 20 October 1548 she married Antoine de Bourbon, Duke of Vendôme; of their five children only Henry and Catherine reached adulthood.

On the death of her father on 25 May 1555 Jeanne and Antoine became joint rulers of Navarre, and they were crowned at Pau on 18 August. Antoine's frequent absences left her to rule Béarn alone. Influenced by her mother's leanings towards religious reform, she publicly embraced the teachings of John Calvin on Christmas Day 1560, which made her the highest-ranking Protestant in France. She declared Calvinism the official religion of her kingdom, banished priests and nuns, prohibited Catholic ritual and commissioned a translation of the New Testament into Basque and Béarnese. She also reformed the economic and judicial systems of her domains.

When the French Wars of Religion began in 1562 Antoine sided with the Catholics, and Jeanne left Paris for Béarn. He died that year of wounds suffered at the siege of Rouen. She refused an offer of marriage from Philip II of Spain that required her return to Catholicism, and she was summoned to Rome by Pius IV to be examined for heresy; the threat was never carried out. When the third war broke out in 1568 she took refuge at La Rochelle with her son, wrote manifestos, borrowed from Elizabeth I of England on the security of her jewels and worked with Admiral de Coligny.

Jeanne was the chief negotiator of the Peace of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in August 1570. Its terms led to the marriage contract between her son Henry and Marguerite, sister of Charles IX, signed on 11 April 1572 after talks with Catherine de' Medici at Chenonceaux. She fell ill in Paris on 4 June 1572 and died five days later; a rumour that Catherine had poisoned her with perfumed gloves was not borne out, since an autopsy showed natural causes. She wrote poetry and memoirs justifying her leadership of the Huguenots. Her son succeeded as Henry III of Navarre and in 1589 became Henry IV of France, founding the Bourbon line of kings.
jebe: Jebe, whose birth name was Jirqo'adai, was one of the most prominent noyans, or generals, of Genghis Khan. He belonged to the Mongol Besüd tribe and fought among the Tayichi'ut before entering Temüjin's service. After the Battle of the Thirteen Sides in 1202, Genghis asked the defeated who had shot the arrow. Jirqo'adai confessed and said it was Genghis's choice to kill him, but that if allowed to live he would serve loyally. Genghis valued skill and loyalty, pardoned him and gave him the name Jebe, meaning arrow and weapon in Mongolian.

Jebe quickly became one of Genghis Khan's best commanders and led the left wing, with Subutai, in the 1211 invasion of Jin China. His unit went round the wall to the east, took two fortresses and destroyed the second Jin army at Wusha Fortress. Using feigned retreats he captured chains of fortresses; in winter 1211 he took Liaoyang by luring its defenders on a retreat of over 100 miles, then riding 100 miles in 24 hours to rout them. In 1213 he found a way round the defences of the Juyong Pass, forcing the defenders into the field.

In 1218 Jebe was sent with 20,000 men against Kuchlug to conquer Kara-Khitai, which he did partly by inciting and backing religious revolts between its ruling Buddhists and oppressed Muslims; Kuchlug was hunted down after a long chase through the mountains. Genghis was said to be concerned that Jebe might rebel, and Jebe returned and offered him 100 white horses as a sign of loyalty. In the invasion of the Khwarezm Empire in 1219 he crossed the Tian Shan in winter to threaten the Ferghana Valley, and he and Subutai then pursued Shah Mohammed II across his own empire. They failed to catch him, but the pursuit kept him from rallying new armies.

Jebe and Subutai raided around the Caspian Sea, defeating the Georgians, who were set to join the Fifth Crusade, and the tribes of the Caucasus steppe, and then defeated the Rus' and Cumans at the Battle of the Kalka River. Jebe likely died soon after the battle, but the circumstances are mysterious. Stephen Pow suggests that Kipchak forces allied with the Rus' may have killed him near a kurgan close to Khortytsia Island, while the Russian scholars D. M. Timokhin and V. V. Tishin hold that this is not proven. He has been described as the best cavalry general in history for his unorthodox and daring maneuvers, though few sources survive about his life.
jebel-ali: Jebel Ali is a port city in the Emirate of Dubai, about 35 kilometres south-west of the city of Dubai on the southern coast of the Persian Gulf. Jebel means mountain or hill in Arabic. Many Arab historians argue that it was named after Ali, cousin and son-in-law of Muhammad, who stood on a hill and looked towards the sea, though no recorded proof has been found. It was initially a sparsely inhabited coastal area.

In 1968 Overseas AST began building Dubai's first communications station in the Jebel Ali area, on raised ground; it was commissioned in 1970 and gave the first telecommunication links with the rest of the world. In the 1970s Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum planned to develop Jebel Ali into an industrial area with its own airport, port and township. The original Jebel Ali Village, built in 1977 to house the staff of construction contractors, was a small British-style garden city by Sir William Halcrow and Partners and a prototype for later residential areas such as Emirates Hills.

The Port of Jebel Ali opened in 1979 at the decree of Sheikh Rashid and was inaugurated by Queen Elizabeth II. It is one of the largest man-made harbours in the world and is operated by DP World. Its depth allows a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier and several ships of its strike group to dock pierside. The Jebel Ali Free Zone was created in 1985 as an industrial area around the port, with privileges that included exemption from corporate tax for 50 years, no personal income tax and no import or re-export duties. On 23 September 1983 Gulf Air Flight 771 crashed at Jebel Ali, killing all 112 people on board; a bomb planted by the Abu Nidal Organization caused the crash.

The area holds the Jebel Ali Power and Desalination Complex, an aluminium smelter run by Emirates Global Aluminium, oil storage and bunkering terminals and warehousing. It is Sector 5 of the Emirate of Dubai and is split into 18 communities. Sheikh Zayed Road, the Dubai Metro Red Line and Al Maktoum International Airport in Dubai South connect it to other places. Off its coast lies the artificial archipelago Palm Jebel Ali, developed by Nakheel, and the area includes Expo City Dubai, the legacy site of Expo 2020, and Dubai Investment Park.
jebel-barkal: Jebel Barkal is a flat-topped mesa 104 metres tall, standing 400 km north of Khartoum beside Karima in Northern State, near the Nile in Nubia. It acquired religious significance for both ancient Kush and the Egyptians who occupied it. The earliest occupation is known so far only from scattered potsherds of the Kerma culture, whose people seem to have venerated the mesa in an animistic fashion and to have passed the tradition on to the New Kingdom Egyptians and later to the Napatans and Meroites.

Around 1450 BCE the pharaoh Thutmose III conquered Jebel Barkal and built a fortified settlement there as the southern limit of the Egyptian empire. The city and region became known as Napata, and Egyptian occupation lasted through most of the New Kingdom. The Egyptians built a complex of temples centred on a temple of Amun of Napata, a local, ram-headed form of the god of Thebes. Little was built in the last years of the New Kingdom or after its collapse in 1169 BCE.

Jebel Barkal was the capital of the Kingdom of Kush as it returned to power after 800 BCE as the Dynasty of Napata. The Kushite kings who ruled Egypt as the 25th Dynasty, among them Kashta, Piankhy and Taharqa, built, renovated and expanded monuments there. After the Assyrian conquest of Egypt in the mid-7th century BCE, the Kushites kept Jebel Barkal and Meroë as the main centres of their kingdom, and palaces and temples were renewed there until the early 3rd century BCE.

In 270 BCE royal burials moved to Meroë, but Jebel Barkal remained an important city, and King Natakamani built a sequence of palaces. Pyramids of the Meroitic period were built at the site, and occupation continued in the Christian period of Nubia after Kush collapsed in the 4th century CE.

The ruins include at least 13 temples built, renovated and expanded over more than 1,500 years. European explorers began describing them in the 1820s, among them Frédéric Cailliaud, Louis Maurice Adolphe Linant de Bellefonds and Karl Richard Lepsius, whose drawings record details that have since disappeared. Scientific excavation began in 1916 with a joint expedition of Harvard University and the Museum of Fine Arts of Boston under George Reisner, followed from the 1970s by a team from the University of Rome La Sapienza under Sergio Donadoni. The larger temples, such as the Temple of Amun, are still regarded as sacred by the local population. In 2003 UNESCO named the mountain and the archaeological site at its base a World Heritage Site.
jebusites: The Hebrew Bible is the only surviving ancient text that uses the term Jebusite for the inhabitants of Jerusalem, which it calls Jebus, a name meaning 'trampled place'. In the Generations of Noah in Genesis 10 the Jebusites are listed among the Canaanites, in third place between the Hittites and the Amorites. Scholars have long debated who they were.

Many once took them to be Hittites, a view that has lost ground. Edward Lipiński has proposed that they were an Amorite tribe, linking them with the Yabusi'um named in a cuneiform letter from the archive of Mari. The Amarna letters name a king of Jerusalem, Abdi-Heba, whose name invokes the Hurrian goddess Ḫepat, which suggests Hurrian influence or a Hurrian warrior elite in the city.

In the biblical account the Jebusites lived in the hill country beside Jerusalem. Joshua 10 tells of Adonizedek leading a confederation of Jebusites and neighbouring cities against Joshua, who defeated and killed him. Joshua 15:63 and Judges 1:21 say the Jebusites remained in the city, where the Judahites could not dislodge them. According to 2 Samuel, they still held Jerusalem in the time of King David and boasted that even the blind and lame could defend it.

David took the city by a surprise attack led by Joab, which in the Masoretic Text goes through the water tunnels; the version in 1 Chronicles does not mention them. According to some biblical chronologies the conquest fell in 1003 BCE. A majority of scholars hold that the Book of Joshua has little historical value for the early settlement of the Hebrew tribes. 1 Kings 9:20-21 says Solomon made the surviving Jebusites serfs. The Jebusite Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles, sold David the threshing floor on which he built an altar.

Niels Peter Lemche has argued that no evidence for Jebus or the Jebusites exists outside the Old Testament, and that every non-biblical source calls the city Jerusalem. He suggests that Jebus may be a different place or a pseudo-ethnic name. What became of the Jebusites is unknown. The 'Jebusite hypothesis' holds that they remained in Jerusalem and formed an important faction in the Kingdom of Judah, with the priest Zadok among them.

Rabbinic tradition has its own stories, including a covenant between Abraham and the Jebusites cast in bronze. In modern times Yasser Arafat and Faisal Husseini, among others, have claimed that Palestinian Arabs descend from the Jebusites. Eric H. Cline holds that historians and archaeologists generally find no significant connection between them.
jeddah: Jeddah lies on the Red Sea coastal plain, called Tihamah, in the lower Hijaz mountains. Mecca, the holiest city in Islam, is 65 kilometres to the east, and Medina, the second holiest, is 360 kilometres to the north. The climate is arid, and unlike other Saudi cities Jeddah keeps warm temperatures in winter, while summers often pass 40 °C. Traces of early activity are attested by Thamudic inscriptions found in Wadi Briman and Wadi Boweb, and the oldest mashrabiya, a type of carved wooden screen, found in Jeddah dates to the pre-Islamic era. One account of the name derives it from the Arabic word jaddah, meaning grandmother, and a folk belief places the tomb of Eve, the grandmother of humanity, in the city.

Jeddah first achieved prominence around 647 CE, when the third caliph, Uthman ibn Affan, made it the port of Mecca in place of the Al Shoaib port, southwest of Mecca. In 969 the Fatimids, who had taken Egypt from the Abbasid governors of the Ikhshidid dynasty, extended their empire to the Hijaz and Jeddah, and developed trade networks in the Mediterranean and Indian Ocean through the Red Sea, with diplomatic ties reaching the Song dynasty of China. In 1517 the Ottomans, under Selim I, conquered the Mamluk Sultanate, and in 1802 forces from Nejd took Mecca and Jeddah from them. Sultan Mahmud II ordered his Egyptian viceroy, Muhammad Ali Pasha, to retake the city, and he did so in the Battle of Jeddah in 1813.

During the First World War Sharif Hussein bin Ali declared a revolt against the Ottoman Empire, seeking a unified Arab state from Aleppo to Aden. Ibn Saud, whose clan came from the central Nejd, later conquered Medina and Jeddah by agreement with the people of Jeddah after the Second Battle of Jeddah. He deposed Ali bin Hussein, who fled to Baghdad and eventually settled in Amman, where his descendants joined the Hashemite royal house of Jordan.

Jeddah is the second-largest city in Saudi Arabia after Riyadh and its main commercial centre, and the principal gateway to Mecca. It has long been a port: in the 19th century it exported mother-of-pearl, tortoise shells, frankincense and spices. The old city, Al-Balad, with its multistorey merchant houses, was granted UNESCO World Heritage status in 2014, and it holds the Bayt Naseef museum. The speech of the region is called the Hejazi dialect. The 2022 census counted 3,712,917 people.
jefferson-davis: Jefferson Davis was the youngest of ten children of Jane and Samuel Emory Davis. He was born on 3 June 1808 at Davisburg, a village his father had established that later became Fairview, Kentucky, and was named after President Thomas Jefferson. The family soon moved to Wilkinson County, Mississippi, where Samuel grew cotton. After Samuel died in 1824, Davis's eldest brother, Joseph Emory Davis, who was 23 years older, became a surrogate father and secured his appointment to the United States Military Academy at West Point, from which he graduated 23rd in a class of 33.

After six years as an army lieutenant, Davis left the service in 1835 and married Sarah Knox Taylor, daughter of the future president Zachary Taylor, who died of malaria three months later. He became a cotton planter, building Brierfield Plantation on his brother's land and eventually owning as many as 113 slaves. He married Varina Howell in 1845, sat in the House of Representatives in 1845–1846 and fought in the Mexican–American War as colonel of the First Mississippi Regiment, whose percussion rifles gave it the name Mississippi Rifles.

As a senator from 1847 he argued that slave owners had an equal right to settle the western territories with their slaves. President Franklin Pierce made him secretary of war in March 1853, and he oversaw the Pacific Railroad Surveys, promoted the Gadsden Purchase and won four new regiments for the army. He returned to the Senate in 1857 and resigned in 1861 when Mississippi seceded. On 9 February 1861 a convention at Montgomery, Alabama, unanimously elected him provisional president of the Confederacy, chosen for his political prominence, his military reputation and his moderate approach to secession.

Davis was captured and on 22 May 1865 imprisoned at Fort Monroe, Virginia, where he was at first shackled and denied contact with his family; the fetters came off after five days, and he was released without trial after two years. He later lived at Beauvoir, Mississippi, writing The Rise and Fall of the Confederate Government (1881). He died in New Orleans on 6 December 1889, aged 81, and more than 200,000 mourners were estimated to have attended his funeral. Journalist Edward A. Pollard, who popularised the Lost Cause, blamed Davis for the defeat, and many historians followed him.
jehoahaz-of-israel: Jehoahaz, whose Hebrew name means Yahweh has held, was the eleventh king of Israel and the son of Jehu. He reigned for seventeen years. William F. Albright dated his reign to 815-801 BCE, while E. R. Thiele offered the dates 814-798 BCE. The account in 2 Kings states that he did evil in the sight of Yahweh and that his people followed the religious practices of the house of Jeroboam, which included the worship of a cultic pole of Asherah in Samaria.

According to 2 Kings, the kings of the Arameans, Hazael and Ben-hadad, prevailed over him. Jehoahaz besought the Lord for a deliverer to relieve Israel from Aramean oppression, and the Lord provided a saviour for Israel, who is not named. The Arameans were defeated, but this left Jehoahaz with an army reduced to 50 horsemen, 10 chariots and 10,000 foot soldiers.

The identity of the deliverer is disputed. The verse 2 Kings 13:25 suggests that Jehoahaz's son Joash, who recaptured a number of Israelite cities in three successful battles, could have been the deliverer, and the Geneva Study Bible maintains this view. The Jerusalem Bible and the Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges argue instead that Jeroboam II, the son of Joash, was the deliverer, citing 2 Kings 14:27, which says that the Lord saved them by the hand of Jeroboam the son of Joash.

The Pulpit Commentary agrees that this was probably the case. Adad-nirari III, king of Assyria from 812 to 783 BCE, also made campaigns into the west between 804 and 797 BCE and on one of them captured and sacked Damascus, removing the worst enemy of Israel's prosperity, so that he too could be considered the deliverer.
jehoahaz-of-judah: Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, was the fourth son of King Josiah and the seventeenth king of Judah. His mother was Hamautal, daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah, and he was born in 633/632 BCE. In the spring or early summer of 609 BCE Pharaoh Necho II began his first campaign against Babylon, in aid of the Assyrians. He moved his forces along the coastal route towards Syria and prepared to cross the hills that close the Jezreel Valley on the south, where he found his way blocked at Megiddo by the Judean army under Josiah. After a fierce battle Josiah was killed, probably in the month of Tammuz.

Although he was two years younger than his brother Eliakim, Jehoahaz was chosen to succeed his father at the age of 23. This suggests the young man's popularity and probably also that his policy was in line with his father's. According to 2 Kings he reigned for three months and that he disregarded the reforms of Josiah. William F. Albright and E. R. Thiele both dated his reign to 609 BCE.

After the failed siege of Harran, Necho left a sizeable force behind and returned to Egypt. On his march back he found that the Judeans had chosen Jehoahaz as king. Necho brought him to Riblah and imprisoned him, deposed him, and made his older brother Eliakim king, changing his name to Jehoiakim. Necho took Jehoahaz to Egypt as a prisoner, where he ended his days. The prophet Jeremiah said of him that he should be wept for bitterly, since he would never return nor see his native land again.
jehoash-of-israel: Jehoash was the twelfth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, with its capital at Samaria, and the son of Jehoahaz. He reigned for sixteen years. William F. Albright dated his reign to 801-786 BCE, while Edwin R. Thiele offered the dates 798-782 BCE. When he ascended the throne Israel was suffering from the attacks of Aram-Damascus, whose king Hazael was conquering land controlled by Samaria. According to 2 Kings he was sinful and did evil in the eyes of Yahweh by tolerating the worship of the golden calves, yet outwardly at least he worshipped Yahweh.

According to 2 Kings 13:14, Jehoash visited the prophet Elisha, who was sick with the illness that would lead to his death, held him in honour and wept at his bedside. When Jehoash failed to obey Elisha's instructions completely, Elisha predicted that he would defeat Aram-Damascus only three times rather than five or six. In three successive victories Jehoash overcame the Syrians and retook towns Hazael had captured.

Later he defeated king Amaziah of Judah, whom he had warned with a parable of a thistle and a cedar in Lebanon. The author of Chronicles believes that Amaziah's ruin followed from his worship of idols taken from the Edomites. Jehoash utterly defeated Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, advanced on Jerusalem, broke down a portion of its wall, carried away the treasures of the Temple and the palace, took Amaziah prisoner and took hostages to assure good conduct. A conspiracy that took Amaziah's life followed. Soon after the battle Jehoash died and was buried in Samaria.

The excavation at Tell al-Rimah yielded a stele of Adad-nirari III which mentions Jehoash the Samarian and contains the first cuneiform mention of Samaria by that name. A postulated image of Jehoash has been reconstructed from plaster remains recovered at Kuntillet Ajrud, the ruins of a temple built by the northern kingdom when Jehoash gained control over the kingdom of Judah in the reign of Amaziah.
jehoiakim: Jehoiakim was the second son of King Josiah and Zebidah, the daughter of Pedaiah of Rumah. His birth name was Eliakim. When Josiah was killed at Megiddo, the people proclaimed his younger brother Jehoahaz, also called Shallum, as king. Rabbinic literature explains that Jehoiakim, though the elder, was passed over as unworthy to succeed his father.

Pharaoh Necho II returned from the battle at Harran three months after Josiah's death and deposed Jehoahaz, taking him to Egypt, where he died. Necho placed Eliakim on the throne in 609 BCE and changed his name to Jehoiakim.

Jehoiakim at first ruled as a vassal of Egypt and paid a heavy tribute. To raise the money he taxed the land and took silver and gold from the people of the land according to their assessments. After the Egyptians were defeated by the Babylonians at Carchemish in 605 BCE, Nebuchadnezzar II besieged Jerusalem, and Jehoiakim changed allegiance to spare the city. He paid tribute from the treasury, gave up some temple artefacts and handed over members of the royal family and nobility as hostages. The Book of Daniel counts Daniel among them.

He remained a Babylonian vassal for three years, until the failure of a Babylonian invasion of Egypt in 601 BCE weakened Babylon's hold on the region. Jehoiakim then switched his allegiance back to Egypt. The prophet Jeremiah criticised the king's policies and urged repentance and strict observance of the law. Another prophet, Uriah ben Shemaiah, proclaimed a similar message, and Jehoiakim ordered his execution.

In late 598 BCE Nebuchadnezzar invaded Judah and laid siege to Jerusalem. Jehoiakim died before the siege ended. The Book of Chronicles says Nebuchadnezzar bound him in fetters to take him to Babylon, while Jeremiah foretold that he would be buried with the burial of a donkey, dragged and cast out beyond the gates of Jerusalem. Josephus writes that Nebuchadnezzar killed him and ordered his body thrown before the walls without burial.

His son Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, reigned three months before Nebuchadnezzar deposed him and installed Jehoiakim's younger brother Zedekiah. Jehoiachin, his household and much of Judah's population were exiled to Babylon. The Babylonian Chronicles record that Jerusalem fell on 2 Adar, which is 16 March, in 597 BCE. Rabbinic literature portrays Jehoiakim as a godless tyrant guilty of atrocious crimes.
jehoram-of-israel: Jehoram, also Joram, was the ninth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel, son of King Ahab and Jezebel and brother of Ahaziah and Athaliah. According to 2 Kings 3:1 he began his reign in the 18th year of Jehoshaphat of Judah and ruled 12 years. In the fifth year of Jehoram of Israel a different Jehoram became king of Judah; the two were brothers-in-law, since Jehoram of Judah married Athaliah. Unlike his predecessors, Jehoram did not worship Baal: 2 Kings 3:2 says he removed the pillar of Baal, probably a special pillar Ahab had erected near his palace at Jezreel. The writer still says he followed in the ways of Jeroboam, son of Nebat, who led the Israelites to sin.

With Jehoshaphat of Judah, Jehoram attacked Moab, ruled by Mesha. In the war between Aram-Damascus and Israel, the prophet Elisha befriended him and revealed the enemy's plans. When Ben-hadad of Aram-Damascus besieged Samaria, the capital, the city was reduced almost to starvation and cannibalism, and Jehoram sought to behead Elisha. Elisha foretold a period of plenty, the siege was soon lifted, the food supplies were replenished and the old relation between king and prophet was restored.

When Hazael, king of the Arameans, violently revolted in Damascus, as Elisha had predicted in 2 Kings 8:12, Jehoram allied with his nephew Ahaziah, king of Judah, and the two set out to take Ramoth-Gilead from Aram-Damascus. The battle failed, and Jehoram was wounded and withdrew to Jezreel to recover. His defeat there was likely a disaster. While he recovered, his general Jehu incited a revolt, shot him in the back with an arrow and had his body thrown into the field of Naboth, as punishment for his parents' sin of illegally stealing Naboth's land. Jehoram and his other family members died, the Omride dynasty ended and Jehu claimed the throne of Israel.

The Tel Dan Stele, of the 9th century BCE and found in 1993 and 1994, claims that its author slew both Ahaziah of Judah and Jehoram of Israel. Most scholars identify the author as Hazael, whose reign is dated c. 842 to 806 BCE. On the Mesha Stele, dated to about 840 BCE, Mesha of Moab claims a victory against Israel after forty years of oppression by Omri and his son; some scholars understand 'son' to mean a later descendant of Omri, such as Ahaziah or Jehoram.
jehoshaphat: According to the Hebrew Bible, Jehoshaphat was the fourth king of the Kingdom of Judah, succeeding his father Asa; his mother was Azubah. Chronicles gives chapters 17 to 21 to his reign, and the First Book of Kings treats him more briefly. He ascended the throne at the age of thirty-five and reigned twenty-five years. He is said to have walked in the ways of David, spent his first years fortifying his kingdom against Israel and suppressed worship at the high places. In his third year he sent priests and Levites through the land to teach the Law.

His later reforms appear to have included judges in the cities of Judah and a form of court of appeal in Jerusalem. The Chronicler praises his reign for peace and prosperity, though modern commentary treats the figure of a vast army of 1,160,000 men and the rich tribute from the Philistines and Arabs as not historical.

He allied himself with the northern kingdom: his son Jehoram married Athaliah, a daughter of King Ahab of Israel. He nearly lost his life accompanying Ahab to the siege of Ramoth-Gilead, and the prophet Jehu, son of Hanani, rebuked him for the alliance. He joined Jehoram of Israel in a war against the Moabites, who were under tribute to Israel; the Moabites were subdued, but when King Mesha offered his own son as a sacrifice on the walls of Kir of Moab, the allies withdrew in horror.

Chronicles also tells of a confederacy of Moabites and neighbouring peoples that marched against Jehoshaphat and camped at Ein Gedi. After the king prayed in the court of the Temple, the Levite Jahaziel announced that the host would be overthrown; the invaders quarrelled and killed one another. Jehoshaphat died soon after, at sixty, and his son Jehoram succeeded him. The medieval commentator Rashi held that he died two years later and gave up his throne earlier. William F. Albright estimated his reign at 873-849 BCE. He appears in the genealogy of Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.
jehu: Jehu was the tenth king of the northern Kingdom of Israel since Jeroboam I, the son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, and possibly a great-grandson of Omri, although the biblical text does not support the last claim. The main source for his reign is 2 Kings, which gives it as 28 years; scholars date it slightly differently, by about a year. Jehu was a military commander at the time of the Battle of Ramoth-Gilead against the Arameans, in which King Jehoram of Israel was wounded and withdrew to Jezreel, attended by his nephew Ahaziah, king of Judah.

According to Kings, the prophet Elisha sent one of his students to anoint Jehu as the agent of divine judgment against the house of Ahab. Jehu at first dismissed the young man as a madman, but his companions blew trumpets and proclaimed him king. At Jezreel he shot Jehoram with an arrow, and Ahaziah died at Megiddo of his wounds. Queen Jezebel was thrown from a palace window at his command. At his order the chief men of Samaria killed the 70 royal princes, and he killed 42 relatives of Ahaziah at Beth-eked. He then trapped and killed the worshippers and priests of Baal.

Little else is known of his reign apart from his tolerance of the golden calves at Dan and Bethel, which was criticised, and the pressure of Hazael, king of the Arameans, who defeated his armies beyond the Jordan River. The Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III depicts Jehu kissing the ground before the Assyrian king and records his tribute of much silver, dated about 841 BCE; it is the earliest preserved depiction of an Israelite. It calls him the son of Omri, which may reflect the Assyrian name for Israel as the House of Omri. The Book of Hosea says God would punish the house of Jehu for the massacre at Jezreel.
jeju-island: Jeju Island lies in the Korea Strait, 82.8 km south of the nearest point on the Korean Peninsula. It covers 1,833.2 km2, which is 1.83% of the area of South Korea, and has an oval shape about 73 km from east to west, with a gentle slope around Hallasan in the centre. The coastline is 258 km long. The island consists chiefly of basalt and lava, and Hallasan, a volcano 1,947 metres high, is the highest mountain in South Korea.

The island formed from volcanic eruptions about two million years ago, in the Pleistocene epoch. A magma chamber formed under the sea floor about 1.2 million years ago and began to erupt, and activity stopped for about 100 thousand years before it restarted along the coast about 300 thousand years ago. Hallasan took shape about 100 thousand years ago, and lateral eruptions about 25 thousand years ago left some 360 oreum, small extinct parasitic cones such as Geomunoreum and Yongnuni Oreum.

The Jeju people are indigenous to the island, which has been populated by modern humans since the early Neolithic period. Its many historical names include Juho, Tammora, Seomna, Tangna and Tamna, and later Samdado, the Island of Three Abundances. Before the Japanese annexation of 1910 Europeans usually called it Quelpart, a name from French attested in Dutch by 1648, which may come from a Dutch ship, the quelpaert de Brack, said to have first sighted the island around 1642. The first European explorers to sight it, the Portuguese, called it Ilha de Ladrones, the Island of Thieves. Under Japanese occupation it was known as Saishū, and Cheju remained the usual spelling until 7 July 2000.

Jeju forms the majority of Jeju Province together with its outlying islands. It has a humid subtropical climate with four seasons, cool winters and hot, very wet summers, and the south around Seogwipo is warmer in winter than Jeju City because Hallasan blocks the continental winds. About 12% of the island is gotjawal, forest on rough lava that stayed uncultivated until the 21st century and is the main source of groundwater for the island's half million people.

The Jeju language is considered critically endangered by UNESCO, and the island is one of the regions of Korea where shamanism is most intact. It contains the natural World Heritage Site named Jeju Volcanic Island and Lava Tubes, and tourism is a large part of its economy.
jelgava: Jelgava lies on a fertile plain only 3.5 metres above mean sea level on the right bank of the Lielupe, about 41 kilometres south-west of Riga. At high water the plain and sometimes the town are flooded. It is the largest town of the Semigallia region and a railway centre at the junction of over six lines. Until 1917 the city was officially called Mitau; Jelgava is believed to derive from a Livonian word meaning town on the river, while the origin of Mitau is unclear.

Settlement began between the rivers Lielupe and Driksa in the 10th century. The crusading Livonian Order, under Grand Master Konrad von Mandern, built a castle on the natural island fortification of Pilssala in 1265–1266, and used it to subdue the surrounding Livonians and Semigallians by 1290. Lithuanians plundered the town in 1345. After the fall of the Livonian Order in the Livonian War it became a town of the Duchy of Courland, received city rights in 1573 and became capital of the united duchies of Courland and Semigallia in 1578.

The duchy was a vassal of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and Swedish invasions subjected Mitau to several sieges, though it grew as a centre of trade and industry. In 1710 Duke Friedrich Wilhelm married Anna Ioannovna, later Empress of Russia, who ruled as duchess from 1711 to 1730. Ernst Johann von Biron expanded the city's cultural life, building the ducal palace and opening its first public library, and the last duke, Peter von Biron, founded the Academia Petrina in 1775. Russia annexed the city in 1795, in the Third Partition of Poland, and the future Louis XVIII lived in the palace in 1798–1801 and 1804–1807. Rail arrived in 1868, and by 1914 Mitau had over 45,000 inhabitants.

In 1919 Mitau was a battleground between Bolshevik Red Guards, German paramilitaries and Latvian forces, and after the Latvian victory in November it was renamed Jelgava. The Soviet Union occupied it in 1940. German police and Latvian auxiliaries murdered its Jewish inhabitants in mass shootings during the German occupation of 1941–1944, and the main synagogue was burned. Fighting in 1944 destroyed almost 90% of the city, including the Kurland Provincial Museum and Athenaeum. It was rebuilt in Soviet style as part of the Latvian SSR.

Jelgava had 54,694 inhabitants on 1 January 2022 and is home to the Latvia University of Life Sciences and Technologies, which occupies the palace. Designed by Bartolomeo Rastrelli and built between 1738 and 1772, the palace holds the sarcophagi of almost all the Courland dukes. Other landmarks include the baroque St Anne's Church, the tower of the destroyed St. Trinity Church and the Academia Petrina.
jena: Jena lies in a hilly landscape in the east of Thuringia, in the wide valley of the Saale river. The city centre stands at about 160 metres, and the hills on both sides of the valley rise to about 400 metres. Until the High Middle Ages the Saale was the border between Germanic regions in the west and Slavic regions in the east. Jena was a river crossing, but its relevance in the Middle Ages was local.

The first unequivocal mention of Jena is in a document of 1182, and its first local rulers were the Lords of Lobdeburg. The Protestant Reformation reached it in 1523, when Martin Luther visited to reorganise church affairs, and the townsmen attacked the Carmelite and Dominican convents, which were abolished in 1525 and 1548. The city remained a small town until the 19th century.

Around 1790 the university became the largest and most prominent among the German states. It made Jena the centre of idealist philosophy, with professors such as Johann Gottlieb Fichte, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Friedrich Schiller and Friedrich Wilhelm Joseph Schelling, and gave rise to Jena Romanticism, the first phase of German Romanticism, with a group led by Caroline Schlegel and poets such as Novalis, August and Friedrich Schlegel and Ludwig Tieck. Goethe and Schiller met at the university in 1794 and formed a long friendship.

On 14 October 1806 Napoleon defeated the Prussian army near the district of Vierzehnheiligen in the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt. Resistance to the French occupation was strong, especially among the students, many of whom fought in the Lützow Free Corps in 1813, and the Urburschenschaft fraternity was founded in the city two years later. Industrialisation then changed the social structure: the former academic town became a working-class city, and its population rose from 8,000 around 1870 to 71,000 at the beginning of the Second World War. The optical and glass industry, around companies such as Carl Zeiss and Schott, grew steadily, and Jena was a world centre of the optical industry for most of the 20th century.

Jena is the second largest city in Thuringia, with about 110,000 inhabitants. The Friedrich Schiller University, founded in 1558, remains the heart of its education and research. Its main church, St Michael's, built between 1422 and 1557, is one of the biggest Gothic monuments in Thuringia, and the botanic garden, established in 1794, is one of the oldest in Germany.
jeongjo-of-joseon: Jeongjo, whose personal name was Yi San, was the second son of Crown Prince Sado and Lady Hyegyŏng. His elder brother, Crown Prince Uiso, died in infancy. In 1762 Yeongjo had Sado executed by confinement in a rice chest, after long conflicts and Sado's years of mental illness. On 21 February 1764 Yi San became the adoptive son of Crown Prince Hyojang and Princess Consort Hyosun by Yeongjo's order, because Yeongjo feared that the heir would be opposed as Sado's son.

The Noron faction protested that Yi San was the son of a prisoner or of a madman and so unfit to succeed. Between 1762 and 1777 some of its members tried to depose him in favour of his half-brothers. Hong Guk-yeong strongly supported his accession, and Kim Jong-su, though a Noron, also helped him. In 1775 Yi San was made regent, but received no military power.

Jeongjo was crowned in the Gyeonghuigung palace on 10 March 1776. His first statement to his officials was that he was the son of Sado, whom the former king had executed. He made his mother a Dowager Queen and spent much of his reign trying to clear his father's name. In 1776 Hong Sang-beom, Hong Kye-neung and other Noron members tried to stage a military coup and assassinate him; he had them executed, along with Prince Eunjeon, Hong In-han and Jeong Hu-gyeom.

He continued Yeongjo's Tangpyeong policy of balancing political factions, favoured members of the Soron and Namin parties over the Noron as a check on them, and relied on Silhak scholars such as Chŏng Yagyong and Pak Chiwŏn. He founded the Kyujanggak Royal Library to improve scholarship and recruit able officers, and opened government posts to men previously barred by social status. From 1782 he chose officers for the Changyongyeong guard, created in 1785, by competitive examination. He ordered the building of Hwaseong Fortress, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. In 1791 he issued the Shinhae Tonggong law, which let anyone sell goods at the market and ended the monopoly of the capital's merchant groups.

In his last years Jeongjo arranged the marriage of his second son and successor, Sunjo, to the daughter of Kim Jo-sun of the Andong Kim clan. He died suddenly in 1800, at the age of 47, in uncertain circumstances, and speculation about the cause continues. He is buried with Queen Hyoui at the royal tomb of Geonneung. His appointment of Hong Guk-yeong let state affairs be swayed by close retainers, and the Andong Kim marriage tilted power to one side and became the background of the era of sedo politics. In 1899 he was honoured as Emperor Seon.
jeonju: Jeonju lies in a basin surrounded by mountains, with Moryongsan to the north and Namgosan to the south, and the Jeonjucheon River flows through the centre of the city. Wanju County almost entirely surrounds it, so the city is both urban and rural. Its name is glossed as "Perfect region". Jeonju is divided into two wards, Deokjin District and Wansan District.

The kingdom of Baekje lay in south-western Korea and included the area of Jeonju, which is believed to have been founded as a market town within Baekje around 57 BCE. Silla conquered Baekje in 660, and in 685 Jeonju became one of the nine provincial capitals of the Silla kingdom. From 889 peasant revolts caused by over-taxation spread across the kingdom, and in Jeonju they gave a base to one of the most powerful rebel leaders, Gyeon Hwon. He renamed the city Wansan and made it the capital of Later Baekje. From there he campaigned against Silla, destroying its capital Geumseong and assassinating King Gyeongae in 927. Wang Geon of Goryeo then invaded Later Baekje in 934, and Jeonju surrendered to him in 935.

Under Goryeo, Jeonju was again a provincial capital and enjoyed relative stability and economic growth. In 1182 peasant rebels took the city with the help of government troops stationed there, who resented being made to do heavy labour alongside slaves, but the rebellion was suppressed forty days after it began. The Joseon dynasty, founded in 1392, regarded Jeonju as its ancestral home. It became the capital of a reorganised Jeolla province, and in 1413 it was one of four cities given copies of the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty to keep. The Donghak Peasant Revolution occupied the town in 1894.

Japan occupied Korea from 1910 to 1945 and renamed Jeonju Zenshū. The Japanese authorities destroyed the old city walls, leaving only the gate Pungnammun. Jeonju received metropolitan status in 1935 and its modern boundaries and government in 1963. It was not on the front line in the Korean War, but suffered bombardment and the loss of many male residents who fought.

Jeonju is the capital and largest city of Jeonbuk province in South Korea, known for its cuisine, historic buildings and festivals. Jeonju bibimbap is a well-known local dish, and UNESCO named the city a Creative City for Gastronomy in 2012. Jeonju Hanok Village holds over 800 traditional hanok buildings. Gyeonggijeon enshrines the portrait of Lee Seonggye, the first king of Joseon, and the Jeongdong Catholic Church, built from 1908 to 1914, stands on the site of the Korean Catholic martyrs of 1791 and 1801.
jerash: Archaeologists have found ruins of Neolithic settlements at Jerash and evidence of Bronze Age settlement in the region. The Greek city of Gerasa, also called Antioch on the Golden River, is traditionally linked to Alexander the Great and his general Perdiccas, who allegedly settled aged Macedonian soldiers there in 331 BCE. Its former name, Antioch on the Chrysorrhoas, points instead to a Seleucid founding, and still others credit Ptolemy II of Egypt. In the early 80s BCE the Hasmonean king Alexander Jannaeus conquered it.

The Roman conquest of 63 BCE ended this rule, and Pompey attached the city to the Decapolis, a league of Hellenistic cities that enjoyed considerable autonomy under Roman protection. In the second half of the 1st century CE Gerasa grew prosperous, and in 106 it was absorbed into the Roman province of Arabia. Hadrian visited in 129–130, and the Arch of Hadrian was built to mark the occasion. The first cathedral was built in the 4th century, the first of at least 14 churches built between the 4th and 7th centuries, many with fine mosaic floors.

The Persian Sassanids invaded in 614, and in 636 the Byzantine army lost the Battle of the Yarmuk, after which the region passed to the Rashidun Caliphate. The city did well under the Umayyad Caliphate, with a mint that struck coins naming Jerash, until the earthquake of 749 destroyed much of it. A fortress built by a garrison sent by Zahir ad-Din Toghtekin, atabeg of Damascus, was captured and burned by Baldwin II, King of Jerusalem, in 1121–1122. In 1596 an Ottoman census recorded 12 Muslim households, and in 1838 the site was described as a ruin.

Jerash is regarded as one of the largest and best preserved sites of Greek and Roman architecture outside Italy. Its monuments include an oval forum about 300 feet long with an Ionic colonnade, sanctuaries of Artemis and Zeus, two theatres, the colonnaded cardo, two tetrapyla, two baths, a nymphaeum and an almost complete circuit of walls. Wealthy citizens paid for most of these buildings. Excavation has gradually revealed the ancient city since 1925, and the western side with its monuments has been preserved, while the modern city lies east of the river.
jeremiah: According to the biblical narrative, Jeremiah was the son of Hilkiah, a priest from the village of Anathoth in the land of Benjamin.
