He was called to prophecy in about 626 BCE, the thirteenth year of Josiah, king of Judah, and he remained a prophet until after the fall of Jerusalem and the destruction of Solomon's Temple in 587 BCE, a span covering the reigns of five kings of Judah. He is said to have resisted the call, protesting that he was only a child and did not know how to speak. He was to proclaim that invaders from the north would destroy Jerusalem because the nation had forsaken God.

In his early years Jeremiah was chiefly a preaching prophet, condemning idolatry, the greed of priests and false prophets. His message prompted plots against him: the men of Anathoth, his priestly kin, plotted to kill him, and a temple official, Pashur, had him beaten and put in the stocks. Under King Zedekiah he made a yoke to show that the nation would be subject to the king of Babylon. The prophet Hananiah broke the yoke, and Jeremiah answered that he had made instead a yoke of iron.

After he prophesied that Jerusalem would be handed to the Babylonian army, the king's officials persuaded Zedekiah that he should be put to death. They cast him into a cistern, where he sank into the mud, and Ebed-Melech, an Ethiopian, pulled him out. He stayed imprisoned until Jerusalem fell. The Babylonians then released him, and he went to Mizpah with Gedaliah, whom they had made governor. When Gedaliah was assassinated, Johanan fled to Egypt, taking Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch against his counsel. The prophet probably spent the rest of his life there, and there is no authentic record of his death.

Jewish tradition holds that Jeremiah, with the help of Baruch, wrote the Book of Jeremiah, the Books of Kings and the Book of Lamentations. The consensus among scholars is that there was a historical prophet of the name and that parts of the book were probably written by him or by Baruch. Views range from the belief that its narratives and poems are contemporary with his life to the view that the original prophet's work cannot now be recovered. Rainer Albertz proposed that early collections of oracles were followed by several redactions between about 550 and 520 BCE.

Jeremiah is an essential figure in both Judaism and Christianity. His words are read in synagogues as part of the haftara and quoted about forty times in the New Testament. Islam regards him as a prophet, and the word jeremiad, a mournful complaint, derives from his name.
jeremie: Jérémie, in Haitian Creole Jeremi, is a commune and the capital city of the Grand'Anse department in Haiti. It is relatively isolated from the rest of the country, and the Grande-Anse River flows near the city. At the census of 2015 it had a population of about 134,317. About 40 nautical miles, or 74 kilometres, to the west lies Navassa Island, which is claimed by both Haiti and the United States. The city has an airport, Jérémie Airport, whose area is known as Numero Deux, and its districts include Beaudrouin, Campagne, Carrefour Sanon, La Forêt and Rampe des Lions.

General Thomas-Alexandre Dumas, a Creole, was born here in 1762, the son of a French nobleman and his African slave. His father took him to France at the age of 18, and he became known for fighting under Napoleon in Italy and Egypt and as the father of the writer Alexandre Dumas. In 1954 Hurricane Hazel hit Jérémie and destroyed much of the city and many neighbouring inland villages. In 1964, during the event known as the Jérémie Vespers, the Haitian army and the Tonton Macoutes massacred 27 people in the city.

In the early 2000s archaeologists uncovered an ancient synagogue of Crypto-Jews in the city, the only one found on the island, and Jérémie has historically been inhabited by many mixed-race families of Jewish descent. After the earthquake of 2010 a food aid convoy that had been delivered to Jérémie Airport met a hijacking attempt by 20 men on 30 January 2010, and medical supplies were also flown in through the airport for injured refugees arriving after the quake. In October 2016 Hurricane Matthew almost completely destroyed the city.

Jérémie is called the city of the poets because of the many writers, poets and historians born there. Among them are the poets Emile Roumer, who lived from 1903 to 1988, and Etzer Vilaire, from 1872 to 1951. Joseph Serge Miot, Archbishop of Port-au-Prince, who was killed in the earthquake of 2010, was also born in the city. So was Modeste Testas, an Ethiopian woman who was formerly enslaved and who lived from 1765 to 1870; a statue of her in Bordeaux commemorates the transatlantic slave trade. Elisabeth Dieudonné Vincent, who lived from 1798 to 1883, was a free colored businesswoman.
jeremy-bentham: Jeremy Bentham was born in Houndsditch, London, in February 1748, the son of the attorney Jeremiah Bentham, in a wealthy Tory family. He was reportedly a child prodigy: found as a toddler reading a multi-volume history of England at his father's desk, he began Latin at three and at seven played Handel sonatas on the violin at dinner parties. His one surviving sibling, Samuel Bentham, became a close companion. In 1786 and 1787 he visited Samuel in Krichev, in the Russian Empire, where Samuel had conceived a circular building from which a few managers could oversee a large workforce. Bentham developed the idea as a prison design, the Panopticon, and acknowledged that the basic idea was his brother's.

Bentham took as the fundamental axiom of his philosophy that right and wrong are measured by the happiness of the largest number of people, a principle he said he had borrowed from Joseph Priestley. His ambition was a Pannomion, a complete utilitarian code of law, and he coined the verb to codify; his efforts were unsuccessful in his lifetime, though they laid a foundation for David Dudley Field II's codification work in the United States. In A Fragment on Government (1776), published anonymously, he criticised William Blackstone's defence of judge-made law, legal fictions and the social contract. He argued that the ability to suffer, not to reason, should decide who has rights, and he is regarded as an early voice for animal rights.

He favoured the separation of church and state, equal rights for women including the vote and divorce, and the abolition of slavery, capital punishment and physical punishment. He opposed empire, writing Emancipate Your Colonies! in 1793. In 1823 he co-founded The Westminster Review with James Mill, a journal for the Philosophical Radicals, among them John Bowring and Edwin Chadwick.

Bentham died on 6 June 1832 at his home in Queen Square Place, Westminster, aged 84, having written until a month earlier. His instructions, attached to his will of 30 May 1832, directed Thomas Southwood Smith to dissect his body and preserve it as an auto-icon, which is now on display at University College London. Although he is called the spiritual founder of the college, he only bought a single £100 share. He left manuscripts of an estimated 30 million words, now largely held by UCL and the British Library.
jerez-de-la-frontera: Jerez de la Frontera lies in southwestern Iberia on the Campiña de Jerez, an inland lowland plain crossed by the Guadalete River, midway between the Atlantic Ocean, the Guadalquivir and the western reaches of the Subbaetic System. The municipality covers 1,188.14 square kilometres and includes Los Alcornocales Natural Park. Its inland position gives mild winters and hot, long summers.

Human presence in the area goes back at least to the Copper or Neolithic Age. The first major protohistoric settlement, around the third millennium BCE, is attributed to the Tartessians, and the Roman city of Asta Regia stood about 8 kilometres to the north. The Vandals and Visigoths ruled the area until the Umayyad conquest of Hispania in the early 8th century. In the 11th century it briefly became the seat of an independent taifa, and it was annexed to Seville in 1053. Under the Almohads it grew into the largest urban centre between Seville and the Strait of Gibraltar.

The Crown of Castile conquered Jerez in the 13th century. After the conquest of Granada in 1492 and the discovery of the Americas it became one of the most prosperous cities of Andalusia through trade. English, Flemish, Portuguese and above all Genoese merchants settled there, drawn by winemaking. In January 1892 a peasant uprising was violently repressed.

Jerez is the most populated municipality in the province of Cádiz, with 214,844 people. Winegrowing has long been its main economic driver, and its grapes are made into sherry; through most of the 19th century the wine was produced overwhelmingly for export. It is home to the Spanish Military Stud farm. The Alcázar, a Moorish fortress, dates to the 11th century, and the Old City Hall was built in 1575. Motorcycle Grand Prix racing has been held at the Circuito de Jerez since 1987.
jericho: Jericho lies in the Jordan Valley, with the Jordan River to the east and Jerusalem to the west, in an oasis in Wadi Qelt 258 metres below sea level. The nearby spring of Ein es-Sultan irrigates some 10 square kilometres through channels. The Bible calls it the city of palm trees. Its Arabic name, Arīḥā, means fragrant and, like its Hebrew name, is generally thought to derive from a Canaanite word rēḥ.

The earliest excavated settlement lies at Tell es-Sultan, a couple of kilometres from the present town, where archaeologists have found the remains of more than 20 successive settlements, the first from about 9000 BCE. Jericho is the type site for the Pre-Pottery Neolithic A and B periods. In the Early Bronze Age it became a fortified town, reaching its largest extent around 2600 BCE. In the Middle Bronze Age it had extensive walls with rectangular towers and a large cemetery whose rich offerings may reflect the emergence of local kings. It was destroyed in the Late Bronze Age and settled again from the 11th century BCE until the Babylonian conquest of Judah.

In the second half of the 2nd century BCE Jericho became part of the kingdom of Judea under the Hasmoneans. Around 135 or 134 BCE the local commander Ptolemy son of Abubus assassinated the Hasmonean leader Simon Thassi, his father-in-law, at the nearby fortress of Duq. Josephus calls its district the most fruitful country of Judea, rich in date palms and balsam. By the Byzantine period the built-up area had moved about 1,600 metres east to the site of the modern town, and monasteries and churches were built.

An earthquake destroyed Jericho in 659. The Crusaders ran large-scale sugar production there until Saladin's forces evicted them in 1187. It became part of the Ottoman Empire in 1517, came under British rule after the First World War, under Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War, and was occupied by Israel in 1967. In 1994 it became the first city handed to Palestinian Authority control.

Jericho is a city in the West Bank and capital of the Jericho Governorate, with 20,907 people in 2017. In 2023 Tell es-Sultan was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List. Other sites include the Umayyad palace at Khirbet al-Mafjar, known as Hisham's Palace, the Crusader sugar works at Tawahin es-Sukkar and Qasr al-Yahud on the Jordan, traditionally identified as the place of the baptism of Jesus.
jeroboam-i: According to the Hebrew Bible, Jeroboam was the son of Nebat, an Ephraimite of Zereda, and of Zeruah, a widow. King Solomon made the young man a superintendent over his tribesmen in the building of the fortress Millo in Jerusalem and other public works. There he became familiar with the widespread discontent that the extravagance of Solomon's reign had caused.

Encouraged by the prophet Ahijah, he began to plot to become king. The plots were discovered, and he fled to Egypt, where he stayed under the protection of Pharaoh Shishak until Solomon died. He had at least two sons, Abijah and Nadab.

Hearing of Solomon's death, Jeroboam returned and joined a delegation that asked the new king Rehoboam to reduce taxes. Rehoboam refused, and ten of the tribes withdrew their allegiance to the house of David and proclaimed Jeroboam king, forming the northern kingdom of Israel. Only Judah and Benjamin stayed loyal to Rehoboam. According to 1 Kings he reigned for 22 years. Edwin Thiele dates the reign from 931 to 910 BCE and William F. Albright from 922 to 901 BCE.

Jeroboam rebuilt and fortified Shechem as his capital. Fearing that pilgrimages to the temple in Jerusalem might draw his people back to their old allegiance, he built two state temples with golden calves, at Bethel and at Dan. An unnamed prophet condemns this in 1 Kings 13, and the biblical writers often describe the king as doing evil in the sight of the Lord. He also moved the festival of Sukkot to the eighth month instead of the seventh.

The Bible reports constant war between Jeroboam and the house of Judah, with a long boundary dispute that lasted most of his reign. Chronicles says that Abijah, Rehoboam's son, defeated him in the mountains of Ephraim, with forces of 400,000 against 800,000, and that 500,000 of Jeroboam's men were killed. He is said to have lost Bethel, Jeshanah and Ephron, and he died soon after Abijah.

Later Jewish tradition made him a prototype of the evildoer. Some modern scholars have asked in recent years whether Jeroboam I existed and whether he may be a retrojection of the later Jeroboam II, though there is no consensus on the question.
jeroboam-ii: Jeroboam II, also called Jeroboam son of Jehoash, succeeded Jehoash as the thirteenth king of the ancient Kingdom of Israel and was the fourth king of the House of Jehu. He ruled for about four decades from Samaria and was the longest-reigning king of the northern kingdom; scholars date his reign differently, William F. Albright giving 786 to 746 BCE. His reign was contemporary with those of Amaziah and Uzziah of Judah. He is described as a military commander who fought Syria, and he extended Israel to its former limits, from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain.

Archaeological evidence confirms the biblical account of his reign as the most prosperous the northern kingdom had known. In 1910 G. A. Reisner found 63 inscribed potsherds at the royal palace at Samaria, later dated to his reign, which give information about the script, language, religion and administration of the period. A Hebrew seal found at Megiddo in 1904 reads Belonging to Shema, servant of Jeroboam. By the late 8th century BCE the territory of Israel was the most densely settled in the Levant, with about 350,000 people, and its prosperity rested on trade in olive oil, wine and possibly horses with Egypt and especially Assyria.

His reign was the period of the prophets Hosea, Joel, Amos and Jonah, who condemned the materialism and selfishness of the Israelite elite. According to Amos, the king's triumphs bred boastful overconfidence, the oppression of the poor by the mighty and luxury in palaces. The Book of Kings condemns him for doing evil in the eyes of the Lord, meaning both the oppression of the poor and his support of the cult centres at Dan and Bethel. The archaeologist Israel Finkelstein has argued that many stories of Solomon's rule over a large, prosperous kingdom were inspired by memories of the reign of Jeroboam II.

The Book of Amos mentions a major earthquake in the days of Jeroboam son of Jehoash. It is dated to about 760 BCE, and Yigael Yadin and Finkelstein dated the destruction level at Tel Hazor to it, as David Ussishkin did the destruction at Lachish. His name occurs in the Old Testament only in 2 Kings, 1 Chronicles, Hosea and Amos; elsewhere Jeroboam I is meant.
jerome: Eusebius Sophronius Hieronymus was born at Stridon and was of Illyrian ancestry. He went to Rome with his friend Bonosus of Sardica to study rhetoric and philosophy, learned Latin under the philologist Aelius Donatus, and was baptized there. He described the guilt that followed the escapades of his student days, and how he visited the tombs of the martyrs in the catacombs on Sundays. Drawn to ascetic penance, he went for a time to the desert of Chalcis, south-east of Antioch, known as the Syrian Thebaid for its many hermits. There he began to learn Hebrew under a converted Jew.

As a protégé of Pope Damasus I, Jerome revised the Vetus Latina Gospels in Rome against Greek manuscripts. He gathered around him well-born women, among them the widows Marcella and Paula and Paula's daughters Blaesilla and Eustochium, who turned towards the monastic life. His unsparing criticism of the Roman clergy brought hostility, and after Damasus died on 10 December 384 he was forced to leave Rome after an inquiry into allegations of an improper relationship with Paula. Paula's money later paid for his stay in a monastery at Bethlehem, next to the Church of the Nativity, where he completed his translation of the Bible. He died on 30 September 420.

Jerome began in 382 by correcting the Vetus Latina New Testament. By 390 he was translating the Hebrew Bible from Hebrew, and he finished by 405. Earlier Latin versions of the Old Testament rested on the Septuagint, and his choice of a Hebrew text went against the advice of most Christians, among them Augustine, who thought the Septuagint inspired. The result became known as the Vulgate, and in 1546 the Council of Trent declared it authoritative. From 405 to 420 he wrote commentaries on Scripture.

His other writings include the Chronicon, a translation and continuation of the chronicle of Eusebius, and On Illustrious Men, a biobibliography of Christian writers written in 392 and 393. His letters give a vivid picture of the age. After Augustine, he is the most voluminous writer of ancient Latin Christianity, and the Catholic Church counts him among the four Great Latin Church Fathers and as patron saint of translators, librarians and encyclopedists. Artists often show him with a lion.
jerome-bonaparte: Jérôme Bonaparte was born Girolamo Buonaparte at Ajaccio, Corsica, on 15 November 1784, the eighth and last surviving child of Carlo Buonaparte and Letizia Ramolino. He studied at the Catholic College of Juilly and at the Irish College in Paris, and joined the French Navy in January 1800. Given a frigate in the West Indies, he fled to the United States under the name Mr. Albert after accidentally firing on a British ship. In Baltimore he married Elizabeth Patterson on 24 December 1803. Napoleon, who wanted to marry his siblings into royal houses, had the marriage annulled by imperial decree on 11 March 1805, and Jérôme submitted.

In return Jérôme was made an admiral, a general and an imperial prince, and in 1807 King of Westphalia, a realm formed from several states of north-western Germany in the Confederation of the Rhine, with its capital at Kassel. Napoleon had arranged his marriage to Princess Catharina of Württemberg, daughter of King Frederick I. The kingdom received the first constitution and parliament on German soil, and Jérôme brought the Empire style from Paris and had Leo von Klenze design a court theatre beside the summer residence, renamed Napoleonshöhe. His spending emptied the treasury, and Napoleon refused to support him financially.

In 1812 he commanded a corps of the Grande Armée marching towards Minsk. Reprimanded for travelling in state, he returned to Westphalia with his court after the Battle of Mir, and historians hold that tens of thousands of lives were probably lost in the invasion of Russia as a result. In 1813 the main allied force took Kassel, the kingdom was dissolved and Jérôme fled to France. At Waterloo his division was drawn into a prolonged assault on Hougoumont. Frederick I forced him and Catharina to leave Württemberg in 1814, and in July 1816 he gave Jérôme the title Prince of Montfort.

After his nephew Louis Napoleon became president of the Second Republic in 1848, Jérôme was made Governor of Les Invalides, Marshal of France in 1850 and President of the Senate in 1852. He was for a time heir presumptive to the imperial throne. He died on 24 June 1860 at Villegenis (now Massy) and is buried in Les Invalides. Historians such as Owen Connelly stress his financial, military and administrative successes, while others, including Helen Jean Burn, stress his failures; most agree he was the least successful of Napoleon's brothers. His grandson Charles Joseph Bonaparte served as United States Secretary of the Navy and Attorney General.
jeronimos-monastery: The Jerónimos Monastery, near the Tagus in the parish of Belém, replaced a church of Santa Maria de Belém, where monks of the Order of Christ assisted seafarers. Manuel I ordered the new building at the cortes of Montemor o Velho in 1495 as a final resting place for the House of Aviz, and in 1496 he petitioned the Holy See for permission to build the monastery. Vasco da Gama and his men spent the night in prayer at the old church before leaving for India in 1497.

Construction began on 6 January 1501 and took a century. It was funded by the Vintena da Pimenta, a 5 percent tax on commerce from Africa and the Orient, equal to 70 kilograms of gold a year. Manuel I chose Hieronymite monks to pray for his soul and to give spiritual help to navigators leaving from Restelo, which they did until 1833.

The monastery is among the most prominent examples of the Manueline style, a richly ornate architecture carved in limestone with maritime themes and objects found on naval expeditions. Diogo de Boitaca drew the plans, and the Spaniard Juan de Castillo took charge around 1517, moving gradually towards the Spanish Plateresque. Building halted when Manuel I died in 1521. Diogo de Torralva resumed work in 1550 and added the main chapel and choir, and Jérôme de Rouen continued from 1571.

The church is a hall church with a single-span ribbed vault over a nave 19 metres wide and a transept vault without piers, which seems to float in the air. Six slender octagonal columns, 25 metres high, are carved with Renaissance decoration. The south portal, designed by Castillo, is 32 metres high, while Nicolau Chanterene built the western portal in 1517. The cloister, 55 by 55 metres, carries Manueline motifs with nautical elements and symbols of Portugal's growing world power.

Work stopped in 1580 with the union of Spain and Portugal, when the building of the Escorial drained funds. In 1604 Philip of Spain made it a royal funerary monument. The monastery withstood the Lisbon earthquake of 1755 with little damage, but on 28 December 1833 it was secularized and transferred to the Real Casa Pia de Lisboa. Restoration began after 1860.

The church holds the tombs of kings Manuel I and John III, and of the explorer Vasco da Gama and the poet Luís de Camões, whose remains were moved to carved tombs in 1880. The monastery and the nearby Tower of Belém were classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983, and the Treaty of Lisbon was signed there on 13 December 2007. Its west wing houses the Maritime Museum, inaugurated in 1963.
jerriais: Jèrriais is the traditional language of the Jersey people, a Romance language and the form of Norman spoken on the island. Its closest relatives are the other Norman languages, such as Guernésiais in Guernsey, and the other langues d'oïl. It is more accurately described as Norse adapted to the langue d'oïl than as a mixture of Old Norse and French: when Norse-speaking Normans conquered Normandy they began speaking the language of their new subjects, and kept some Norse vocabulary, such as mielle for sand dune and mauve for seagull. The language of Sark, Sercquiais, descends from the Jèrriais brought by Jersey colonists who settled the island in the 16th century.

A feature that distinguishes Jèrriais from its neighbours is the voiced dental fricative, written th, which typically occurs between vowels. Vowel length matters, and long vowels are usually written with a circumflex accent. Verb tenses show regular doubling of consonants, written with an apostrophe, as in pâl'la, "she will speak". It is distinct from Jersey Legal French, the language used for contracts, laws and official documents.

Until the 19th century Jèrriais was the everyday language of the majority of the population, and at the beginning of the Second World War up to half the population could still communicate in it. Louis Lucien Bonaparte visited the island and interested himself in the language, and Victor Hugo, in exile in Jersey, knew some Jèrriais writers. During the German occupation islanders used it among themselves as a language that neither the Germans nor their French interpreters could understand. English use then increased sharply after the Liberation, and the last monolingual adult speakers probably died in the 1950s.

Jersey fishing companies took the language to the cod fisheries of the Gaspé peninsula in Quebec, where it was the common language of business, and some speakers remained there in the 1960s. Efforts to preserve it include a Jèrriais section at the Jersey Eisteddfod since 1912, the Assembliée d'Jèrriais, founded in 1951, and Le Don Balleine, a trust set up under the will of Arthur E. Balleine. Dictionaries include the Glossaire du Patois Jersiais of 1924 and a Dictionnaire Jersiais–Français of 1966. On 13 February 2019 the States of Jersey adopted Jèrriais as an official language.
jesenik: Jeseník lies about 70 kilometres north of Olomouc, in the historical land of Czech Silesia, at the confluence of the Bělá River and the Staříč Stream. The southern part of its territory lies in the Hrubý Jeseník mountain range and the northern part extends to the Golden Mountains. The original name, Freiwaldau or Frývaldov, comes from the German frei vom Walde, meaning free from the woods. After the Second World War the town took its present name from the surrounding mountains, called Hrubý Jeseník or Jeseníky.

The first written mention dates from 1267. The town was probably founded during the colonisation of the area by the bishops of Wrocław, who acquired it in 1199, and it gained town status between 1284 and 1295, helped by its position on a trade route from Moravia to Silesia and by iron ore deposits. In 1326 thirteen hammer mills were already working iron. From 1378 to 1463 the Mušín family owned it, and in 1506 the Swabian Fugger family bought it and resumed mining. They sold it back to the Wrocław bishops in 1547, and linen weaving became its most important source of income.

The Thirty Years' War damaged the town several times, and between 1622 and 1684 it stood at the centre of the Northern Moravia witch trials. A fire in 1696 caused severe damage. In 1742, after the First Silesian War, it became part of Austrian Silesia and lost its Silesian markets, so that the linen trade fell into crisis. Industrialisation brought new factories in the 19th century, among them a textile works founded in 1822, and a railway opened in 1888. In 1938 the Munich Agreement ceded the town to Nazi Germany, and in 1945 it returned to Czechoslovakia and its German population was expelled.

Jeseník has about 10,000 inhabitants and is known for the Priessnitz Medical Spa, founded by Vincenz Priessnitz in 1822 as the world's first hydrotherapy institute; his birth house is now a museum, and his tomb dates from 1853. The Gräfenberg hamlet, founded in 1808, was incorporated into the town in 1868. The oldest monument is the Jeseník Water Fortress, a Gothic castle of the 13th century first documented in 1374, which houses the regional museum. The town hall dates from 1710.
jesuits: Ignatius of Loyola, a Basque nobleman of Spanish origin with a military background, discerned his vocation while recovering from a wound received at the Battle of Pamplona. On 15 August 1534 he and six companions, students at the University of Paris, met in a crypt at Montmartre to promise poverty, chastity and obedience. They were Francis Xavier, Alfonso Salmerón, Diego Laínez, Nicolás Bobadilla, Peter Faber and Simão Rodrigues. The society was founded in 1540 with the approval of Pope Paul III.

The Jesuits arose just before the Council of Trent and the Counter-Reformation, but Ignatius and the early Jesuits recognised that the hierarchical church needed reform. They struggled against corruption and spiritual lassitude, and Ignatius insisted on a high level of academic preparation for the clergy. A Jesuit professes perpetual poverty, chastity and obedience and promises special obedience to the pope regarding missions. The order is led for life by a superior general.

Jesuit missionaries established missions around the world from the 16th to the 18th century, with successes and failures. In Japan the government granted them the fiefdom of Nagasaki in 1580 and removed it in 1587 out of fear of their growing influence. In Latin America their ascendancy grew in the 17th century, with new missions in Peru, Colombia and Bolivia, and by 1603 there were 345 Jesuit priests in Mexico alone. In some places they protected indigenous peoples from slavers, notably the Guaraní, but elsewhere they enslaved indigenous people after wars in which resistance to European colonisation was defeated.

The Jesuits were always controversial and often clashed with governments. They were banished from France in 1594 after Jean Châtel, who had studied at their Collège de Clermont, tried to kill Henri IV, though the ban was soon lifted. The Jesuit scholar Andrew Dial calculated that the order owned more than 20,000 slaves worldwide in 1760, mostly in the Americas, and Jesuits also took part in the Atlantic slave trade. From 1759 the Church expelled them from most of Europe and its colonies, and on 21 July 1773 Pope Clement XIV suppressed the order. The suppression was lifted in 1814.

Jesuit spirituality draws on the Spiritual Exercises of Ignatius, which aim to find God in all things, and on the Examen, a daily review of the day's events. Formation for the priesthood takes eight to fourteen years. The Decree de genere of 1593 barred anyone of Jewish or Muslim ancestry, contrary to Ignatius's own wishes, and was repealed only in 1946. Jesuit schools, whose studies followed Aristotle under the Ratio Studiorum of 1599, were joined by scientific work in fields from cosmology to seismology, and the order has been described as the most important contributor to experimental physics in the seventeenth century.
jesus: A Jewish person in the time of Jesus usually had only one name, sometimes followed by a patronymic or a home town, and so Jesus is commonly called Jesus of Nazareth in the New Testament. His name is the English transliteration, through Latin Iesus, of the Greek rendering of the Hebrew Yehoshua, shortened by that period to Yeshua; it means God saves. The word Christ is a title, not a given name, from the Greek Christos, meaning anointed, a calque of the Hebrew mashiakh, or messiah.

According to Christian tradition as represented in the Gospels and the Acts of the Apostles, Jesus was circumcised at eight days old and presented at the Temple in Jerusalem at 40 days. He was baptized by John the Baptist as a young adult. After 40 days and nights of fasting in the Judean wilderness he began his public ministry.

The four canonical gospels, Matthew, Mark, Luke and John, are the foremost sources for his life and message. By the usual scholarly view, Mark was written first, and Matthew and Luke used it as a source.

According to the New Testament accounts, Jesus was an itinerant teacher whom his followers believed to possess divine authority in interpreting Jewish law. He debated with other Jews, most commonly the Pharisees and Sadducees, engaged in healings, taught in parables, and gathered followers, 12 of whom he appointed as his apostles. He was arrested in Jerusalem, tried by the Sanhedrin, and handed over to the Roman authorities, and was crucified on the order of Pontius Pilate.

Christians hold that Jesus rose from the dead on the third day after his death, a belief that became the foundation of the early Christian Church. His first followers were Jews, and the first Christian community was centred in Jerusalem, with Peter, James the brother of Jesus, and John the Apostle among its leaders. After his conversion Paul the Apostle spread his teachings to non-Jewish communities in the eastern Mediterranean. By the end of the 1st century Christianity began to be recognised as a separate religion from Judaism.

Scholars have pursued three quests for the historical Jesus since the 18th century. They agree that he existed, though their portraits differ from each other and from the gospels. Mainstream Judaism rejects the belief that he was the awaited messiah. In Islam he is considered the messiah and a prophet of God, and most Muslims do not believe he was crucified.
jet-engine: Before the Second World War, engineers were beginning to realise that engines driving propellers were approaching performance limits, because propeller efficiency declined as the blade tips approached the speed of sound. A different means of propulsion was needed to raise aircraft performance further, and this motivated the development of the gas turbine, the most common form of jet engine. Its key feature is that the turbine extracts power from the engine itself to drive the compressor.

The gas turbine was not a new idea. John Barber was granted a patent for a stationary turbine in England in 1791, and the Norwegian engineer Ægidius Elling built the first gas turbine to run self-sustaining in 1903. Such engines did not reach manufacture because of problems of safety, reliability, weight and above all sustained operation. Maxime Guillaume's patent of 1921 described an axial-flow turbojet that would have needed considerable advances in compressors. Alan Arnold Griffith published An Aerodynamic Theory of Turbine Design in 1926, which led to experimental work at the RAE.

A jet engine discharges a fast-moving jet of heated gas, usually air, and generates thrust by jet propulsion. The term usually means an internal combustion air-breathing engine such as a turbojet, turbofan, ramjet, pulse jet or scramjet, although the broad definition can include rocket, water jet and hybrid propulsion. A turbojet compresses air, mixes fuel with it, burns the mixture in a combustor and passes the hot, high-pressure gas through a turbine, which drives the compressor, and then a nozzle. The turbofan adds a fan at the front that accelerates air through a duct around the core, and it is the dominant type for medium and long-range airliners.

A rocket engine uses the same basic principle of thrust but carries all its reaction mass, so it can work at any altitude and in space. Ramjets and scramjets use the ram effect of the vehicle's speed instead of a mechanical compressor, and turboshaft and turboprop engines share components with jet engines.

Early jet aircraft used turbojets, which were relatively inefficient for subsonic flight, and most modern subsonic jet aircraft use high-bypass turbofans, which give higher speed and better fuel efficiency than piston and propeller engines over long distances. The thrust of a typical jetliner engine rose from 5,000 lbf in the de Havilland Ghost turbojet of the 1950s to 115,000 lbf in the General Electric GE90 turbofan of the 1990s, while in-flight shutdowns fell from 40 to fewer than 1 per 100,000 engine flight hours. This allowed routine transatlantic flights by twin-engined airliners.

Jet engines also power cruise missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles. Designs derived from military turbojets such as the Pratt & Whitney J57 and J75 serve as industrial gas turbines for generating electricity, driving pumps and propelling ships and locomotives.
jever: Jever is the capital of the district of Friesland in Lower Saxony. It lies in Jeverland, in the north-eastern part of the East Frisian peninsula near the North Sea coast, about 15 kilometres west of Wilhelmshaven. The town stands on a flat tongue of the Oldenburg–East Frisian geest, which rises 7 to 8 metres above the surrounding marshes. Several tiefs, watercourses close to the sea that drain the land behind the dikes, surround it. Archaeological finds show that the area has been inhabited since the Neolithic: a dolmen stood near the town until at least 1880, and flint tools, urns, a bronze spear tip and a socket axe have been found.

Jever was granted city status in 1536, and the ring of moats and earthen walls called the Gräfte was built that year to protect it. Three wooden gates with bridges gave access. At the start of the 19th century the earth walls were removed and the canals filled where the gates had stood, leaving the Graften that still surround the historic centre. The town is sometimes called Marienstadt after Maria of Jever (1500–1575), the last independent ruler of the Lordship of Jever, who ruled from 1517. From 1560 to 1564 she had the castle altered in Renaissance style.

Jever Castle grew from a fortified complex of the 14th century and was the seat of the lordship, with a mighty Bergfried at its centre that was integrated from the 16th century into a four-wing complex with moats and ramparts. Under Prince Friedrich August of Anhalt-Zerbst, a well decree of 9 October 1756 made each public fountain the charge of a named group of residents, the Püttacht, a custom the Püttbierfest still recalls each January. In 1825 the mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss stayed in Jever for survey work, and the town served as a triangulation station.

Jever is known for its castle, which has housed the Castle Museum of cultural history since 1921, and for its brewery, the maker of Jever Pilsener, with a historical brewery museum. The Evangelical Lutheran town church, consecrated in 1736, burned down on 1 October 1959. Natives include the agricultural economist Johann Heinrich von Thünen (1783–1850) and the historian Friedrich Christoph Schlosser (1776–1861), and the psychiatrist and philosopher Karl Jaspers (1883–1969) often visited his grandparents there.
jewish-agency-for-israel: The body began in Jaffa in 1908 as the Palestine Office of the Zionist Organization in Ottoman-controlled Palestine, headed by Arthur Ruppin. Its tasks were to represent the Jews of the region in dealings with the Sultan and foreign dignitaries, to aid immigration and to buy land for Jewish communities. With the Jewish National Fund it bought land for newcomers of the Second Aliyah at Chavat Kinneret and Kibbutz Ruhama, and over the following decades established hundreds more moshavim and kibbutzim. It was later renamed the Zionist Commission and then the Palestine Zionist Executive.

The League of Nations Mandate for Palestine required a Jewish agency to help establish the Jewish National Home, and in 1929 the 16th Zionist Congress restructured the executive as the Jewish Agency for Palestine, at the initiative of Chaim Weizmann. It was founded on parity between Zionist and non-Zionist Jews, who were given mandatory representation.

Weizmann was criticised as too pro-British and resigned from the Agency after the 1930 White Paper recommended restricting Jewish immigration, protesting that the British had betrayed the Balfour Declaration. Nahum Sokolow remained in post, Arthur Ruppin became chairman in 1933 and in 1935 David Ben-Gurion was elected chairman of its executive. Before the founding of Israel the Agency oversaw the creation of about 1,000 towns and villages in Mandatory Palestine. On 14 May 1948 Ben-Gurion, in that capacity, proclaimed Israel's independence and became its first prime minister. The Agency then took the name Jewish Agency for Israel and shifted towards economic development and absorbing immigrants, replacing its Security and Government departments with ones for agriculture and settlement and for Israel.

In 1949 it brought 239,000 Holocaust survivors from displaced persons camps in Europe and detention camps in Cyprus, and airlifted 49,000 Yemenite Jews in Operation Magic Carpet. About 700,000 immigrants reached the new state between 1948 and 1952. The Agency ran Hebrew schools for them from Ulpan Etzion in 1949 and provided food, housing and training, though for a time many lived in transit camps, the ma'abarot.

The Agency says it has brought 3 million immigrants to Israel since 1948. It is a parastatal body that receives no core funding from the Israeli government, drawing on the Jewish Federations of North America, Keren Hayesod, communities and donors. In February 2010 Natan Sharansky announced a shift of priority from immigration to strengthening the Jewish identity of young adults abroad. In 2008 it received the Israel Prize for its historical contribution.
jezebel: Jezebel is introduced in the Book of Kings as a Phoenician princess, the daughter of a king of Tyre. The first Book of Kings, chapter 16, calls her Sidonian, a biblical term for Phoenicians in general. She married King Ahab of Samaria, in the northern kingdom of Israel. Israel Finkelstein calls the marriage a brilliant stroke of international diplomacy that showed the power and prestige of Ahab and his kingdom. The name is an Anglicized form of the Hebrew ʾIzeḇel, often interpreted as Where is the Lord?, a ritual cry in worship of Baal. Ahab built a Baalist altar in a house of Baal in Samaria.

As queen, Jezebel according to the Hebrew Bible institutionalised Baal worship, killed Yahwist prophets and desecrated their altars. The prophet Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal and Asherah to a contest at Mount Carmel to see which god would burn a bull sacrifice. Her prophets failed, and Elijah then ordered the people to seize and kill them. Jezebel vowed to kill Elijah, who fled to Mount Horeb. In the account of Naboth she resolved a failed deal between Ahab and Naboth over a vineyard by ordering the execution of Naboth and his sons on false charges of blasphemy. Elijah condemned this and foretold doom for her family.

After Ahab's death in battle their son Ahaziah inherited the throne, and his brother Jehoram succeeded him. Jehu usurped the throne and killed Jehoram. When he came to Jezreel, Jezebel put on make-up and a wig and looked out of a window to taunt him. Geoffrey Bromiley reads this as the defiance of a queen mother. Jehu had her eunuch servants throw her from the window, and only her skull, feet and palms were left of her body, as Elijah had prophesied.

Scholars disagree about the historicity of the story. Finkelstein considers it more of a historical novel than a chronicle, shaped by the theology of 7th-century BCE writers, while Brian R. Doak argues for its plausibility. A 9th-century BCE seal inscribed YZBL may once have read as belonging to Jezebel, but scholars do not agree. The name later came to stand for false prophets and then for fallen or promiscuous women.
jezreel-valley: The Jezreel Valley is a large fertile plain in the Northern District of Israel. It is bordered by the highlands of the Lower Galilee to the north, by those of Samaria to the south, by Mount Carmel to the west and northwest, and by the Jordan Valley to the east, and Mount Gilboa marks its southern extent. It takes its name from the ancient city of Jezreel, on a low hill above its southern edge, and the Hebrew name is taken to mean God sows. Its Arabic name, Marj Bani Amir, means meadow of the Banu Amir.

Excavations have shown nearly continuous settlement from the Chalcolithic Ghassulian culture, about 4500 to 3300 BCE, to the Ayyubid period. Biblical cities in the valley include Jezreel, Megiddo, Beit She'an and Shimron. The 15th-century BCE Battle of Megiddo has a detailed surviving account, which shows that it was fought in the valley, because the terrain allowed Egyptian chariots to travel from Egypt only as far as the Jezreel Valley. According to the Hebrew Bible, it was the scene of several battles: Deborah and Barak against the Canaanites, Gideon against the Midianites and Amalekites, the defeat of King Saul by the Philistines and that of King Josiah by the Egyptians.

In the Mamluk period the valley formed the southern part of the province of Safed, and in the early Ottoman period it was the core territory of the Turabay Emirate, from 1517 to 1683. In the late Ottoman era malaria was widespread and the population sparse. The Ottomans built the Jezreel Valley railway in the early 1900s. The Sursock family of Beirut bought land there in 1872, and in 1921 sold about 80,000 dunams, with some twenty-two villages, to the American Zion Commonwealth. Some tenant farmers were expelled, and the first moshav, Nahalal, was settled on 11 September 1921.

The valley is green farmland, producing wheat, cotton, sunflowers, corn, melons and oranges, with grazing for sheep and cattle. Afula, near its centre, is its largest city, and the valley is governed by the Jezreel Valley Regional Council. Archaeological sites such as Tel Megiddo are excavated by the Jezreel Valley Regional Project.
jharkhand: Jharkhand is a landlocked state of eastern India, bordered by West Bengal to the east, Chhattisgarh to the west, Uttar Pradesh to the north-west, Bihar to the north and Odisha to the south. Its name means 'the land of forests', from jhar, 'forest', and khand, 'land'. It covers 79,716 square kilometres, much of it on the Chota Nagpur Plateau, crossed by the Damodar, North Koel, Barakar, South Koel, Sankh and Subarnarekha rivers. Forests still cover much of the state and sustain elephants and tigers. The Parasnath Hill in Giridih district, 1,365 metres high, is the chief Jain pilgrimage site and is called Marang Buru by the Santal, whose supreme deity it names.

The region has been inhabited since the Mesolithic and Chalcolithic periods, as cave paintings at Isko in Hazaribagh district, dated to between 9000 and 5000 BCE, show. In the second millennium BCE copper tools spread across the Chota Nagpur Plateau in what is known as the Copper Hoard Culture, and iron slag from Singhbhum district has been dated by carbon to 1400 BCE. The Nanda, Maurya and Gupta empires ruled the region in ancient times. The Chinese traveller Xuanzang passed through it in the seventh century and described the kingdom of Karnasuvarna under Shashanka. In the medieval period the Nagvanshi, Pala, Khayaravala, Ramgarh Raj and Chero rulers governed it.

Mughal influence reached Palamu when the Rajput Raja Mansingh conquered it in 1574 under Emperor Akbar. A separate tribal state was demanded in 1928, when Unnati Samaj, the political wing of the Christian Tribals Association, submitted a memorandum to the Simon Commission. In 1955 the Jharkhand Party, led by Jaipal Singh Munda, asked the States Reorganization Commission for a state of the tribal area of south Bihar, which was rejected. Jharkhand was finally carved out of the southern part of Bihar in 2000, with 18 districts that were formerly part of south Bihar.

Hindi is the official language, and Ranchi is the capital with Dumka as sub-capital. The census of 2011 counted 32.96 million people, of whom 26.21 percent belong to Scheduled Tribes. Besides Hindi, speakers of Indo-Aryan, Dravidian and Austroasiatic languages live in the state, and sixteen further languages, among them Santali, Mundari, Ho, Kurukh and Nagpuri, have additional official status. Hinduism is the largest religion, with 67.8 percent, and Sarnaism, a tribal faith, is the second largest of its kinds, with 12.5 percent. The state has large reserves of iron ore, coal, copper ore, mica, bauxite and uranium.
jiajing-emperor: Zhu Houcong was born on 16 September 1507, the eldest son of Zhu Youyuan, Prince of Xing, a fourth son of the Chenghua Emperor known for his poetry and calligraphy. His parents had lived since 1494 at Anlu in Huguang, in central China, where he was born. When the Zhengde Emperor died on 20 April 1521, Grand Secretary Yang Tinghe, with the support of court eunuchs and Empress Dowager Zhang, issued an edict calling the prince to Beijing to take the throne.

The new emperor wished to raise his father posthumously to imperial rank, while Yang Tinghe insisted that he be formally adopted by the Hongzhi Emperor and so become the younger brother of the late Zhengde Emperor. The emperor and his mother rejected the adoption, and he did not want to declare his parents his uncle and aunt. After three years of the Great Rites Controversy he emerged victorious, and his main opponents were banished or executed. In the late 1530s he introduced separate sacrifices to the Heavens, Earth, Sun and Moon. He brought eunuchs from Anlu to fill palace posts, and their influence kept growing.

On 27 November 1542 a group of palace women tried to strangle him with a silk cord. He lay unconscious for eight hours, and Empress Fang had the women executed. He moved that year to the West Park, where he built palaces and Taoist temples and was served by eunuchs, Taoist monks and advisers such as Zhang Cong, Xia Yan, Yan Song and Xu Jie. His pursuit of immortality led to elixirs holding arsenic, lead and mercury.

In the 1540s Altan Khan united the Mongols and demanded the restoration of free trade; the emperor refused, and in 1550 Altan's raids reached the outskirts of Beijing. Wokou piracy reached its peak in the 1550s. The deadly 1556 Shaanxi earthquake struck, yet agriculture, industry and trade continued to grow, and Wang Yangming's more individual teaching gained ground over the traditional Confucian interpretation.

In the 1560s the emperor suffered from the effects of the potions, insomnia and mood swings, and after 11 November 1566 he issued no written orders because of illness. On 23 January 1567 he moved from the West Park to the Forbidden City, where he died around midday. He was buried in the Yong Mausoleum in the Ming tombs near Beijing and received the temple name Shizong.
jiang-qing: Jiang Qing was born in Zhucheng, Shandong, in March 1914. Her father, Li Dewen, was a carpenter, and her mother was his subsidiary wife. He abused her mother almost every day, and after he broke her finger one Lantern Festival the mother fled with the child and found work as a domestic servant. At 14 Jiang joined a local underground theatre troupe and then trained at the Experimental Arts Academy in Jinan. In Shanghai she joined the Communist Youth League and returned to the stage. She joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1933.

Jiang went to Yan'an, where in 1938 she became a drama instructor at the new Lu Xun Academy of Arts, and she married Mao Zedong that year. After the People's Republic was founded in 1949 she wielded considerable influence over the arts. She organised campaigns against the film The Life of Wu Xun and the Peking opera Hai Rui Dismissed from Office and promoted revolutionary operas known as yangbanxi. From 1962 she appeared in public as Mao's wife and gave speeches in the cultural and propaganda sectors, condemning various figures.

By late 1965 she had gathered allies such as Zhang Chunqiao and Yao Wenyuan, and her campaign against Hai Rui Dismissed from Office marked the start of the Cultural Revolution. She became a major figure from 1966 to 1976, a Politburo member at the Ninth and Tenth Central Committees and the de facto leader of the Cultural Revolution Group. She also used the movement against personal enemies, among them people who had slighted her during her acting career in the 1930s. With Zhang, Yao and Wang Hongwen she formed the group Mao called the Gang of Four.

In the mid-1970s Jiang led the campaign against Deng Xiaoping. When Mao lay critically ill in September 1976 she proposed expelling Deng at a Politburo meeting but did not succeed, and after Mao's death she was arrested and expelled from the party. The indictment against the Gang of Four had 48 counts. In the televised trial she was sentenced to death with a two-year reprieve, and in 1983 the sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. She was held at Qincheng Prison.

According to Ross Terrill's biography, she died by suicide in a Beijing hospital on 14 May 1991, a claim disputed by a former Qincheng official who said she died in prison. The Chinese public blamed her for the upheavals of the Cultural Revolution.
jiang-zemin: Jiang Zemin was born in Yangzhou, Jiangsu, on 17 August 1926 and grew up during the Japanese occupation. His uncle and foster father, Jiang Shangqing, died fighting the Japanese and was regarded as a national hero, and Jiang became his male heir. He studied electrical engineering at the National Central University, joined the Chinese Communist Party while in college, and graduated from the National Chiao Tung University in 1947. In the 1950s he trained at the Stalin Automobile Works in Moscow. From 1970 to 1972 he led an expert team that set up fifteen machinery plants in Romania. He became a member of the Central Committee in 1982.

Jiang became mayor of Shanghai in 1985, and in 1987 its party secretary and a member of the Politburo. After the Tiananmen Square protests and massacre of 1989 he unexpectedly replaced Zhao Ziyang as general secretary, as a compromise candidate, appointed on 24 June 1989 with a small power base. He also took over the chairmanship of the Central Military Commission from Deng Xiaoping, and he became president in 1993. After Deng's southern tour of 1992 he introduced the term socialist market economy, and his administration oversaw the breaking of the iron rice bowl and the privatization of many state-owned enterprises. He forbade the military to engage in business. In 1999 he began a crackdown on Falun Gong.

Hong Kong returned from the United Kingdom in 1997 and Macau from Portugal in 1999, and China entered the World Trade Organization in 2001. Relations with the United States were marked by tensions, including the Third Taiwan Strait Crisis of 1996. On 25 February 2000 he introduced the theory of the Three Represents, which justified admitting private business owners to the party and was written into its constitution in 2002.

Jiang gave up his leadership posts between 2002 and 2005, handing them to Hu Jintao, though he and his faction kept an influence on affairs for some time. He died in Shanghai on 30 November 2022, at 96, and was given a state funeral. In China his reputation is mixed: some credit his term with the relative stability and growth of the 1990s, while others argue that he did little to correct the imbalances built up by years of fast economic reform.
jiangsu: Jiangsu is a coastal province of East China, bordering Shandong to the north, Anhui to the west, and Zhejiang and Shanghai to the south. It has a coastline of over 1,000 kilometres along the Yellow Sea. The land is flat: plains cover 68 percent of the province, and most of it stands no more than 50 metres above sea level. The well-developed irrigation system earned the south the name shuixiang, land of water, and Suzhou has so many canals that it has been called the Venice of the East. The Grand Canal crosses the province from north to south, and the Yangtze flows through its southern part.

In the earliest Chinese dynasties the area lay far from the centre of Chinese civilisation and was home to the Huai people. Under the Zhou the state of Wu appeared in southern Jiangsu. Near the end of the Spring and Autumn period it became a great power under King Helu and in 484 BCE defeated Qi, but in 473 BCE it was conquered by the state of Yue. Yue was in turn subjugated by Chu in 333 BCE, and Qin unified China in 221 BCE. Since the Sui and Tang dynasties Jiangsu has been a national economic and commercial centre, partly because of the Grand Canal.

The name combines the first elements of two cities, Jiangning, now Nanjing, and Suzhou. In April 1927 Chiang Kai-shek established a government at Nanjing, and Shanghai separated from Jiangsu in 1927. Nanjing fell to the Japanese on 13 December 1937, and the atrocities of the following three months became known as the Rape of Nanjing. It then became the seat of the collaborationist government of East China under Wang Jingwei, and most of Jiangsu stayed under Japanese occupation until 1945.

Jiangsu is a province of the People's Republic of China with its capital at Nanjing and a population of about 85 million, the most densely populated of the country's provinces. It is divided into thirteen prefecture-level cities, among them Nanjing, Suzhou, Wuxi, Changzhou and Zhenjiang. Most residents are ethnic Han Chinese, with Hui and Manchu minorities. The southern part, centred on the Shanghai-Nanjing corridor, is the more urban and prosperous, while the north is more rural.
jiangxi: Jiangxi lies on the banks of the Yangtze in the north and rises into hillier country in the south and east. Mountains surround it on three sides, and the highest point is Mount Huanggang in the Wuyi Mountains, at 2,157 metres. The Gan River flows through the whole province from south to north into Lake Poyang, the largest freshwater lake in China, which empties into the Yangtze. The Gan valley was historically the main north-south transport route of south China, one of the few easy corridors through the rugged south-eastern mountains. It carried trade between the North China Plain and the Yangtze valley and the territory of modern Guangdong, so the region was strategically important throughout much of Chinese history.

Jiangxi lay outside the sphere of early Chinese civilisation under the Shang, and peoples collectively known as the Baiyue probably lived there. Its north formed the western frontier of the state of Wu, and after Yue conquered Wu in 473 BCE, Chu took northern Jiangxi. Yuzhang Commandery, established at the start of the Han dynasty, was the first commandery set up there by a Chinese dynasty. It took its name from the original name of the Gan River, and Gan is now the province's abbreviation. In 291 it became its own zhou, Jiangzhou, under the Western Jin. In 733 the Tang divided the Jiangnan Circuit, and the western half, the Jiangnanxi Circuit, gave the province its modern name.

After the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period, Jiangxi Province was established for the first time, and it took roughly its modern borders. After the fall of the Qing it became one of the earliest Communist bases. The Nanchang Uprising took place there on 1 August 1927. The government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established at Ruijin in 1931, and in 1935, encircled by Nationalist forces, the Communists broke through and began the Long March to Yan'an. The brutal campaigns and purges of those years reduced the population by 40 per cent, to 13.8 million in 1936.

Nanchang is the provincial capital, and Ganzhou and Jiujiang are other major cities. Most of the population is Han Chinese, and the province is the centre of Gan Chinese, with some Hakka also spoken. It has deposits of copper, tungsten, gold, silver, uranium and lithium. After the opening of the Yuehan Railway in 1936 and of the Zhegan Railway in 1937, Jiujiang's port declined in importance. The province was fully under Communist control from the establishment of the People's Republic of China in 1949.
jiaqing-emperor: The Jiaqing Emperor was born Yongyan on 13 November 1760 at the Old Summer Palace, near Beijing, the 15th son of the Qianlong Emperor. His mother was Noble Consort Ling, daughter of an ethnic Han Chinese official whose family had long been part of the Manchu Eight Banners. Two other sons the emperor had in mind as heir died young, and in December 1773 he secretly chose Yongyan as his successor. In 1789 he made him Prince Jia of the First Rank.

In October 1795 the Qianlong Emperor announced that he would abdicate, since he thought it disrespectful to rule longer than his grandfather, the Kangxi Emperor. Prince Jia took the throne in February 1796 under the era name Jiaqing, but for three years his father, now emperor emeritus, still made the decisions. After Qianlong died in February 1799 the new emperor took control and prosecuted Heshen, his father's corrupt favourite, who was stripped of his titles, lost his property and was ordered to commit suicide.

The state faced disorder and an empty treasury. The White Lotus Rebellion (1796 to 1804) and the Miao rebellion (1795 to 1806) were put down at a steep fiscal cost. In 1813 the Eight Trigrams, a millenarian Buddhist sect, attacked the Forbidden City, intending to kill the emperor on his return from a hunt; the attempt failed. In 1816 the ambassador Lord Amherst came to improve trade with Britain, but his refusal to perform the kowtow ended the embassy. The emperor refused the Vietnamese ruler Gia Long's request to call his country Nam Viet, but agreed to the name Viet Nam. In 1811 a clause added to the legal code made spreading Christianity among Han Chinese and Manchus punishable by death for Europeans.

He died on 2 September 1820 at the Rehe summer palace, 230 kilometres north-east of Beijing, and was buried in the Chang mausoleum among the Western Qing Tombs. The Draft History of Qing gives no cause of death; some have alleged lightning, others prefer a stroke, as he was very heavy. His second son Mianning succeeded him as the Daoguang Emperor.

Assessments of his reign are mixed. Some see it as the beginning of the end of the Qing dynasty, others as a period of moderate reform. Jonathan Spence thought he relied on rhetoric more than on specific policies. He was a keen scholar of the Confucian classics, with 15,267 poems attributed to him, and had printed compendia of court collections made, which are an important source for Qing court art.
jie-of-xia: Jie, also known by the temple name Di Gui, is traditionally the 17th and last sovereign of the Xia dynasty, which lasted about 500 years. His given name was Lü Gui, and his parents were Fa of Xia and his wife. According to the traditional record he first had his capital at Zhenxun, where he built a tilt palace, and put down a rebellion by the Quanyi people. His name Jié means outstanding and later hero, but a later dictionary linked it with a word meaning to cut asunder, and the Rules for Posthumous Names say that the name was given to those who harmed and killed many people.

Later texts describe him as lavish and cruel, fond of luxury and disliking criticism. In his 11th year he summoned his vassals, and when the kingdom of Youmin did not come he attacked and conquered it. Later he took two daughters of the King of Minshan as wives and abandoned his first wife, Mo Xi.

Liu Xiang's book Lienü zhuan, written much later, around 18 BCE, tells that Mo Xi had a lake of wine made and ordered 3,000 men to drink it dry, laughing when they drowned. The Song scholar Luo Mi observed that such tales of Jie echo those told of Di Xin, and argued that this copying greatly exaggerated both rulers' crimes. Yuri Pines notes that the Rong Cheng Shi, excavated in 1994, depicts Jie's crimes fairly mildly.

Meanwhile Shang, a vassal kingdom, grew in strength under Tang of Shang, who won the support of as many as 40 smaller kingdoms by pointing to Jie's mistreatment of his people. The histories record omens in Jie's reign: an alignment of five stars, a meteor shower and an earthquake in his 10th year, a landslide at Qu mountain and, in his last year, summer frost and failed crops. In his 32nd year Tang attacked Xia and Kunwu, and Jie's army was defeated at Mingtiao in a heavy thunderstorm.

Jie fled, was pursued by the Shang general Wuzi, captured and deposed, and the Xia dynasty ended. He was eventually released at Nanchao and is said to have died of illness 12 years later during a drought. Tang became king and began the Shang dynasty. No contemporary evidence of Jie survives: the Erlitou culture has been proposed as a Xia site, but no writing was found there, records of Xia appear only under the Zhou, and its historicity, and so Jie's, is disputed, especially by Western scholars.
jigawa-state: Jigawa State lies in the north-west of Nigeria, between latitudes 11°N and 13°N, and covers about 22,410 square kilometres. It borders Kano and Katsina states to the west, Bauchi State to the east and Yobe State to the north-east, and along its northern edge it shares a 70 km international border with the Zinder Region of Niger. Its land is undulating, with sand dunes spanning several kilometres in places. The main rivers are the Hadejia, Kafin Hausa and Iggi, and the Hadejia–Kafin Hausa river crosses the state from west to east through the Hadejia-Nguru wetlands into the Lake Chad Basin. Most of the state lies within the Sudan savannah.

The state is known for the Dutsen Habude cave paintings at Birnin Kudu, which have been dated to the Neolithic period. The town of Hadejia, formerly Biram, is notable as one of the traditional seven true Hausa states. The area was formerly the north-eastern part of Kano State. Agitation for a separate state was led by Malam Inuwa-Dutse, a former commissioner in the ministry of agriculture and natural resources under Audu Bako, governor of the old Kano State. Jigawa was created on 27 August 1991 under the military administration of General Ibrahim Babangida.

The capital and largest city is Dutse, and the state has twenty-seven local government areas. The people are predominantly Hausa and Fulani, with Kanuri mainly in the Hadejia Emirate, and Islam and a long history of intermarriage bind the three groups together. The state is governed under Sharia law. Over 80% of the population is engaged in subsistence farming and animal husbandry, and trade is mostly small and medium in scale. The state has universities at Dutse, Babura, Kafin Hausa and Majia, and a federal polytechnic at Kazaure.
jigme-dorji-wangchuck: Jigme Dorji Wangchuck was born at Thruepang Palace in Trongsa and trained as a young man in etiquette and leadership at the royal court of his father, the king. He was educated in a British manner in Kalimpong and at Bishop Cotton School in Simla, and went on study tours to countries such as Scotland and Switzerland, from which he drew ideas for developing Bhutan with suitable adaptations. He was appointed Trongsa Dronyer in 1943 and became the 25th Paro Penlop in 1950. On 5 October 1951 he married Ashi Kesang Choden Wangchuck. He became king on 30 March 1952 after his father's death and was crowned at Punakha Dzong on 27 October 1952.

His reign of about twenty years began the reorientation of Bhutanese society. Labourers on the royal lands were made tenants and sharecroppers instead of indentured workers, and similar labourers were later freed in other areas, especially in eastern Bhutan. In 1953 he opened the National Assembly at Punakha Dzong, inviting elders from the gewogs to voice their concerns. The Assembly passed the Thrimzhung Chenmo, or Supreme Law, in 1959. Judges called Thrimpons were appointed in the districts, a High Court was set up in 1968, the Royal Bhutan Army was formally established in 1963 and new ministries followed in 1968. In 1955 he began converting taxes paid in goods into cash taxes by assessing land.

He also promoted Bhutanese culture, commissioning Buddhist monuments and copies of the Kangyur and Tengyur, founding Simtokha Rigzhung Lobdra in 1967 and the public schools of Kanglung and Yangchenphug. The rules of the Dzongkha language were systematically devised in his reign. Bhutan joined the Colombo Plan in 1962, and India became the main source of financial and technical help. After Jawaharlal Nehru visited Bhutan in September 1958, road building began in 1959, and the first Five Year Plan of 1961 envisaged 177 km of road, 108 schools, three hospitals and 45 clinics. More than 1,200 km of road had been built by his death. In 1971 Bhutan became the 125th member of the United Nations.

The king had long-term heart problems. In July 1972 he travelled to Nairobi for treatment and died suddenly there, and his body was flown back to Bhutan to be cremated. He is remembered as the father of modern Bhutan, who modernised the country without, in the view of those who praise him, destabilising its culture and tradition.
jihlava: Jihlava began as a Slavic market village on a trade route around 1200 and is first mentioned in 1233. Silver mining began in 1234, and the royal mining town was established between 1233 and 1240, making it the oldest mining town in what is now the Czech Republic. It was the first city in central Europe where mining law was codified. Miners came from Bavaria, Saxony and other German-speaking lands, and King Ottokar II's building regulations of 1270 set its rectangular plan around a large square.

By the end of the 14th century the richest deposits were exhausted and Jihlava turned to trade and cloth making. During the Hussite Wars it stayed a Catholic stronghold, and on 5 July 1436 a treaty was made there in which the Hussites acknowledged Sigismund as king of Bohemia. A fire in 1523 badly damaged the town, and Swedish troops captured it twice in the Thirty Years' War.

In the second half of the 18th century Jihlava was the second largest cloth producer in the Austrian Empire. In 1921 about 54 per cent of its people were German speakers, and it formed the centre of a German-speaking enclave. The synagogue was burnt in 1939, and most of the town's Jewish population, over 1,000 people, was deported and killed. After the Second World War most German speakers were expelled under the Beneš decrees.

Jihlava is the capital of the Vysočina Region, on the historic border of Moravia and Bohemia, about 110 kilometres south-east of Prague, with about 54,000 inhabitants. Its historic centre, a mixture of Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque buildings, is protected as an urban monument reservation, and the early Gothic Church of Saint James the Great is a national cultural monument. Gustav Mahler lived there from 1860 to 1875, and his parents lie in the Jewish cemetery.
jikji: Jikji is the abbreviated title of a Korean Buddhist document whose title translates as Anthology of Great Buddhist Priests' Zen Teachings. It comes from the phrase Jikji Insim Gyeonseong Seongbul, which means that when a person's heart is seen correctly through meditation, its nature is realised as the mind of Buddha. The text was compiled by the monk Baegun (1298–1374), whose Buddhist name was Gyeonghan. In May 1351 he sought the teachings of the Chinese master Seok-ok, and he was also taught by the Indian priest Jigonghwasang. He later served as chief priest of the Anguksa and Shingwangsa temples in Haeju, and he wrote and edited the Jikji at Chwiamsa Temple in Yeoju in 1374, where he lived until his death.

The Jikji is a collection of excerpts from the analects of the most revered Buddhist monks of successive generations. Baegun compiled it as a guide for students of Buddhism, then Korea's national religion under the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392). It sets out the essentials of Korean Seon, the predecessor of Japan's Zen Buddhism. The work originally consisted of two volumes totalling 307 chapters.

The last page records that it was printed with metal type at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju in the third year of King U, in July 1377. Baegun's students, the priests Seoksan and Daldam, helped to publish it, and the priestess Myodeok also contributed. Its printing methods differed from those of Johannes Gutenberg. The surviving volume measures 24.6 by 17.0 centimetres on very thin white paper. The lines are askew, the ink varies in thickness, and a few characters, such as 日 and 一, are printed in reverse. A woodblock edition made at Chwiamsa in 1378 survives complete in two volumes.

The metal-printed volume became known in 1901, when the French scholar Maurice Courant listed it in the appendix of his Bibliographie coréenne. The French diplomat Victor Collin de Plancy had collected it in Seoul, and in 1911 Henri Véver bought it for 180 francs and later left it to the National Library of France in his will. It drew wide attention when shown in Paris in 1972, and Cheongju University confirmed the site of Heungdeok Temple by excavation in 1985. UNESCO inscribed it on the Memory of the World Register on 4 September 2001. Ownership remains disputed: the French library holds that it is a shared heritage of humanity, while Korean organisations argue that it belongs in Korea.
jilin: In ancient times the Jilin area was inhabited by the Xianbei, Sushen, Mohe, Jurchens and Wùjí, and the kingdoms of Buyeo and Goguryeo ruled parts of it. The region then fell successively under the Xiongnu, the Xianbei state, Goguryeo, Balhae, the Khitan Liao dynasty, the Jurchen Jin dynasty and the Mongol Yuan dynasty. Under the Qing, much of the area was controlled by the General of Jilin, whose territory extended to much of what is now Russia's Primorsky Krai.

After Primorsky Krai was ceded to Russia in 1860, the government began to open the area to Han Chinese migrants, most of them from Shandong, and by the early 20th century the Han had become the dominant ethnic group of the region. In 1932 the area was incorporated into Manchukuo, a puppet state set up by Japan, with Changchun, then called Xinjing, as its capital. After Japan's defeat in 1945 the Red Army captured Jilin in Operation August Storm, and the region, with the rest of north-eastern China, passed to the Communists. Manchuria was the staging ground from which they conquered the rest of China in the Chinese Civil War.

In 1949 the province was smaller, taking in only the environs of Changchun and Jilin City, with its capital at Jilin City, while Changchun was an independent municipality. It was expanded to its present borders in the 1950s. During the Cultural Revolution it was enlarged again to include part of Inner Mongolia, giving it a border with Mongolia, but this was later reversed. The name comes from the Manchu phrase girin ula, meaning along the river, written in Chinese as jilin wula and shortened to Jilin.

Jilin is one of the three provinces of Northeast China, bordering North Korea and Russia to the east and south and Heilongjiang, Liaoning and Inner Mongolia. Its capital and largest city is Changchun, 113 kilometres west of Jilin City. The Changbai Mountains in the south-east hold its highest peak, Paektu Mountain at 2,744 metres, and the Yalu and Tumen rivers form parts of the border with North Korea. Agriculture centres on rice, wheat, maize and sorghum, and the province is known for ginseng and deer antlers used in Chinese medicine.
jilin-city: Jilin City lies in central Jilin Province, in a hilly area on the Songhua River, which surrounds much of the city and gives it the nickname River City. Four mountains stand round it: North Mountain (Beishan) to the west, Long Tan Mountain to the east, Zhuque Mountain to the north and Turtle Mountain to the south. With the river they form a bagua in the Taiji pattern. Beishan is the best known of them and is home to several Buddhist temples. The climate is humid continental, with long, cold winters. The Songhua is the only river in the region that does not freeze in winter, and water vapour rising from it crystallises on willow branches as rime ice in January and February.

Jilin City is one of the oldest cities in Northeast China. Under the Yongle Emperor, the Ming sought to extend control throughout Manchuria, and river fleets built here sailed several times to make local chieftains swear allegiance. After the Manchu-led Qing dynasty was established, the territory of today's Primorsky Krai was placed under Jilin's administration. As the Russian Empire advanced east towards the Pacific coast, the Qing government ordered a naval shipbuilding factory set up here in 1661.

Jilin was officially established as a fort city in 1673, when the Deputy Lieutenant-General Anzhuhu was ordered to build a castle. In 1676 the Military Governor of Ninguta was transferred to Jilin because of its more convenient location and growing military importance, and the city then developed rapidly. Its nickname comes from a line of a poem written by the Kangxi Emperor on his visit in 1682. Jilin remained important in the 18th and 19th centuries as one of the few cities beyond the Willow Palisade, with Qiqihar, Ninguta and Mukden.

When Manchukuo made Xinjing, now Changchun, its capital, Jilin's importance fell. By 1940 Jilin had 173,624 people and Xinjing 544,202. Soviet forces captured Jilin during the August Storm operation. It was the provincial capital of Jilin Province from the founding of the People's Republic of China in 1949 until Changchun took that role in 1956.

Jilin City is a prefecture-level city and the only major city in China that shares its name with its province. It co-hosted the Asian Winter Games in 2007, and winter sports such as skiing and skating are popular. Among its sights is Wulajie Old City, a walled Qing town downstream on the Songhua. It was a collecting point for local products sent to the imperial court, and the Kangxi Emperor went there in 1682 to fish for sturgeon. A Meteorite Museum there displays the largest stony meteorite of a documented meteorite fall.
jim-crow-laws: The Thirteenth Amendment abolishing slavery was ratified on 18 December 1865. During Reconstruction, between 1865 and 1877, federal laws protected the civil rights of freedmen in the South. In the 1870s Democrats gradually regained power in Southern legislatures while paramilitary groups such as the Ku Klux Klan, the White League and the Red Shirts drove out Republican officeholders and lynched Black voters to suppress the Black vote.

The term Jim Crow probably derives from Jump Jim Crow, a minstrel dance performed in blackface by the white actor Thomas D. Rice, first staged in 1828. By the end of the nineteenth century the name meant the social separation of the races.

The laws were passed by white-dominated state legislatures to remove the gains that African Americans had made during Reconstruction. Beginning in the 1870s they mandated segregation in public facilities across the South, and companion laws excluded most African Americans from the vote. The Civil Rights Act of 1875 guaranteed equal treatment in public accommodations but had little effect, and an 1883 Supreme Court decision found it unconstitutional in some respects.

In Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896 the Supreme Court upheld the doctrine of separate but equal facilities. In practice the facilities for African Americans were consistently inferior and underfunded, and sometimes did not exist. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, founded in 1909, campaigned against the laws and the doctrine.

In Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka in 1954 the Supreme Court unanimously held public school segregation unconstitutional and overturned Plessy. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, and the Montgomery bus boycott that followed lasted more than a year. Mass demonstrations organised by the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, headed by Martin Luther King Jr., drew national attention on television.

Congress overcame Southern filibusters to pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which overturned most remaining Jim Crow laws. Laws against interracial marriage were struck down in Loving v. Virginia in 1967. Historians count the laws among the causes of the Great Migration, in which African Americans left the rural South for cities in the Northeast, Midwest and West.
jimena-diaz: Jimena, whose name is also spelled Ximena, was born before July 1046. She was the daughter of Diego Fernández, Count of Oviedo, himself the son of Count Fernando Flaínez, and of his wife Cristina, and she was a sister of Fernando Díaz, Count of Asturias. She married Rodrigo Díaz between July 1074 and 12 May 1076.

It is unclear whether she lived with her husband in the Taifa of Zaragoza during his first exile, from 1080 to 1086, when he led the army of its rulers, or whether she went to Asturias in those years. A legal action from Tol dated 1083 suggests that she kept a presence there even while the two were apart.
