In 1363 John's son Louis, a hostage in exchange for him, broke his parole and escaped from Calais. John resolved to return to captivity, replying that if good faith were banned from the earth, it should find asylum in the hearts of kings. He landed in England in January 1364 and fell ill with an unknown malady. He died at the Savoy Palace in April 1364 and was buried at the Basilica of Saint Denis. He created seven duchies and counties, more than any other French monarch.
john-ii-of-portugal: John, called the Perfect Prince, was born in Lisbon on 3 May 1455, the second son of Afonso V of Portugal and Isabella of Coimbra. At one month old he was declared legitimate heir and received an oath of allegiance from the three estates. In 1471 he married his first cousin Eleanor of Viseu, and he was knighted that year after the conquest of Arzila in North Africa. At Toro in March 1476 he defeated the Castilian right wing. From 1477 to 1481 he and his father were practically co-rulers, and he helped negotiate the Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1479 with Spain, which gave Portugal hegemony in the Atlantic south of the Canary Islands.

John became king on his father's death on 28 August 1481. He set out to reduce the power the nobility had gained, requiring magnates at the Cortes of Évora to swear allegiance to him as their superior and taking from nobles the right to administer justice on their estates. Fernando, Duke of Braganza, was arrested, convicted of treason and beheaded in June 1483. In September 1484 John himself stabbed to death Diogo, Duke of Viseu, his cousin and the brother of the queen, after confronting him with evidence of treason.

African trade became a crown monopoly, and its profits paid for exploration. The fortress of São Jorge da Mina was founded in 1482, Diogo Cão found the Congo River in 1484, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope. John received Christopher Columbus twice, in 1484 and 1488, and rejected his plan, as the king's advisers judged his estimate of the distance far too small. When Columbus returned in 1493, John claimed his discoveries under the Treaty of Alcáçovas, and the dispute led to the Treaty of Tordesillas.

After Spain expelled its Jews in 1492, John admitted tens of thousands of them at eight cruzados a head, for no more than eight months. About 20,000 families entered, and only 600 of the wealthiest won permanent residence. Those who could not leave in time were enslaved until Manuel's reign.

His only legitimate son, Afonso, died in a horse accident in July 1491. John named Queen Eleanor's brother Manuel as his heir in his will in September 1495, and he died of dropsy at Alvor on 25 October 1495. His remains were moved to the Monastery of Batalha in 1499. His epithet is taken to refer to Machiavelli's The Prince.
john-iii-doukas-vatatzes: John Doukas Vatatzes, born about 1192 at Didymoteicho, came from a military family and by about 1216 held the post of protovestiarites. Emperor Theodore I Komnenos Laskaris chose him as the second husband of his daughter Irene Laskarina. When John became emperor in December 1221 he had to suppress opposition from Theodore's brothers Alexios and Isaac, which ended at the Battle of Poimanenon in 1224, where his opponents were defeated despite support from the Latin Empire of Constantinople. The Latin Empire made territorial concessions in 1225, and John crossed into Europe and seized Adrianople.

Theodore Komnenos Doukas of Epirus and Thessalonica drove the Nicaean garrison out of Adrianople in 1227. When Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria eliminated Theodore in 1230, John allied with Bulgaria against the Latin Empire. The alliance brought the restoration of the Bulgarian patriarchate in 1235 and the marriage of his son Theodore II to Elena of Bulgaria, and in 1236 the two allies attempted a joint siege of Constantinople.

Pope Gregory IX called for a crusade against Nicaea in 1237. John sought allies elsewhere and turned to Emperor Frederick II, who recognised him as Byzantine emperor under the title Emperor of the Greeks in exchange for mutual aid. In 1238 John sent troops to the Siege of Brescia. After his first wife died in 1240 he married Frederick's ten-year-old daughter Constance, who took the Greek name Anna, and the alliance lasted until Frederick's death in 1250. At the Council of Lyon in 1245 Pope Innocent IV, who called John that enemy of God and the church, deposed Frederick, and John sent troops and subsidies to Italy between 1247 and 1250.

John annexed Thessalonica and much of Bulgarian Thrace in 1246. By 1247 he had established a stranglehold on Constantinople, and his authority reached far to the west. He also extended Nicaean control over much of the Aegean and annexed Rhodes. Large Cuman communities he settled guarded western Anatolia against Oghuz-Turkmen invasions. He died at Nymphaion in 1254 and was buried in the monastery of Sosandra, which he had founded near Magnesia.

Later generations called him the Father of the Greeks. He was canonised about half a century after his death as John Vatatzes the Merciful, and his feast day is 4 November. He collected and copied manuscripts, and he ruled despite epilepsy.
john-iii-of-portugal: John was born in Lisbon on 6 June 1502, the eldest son of King Manuel I and his second wife Maria of Aragon. He was educated by scholars including the humanist Luís Teixeira Lobo and studied Latin, Greek, mathematics and cosmography. At sixteen he was chosen to marry his first cousin Eleanor of Austria, but she married his widowed father instead. His chroniclers say he was deeply offended, and some historians see in this one reason for the piety that gave him his nickname. He was crowned on 19 December 1521 in the Church of São Domingos in Lisbon.

John continued the absolutist politics of his predecessors and called the Cortes only three times, in 1525, 1535 and 1544. He married Catherine of Austria, sister of Emperor Charles V, and his sister Isabella of Portugal married Charles, which secured peace with Spain. The empire was costly to run and burdened with debt, and pressure from the Ottoman Empire in the Indian Ocean and North Africa raised the cost of defence. To pay for it he gave up several North African strongholds, among them Safim and Azemmour in 1541 and Arzila in 1549. By the Treaty of Zaragoza of 22 April 1529 Portugal paid Charles 350,000 ducats and secured the Maluku Islands.

In Asia the Portuguese reached Japan in 1543 and gained a footing at Macau. In Brazil, French privateers and the attempted colony of France Antarctique prompted the twelve captaincies founded from 1534; the French were not expelled until 1565. John created the Governorate General in 1549 under Tomé de Sousa, who founded Salvador, and sugar began to compensate for falling revenue from Asia. The first enslaved Africans reached Brazil in 1539.

John's rule was marked by support for humanist writers and scholars, among them Gil Vicente and Luís de Camões. He moved the university to Coimbra in 1537 and appointed Francis Xavier to the East Indies in 1540. The Jesuits took over the Coimbra College of Arts in 1555. After ten years of negotiation with Rome he established the Portuguese Inquisition in 1536, with his brother Cardinal Henry as first Grand Inquisitor; it chiefly targeted New Christians, and at least 1,379 people were burned between 1543 and 1684.

Nine of his children died young. His heir, Prince John, died aged sixteen, eighteen days before the birth of his son Sebastian on 20 January 1554. John died of apoplexy in 1557, leaving his three-year-old grandson as heir. He is buried in the Monastery of Jerónimos in Lisbon.
john-iii-of-sweden: John was born at Stegeborg Castle on 20 December 1537, the son of Gustav I and his second wife Margareta Leijonhufvud. As Duke of Finland he quarrelled with his father by meddling in Livonian affairs, and he travelled to London for his brother Erik to woo Queen Elizabeth I; the mission failed, but John observed the new Book of Common Prayer. When Erik XIV became king and centralised power, the brothers fell out, and John signed the Articles of Arboga of 1561, which restricted his power, only with great reluctance. In 1562 he married Catherine Jagiellon in Vilnius against Erik's will.

The Estates found John guilty of treason in June 1563. He held out in Turku Castle for some weeks and surrendered on 12 August 1563. He was imprisoned at Gripsholm Castle with his wife for more than four years, in light conditions, and two of their children were born there. He was freed in October 1567, during Erik's insanity. In July 1568 John and his brother Charles rose against Erik; Stockholm opened its gates on 29 September 1568, Erik was captured, and John was recognised as king by the Riksdag in January 1569, after granting concessions to the nobility and to Charles.

John ended the Northern Seven Years' War, then fought Russia in the Livonian War, which the Treaty of Plussa in 1583 concluded with Narva confirmed as Swedish. His son Sigismund became king of Poland in 1587. John regretted this and demanded his return, but the high nobility opposed it, and he turned to Charles for support. Erik died in 1577 in captivity, probably as a result of John's order of 1571 to kill him if a rescue were attempted. John died in Stockholm on 17 November 1592 and is buried in Uppsala Cathedral.

John was a learned follower of the mediating theologian George Cassander and sought reconciliation between Rome and Wittenberg. He issued the Red Book liturgy, which reintroduced Catholic customs and caused the twenty-year Liturgical Struggle, and his talks with the Pope failed. He rewarded the nobility with privileges and estates, and was the most building-minded monarch Sweden ever had, restoring cathedrals and extending Kalmar, Vadstena and Tre Kronor and starting Borgholm Castle.
john-iv-laskaris: John IV Doukas Laskaris was born on 25 December 1250, a son of Theodore II Doukas Laskaris, the third emperor of Nicaea, and Elena of Bulgaria. His maternal grandparents were Emperor Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria and his second wife Anna Maria of Hungary, a daughter of Andrew II of Hungary. The Nicaean Empire was one of the Greek successor states formed after the sack of Constantinople by the Roman Catholics in the Fourth Crusade, and the Laskarid dynasty had done much to restore the Byzantine Empire.

John was only seven when he inherited the throne on his father's death, and he reigned from 16 August 1258. His first regent was the bureaucrat George Mouzalon, but the nobility murdered Mouzalon, and their leader Michael Palaiologos took over the post. On 1 January 1259 Palaiologos made himself co-emperor as Michael VIII; the two were second cousins once removed, both descended from Empress Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera.

Michael took Constantinople from the Latin Empire on 25 July 1261, and John was left behind at Nicaea. On his eleventh birthday, 25 December 1261, he was blinded on Michael's orders, which made him ineligible for the throne, and he was exiled and imprisoned in a fortress in Bithynia. The Patriarch Arsenius Autoreianus excommunicated Michael VIII for the act, and a revolt led by a Pseudo-John IV later broke out near Nicaea.

John spent the rest of his life as a monk at Dacibyza. A rescript of Charles of Anjou dated 9 May 1273 refers to a report that John had escaped and invites him to Charles's court, and further documents attest a pension. This contradicts the historians George Pachymeres and Nikephoros Gregoras, who record that John stayed at Dacibyza until long after Michael's death; Deno John Geanakoplos concluded that the documents were propaganda meant to attract Greek supporters of the Laskarid dynasty. In 1290 Andronikos II Palaiologos, Michael's son and successor, visited John to seek forgiveness for the blinding. John died about 1305 and was eventually recognised as a saint, whose memory was revered in Constantinople in the 14th century.
john-iv-of-portugal: John was born at Vila Viçosa on 19 March 1604. He succeeded his father Teodósio II as Duke of Braganza in 1630, when Teodósio died insane, and in 1633 he married Luisa de Guzmán, eldest daughter of Juan Manuel Pérez de Guzmán, 8th Duke of Medina Sidonia. His claim to the crown came through his grandmother Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, who had been a claimant during the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580. Since then Portugal had been joined to Spain in the Iberian Union.

Under Philip III of Portugal (IV of Spain) taxes on Portuguese merchants were raised, the Portuguese nobility lost influence and government posts were increasingly held by Spaniards. The king is also said to have tried to make Portugal a Spanish province. On 1 December 1640 a group known as the Forty Conspirators, drawn from the nobility and the bourgeoisie, killed the Secretary of State, Miguel de Vasconcelos, and imprisoned the Vicereine of Portugal, Margaret of Savoy, the king's cousin. Spanish troops were then occupied with the Thirty Years' War and a revolution in Catalonia.

Within hours, and with popular support, John was acclaimed king; according to legend his wife persuaded him to accept. Portugal allied with France on 1 June 1641 and with Sweden in August 1641, and the war with Spain lasted from 1641 to 1668. A Portuguese force defeated the Spanish at Montijo, near Badajoz, in 1644. Overseas the Dutch took Malacca in January 1641 and the Imam of Oman captured Muscat in 1650, but the Portuguese retook Luanda in 1648 and by 1654 had recovered northern Brazil. Colombo fell to the Dutch in 1656.

John died in 1656 and was succeeded by his son Afonso VI. His daughter Catherine of Braganza married King Charles II of England, and Bombay was given to the English as her dowry. John was also a composer and a writer on music, author of a Defence of Modern Music (Lisbon, 1649) and a defence of Palestrina, and he built up a very large library that was destroyed in the Lisbon earthquake of 1755. In 1646 he proclaimed the Immaculate Conception of Mary patroness of Portugal by royal decree.
john-j-pershing: John Joseph Pershing was born on a farm near Laclede, Missouri, on 13 September 1860, the son of the farmer and store owner John Fletcher Pershing and Ann Elizabeth Thompson. He became a West Point cadet in July 1882 and rose to First Captain, the highest cadet rank. He served with the 6th Cavalry in New Mexico, Arizona and South Dakota and was cited for bravery against the Apache. As a West Point instructor from 1897 he was unpopular for his strictness, and the nickname Black Jack that cadets gave him stayed with him for life.

In the Spanish–American War Pershing fought on Kettle and San Juan Hills in Cuba and was cited for gallantry; Theodore Roosevelt called him the coolest man under fire he had ever seen. In 1940 he was awarded the Distinguished Service Cross for leading an assault against Moro defenders at Mount Bagsak, on Jolo in the Philippines, on 15 June 1913. On 27 August 1915 a fire at the Presidio in San Francisco killed his wife, Frances Warren Pershing, and three of their daughters; only his son Warren survived. On 15 March 1916 he led an expedition of 10,000 men some 350 miles (560 km) into Mexico against Pancho Villa, which routed Villa's followers but failed to capture him.

President Woodrow Wilson chose Pershing to command the American Expeditionary Forces, and he was installed on 10 May 1917, with headquarters at Chaumont. He resisted British and French demands that American troops serve as replacements in their armies, although in March 1918, when General Philippe Pétain said he had few reserves left, he put all available American divisions at Pétain's disposal. American soldiers fought at Cantigny, Château-Thierry and Belleau Wood in June 1918, and at St. Mihiel in September the First Army, under his direct command, overwhelmed a German salient. In the Meuse-Argonne Offensive he kept about 600,000 soldiers in hard fighting for 47 days.

In September 1919 Congress authorized the promotion of Pershing to General of the Armies, a rank created for him. His memoirs, My Experiences in the World War, won the 1932 Pulitzer Prize for history. Historians have criticised his reliance on costly frontal assaults, and his failure to halt attacks in the last hours before the armistice of 11 November 1918; he said he followed the orders of Ferdinand Foch, and Congress found that no one was culpable. He mentored many later generals, among them George C. Marshall and Dwight D. Eisenhower. Pershing died on 15 July 1948 and was buried in Arlington National Cemetery.
john-king-of-england: John was the youngest son of King Henry II of England and Eleanor, Duchess of Aquitaine. He was born around Christmastide in 1166 or 1167, and historians debate the precise date. His father's lands, Anjou, Normandy and England, with Eleanor's Aquitaine, formed the Angevin Empire, a fragile union whose parts had their own traditions and governments. As a younger son John was not expected to inherit significant lands, and his father jokingly called him Lackland. In 1177 Henry appointed him Lord of Ireland. When Richard became king in 1189 he made John Count of Mortain and married him to the wealthy Isabella of Gloucester.

After Richard died on 6 April 1199, John's claim rivalled that of Arthur of Brittany, son of John's elder brother Geoffrey. John had the support of most English and Norman nobles and was crowned at Westminster Abbey, while Philip II of France backed Arthur. The peace treaty of Le Goulet in 1200 recognised John's continental lands. War returned after he married Isabella of Angoulême in August 1200, having set aside his first wife. Shortages of resources and his treatment of Norman, Breton and Anjou nobles led to the collapse of his empire in northern France in 1204. He spent the next decade trying to regain it, raising large revenues and reforming his forces. His judicial reforms had a lasting effect on English common law.

A dispute with Pope Innocent III over the election of Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury led Innocent to ban church services in England from 1208 until 1214 and to excommunicate John from 1209 until 1213. In 1209 John invaded Scotland and forced William the Lion to sign the Treaty of Norham, with a payment of £10,000.

In 1214 John's final campaign to retake Normandy failed when the French defeated his allies at the Battle of Bouvines. Barons who were unhappy with his fiscal policies and his treatment of nobles rebelled, many of them northerners who owed him large sums. John and the barons agreed to Magna Carta in 1215 as a peace treaty, but neither side complied with it, and civil war began. He died on 19 October 1216. Contemporary chroniclers mostly criticised him. Jim Bradbury describes the present view as that of a hard-working administrator, an able man and an able general, while historians also point to faults such as pettiness, spitefulness and cruelty.
john-knox: Knox was born in or near Haddington, East Lothian, sometime between 1505 and 1515, the son of a merchant. He studied at the University of St Andrews or possibly Glasgow, under John Major, and was ordained a Catholic priest in Edinburgh on Easter Eve 1536. He appears in the records as a priest and notary in 1540 and became tutor to the sons of two lairds who had embraced the new religious ideas. After the murder of Cardinal David Beaton in 1546 he became chaplain to the garrison of St Andrews castle. French galleys besieged it, and on 31 July 1547 the garrison surrendered; Knox was taken to France and forced to row in the galleys until 1549.

Knox took refuge in England and on 7 April 1549 was licensed to work in the Church of England. He became a royal chaplain to Edward VI and influenced the wording of the Book of Common Prayer. When Mary I restored Catholicism he left England for Frankfurt and then Geneva, where he met John Calvin. He was elected minister of the English congregation there and arrived on 13 September 1556.

Back in Scotland in 1559, Knox preached a sermon at Perth on 11 May after which a mob gutted the church and attacked two friaries. In August 1560 the Scottish Parliament asked him and five other ministers named John to draw up a confession of faith. The Scots Confession was presented within four days and approved, and Parliament abolished papal jurisdiction and forbade the Mass. The Book of Discipline of January 1561 was not approved, mainly for reasons of finance.

After Mary, Queen of Scots, arrived in August 1561 and heard Mass at Holyrood, Knox protested from the pulpit of St Giles' and refused to moderate his preaching when she summoned him. In 1564 he married Margaret Stewart, aged seventeen, when he was a widower of fifty. His influence waned as the nobility supported Mary. He died on 24 November 1572. His will declared that he had corrupted and defrauded none, and the small sum he left showed that he had not profited from the Kirk. He wrote his History of the Reformation in Scotland between 1559 and 1566.
john-lewis: John Robert Lewis was born near Troy, Alabama, on 21 February 1940, the third of ten children of Willie Mae and Eddie Lewis, sharecroppers in rural Pike County. His great-grandfather Frank Carter had been born enslaved in the same county in 1862 and lived until Lewis was seven. Troy University, then Troy State, denied him admission in 1957 because of racial segregation. As a student he became an activist, attending nonviolence workshops held by the Rev. James Lawson and the Rev. Kelly Miller Smith at Clark Memorial United Methodist Church in Nashville, and he practised the discipline of nonviolence for the rest of his life.

In the Nashville Student Movement Lewis organised sit-ins at segregated lunch counters, which brought the desegregation of the city's downtown lunch counters, and he was arrested and jailed many times. In 1961 he was one of the 13 original Freedom Riders, seven Black and six white riders who planned to travel on interstate buses from Washington, D.C. to New Orleans to challenge segregated seating, in support of the Supreme Court's decision in Boynton v. Virginia. After extreme violence broke out in South Carolina and Alabama, the Kennedy administration called for a cooling-off period.

In 1963 Lewis, a founding member, was elected chairman of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, and he was the youngest of the Big Six leaders who organised the March on Washington. He was the fourth of twelve speakers that day, before Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech. In 1965 he led the first of three Selma to Montgomery marches across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, where state troopers and police attacked the marchers on what became known as Bloody Sunday. From 1970 to 1977 he directed the Voter Education Project, which added nearly four million minority voters to the rolls. He served on the Atlanta City Council from 1981 to 1986, then won Georgia's 5th district in 1986.

Lewis served 17 terms in the House and from 1991 was a chief deputy whip. His awards included the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2011. His memoir Walking with the Wind (1998) won several prizes, and in 2013 he became the first member of Congress to write a graphic novel, the March trilogy. He died in Atlanta on 17 July 2020, the last surviving Big Six leader. His casket crossed the Edmund Pettus Bridge in a horse-drawn caisson on 26 July before he lay in state at the Alabama State Capitol.
john-locke: John Locke was born on 29 August 1632 in the village of Wrington, Somerset, to Puritan parents. His father, also John Locke, was an attorney who served as clerk to the Justices of the Peace in Chew Magna, one of whom was Alexander Popham, a Member of Parliament for Bath. Locke was 10 when the English Civil War began, and his father fought for the Parliamentarian side as a captain of cavalry under Popham.

In 1647, under Popham's sponsorship, he became a student at Westminster School in London. Locke wrote of those years, "I found myself in a storm." He then won a place at Christ Church, Oxford, where he spent 15 years, first as a student and then as a tutor, pursuing medical and other scientific interests.

In 1665 Locke travelled outside England for the first time, as secretary to Sir Walter Vane on a failed diplomatic mission to the Elector of Brandenburg. In 1666 he met Anthony Ashley Cooper, later Lord Shaftesbury, and in 1667 moved into Shaftesbury's London home as his personal physician. He studied medicine there under Thomas Sydenham, and was probably instrumental in persuading Shaftesbury to undergo the surgery that saved his life. Locke was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1668.

After Shaftesbury fell from royal favour and died, Locke spent five years in political exile in the Netherlands (1683–85), where he wrote some of his most important works. He returned to England in 1689, served as a Commissioner of Trade and Plantations and retired because of ill health. He is also listed as a shareholder in the Royal Company of Adventures Trading to Africa, which traded in slaves from 1663. He died on 28 October 1704.

In his Letters Concerning Toleration (1689–1692) Locke argued that earthly judges cannot dependably evaluate competing religious truth-claims, that belief cannot be compelled by violence, and that enforcing uniformity would cause more disorder than allowing diversity. In the Essay Concerning Human Understanding he held that the mind is at birth a blank slate, tabula rasa, and that knowledge comes only from experience. He is often credited with describing private property as a natural right, arising when a person mixes labour with nature. The phrase "long train of abuses" in the Declaration of Independence is taken from the Second Treatise.
john-magufuli: John Pombe Joseph Magufuli was born on 29 October 1959 in north-western Tanzania, then Tanganyika, on the shores of Lake Victoria, into a poor family. As a boy he looked after cattle and sold milk and fish to help support them. He attended Chato Primary School from 1967 to 1974, then Katoke Seminary, Lake Secondary School and Mkwawa High School. He earned a Bachelor of Science in education from the University of Dar es Salaam in 1988, majoring in chemistry and mathematics, and a master's degree in chemistry in 1994 and a doctorate in 2009 at the same university.

He taught chemistry and mathematics at Sengerema Secondary School in 1982 and 1983, then worked as an industrial chemist for the Nyanza Cooperative Union Limited from 1989 to 1995. In 1995 he was elected a Member of Parliament for Chato and served as Deputy Minister of Works until 2000, when he became Minister of Works. From January 2006 he was Minister of Lands and Human Settlement, from 2008 to 2010 Minister of Livestock and Fisheries, and from 2010 to 2015 Minister of Works again.

The ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi nominated him as its presidential candidate on 12 July 2015. He won the election of October 2015 with 58 per cent of the vote, with Samia Suluhu as running mate, and was sworn in as president on 5 November 2015. He was re-elected in 2020. Magufuli died on 17 March 2021 and was succeeded by his vice-president, Samia Suluhu.
john-marshall: John Marshall was born on 24 September 1755 in a log cabin in Germantown, in the Colony of Virginia. He was the oldest of 15 siblings. After the outbreak of the American Revolutionary War, John Marshall joined the Continental Army and served in numerous battles. Late in the war he was admitted to the state bar, and in early 1782 he won election to the Virginia House of Delegates.

He built a legal practice in Richmond. He favoured ratification of the United States Constitution and played a major role in Virginia's ratification. In 1797 President John Adams sent him to France with Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and Elbridge Gerry. Talleyrand's agents refused to negotiate unless the United States paid enormous bribes, an episode known as the XYZ Affair, and Marshall returned in 1798.

Marshall was appointed secretary of state in 1800, and Adams appointed him to the Supreme Court in 1801. He quickly became the key figure on the court, in large part through personal influence on the other justices, and it moved from seriatim opinions to a single majority opinion stating a clear rule. In Marbury v. Madison, decided in 1803, he upheld judicial review, the principle that courts may strike down laws conflicting with the Constitution, while avoiding a direct clash with the Jefferson administration.

Later decisions confirmed the supremacy of the federal government over the states. Fletcher v. Peck in 1810 was the first case in which the court ruled a state law unconstitutional, applying the Contract Clause. In McCulloch v. Maryland in 1819 Marshall upheld the Second Bank of the United States and laid down the theory of implied powers. In Worcester v. Georgia he held a Georgia statute on Native American lands unconstitutional.

Marshall wrote The Life of George Washington, a five-volume work published from 1804 to 1807, the first biography of a US president. He also owned slaves throughout his life and wrote seven of the court's fourteen decisions on slavery, siding against the enslaved in each. He died on 6 July 1835 in Philadelphia, after more than 34 years as chief justice, and was buried in Shockoe Hill Cemetery in Richmond beside his wife Polly.

Before him the court had been a minor organ of government. In his tenure it gained the weight of a co-equal branch, and the Marshall Court struck down an act of Congress in only one case, Marbury v. Madison, which established the court's power to overrule Congress, the president and the states. His Richmond home is preserved as a museum.
john-maynard-keynes: John Maynard Keynes was born in Cambridge on 5 June 1883 into an upper-middle-class family. His father, John Neville Keynes, was an economist and lecturer in moral sciences at the University of Cambridge, and his mother, Florence Ada Keynes, was a social reformer who became the town's second female mayor. He studied at King's College, Cambridge, graduating in 1904 in mathematics. In October 1906 he became a clerk in the India Office but resigned in 1908 to return to Cambridge and work on probability theory. He became a fellow of King's College in 1909.

In the First World War the British government sought his advice. A few days before hostilities began he went to London at its request and helped persuade the Chancellor, Lloyd George, not to suspend specie payments. At the Versailles peace conference he tried to stop German reparations being set so high that they would damage Germany's ability to pay and buy exports, and so harm the wider world economy; the experience shaped his outlook, though he was unsuccessful. In the 1920s he published A Treatise on Probability and criticised the return to the gold standard in 1925 at the pre-war valuation.

During the Great Depression he challenged the neoclassical view that free markets would automatically provide full employment. He argued that aggregate demand determined the level of economic activity and that inadequate demand could cause prolonged unemployment, and he advocated fiscal and monetary policy to counter recessions. He set out these ideas in The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money, published in early 1936. In How to Pay for the War, published in 1940, he proposed financing the war through higher taxation and compulsory saving rather than deficit spending. He received a hereditary peerage in 1942 and helped to design the new international economic institutions, though the American delegation overruled him on several points.

Keynes suffered a series of heart attacks in 1946, beginning during the negotiations over the Anglo-American loan in Savannah, Georgia. He died at Tilton, his farmhouse near Firle in East Sussex, on 21 April 1946, aged 62. By the late 1930s leading Western economies had begun adopting his recommendations, and almost all capitalist governments had done so within two decades of his death. His influence waned in the 1970s, amid stagflation and criticism from Milton Friedman and other monetarists.
john-newton: John Newton was born at Wapping, London, on 4 August 1725, the son of a Mediterranean shipmaster. His mother died of tuberculosis in 1732. He first went to sea at 11 with his father and sailed six voyages. In 1743 he was pressed into the Royal Navy and became a midshipman aboard HMS Harwich. After he tried to desert he was flogged and reduced to common seaman.

He then moved to a slave ship, Pegasus, bound for West Africa. In 1745 he was traded to a slaver and taken as a servant to the coast of Sierra Leone, a time he later called being a servant of slaves in West Africa. Early in 1748 a sea captain sent by his father rescued him, and in a severe storm off County Donegal during the voyage home he began to pray for mercy. He dated his conversion to 21 March 1748, though he later said that he was not a believer in the full sense until considerably afterwards.

Newton returned to Liverpool in 1748 and became first mate of the slave ship Brownlow. He then made three voyages as captain, of the Duke of Argyle (1750) and the African (1752 to 1753 and 1753 to 1754). After a severe stroke in 1754 he gave up the sea but continued to invest in the slaving operations of Joseph Manesty. He married Mary Catlett on 12 February 1750. In 1755 he became tide surveyor at Liverpool and studied Greek, Hebrew and Syriac.

He applied to be ordained in 1757 and was accepted only after more than seven years. He became deacon on 29 April 1764 and priest on 17 June, as curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire, where John Thornton helped to pay his stipend. His preaching drew so many that a gallery was added to the church. In 1779 he became rector of St Mary Woolnoth in London. Visitors who sought his advice included the writer Hannah More and the young William Wilberforce, whom he encouraged to stay in Parliament.

The poet William Cowper moved to Olney in 1767 and worked with Newton on Olney Hymns, published in 1779. It included Glorious Things of Thee Are Spoken, How Sweet the Name of Jesus Sounds and Faith's Review and Expectation, which came to be known by its opening phrase. Newton also published an anonymous autobiography, An Authentic Narrative, in 1764.

In 1788 he broke a silence of 34 years with Thoughts Upon the Slave Trade, which described conditions on the slave ships in the Middle Passage. He called his part in the trade a subject of humiliating reflection and sent a copy to every Member of Parliament. He died on 21 December 1807, aged 82, after the Slave Trade Act had passed.
john-of-austria: John of Austria was born on 24 February 1547 in Regensburg. His mother was Barbara Blomberg, the daughter of a burgher, and his father was Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, who had been a widower since 1539. In 1554 the boy was taken to the castle of Luis de Quijada at Villagarcía de Campos, where Quijada's wife, Magdalena de Ulloa, took charge of his education. Charles recognised him in a codicil of 6 June 1554 and again in his last will of 1558.

Philip II returned from Brussels in 1559 and met his half-brother on 28 September at the Monastery of Santa María de La Santa Espina. Philip told him they shared a father and that he was a Habsburg, but that he was not to be addressed as Your Highness. John was styled Don Juan de Austria and Your Excellency, the form for a grandee. He studied at the University of Alcalá de Henares beside Prince Carlos and Alessandro Farnese.

In 1568 Philip gave John a naval command, and he spent three months fighting corsairs off North Africa. The Moriscos of the Kingdom of Granada had been ordered to give up their customs, language, clothing and religious practices, and almost 200 towns rose against the decree. Philip made John supreme commander of the royal forces. After the siege of Galera, which fell on 10 February 1570, the village was levelled and salt ploughed into its soil; between 400 and 4,500 inhabitants were killed and 2,000 to 4,500 more sold into slavery.

Philip joined the Holy League of Pope Pius V and Venice and named John commander-in-chief of its fleet. On 7 October 1571 John, with 207 galleys and six galleasses against nearly 300 Ottoman vessels, fought the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras at Lepanto. The Ottoman fleet was destroyed; the League suffered over 13,000 casualties and freed over 10,000 Christian slaves. Among the wounded was Miguel de Cervantes.

After Luis de Requesens died in March 1576, Philip appointed John governor-general of the Spanish Netherlands, and he entered Brussels on 1 May 1577. He took Namur on 24 July 1577 and defeated the rebels at the Battle of Gembloux in January 1578, which forced William of Orange to leave Brussels. John was beaten at Rijmenam, then fell ill with a fever and died on 1 October 1578, aged 31. His body was carried secretly overland to Madrid and buried at El Escorial.
A monument to him was raised at Messina in 1572, and a copy stood in Regensburg from 1978. G. K. Chesterton's poem Lepanto of 1911 called him the last knight of Europe.
john-of-bohemia: John was the eldest son of Emperor Henry VII and Margaret of Brabant. Born in Luxembourg and raised in Paris, he was French by education but deeply involved in the politics of Germany. In 1310 his father arranged his marriage, at the age of fourteen, to Elizabeth of Bohemia. The couple travelled to Prague under the protection of imperial regiments.

Czech forces took control of Prague and deposed the reigning king, Henry of Carinthia, on 3 December 1310. John and Elizabeth were crowned on 7 February 1311. His attempt to follow his father as King of the Romans failed when Louis IV of Bavaria was elected in 1314.

Much of the Czech nobility disliked John as an alien king. In 1311 he reached an agreement with the Bohemian and Moravian aristocracy, the so-called inaugural diplomas, which kept the right to elect the king and to decide extraordinary taxation with the nobles and abolished the king's right to appoint foreign officials. The settlement did not hold, and John, who preferred foreign politics, gave up the administration of Bohemia and travelled, leaving the country to be ruled by the barons. By 1318 he had reconciled with the nobility and recognised their rights.

Abroad he served his father as Imperial Vicar and pressed the Habsburgs and the House of Wettin for territory. After the House of Ascania died out in Brandenburg he regained Bautzen in 1319 and Görlitz in 1329. He supported Louis IV against Frederick the Fair at the Battle of Mühldorf in 1322 and received the region of Egerland as a reward, but allied with France and Austria against Louis in 1322 or 1323. In 1335, at the Congress of Visegrád, Casimir III of Poland paid a large sum for John to give up his claim to the Polish throne.

John lost his sight to ophthalmia while crusading in Lithuania. After the Hundred Years' War began in 1337 he allied with Philip VI of France and served as governor of Languedoc from 30 November 1338 to November 1340. On 26 August 1346 he commanded the French vanguard at the Battle of Crécy and was killed. Jean Froissart records that his companions tied their bridles together and led him into the fight.

His eldest son Charles succeeded him in Bohemia and his son Wenceslaus, by his second wife Beatrice of Bourbon, in Luxembourg. His remains were placed in the crypt of Notre-Dame Cathedral, Luxembourg, in 1945. He is regarded as a national hero in Luxembourg.
john-of-capistrano: John was born on 24 June 1386 and was named after the village of Capestrano in the Abruzzi; his father had come to Italy with the Angevin court of Louis I of Anjou. He studied law at the University of Perugia, and in 1412 King Ladislaus of Naples appointed him governor of Perugia. In 1416, sent as ambassador to broker peace in a war between Perugia and the House of Malatesta, he was thrown into prison, and began to study theology there. On his release he decided to become a Franciscan, citing a dream of Saint Francis; he had married before the war but asserted that the marriage was never consummated. He entered the Order at Perugia on 4 October 1416.

From 1420 John preached in many cities, and he was ordained in 1425. Unlike most Italian preachers of repentance, he was effective in northern and central Europe; at Brescia he preached to a crowd of 126,000. With Bernardine of Siena he worked to reform the Franciscan Order, and in 1429 both were acquitted by a commission of cardinals of charges of heresy raised over their devotion to the Holy Name of Jesus. In 1451 he went as apostolic nuncio to Austria, and as legate or inquisitor he persecuted the last Fraticelli of Ferrara, the Jesuati of Venice, Crypto-Jews, and above all the Hussites.

John preached extensively against Judaism in Germany, Bohemia, Moravia and Silesia and was called the scourge of the Hebrews. Between 1451 and 1453 his sermons persuaded many southern German regions to expel their entire Jewish populations. At Breslau, after an accusation that Jews had desecrated the communion bread, he supervised the torture of Jewish prisoners until they confessed; forty were burned alive, a rabbi hanged himself and the rest were expelled. Scholars of Catholicism and of Judaism have judged him differently: a 2005 encyclopedia of antisemitism said he was a forerunner of modern antisemitism in seeking the social isolation of Jews.

After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, Pope Callixtus III sent John, then aged 70, to preach a crusade against the Ottomans. Meeting little response in Bavaria and Austria, he concentrated on Hungary, and by July 1456 had raised a large but poorly trained force of peasants and landlords. With John Hunyadi he advanced to Belgrade, where together they had gathered about 40,000 to 50,000 troops. After a fierce battle the Ottomans withdrew and the siege was lifted, and John was called the Soldier Priest. He died of plague on 23 October 1456 at Ilok. His canonisation was marked in 1690 by Pope Alexander VIII. He is the patron saint of military chaplains and jurists.
john-of-gaunt: John was the son of Edward III and Philippa of Hainault, born in March 1340, most likely at Saint Bavo's Abbey in Ghent. The name Gaunt is an anglicised form of Ghent, though in his lifetime he was not called by it after the age of three, and its use was popularised by Shakespeare's Richard II. On 19 May 1359 he married his third cousin Blanche of Lancaster, younger daughter of Henry of Grosmont, Duke of Lancaster. The wealth she brought was the foundation of his fortune, and he was created Duke of Lancaster on 13 November 1362 after her father's death. Blanche died in 1368, and only three of their seven children survived to adulthood.

John was one of England's principal commanders in France in the 1370s and 1380s, though without the success of his elder brother, Edward the Black Prince. From 1374 to 1377, with his father and brother ill, he was effectively head of the English government. His vast estates made him the richest man in England, and his wealth and autocratic manner, and the failed peace talks at Bruges, made him a target of resentment. After Richard II's accession in 1377 there was rioting in London, and the rumour that he meant to seize the throne was believed by many, though he sought no regency. His expedition to St Malo in 1378 failed, and rebels destroyed his Savoy Palace in the Peasants' Revolt of 1381.

On marrying Constance of Castile in 1371 he took the title King of Castile and León, and insisted that nobles address him as my lord of Spain. In 1386 he landed at Corunna on 29 July with an Anglo-Portuguese fleet, but in 1387 England neared civil war and he returned in 1389, having given up his claim in 1388. His intervention persuaded the Lords Appellant and Richard to compromise, and Richard invested him with the Duchy of Aquitaine in March 1390. His daughter Philippa married John I of Portugal, which sealed the Anglo-Portuguese alliance of 1386. He was a friend and patron of Geoffrey Chaucer.

John died of natural causes on 3 February 1399 at Leicester Castle, with his third wife Katherine Swynford beside him, and was buried next to Blanche in St Paul's Cathedral. After his death Richard II seized the Lancastrian estates and exiled his son Henry Bolingbroke, who raised an army, deposed Richard and reigned as Henry IV from 1399 to 1413. The House of Lancaster ruled England until the Wars of the Roses. Katherine's children, surnamed Beaufort, were legitimised after their marriage, and through them he was an ancestor of Edward IV, Richard III and Henry VII. All English monarchs from Henry IV are descended from him.
john-of-the-cross: John of the Cross was born Juan de Yepes y Álvarez at Fontiveros, a town of about 2,000 people near Ávila. His father, Gonzalo, a weaver who had been rejected by his family for marrying below him, died around 1545, and the family lived in poverty. His mother, Catalina, moved with her sons to Medina del Campo in 1551, where John entered a school for 160 poor children and later studied the humanities at a Jesuit school from 1559 to 1563. In 1563 he entered the Carmelite Order, and in 1564 he enrolled at Salamanca to study theology and philosophy. He was ordained a priest in 1567.

In Medina del Campo in 1567 John met Teresa of Ávila, who persuaded him to delay joining the Carthusian order and to follow her reform, which sought to restore the Primitive Rule of the Carmelite Order. On 28 November 1568 he founded a monastery for friars at Duruelo and took the name John of the Cross. After tensions among the Carmelites, a General Chapter at Piacenza in 1576 ordered the suppression of the Discalced houses.

On the night of 2 December 1577 Carmelites opposed to reform seized John in Ávila and took him to Toledo, where a court of friars sentenced him to imprisonment. He was lashed publicly at least weekly and held in a cell barely 10 by 6 feet. There he composed a great part of the Spiritual Canticle, and he escaped through a small window on 15 August 1578.

In 1580 Pope Gregory XIII authorised the separation of the Discalced Carmelites. John became a leader of the new order and in 1585 Vicar Provincial of Andalusia, founding seven monasteries there. After disagreeing with the order's leadership he was sent to La Peñuela in June 1591, fell ill and died of erysipelas at Úbeda on 14 December 1591. He was beatified in 1675, canonized in 1726 and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926.

John's poems add up to fewer than 2,500 verses, and his theological works are largely commentaries on them. The Spiritual Canticle, in which the bride, representing the soul, searches for the bridegroom, Christ, is seen as a free Spanish version of the Song of Songs; its first 31 stanzas date from 1578, and it survives in versions of 39 and 40 stanzas. The Dark Night narrates the soul's journey to union with God through detachment, and the Ascent of Mount Carmel, composed between 1581 and 1585, is a systematic study of that ascetical path. His works were first published in 1618, and his writing influenced T. S. Eliot, Thérèse de Lisieux and Thomas Merton.
john-sigismund-elector-of-brandenburg: John Sigismund was born in Halle an der Saale, the son of Joachim III Frederick, Elector of Brandenburg, and his first wife Catherine of Brandenburg-Küstrin. On 30 October 1594 he married Anna of Prussia, the eldest daughter of Albert Frederick, Duke of Prussia, who had no sons. She was the elder sister of his stepmother. The marriage made possible the union of Brandenburg and Prussia, and through his wife he became a major claimant in the War of the Jülich Succession.

He succeeded his father as margrave and elector in 1608. In 1611 he travelled from Königsberg to Warsaw, where on 16 November he did feudal homage to Sigismund III Vasa, King of Poland, whose fief the Duchy of Prussia then was. For several years before 1618 he acted as regent for the mentally disturbed Albert Frederick, and when the duke died he officially became Duke of Prussia. In the Treaty of Xanten of 1614 he received Cleves, Mark and Ravensberg. A stroke in 1616 left him without full recovery, and he died in 1619.

His most significant act was his move from Lutheranism to Calvinism. He had earlier equalised the rights of Catholics and Protestants in Prussia under pressure from the King of Poland. He probably became a Calvinist during a visit to Heidelberg in 1606, but he took communion publicly in the Calvinist rite only on 25 December 1613. Most of his subjects, and his wife Anna, stayed deeply Lutheran.

In February 1614 the elector and his Calvinist officials drew up plans for a mass conversion of the population, under the rule cuius regio, eius religio, and serious protests followed. In 1615 he gave up all attempts at forcible conversion and allowed his subjects to be Lutheran or Calvinist as conscience dictated, so that Brandenburg-Prussia became a bi-confessional state. His son George William succeeded him, and his daughter Maria Eleonora married Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden and was the mother of Christina of Sweden.
john-sigismund-zapolya: John Sigismund was born in Buda on 7 July 1540, the only son of John Zápolya and Isabella Jagiellon. His father had been elected king in 1526 after the Battle of Mohács, while a rival group of lords had proclaimed Ferdinand I of Habsburg. The Treaty of Várad of 1538 confirmed Ferdinand's right to reunite Hungary after John's death, but on his deathbed John Zápolya made those present swear to prevent the transfer of his realm to Ferdinand. The Diet elected the infant king on 13 September 1540, though he was never crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary.

Sultan Suleiman invaded, saying he came to protect the child, and in 1541 his janissaries took Buda without opposition. Suleiman let John Sigismund keep the lands east of the river Tisza in exchange for a yearly tribute of 10,000 florins. The family settled in Gyulafehérvár in Transylvania, but in 1551 his father's treasurer, George Martinuzzi, forced Isabella to give up her son's realm to Ferdinand in return for two Silesian duchies and 140,000 florins, and they went to Poland. At Suleiman's urging the Transylvanian Diet called them back in 1556. Isabella ruled in her son's name until her death in 1559, and then he ruled for himself under the title king-elect.

A powerful lord, Melchior Balassa, deserted to Ferdinand in 1561, and most counties outside Transylvania followed. The Székely commoners also rose, and the king's army crushed them in 1562. John Sigismund paid homage to Suleiman at Zemun in 1566, and the Treaty of Adrianople of 1568 confirmed him in Transylvania and the Partium. Originally Catholic, he converted to Lutheranism in 1562 and to Calvinism in 1564. Influenced by his physician Giorgio Biandrata and his court preacher Ferenc Dávid, he later adopted Anti-Trinitarian views, becoming the only Unitarian monarch in history.

In 1568 the Diet at Torda passed the Edict of Torda, declaring that nobody should suffer for religious reasons and that faith is a gift of God. It expanded religious freedom beyond the standards of 16th-century Europe. By the Treaty of Speyer of 16 August 1570 John Sigismund acknowledged Maximilian II as the sole king of Hungary and took the title Prince of Transylvania and Lord of Parts of the Kingdom of Hungary. He died childless in Gyulafehérvár on 14 March 1571 and was buried in St Michael's Cathedral in Gyulafehérvár according to Unitarian rite. The Diet elected the Catholic Stephen Báthory to succeed him.
john-smith-explorer: John Smith was baptised on 6 January 1580 at Willoughby near Alford in Lincolnshire, where his parents rented a farm. After his father died he went to sea at sixteen and served as a mercenary in the army of Henry IV of France against the Spaniards, then traded and engaged in piracy in the Mediterranean and fought the Ottoman Turks in the Long Turkish War.

He became a cavalry captain fighting for the Austrian Habsburgs in Hungary in 1600 and 1601. He was knighted by the Prince of Transylvania after reputedly killing three Ottoman challengers in single combat. In 1602 he was wounded, captured by Crimean Tatars and sold as a slave, then sent to Rostov. He killed his master and escaped to Muscovy, reaching England in 1604.

In 1606 Smith joined the Virginia Company of London's plan to colonise Virginia, and the expedition sailed on 20 December 1606. He was charged with mutiny during the voyage and held under arrest, but when the ships landed at Cape Henry on 26 April 1607 the company's sealed orders named him one of the colony's leaders. Jamestown was founded on 14 May 1607 on a site chosen by Edward Maria Wingfield.

In December 1607 men led by Opechancanough captured Smith on the Chickahominy River and took him to Powhatan at Werowocomoco. In the summer of 1608 he explored the Chesapeake Bay region for food, and he was elected president of the council in September. He insisted that he who works not, eats not. Smith left in October 1609 after a gunpowder accident. In 1614 he explored the coast from Monhegan Island to Cape Cod and named the region New England.

Smith published eight volumes in his lifetime, including A True Relation of Virginia (1608), A Map of Virginia (1612) and The Generall Historie of Virginia, New-England, and the Summer Isles (1624). He wrote to encourage English colonisation, and the scholar Leo Lemay argues that he was straightforward about its dangers and offered industry rather than gold. The story of Pocahontas saving his life is missing from A True Relation but appears in the Generall Historie, and it is the episode critics scrutinise most. Lemay notes that no one in Smith's day doubted it.

Smith died in London on 21 June 1631 and was buried in 1633 in the south aisle of Saint Sepulchre-without-Newgate Church, the largest parish church in the City of London, where a stained glass window commemorates him. His books and maps encouraged English colonisation.
john-stuart-mill: Mill was born at 13 Rodney Street in Pentonville, then on the edge of London, the eldest son of Harriet Barrow and the Scottish philosopher James Mill. His father educated him, with the advice of Jeremy Bentham and Francis Place, and deliberately shielded him from children other than his siblings, aiming to create a genius intellect that would carry on the cause of utilitarianism. John Stuart was taught Greek at three, and by eight he had read Aesop's Fables, Xenophon's Anabasis and the whole of Herodotus, and had been taught arithmetic, physics and astronomy.

From 1823, at seventeen, until 1858 Mill worked for the East India Company. In 1836 he was promoted to its political department, handling correspondence with the princely states, and in 1856 he became Examiner of Indian Correspondence. When the Crown moved to take direct control of the Company's territories he defended Company rule and declined a seat on the Council of India, citing disapproval of the new system. He defended what he called a benevolent despotism over peoples he regarded as backward.

On 21 April 1851 Mill married Harriet Taylor after 21 years of friendship, declaring on marriage that he repudiated the rights the law gave him over her. He called himself, in the cause of women's rights, chiefly an amanuensis to his wife, who died in 1858. A member of the Liberal Party, he was the second Member of Parliament, after Henry Hunt in 1832, to call for women's suffrage. He died of erysipelas at Avignon on 7 May 1873, aged 66, and was buried beside his wife.

In A System of Logic (1843) Mill held, against William Whewell, that laws are found by observation and induction and need empirical verification. On Liberty (1859) addresses the limits of the power society may legitimately exercise over the individual: the only purpose for which power can rightfully be exercised over a member of a civilised community against his will is to prevent harm to others.

In Utilitarianism he defended the principle, drawn from Bentham and his father, that actions are right in proportion as they tend to promote happiness. In The Subjection of Women, published in 1869, he argued that the legal subordination of one sex to the other is wrong and should be replaced by perfect equality. In 1850 he answered Thomas Carlyle's defence of slavery in an anonymous letter, and he supported abolition in the United States.
john-the-baptist: John is named in all four canonical Gospels. Only the Gospel of Luke tells of his infancy: he was the miraculous son of Zechariah, an old priest, and his wife Elizabeth, who was past menopause. The angel Gabriel is said to have announced his birth to Zechariah while he served in the temple at Jerusalem. Luke also states that John and Jesus were relatives, and on this account the Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran calendars place the feast of his nativity on 24 June, six months before Christmas. Some scholars think that John belonged to the Essenes, a semi-ascetic Jewish sect that expected a messiah and practised ritual baptism.

The Gospel of Mark introduces John as the fulfilment of a prophecy, a messenger sent ahead and a voice crying out in the wilderness. John wore clothes of camel's hair and lived on locusts and wild honey. He proclaimed a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sin and said that another would come who would baptise not with water but with the Holy Spirit.

Baptism was the central symbol of his movement. The majority of biblical scholars agree that John baptised Jesus, and several New Testament accounts report that some of Jesus's early followers had earlier followed John. The Gospel of Matthew has Jesus identify John as the Elijah who is to come, while the Gospel of John has John deny that he is the Christ or Elijah.

According to the New Testament, Herod Antipas had John executed around 30 CE, after John rebuked him for divorcing his wife and unlawfully marrying Herodias, the wife of his brother Herod Philip I. The Jewish historian Josephus also mentions John in his Antiquities of the Jews and states that Herod Antipas had him executed at the fortress of Machaerus.

Followers of John persisted into the second century, and some proclaimed him the Messiah. The Mandaeans, an ancient ethnoreligious group, regard him as their most important and final prophet. In Islam he is the prophet Yahya ibn Zakariya, and he is also honoured as a prophet in the Baháʼí Faith and the Druze faith. In Catholic martyrology he is the only saint whose birth and death are both commemorated.
john-the-fearless: John was born at the Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy in Dijon on 28 May 1371, the son of Philip the Bold and Margaret III, Countess of Flanders. His paternal grandfather was King John II of France, which made him a prince of the blood. In 1384 he received the County of Nevers, and in 1385 he married Margaret of Bavaria in a double wedding at Cambrai that consolidated his position in the Low Countries.

He led the French forces sent to aid Sigismund, King of Hungary, against Sultan Bayezid I, and at the Battle of Nicopolis on 25 September 1396 fought so bravely that he was given the name Fearless. His impetuous leadership ended in disaster; he was captured and freed only the next year after a very large ransom.

John inherited the Duchy of Burgundy on 27 April 1404 and the counties of Burgundy, Flanders and Artois on his mother's death in 1405. He at once clashed with Louis I, Duke of Orléans, the younger brother of the mentally ill King Charles VI, as both tried to fill the power vacuum. Though their uncle John, Duke of Berry, secured a vow of reconciliation on 20 November 1407, Louis was killed in the streets of Paris on 23 November. John admitted the deed and called it a justifiable act of tyrannicide, and in the treaty of Chartres of 9 March 1409 the king absolved him. Louis's son Charles allied with Bernard VII, Count of Armagnac, and the factions became known as Armagnacs and Burgundians.

When Henry V of England invaded France, John kept in contact with him but, wary of losing his popularity, allied himself with the Armagnacs; his troops took no part in the Battle of Agincourt in 1415. On 30 May 1418 his troops captured Paris, the new Dauphin, the future Charles VII, escaping to the Bastille, and John made himself protector of the king.

The Dauphin sought reconciliation, and the two swore peace on the bridge of Pouilly-le-Fort in July 1419. A second meeting was proposed for 10 September 1419 on the bridge at Montereau. John came with his escort, thinking it a diplomatic occasion, and was killed by the Dauphin's bodyguards, among them Tanneguy III du Châtel and Jean Louvet. He was buried at Dijon in 1420. His son and successor Philip the Good then allied with the English, which prolonged the Hundred Years' War. John and his father also played a part in the development of gunpowder artillery in European warfare.
john-v-of-portugal: John was born on 22 October 1689 at Ribeira Palace in Lisbon, the eldest surviving son of Peter II of Portugal and Maria Sophia of Neuburg. His education was first supervised by women, in the custom of the Portuguese nobility. In December 1696 he was invested as Prince of Brazil and Duke of Braganza. His mother died in 1699, and his aunt Catherine of Braganza, former queen consort of England, Scotland and Ireland, then directed his education until her death in 1705. Peter II died on 9 December 1706, and John was acclaimed king a month later. In 1708 he married Archduchess Maria Anna of Austria, his first cousin and the sister of Emperor Joseph I, a match meant to secure the Habsburg alliance.

John ruled as an absolute monarch. He never convened the Cortes and ignored meetings of the Council of State, preferring weekly private audiences with members of the three estates and a close circle of advisers. His main minister was Diogo de Mendonça Corte-Real, and the diplomat Luís da Cunha called him a despot. His foreign policy aimed at neutrality, except for Portugal's part in the War of the Spanish Succession, which he inherited through the Methuen Treaty of 1703. He cultivated Rome: a lavish entry for his ambassador in 1716 helped persuade Pope Clement XI to raise Lisbon to a Patriarchate, and he later received the title Most Faithful Majesty.

Under John the Americas became the base of Portuguese imperial power, as returns from Asia and Africa fell. Gold from Brazil and Maranhão, collected through the royal fifth, filled the treasury. It paid for embassies to Paris in 1715 and Rome in 1716 and for the Royal Palace-Convent of Mafra, begun in 1717 as a modest convent for a hundred friars and enlarged, with gold produced by slave labour in the colonies, into a convent-palace for three hundred friars with a basilica and library. A Swiss resident remarked in 1726 that the king meant to build a second Escorial.

John suffered three strokes in 1742, which left him paralysed on his left side. He remained active in government and would not let Crown Prince José take a role in it. He died on 31 July 1750, aged 60. Admirers called him the Magnanimous and the Portuguese Sun King. His reign marks the high point of Portugal's dependence on wealth from Brazil.
john-vi-kantakouzenos: John Kantakouzenos was born in Constantinople, the son of Michael Kantakouzenos, governor of the Morea. Through his mother he was related to the reigning Palaiologos house, and through his wife Irene Asanina to Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos. He supported Andronikos III against his grandfather Andronikos II Palaiologos and, after the accession in 1328, served as grand domestic. When Andronikos III died in June 1341, Kantakouzenos became regent for the nine-year-old John V Palaiologos. By his own account he had refused several times to be crowned co-emperor.

In September 1341, while Kantakouzenos was away raising an army, the Patriarch John XIV of Constantinople and Alexios Apokaukos overthrew his regency. His relatives were exiled or imprisoned and his mother died under house arrest. His army proclaimed him emperor at Didymoteichon in Thrace, and he accepted while still styling himself the junior ruler.

The civil war lasted six years and nearly ruined the empire. Kantakouzenos fled to Serbia, where Stefan Dušan sheltered him, but the Serbs later changed sides, and Umur of Aydin twice rescued him. He then allied with the Ottoman ruler Orhan Bey, giving him his daughter Theodora in marriage. Kantakouzenos entered Constantinople on 8 February 1347, agreeing that he would rule as senior emperor for ten years.

His reign was one of continuing decline. The Genoese fortified their colony at Galata and took as much as 87 per cent of the Bosphorus revenue. Kantakouzenos built a fleet to break their hold, but Genoa destroyed or captured it by early 1349. In 1351 he oversaw the Fifth Council of Constantinople, which declared the hesychastic theology of Gregory Palamas Orthodox. In 1354 the Ottomans annexed Gallipoli, their first foothold in Europe, as part payment of his debts.

John V removed him from power, and he became a monk on 10 December 1354 under the name Joasaph Christodoulos. In retirement he wrote a four-volume History of the years 1320–1356, an apologia for his actions and the only surviving account by a Byzantine emperor of his own reign.
john-vi-of-portugal: John was born in Lisbon on 13 May 1767, the second son of Maria, Princess of Brazil, later Queen Maria I, and Infante Peter, her paternal uncle, who became King Peter III. He grew up in the shadow of his elder brother José, and little is known of the substance of his education beyond instruction in religion, law, French and etiquette. In 1785 he married Carlota Joaquina of Spain, then ten years old, with a papal dispensation, since they were second cousins; the marriage was consummated five years later. After José died of smallpox in 1788, John became heir to the throne.

As his mother's mental illness grew, John took control of the country, though he rejected a formal regency, and from 1799 he was prince regent. He tried to gain time against Napoleon's pressure, refusing to obey the Continental System while a secret treaty with Britain promised help if the royal family had to flee. In October 1807 news came that a French army was approaching, and a British squadron arrived at Lisbon on 16 November. John chose British protection and sailed for Brazil, reaching Salvador on 22 January 1808.

In Brazil his first major act was the decree opening the ports to friendly nations, from which Britain gained most. He founded the Imprensa Régia, the Botanical Garden and the National Library of Brazil, along with schools, academies and a Royal Museum. He succeeded his mother on 20 March 1816 and was acclaimed on 6 February 1818. Carlota Joaquina repeatedly plotted for a monarchy of her own, and John's involvement in Spanish colonial politics led to the capture of Montevideo in 1817 and the annexation of Cisplatina Province in 1821.

The royal ships reached Lisbon on 3 July, and John swore loyalty to a new constitution on 1 October 1822, surrendering various prerogatives. Carlota Joaquina refused and lost her political rights. Meanwhile his son Pedro, who stayed in Brazil, proclaimed independence on 7 September 1822 and took the title of emperor. Tradition holds that John had told him to put the crown on his own head before an adventurer took it. His other son Miguel led a rebellion that sought to depose him. John was recognised as titular emperor of Brazil from 15 November 1825 and died on 10 March 1826.

Contemporaries thought him kind and benevolent, but later generations caricatured him, and historians have in recent decades restored his reputation as a king who balanced competing interests. Many consider him a mastermind of the modern Brazilian state.
john-vorster: Balthazar Johannes Vorster was born on 13 December 1915 at Jamestown, Cape Province, the fifteenth child of a successful sheep farmer. At Stellenbosch University he became chairman of the debating society, deputy chairman of the student council and leader of the junior National Party. He graduated in 1938 and opened law practices at Port Elizabeth and Brakpan.

From 1939 he strongly opposed South Africa's entry into the Second World War on the side of the Allies, and joined the Ossewabrandwag, an anti-British, pro-Nazi organisation that carried out acts of sabotage during the war. He became a general in its paramilitary wing and was detained at Koffiefontein in 1942; he denied taking part in its violence and said he was interned for being anti-British. After his release in 1944 he became active in the National Party and entered the House of Assembly for Nigel in 1953.

Verwoerd appointed him Minister of Justice in 1961, adding Police and Prisons in 1966. The Rivonia Trial, in which Nelson Mandela was sentenced to life imprisonment for sabotage, came under him as Minister of Justice. After Verwoerd was assassinated in 1966 the National Party elected Vorster to succeed him. He continued apartheid legislation, including the abolition of the last four parliamentary seats for white representatives of Coloured voters, but dropped several proposed bills and repealed the ban on multiracial sports teams so that South Africa could attempt to compete at the 1968 Olympics; the IOC refused the team permission. The Terrorism Act and the Soweto Riots fell in his years as prime minister.

In foreign policy he was more pragmatic than his predecessors, allowing Black African diplomats to live in white areas. After Portuguese rule collapsed in Angola and Mozambique in 1975 he pressed Ian Smith of Rhodesia, in September 1976 under US pressure from Henry Kissinger, to accept in principle that white minority rule could not last. After the Soweto Uprising he let the Department of Information carry out secret activities financed from a secret defence account without telling his cabinet; the auditor general's critical report led to a scandal, and he resigned as prime minister in 1978.

Vorster then became State President, a largely honorary post, but a commission of inquiry concluded in mid-1979 that he had known everything about the Muldergate corruption, including a slush fund used to found The Citizen newspaper, and he resigned. He died in September 1983, aged 67, of a blood clot in the lung after a lung infection and emphysema. A building at Stellenbosch University, built on land taken from coloured residents under the Group Areas Act, was named for him and renamed in the 1990s.
john-winthrop: John Winthrop was born in Edwardstone, Suffolk, to Adam and Anne Winthrop, and his birth was recorded in the parish register at Groton. His father's family had succeeded in the textile business, and his father was a lawyer and prosperous landowner. The family lived at Groton Manor, where John became lord of the manor, managing the estate, and later followed his father in practising law in London. He also sat on the county commission of the peace. In the late 1620s, with Charles I on the throne and married to a Roman Catholic, the outlook for Puritans grew bleak, and Puritan religious and business leaders began to consider emigration.

Winthrop took no part in founding the Massachusetts Bay Company in 1628, but joined it in 1629 and was elected governor in October. On 8 April 1630 four ships left the Isle of Wight with him and other leaders, Winthrop sailing on the Arbella with his sons Samuel and Stephen. First Church in Boston was founded on 30 July 1630. Between 1629 and 1649 he served 18 annual terms as governor or lieutenant-governor. He resisted widening the vote beyond a narrow class of religiously approved men and opposed codifying laws that would bind the magistrates. He clashed with Thomas Dudley, Roger Williams and Henry Vane.

In the Antinomian Controversy of 1636 and 1637 he opposed Anne Hutchinson and John Wheelwright, whose views he saw as dangerous heresy. After the Pequot War of 1636–1638 many captured Pequots were shipped to the West Indies as slaves, and Winthrop kept one male and two female Pequots as slaves. In 1643 he refused official aid to Charles de Saint-Étienne de la Tour in Acadia but let him recruit volunteers in the colony.

Winthrop rarely published, but he kept a journal from the voyage across the Atlantic through his years in Massachusetts, in three notebooks. It is acknowledged as the central source for the history of Massachusetts in the 1630s and 1640s. Noah Webster published the first two notebooks in 1790, the third, long thought lost, was found in 1816, and James Savage issued the complete journals in 1825 and 1826 as The History of New England. The second notebook was destroyed in a fire at Savage's office in 1825. Richard Dunn and Laetitia Yeandle produced a modern transcription in 1996.

The sermon A Modell of Christian Charitie, with its image of a city upon a hill, was long credited to him. The image became a lasting symbol in American political discourse. His reputation declined in the late 19th and early 20th century, when writers such as Nathaniel Hawthorne and H. L. Mencken pointed to the harsher sides of Puritan rule.
john-wycliffe: John Wycliffe was born in the village of Hipswell, near Richmond in the North Riding of Yorkshire, though the date is disputed: it is conventionally given as 1324, while records suggest the mid-1320s or, according to one scholar, a date after 1331. He is known to have been at Oxford around 1345. The book On the Cause of God Against the Pelagians by Thomas Bradwardine shaped his views, as did the Black Death, which reached England in the summer of 1348 and which he mentioned often in later life. He became a priest in September 1351 and completed his bachelor of arts at Merton College in 1356. In 1361 he was Master of Balliol College.

In 1374 Wycliffe was part of a group that negotiated at Bruges for the English government with the envoys of Pope Gregory XI, which may have begun his connection with John of Gaunt, the Duke of Lancaster. He then began to write tracts and longer works. In De civili dominio he attacked the temporal rule of the clergy, the collection of annates, indulgences and simony. His theory of dominion held that the Church should not own property and that men in mortal sin could not exercise authority in Church or state, and he insisted on the poverty of all clergy.

In the summer of 1381 he set out his doctrine of the Lord's Supper in twelve short sentences, and the chancellor of the University of Oxford had some of them pronounced heretical. Wycliffe appealed to the king. Once he dismissed the doctrine of transubstantiation, he lost the support of John of Gaunt and many others. In his last years he argued that Scripture was the authoritative centre of Christianity, that the claims of the papacy were unhistorical, and that monasticism was corrupt.

Wycliffe withdrew to Lutterworth, where he sent out tracts against the monks and Pope Urban VI and left his last work, the Opus evangelicum, unfinished. He suffered a stroke while saying Mass on 28 December 1384 and died a few days later. Tradition credits him with a Middle English translation of the Vulgate Bible, now called Wycliffe's Bible, completed before 1384 and revised by John Purvey in 1388 and 1395, but more recent scholars suggest he had at most a minor part. His followers, called Lollards by their opponents, adopted many of his views, and his Latin writings greatly influenced the reformer Jan Hus.
john-zapolya: John was the oldest son of Count Stephen Zápolya and his second wife, Hedwig of Cieszyn. Stephen, descended from a Croatian noble family from Slavonia, became one of the wealthiest lords of Hungary and served as Palatine from 1492 until his death in 1499. John was born at Szepes Castle, now Spiš Castle in Slovakia, and he and his brother George inherited their father's domains in 1499, mostly in Upper Hungary. He wrote letters in Latin, which shows the education his mother gave him.

Zápolya began his public career at the Diet of Rákos in 1505, where a bill he prompted forbade the election of a foreigner as king. King Vladislaus II refused to ratify it. Zápolya became leader of a national party of the lesser nobility, who opposed the pro-Habsburg higher aristocracy. Vladislaus made him Voivode of Transylvania on 8 November 1510. In 1514 he defeated the peasant army of György Dózsa at Temesvár on 15 July, after a crusade proclaimed against the Turks had turned into a rebellion. The Diet hailed him as liberator of the realm.
His sister Barbara married King Sigismund I of Poland in 1512, but she died in 1515, and the same year his defeat by Sinan, Bey of Smederovo, weakened his position.

The Ottomans crushed the royal army at the Battle of Mohács in 1526 and killed King Louis II. Zápolya marched toward the battlefield with a large army but did not take part, for unknown reasons. On 10 November 1526 the lesser nobility proclaimed him king at Székesfehérvár, and he was crowned the next day. The magnates elected Archduke Ferdinand in Pozsony on 17 December. Ferdinand's German mercenaries captured Buda in 1527 and defeated John at Tarcal on 27 September, and in 1528 John fled to Poland.

In 1529 he agreed to make Hungary a vassal state of the Ottomans in return for support. Sultan Suleiman sent armies against Austria, including the Siege of Vienna, and John regained his position through the efforts of George Martinuzzi. In 1533 the Ottomans made peace and ceded western Hungary to Ferdinand. John married Isabella Jagiellon in early 1539, and their son John Sigismund was born on 15 July 1540. John died on 22 July 1540 in Szászsebes.
johor: Johor covers nearly 19,166 square kilometres in the south of the Malay Peninsula, with the South China Sea to the east, the Straits of Johor to the south and the Straits of Malacca to the west. Tanjung Piai is the southernmost point of mainland Eurasia. The landscape is flat, broken by inselbergs and massifs, with Mount Ledang the highest point, and its tropical rainforests include the Endau-Rompin National Park. The area was known to people in Siam as Gangganu or Ganggayu, meaning Treasury of Gems, and Arab traders called it jauhar, from which the name Johor came. The Old Javanese Nagarakretagama called it Ujong Medini, land's end.

A bronze bell estimated to date from about 150 CE was found near the Muar River, and the lost city of Kota Gelanggi, known from an old Malay manuscript, is placed by some in the forests of Kota Tinggi District. After the Portuguese took Malacca in 1511, Ala'udin Ri'ayat Shah II, a son of Sultan Mahmud Shah of Malacca, founded the Johor Sultanate in 1528 by moving the court to the Johor River. It spanned the southern peninsula, the Riau Archipelago including Singapore and parts of Borneo and Sumatra, and fought a three-way contest with the Portuguese and the Aceh Sultanate.

After Mahmud Shah III died, the Dutch recognised one son as heir in 1818 and the British recognised the other the following year. The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 established Johor's modern borders. Sultan Abu Bakar wrote its state constitution in 1895, and in 1914 it became a British protected state within the Unfederated Malay States. Japanese forces invaded in January 1942 after the Battle of Muar. Johor joined the Malayan Union in 1946 and the Federation of Malaya in 1948, and became part of independent Malaya in 1957 and of Malaysia in 1963.

Johor is a state of Malaysia and a constitutional monarchy headed by a sultan, with Johor Bahru as the state capital and Muar as the royal capital. It is divided into ten districts. The 2023 census counted 4,100,900 people, making it the second most populous state.
