Malay is the official language, Islam the state religion, and the population includes Malay, Chinese and Indian communities. Johor keeps a private army, the Royal Johor Military Force, which has protected its rulers since 1886. In 2008 the International Court of Justice awarded Pedra Branca to Singapore.
johor-bahru: Johor Bahru lies along the Straits of Johor at the southern end of Peninsular Malaysia, on mostly flat land with some hills, bordering Singapore. Its climate is equatorial, with steady temperatures, high humidity and an average annual rainfall of around 2,350 mm, and two monsoon periods each year. The name means New Johor in Malay, distinguishing it from Johor Lama, Old Johor. The area was originally Tanjung Puteri, a Malay fishing village, and the city has also been spelt Johore Bahru, Johor Baru or Johor Baharu.

In 1819 a dispute between the Malays and the Bugis split the Johor-Riau Sultanate: the mainland portion came under Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim, and the Riau-Lingga Sultanate under the Bugis. The Temenggong already had a close relationship with the British, who wanted to control trade at Singapore. By a treaty signed in Singapore on 10 March 1855, Sultan Ali was to be crowned Sultan of Johor and receive 5,000 Spanish dollars and an allowance of 500 a month, and in return ceded the sovereignty of Johor, except Kesang in Muar, to the Temenggong. The Temenggong renamed the territory Iskandar Puteri and at first administered it from Telok Blangah in Singapore, then, after he arrived in 1858, from the new settlement.

Under Sultan Abu Bakar the town was modernised from a fishing village, with administrative centres, offices, schools and a railway to Woodlands. The State Mosque and Royal Palace were built with the aid of Wong Ah Fook, a patron of the sultan. Abu Bakar set up his administration under a British style and a state constitution, the Undang-undang Tubuh Negeri Johor. Although the British had long been advisers to the sultanate, it did not come under direct colonial rule until the adviser's status was raised to that of a Resident, as in the Federated Malay States, under Sultan Ibrahim in 1914.

General Tomoyuki Yamashita's Japanese forces invaded the town on 31 January 1942. The British retreated to Singapore and blew up the causeway the day before. The Japanese used the sultan's Bukit Serene Palace as their base, aware that the British would not attack it. After the war Johor Bahru became a cradle of Malay nationalism, and UMNO was formed at the Istana Besar in 1946. The town remained the state capital after Malaysia's formation in 1963 and was granted city status on 1 January 1994.

Johor Bahru is the capital of the Malaysian state of Johor and had a population of 858,118 in the 2020 census. Its people are mainly Malays, Chinese and Indians, and it is part of Iskandar Malaysia. Its cultural sites include the Royal Abu Bakar Museum in the Grand Palace building and the Johor Bahru Chinese Heritage Museum, and the main football club is Johor Darul Ta'zim.
joint-stock-company: A joint-stock company is a business entity whose shares can be bought and sold by shareholders. Each shareholder owns stock in proportion, evidenced by certificates, and may transfer shares to others without affecting the continued existence of the company. It is an artificial person with legal existence separate from its members: it can own property, enter into contracts, and sue and be sued in its own name. In modern corporate law the form is often synonymous with incorporation and limited liability, so that shareholders answer for debts only up to the money they invested. The company is managed on behalf of the shareholders by a board of directors elected at an annual general meeting.

Finding the earliest joint-stock company is a matter of definition. The earliest records appear in China under the Tang and Song dynasties. The Tang developed the heben, with an active partner and one or two passive investors. By the Song this had grown into the douniu, a large pool of shareholders whose funds were managed by merchants called jingshang, with compensation based on profit-sharing.

In Europe an early form was the medieval commenda, usually used for a single commercial expedition. Around 1350 at Toulouse, 96 shares of the Société des Moulins du Bazacle were traded at a value that depended on the profits of the mills it owned, making it probably the first company of its kind. The Swedish company Stora has documented a transfer of an eighth of the company as early as 1288. The Hudson's Bay Company, the oldest corporation in Canada, received its royal charter from Charles II in 1670.

A corporation requires a legal framework that grants it legal personality and shields its owners from corporate losses, which also encourages new investors by making stock marketable. Where shareholders have limited liability, many jurisdictions require the company to publish annual financial statements so that creditors can judge its standing. Most of the largest businesses in the world are publicly traded companies whose shares are sold on a stock exchange, but most corporations are privately held, with no ready market for their shares.
jokhang: The Jokhang stands in the centre of Lhasa, in Barkhor Square, about 1,000 metres east of the Potala Palace. It was built under Songtsen Gampo, the first king of a unified Tibet, who planned twelve temples across the country, with the Jokhang at its heart. After the king's death the city, once called Rasa, became Lhasa, place of the gods, and the temple took the name Jokhang, house of the Jowo, after its main image.

Tradition tells how the king tossed his hat and promised to build where it landed, in a lake where a white stupa then appeared. The lake was filled, leaving a small pond now seen as a well. In another version Queen Bhrikuti, the Nepalese wife of the king, founded the temple to hold the statue of Akshobhya Buddha she had brought. Craftsmen from Nepal and India are credited with its design and construction.

The temple covers 2.51 hectares and faces west, towards Nepal, in honour of Bhrikuti. It is built of wood and stone in the Tibetan style, with influences from China, Nepal and Indian vihara design, and its roof is covered with gilded bronze tiles and topped with golden deer flanking a Dharma wheel.

The four-storey Buddha Hall holds the Jowo Shakyamuni, a gilded bronze statue 1.5 metres tall showing the Buddha at the age of twelve. It was brought to Tibet by the Tang princess Wencheng, kept first at the temple of Ramoche and later moved to the Jokhang, and it has become the most revered statue in Tibet. Outside stands a pillar 5.5 metres high with an inscription dated 821 or 822 recording a treaty between the Tibetan king Ralpacan and the Chinese emperor Muzong that set the frontier between their lands.

Pilgrims walk around the temple on the Barkhor, spin prayer wheels and prostrate themselves before the Jowo. The temple's history includes hard times. During the reign of Tresang Detsan, from 755 to 797, Buddhists were persecuted, the images were hidden or moved and the monks were driven out. The Fifth Dalai Lama carried out the last major renovation in 1610. In 1966 Red Guards attacked the temple, and for a decade there was no worship. Renovation began in 1972, and the temple was mostly complete by 1980. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000, as an extension of the Potala Palace.
jolo: Jolo is a volcanic island in the Sulu Archipelago, between Borneo and Mindanao, and the main island of the province of Sulu. Its population is approximately 500,000. The island holds the Jolo Group of Volcanoes, an active volcanic group with many cones and craters, among them the active Bud Dajo cinder cone. Mount Daho is its highest point, and the capital town of the same name stands on the island.

After a series of less successful attempts during the centuries of Spanish rule in the Philippines, Spanish forces captured the town of Jolo, the seat of the Sultan of Sulu, in 1876. The Spanish wanted to curb slave raiding once and for all and feared the presence of other Western powers: the British had established trading centres at Jolo and the French were offering to buy Basilan Island. On 21 February 1876 Admiral José Malcampo landed a force of 9,000 soldiers carried in 11 transports, 11 gunboats and 11 steamboats. Captain Pascual Cervera set up a garrison and served as military governor.

By 1878 the Spanish had fortified the town with a perimeter wall, tower gates, inner forts and two outer fortifications. The town was still attacked from time to time: on 22 July 1883 three juramentado attackers reached the plaza and killed three Spaniards, and Colonel Juan Arolas coined the word after he saw several such acts. A treaty of peace signed with the Sultan of Sulu on 22 July 1878 left Spanish sovereignty limited to military stations and pockets of settlement.

The Americans arrived in 1899. Brigadier General John C. Bates signed a treaty with Sultan Kiram to secure the sultanate's neutrality in the Philippine-American War. Its English text described complete dependency and its Tausug text a protectorate, and Bates later admitted it was a stop-gap. The Japanese occupied Jolo in World War II, and American troops landed in April 1945 and in three weeks of combat killed about 2,600 Japanese soldiers, with 37 Americans dead.

Jolo is the capital of Sulu province, and its Tausug name is Sūg. In February 2005 between 4,000 and 5,000 Philippine troops fought around 800 Islamist militants on the island, and up to 12,000 people fled. The Cathedral of Our Lady of Mount Carmel in Jolo was bombed on 27 January 2019.
jomo-kenyatta: Kenyatta was born with the name Kamau in the rural village of Ngenda, to Kikuyu farmers named Mūigai and Wambūi. The Kikuyu kept no birth records, so his date of birth is not known; one biographer suggested 1890 or 1891, while a fuller analysis suggested about 1897 or 1898. During the First World War he lived among the Maasai, adopting a beaded belt called kĩnyata, from which he took his name.

He joined the Kikuyu Central Association. In February 1929 he sailed to Britain to press the Kikuyu land question. He returned to Britain in 1931 and did not go back to Kenya for fifteen years, studying phonetics at University College London and social anthropology under Bronisław Malinowski at the London School of Economics.

Influenced by his friend George Padmore, Kenyatta embraced Pan-African ideas and co-organised the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester. He returned to Kenya in September 1946, farmed an estate at Gatundu and became vice-principal of the Koinange Independent Teachers' College. In 1947 he was elected President of the Kenya African Union, which lobbied for independence and drew wide African support but the animosity of white settlers. In 1952 he was among the Kapenguria Six, arrested and charged with masterminding the Mau Mau Uprising. He protested his innocence, a view later historians share, but was convicted. He was held at Lokitaung until 1959, then exiled to Lodwar until 1961.

After his release Kenyatta joined the Kenya African National Union in October 1961 and accepted its presidency. KANU won 83 of 124 seats in the May 1963 general election, and on 1 June 1963 he was sworn in as prime minister of the autonomous Kenyan government. In December 1964 Kenya was proclaimed a republic with Kenyatta as executive president. KANU's only rival, Oginga Odinga's Kenya People's Union, was prohibited from competing in elections.

By 1975, in the historian Maloba's words, he had in effect ceased to actively govern. In March 1975 the backbencher Josiah Mwangi Kariuki was kidnapped, tortured and murdered, after which support for the government eroded. Kenyatta died on 22 August 1978 and was succeeded by Daniel arap Moi.

He was called Mzee, meaning grand old man, and Father of the Nation, and a cult of personality surrounded him. His government pursued capitalist policies, expanded education and health care. Critics called his rule dictatorial and neocolonial, accused him of favouring the Kikuyu and of enabling corruption, and noted that Kikuyu still held most important government positions.
jonas-basanavicius: Jonas Basanavičius was born in the village of Ožkabaliai in the Augustów Governorate of Congress Poland, to a family of Lithuanian farmers. After birth complications his devout Catholic parents promised that their firstborn would be educated to be a priest. After the Uprising of 1863 Russification policies, meant to reduce Polish influence, allowed him to attend Marijampolė Gymnasium, where he came to value Lithuanian language, culture and history. After graduating in 1873 he persuaded his parents to let him go to Moscow University rather than a seminary, and after two semesters of history and philology he moved to the Moscow Medical Academy, supported by a fellowship for Lithuanian students.

In January 1880 Basanavičius took charge of a run-down hospital at Lom Palanka in the Principality of Bulgaria. He left in May 1882, afraid of persecution after the crackdown on liberal politicians that followed the assassination of Tsar Alexander II. In Prague he organised the publication of Aušra, the first Lithuanian-language newspaper, whose first issue appeared in March 1883 and is often cited as the beginning of the Lithuanian National Revival. It was smuggled into Lithuania, since Lithuanian publication was illegal in the Russian Empire. He soon lost editorial control to Jonas Šliūpas and could not return to Lithuania until 1905.

Back in Bulgaria he married Gabriela Eleonora Mohl in 1884, survived an assassination attempt in August 1887 that left a bullet lodged under his shoulder blade, and suffered illness that led him to resign his public post in 1893.

He returned to Vilnius in August 1905 and chaired the organising committee of the Great Seimas of Vilnius, held on 4 and 5 December 1905 with over 2,000 participants. It demanded autonomy for Lithuania and called for passive resistance to the Tsarist government. In 1907 he founded the Lithuanian Scientific Society and became its president. In 1917 the Vilnius Conference elected him to the Council of Lithuania. He chaired the session that adopted the Act of Independence on 16 February 1918 and was the first to sign it.

Basanavičius collected and published Lithuanian songs, fairy-tales, legends and riddles. As president of the Lithuanian Scientific Society he edited its journal Lietuvių tauta. In 1913 he and Martynas Yčas visited 84 Lithuanian communities in the United States in 120 days and raised $23,799 for a National House; the money was lost in a Russian bank during World War I. He held that Lithuanians descended from Thracians and Phrygians and were closely related to the Bulgarians, a thesis other scholars have not accepted.
jonesborough-tennessee: Jonesborough is the county seat of Washington County in the far north-eastern corner of Tennessee, and part of the Johnson City metropolitan area, within the Tri-Cities region. It lies where the watershed of the Watauga River meets that of the Nolichucky River, among the low hills and elongated ridges of the Appalachian Ridge-and-Valley Province. The main crest of the Appalachians rises a few miles to the south-east. It was named after the North Carolina legislator Willie Jones, who had supported the state's westward expansion across the Appalachian Mountains, and for a time it was spelled Jonesboro.

Settlers of European origin founded the town in 1779, seventeen years before Tennessee became a state, while the area was under North Carolina. It was first part of the Washington District. In 1784 it became the capital of the autonomous State of Franklin, named after Benjamin Franklin. Congress never recognised Franklin, and North Carolina reclaimed it in late 1788. In 1788 the future president Andrew Jackson spent several months practising law in Jonesborough, lodging in a cabin of Major Christopher Taylor.

The town was a centre of abolitionism. The Tennessee Manumission Society was founded in 1815, and in 1819 Elihu Embree of Jonesborough began the Manumission Intelligencier, renamed The Emancipator the next year, the first American periodical devoted only to the abolition of slavery. In the 1840s William G.

Brownlow published the Jonesborough Whig here, and in May 1840 he brawled in the street with the rival editor Landon Carter Haynes. In the summer of 1873 cholera reached the town. Of about 75 people who remained, 30 died by early August and 30 more fell ill but survived. The victims included the publisher George E. Gresham, who had cared for the sick.

Jonesborough styles itself Tennessee's oldest town, and its 2020 census population was 5,860. Its historic district was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1969. The Chester Inn, built in 1797, still stands downtown, and the Christopher Taylor House, built in 1777, was moved into the district and rebuilt there in 1974. The International Storytelling Center holds the National Storytelling Festival on the first full weekend in October, drawing on Appalachian traditions of storytelling.
jonestown: Jonestown, formally the Peoples Temple Agricultural Project, was a remote commune in Guyana established by the Peoples Temple, an American religious organisation led by Jim Jones. Jones formed the Temple in Indianapolis, Indiana, in 1955, and it moved to Redwood Valley, California, in 1965 after criticism of his integrationist views. In the early 1970s it opened branches in Los Angeles and San Francisco and made San Francisco its headquarters.

In the autumn of 1973, after critical newspaper articles and the defection of eight members, Jones and a Temple attorney prepared a plan for a crackdown. In October 1973 the Temple's directors resolved to establish an agricultural mission in Guyana. In the summer of 1977, under pressure from San Francisco media investigations, Jones and several hundred members moved to Jonestown. Its population was slightly under 900 at its peak in 1978. About 70 per cent of the residents were African American. Life there changed after Jones arrived, with lessons and lectures turned to his talk of revolution and enemies.

Leo Ryan, a US congressman from California, flew to Georgetown on 14 November 1978 with a delegation that included journalists, and reached Jonestown on 17 November. When the party left for the airstrip at Port Kaituma on 18 November with some defectors, Temple members murdered Ryan and four others, an act Jones had ordered.

At Jonestown itself 909 people died that day, all but two from apparent cyanide poisoning. Seventy or more were injected with poison, a third of the victims were minors, and armed guards had been ordered to shoot anyone who tried to flee. Jones and some members called the act revolutionary suicide, in a recording of the event and in earlier discussions. In Georgetown four Temple members died in a murder-suicide at the Temple's headquarters, making 918 deaths in all.

Terms for the deaths have changed. Many reports at the time called them a mass suicide, while later sources speak of a mass murder-suicide, a massacre or mass murder. After the deaths the Guyanese government tended the deserted compound and for a few years in the early 1980s let Hmong refugees from Laos live there. Local people looted the buildings, which were mostly destroyed by a fire in the mid-1980s, and the ruins were left to be reclaimed by the jungle.
jordanes: Jordanes, also written Jordanis or Jornandes, was an Eastern Roman bureaucrat of Gothic descent who became a historian later in life. His paternal grandfather Paria was secretary to Candac, a leader of the Alans who held Scythia Minor and Lower Moesia, a small client state on the Roman frontier. Jordanes himself served as notarius, or secretary, to Candac's nephew Gunthigis, also called Baza, a master of the soldiery of the Amali, the leading Gothic clan. He calls himself an unlearned man before his conversion. The nature of that conversion is obscure: it may have been from Arianism to the Nicene Creed, or it may mean that he became a monk or clergyman.

Jordanes wrote two works. The Romana is a history of Rome, written at the request of a certain Vigilius. The Getica, written in Constantinople about 551, interrupted the Romana at the request of a brother Castalius, who knew that Jordanes held the twelve volumes of the History of the Goths by Cassiodorus. Jordanes wrote an excerpt largely from memory, with his own knowledge and perhaps other material, and says he had only three days to review the work. He wrote in Late Latin rather than classical Latin.

The Getica opens with a geography of the north, especially Scandza, and begins the history of the Goths with the emigration of Berig in three ships from Scandza to Gothiscandza. The less fictional part begins when the Goths met Roman forces in the third century CE, and the work ends with their defeat by the Byzantine general Belisarius. With Isidore of Seville's Historia Gothorum, it is one of only two surviving ancient works on the early history of the Goths. Jordanes wrongly equated the Getae with the Goths, so that records concerning Dacians and Getae were attributed to Goths, and some scholars argue that he added fictional events, such as a Gothic war against Egypt.
jorge-amado: Jorge Leal Amado de Faria was born on 10 August 1912 on a farm in the village of Ferradas near Itabuna in the south of Bahia, the eldest of four sons. The village was then administered by the coastal city of Ilhéus, and he considered himself a citizen of Ilhéus. After a smallpox epidemic the family moved there when he was one year old. He attended high school in Salvador and by the age of 14 was writing for magazines and had helped found the modernist Rebels' Academy. His boyhood among the large cocoa plantations showed him the misery of workers living in almost enslaved conditions, a theme of several works, including The Violent Land.

Amado published his first novel, The Country of Carnival, in 1931, aged 18, and his second, Cacau, in 1933. His leftist activities made his life difficult under the regime of Getúlio Vargas: he was arrested for the first time in 1935, and two years later his books were publicly burned. Jubiabá won him a wide readership in France and was praised by Albert Camus. As a Communist militant he went into exile in Argentina and Uruguay in 1941 to 1942. He was later elected to the National Constituent Assembly for the Brazilian Communist Party with more votes than any other candidate in São Paulo.

After the party was declared illegal in 1947 he went into exile again, in France until he was expelled in 1950, and then lived in Czechoslovakia from 1950 to 1952. He won the Stalin Peace Prize in 1951. Back in Brazil in 1954 he left active politics and the party a year later, and gave himself wholly to literature. His second phase began in 1958 with Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon, which Jean-Paul Sartre called the best example of a folk novel. It turned in part from social realism to women characters and a smiling celebration of the traditions of Bahia. Its frank treatment of sexual customs scandalised Brazil, and for some years threats kept him out of Ilhéus.

Amado was elected to the Brazilian Academy of Letters on 6 April 1961 and held its 23rd chair until his death. He received the French Légion d'Honneur in 1984. His books have been translated into 49 languages, adapted for film, theatre and television, and he was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature at least seven times, from 1967 to 1973. He died in Salvador on 6 August 2001, four days before his 89th birthday.

The Fundação Casa de Jorge Amado, created in Salvador in 1987, protects his estate. The Casa do Rio Vermelho, the house where he lived with the writer Zélia Gattai, opened as a memorial in 2014, and the ashes of both are in its garden.
jorge-luis-borges: Borges was born on 24 August 1899 into an educated middle-class family in Palermo, then a poor area of Buenos Aires. His mother, Leonor Acevedo Suárez, worked as a translator and came from a family of criollo origin that had been much involved in the Argentine War of Independence. In 1914 the family moved to Switzerland, where he studied at the Collège de Genève, and travelled widely in Europe, including Spain. When they returned to Buenos Aires in 1921 he had little formal education and few friends, and he brought with him the doctrine of Ultraism. He began publishing poems and essays in literary journals and worked as a librarian and public lecturer.

Borges's father died in 1938. On Christmas Eve that year Borges suffered a severe head injury and nearly died of sepsis. While recovering he began exploring the new style for which he became known. His first story after the accident, Pierre Menard, Author of the Quixote, appeared in May 1939, and his first collection of stories, The Garden of Forking Paths, followed in 1941, composed mostly of works already published in Sur.

Under Juan Perón, he was told he was being promoted from his post at the Miguel Cané Library to inspector of poultry and rabbits at a municipal market; asked why, he was told that he had been on the side of the Allies. He resigned the next day, and the Argentine Society of Writers held a dinner in his honour. In 1955 he was appointed director of the National Public Library and professor of English literature at the University of Buenos Aires. He was completely blind by the age of 55. In 1961 he shared the first International Formentor Prize with Samuel Beckett, and by the 1960s his work was widely translated. He was never awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

His best-known collections, Ficciones and El Aleph, appeared in the 1940s and explore dreams, labyrinths, chance, infinity, archives, mirrors, fictional writers and mythology. He never wrote a novel; he preferred the short story, finding that a novel required padding. He was also a notable translator from English, French, German, Old English and Old Norse, beginning at ten with a Spanish version of Oscar Wilde's The Happy Prince. He held that a translation may improve upon the original, and that different, even contradictory, renderings can be equally valid. He also practised literary forgery and the review of an imaginary work, a form he drew from Thomas Carlyle's Sartor Resartus.
jorge-rafael-videla: Jorge Rafael Videla was born on 2 August 1925 in Mercedes, the third of five sons of Colonel Rafael Eugenio Videla Bengolea. His family was prominent in San Luis Province, where his grandfather Jacinto had been governor from 1891 to 1893. He entered the National Military College on 3 March 1942 and graduated in December 1944 as a second lieutenant. He became a brigadier general in 1971. In August 1975 President Isabel Perón appointed him General Commander of the Army.

After Juan Perón's death his widow Isabel became president amid violence, unrest and economic problems. Videla headed the military coup that deposed her on 24 March 1976. A junta took power, with Admiral Emilio Massera for the Navy and Brigadier General Orlando Ramón Agosti for the Air Force, and two days later Videla assumed the presidency. The junta called its rule the National Reorganization Process. It came to power during attacks by left-wing groups such as the ERP and the Montoneros and by right-wing death squads, and 293 servicemen and police were killed in left-wing attacks in 1975 and 1976.

The repression targeted guerrillas but also the church, unions, artists, intellectuals and students. According to human rights groups, thousands of Argentines disappeared in custody, with estimates as high as 30,000, many held in clandestine detention camps, and between 1,500 and 4,000 were thrown alive from aircraft into the sea. Children born to women prisoners were taken and given to military families, with their identities hidden. On the economy Videla left policy to José Alfredo Martínez de Hoz, who freed prices, exports and imports. Pope John Paul II opened mediation in 1978 in the Beagle conflict over islands at the southern tip of South America. Videla handed power to Roberto Viola on 29 March 1981.

Democracy returned in 1983, and in the Trial of the Juntas Videla was convicted and sentenced to life imprisonment in 1985. President Carlos Menem pardoned him in 1990. He was jailed again in 1998 for the kidnapping of children, and in 2007 a federal court struck down his pardon. In December 2010 he was sentenced to life in prison for the deaths of 31 prisoners and in July 2012 to 50 years for the theft of babies, which the court said involved an estimated 400 to 500 children. He described himself as a political prisoner. He died on 17 May 2013 in a prison at Marcos Paz, an autopsy finding that he had slipped in a shower five days earlier.

The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo began their demonstrations on 30 April 1977, asking where their disappeared children were. In 1980 Adolfo Pérez Esquivel received the Nobel Peace Prize for reporting the abuses to the world.
jorhat: Jorhat lies in Upper Assam, between the Brahmaputra River to the north and the state of Nagaland to the south, at an average elevation of about 116 metres above sea level. It stands on the banks of the Bhogdoi River and has a humid subtropical climate. The name comes from the Assamese words jor, meaning twin, and hat, meaning market. It refers to two historic markets, Macharhat and Chowkihat, which stood on opposite banks of the Bhogdoi.

In 1794 the Ahom king Gaurinath Singha made Jorhat the fifth and last capital of the Ahom Kingdom, after Moamaria rebels had occupied Rangpur. The city keeps monuments of the late Ahom period, among them the Rajamaidam, the maidams of Lachit Borphukan and Captain Gohain, the Rajmao Pukhuri tank and the Burhi Goshani Dewalaya temple. The Burmese Konbaung dynasty later occupied Assam. Its commander Mingimaha Tilwa installed Jogeswar Singha as a puppet king at Jorhat, and a Burmese army under Mingimaha Bandula defeated the deposed king Chandrakanta Singha at Mahgarh, near Jorhat.

Under British rule a narrow-gauge line, the Jorehaut Provincial Railway, opened in 1885 and helped the tea industry of the region to grow quickly. The Jorhat Municipal Board was founded in 1909. Jorhat Theatre was established in 1896 and the Chandrakanta Handique Bhawan, the headquarters of the Asam Sahitya Sabha, in 1926. In 1935 the first Assamese daily newspaper, Dainik Batori, was published in the city by Raibahadur Siva Prasad Barooah. The writer Birendra Kumar Bhattacharya, the first Assamese to win the Jnanpith Award, came from Jorhat.

Jorhat is the headquarters of Jorhat District and the fourth largest city in Assam. The 2011 census gave the municipality 71,398 people, and Assamese is the main language. Its economy rests chiefly on tea cultivation, processing and trade, alongside rice milling, handloom work and trade. The city holds research bodies such as the Tocklai Tea Research Institute and universities including Assam Agricultural University. The Jorhat Gymkhana Club has the oldest golf course in Asia and has held its annual horse races since 1877.
joscelin-i-count-of-edessa: Joscelin came from the Gâtinais, the second son of Joscelin I of Courtenay and Elizabeth, daughter of Guy I of Montlhéry. Nothing is known of his early years; the historian Robert Nicholson suggests that he reached military age by 1101, which would place his birth around 1080. He went east with the Crusade of 1101 in the army of Stephen of Blois. The crusade ended in disaster at the Battle of Mersivan, where as many as four-fifths of the crusaders may have become casualties, and Joscelin reached the Levant with no patrimony and few resources.

In the Levant he entered the service of his cousin Baldwin of Bourcq, count of Edessa, who gave him the lordship of Turbessel, which included Cyrrhus, Duluk and Aintab. At the Battle of Harran on 7 May 1104 he and Baldwin were captured. Joscelin was ransomed for 20,000 dinars in 1107 and then worked to free Baldwin, offering himself as a hostage while Baldwin raised the rest of the ransom. By 1113 he had built a semi-autonomous state around Turbessel, but Baldwin, distrustful of him, imprisoned him and forced him to give it up.

Joscelin went to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, where King Baldwin I made him prince of Galilee. When Baldwin I died childless in 1118, Joscelin urged the nobles to elect Baldwin of Edessa, who became King Baldwin II, and was rewarded with the County of Edessa. On 18 September 1122 Belek Ghazi captured him at the Battle of Saruj, and Baldwin II, taken in April 1123, joined him at Kharput. Armenian soldiers hired by Queen Morphia freed them, and Joscelin then escaped from the besieged fortress, supposedly crossing the Euphrates on inflated wineskins, to seek help.

In 1131, during the siege of a small castle northeast of Aleppo, a sapper's mine collapsed and Joscelin was gravely injured. Hearing that the emir Gazi Gümüshtigin was besieging Kaysun, he had himself carried on a litter at the head of his army, and Gazi lifted the siege. He died soon after, in August 1131, and was succeeded by his son Joscelin II.

Matthew of Edessa called him a brave and mighty warrior, and William of Tyre credited him with temperance and prudence. Muslims seem to have seen him as an intermediary for the Franks. Nicholson calls his death a disaster for a state facing Imad al-Din Zengi. The County of Edessa was conquered by the Zengids in 1146.
jose-antonio-paez: José Antonio Páez was born on 13 June 1790 at Curpa, now part of Acarigua in Portuguesa State, in the Captaincy General of Venezuela. His origins were humble, his father being a low-level employee of the colonial government. By twenty he was married and earning a living by trading cattle. Late in 1810 he joined a cavalry squadron set up to fight the colonial government, and in 1813 he formed his own band of llaneros, plainsmen, and joined the Western Republican Army as a sergeant. He was admired for his horsemanship and was nicknamed the Centaur of the Plains and the Lion of Payara.

In 1818 Páez met Simón Bolívar to coordinate their efforts. In an incident on the Apure River he and fifty men swam on horseback across the alligator-ridden river and seized fourteen enemy boats, a rare cavalry victory over naval forces. He won six major battles that he led by himself, the best known being Las Queseras del Medio. At the Battle of Carabobo on 21 June 1821 he took his division and an additional cavalry regiment through the hills on the northern side and outflanked the Spanish, who lost over 65 per cent of their men. Bolívar promoted him on the spot to General in Chief, and Páez and his men took Puerto Cabello in 1823.

In April 1826 Páez was criticised for his methods of conscription. The central government in Bogotá decided to try him, but he neither submitted nor gave up his post, and Francisco de Paula Santander declared him in open rebellion. This was the Cosiata. When Bolívar returned at the end of 1826 Páez demanded an amnesty, which Bolívar granted in return for his accepting his authority, and Bolívar named him Supreme Civil and Military Commander of Venezuela.

In 1830 Páez declared Venezuela independent from Gran Colombia and became president. From 1830 to 1847 he was the most powerful man in the country, president in 1830 to 1835 and again from 1839 and the power behind other presidents in between, under a constitution largely written by him and an oligarchy allied with him. In 1842 he had Bolívar's remains brought from Santa Marta to Caracas. In 1847 he rebelled against José Tadeo Monagas, was defeated and exiled, and his invasion in 1849 failed. He returned in 1858 and ruled as president and supreme dictator from 1861 for two years. He lived in exile in New York City, and died there on 6 May 1873.
jose-carlos-mariategui: José Carlos Mariátegui was born in Moquegua on 14 June 1894. In 1902, after an accident at school, he spent a long time in a clinic in Lima and was left with a stiff left leg for the rest of his life. In 1909 he began work at the newspaper La Prensa and became a journalist.

In 1918 his interests turned to social problems. With the journalist César Falcón he founded the newspaper La Razón in 1919, which supported university reform and workers' struggles and was closed by the government of President Augusto B. Leguía. He and Falcón then went to Europe on a scholarship from the same government, a covert form of deportation. In Italy he took up Marxism as a method of study.

Mariátegui returned to Lima on 17 March 1923 and gave lectures on the world crisis at the Universidad Popular González Prada. In 1924 his leg was amputated, and he continued to work from a wheelchair. In 1926 he founded the magazine Amauta, which brought together a broad generation of intellectuals around a new appreciation of national life and encouraged the indigenous movement in art and literature.

In 1928 he broke with Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre, with whom he had worked since 1926. On 7 October 1928 he founded the Peruvian Socialist Party, becoming its general secretary a year later, and in 1929 he founded the General Confederation of Workers of Peru. He did not agree to subordinate himself to the Communist International. In February 1930 Eudocio Ravines replaced him as general secretary. He died on 16 April 1930, shortly before a planned journey to Buenos Aires, and was buried in Lima's Presbítero Maestro Cemetery after a massive funeral procession.

In his lifetime Mariátegui published two books, The Contemporary Scene and the Seven Interpretive Essays on Peruvian Reality of 1928. In the Essays he argued that Spanish conquest broke up a solid indigenous communal economy that had grown from the collectivist organisation of Inca society, and replaced it with a feudal economy run by a bureaucracy. He saw Marxism as a method suited to the indigenous masses of the continent, who he thought were its authentic proletariat, and he regarded fascism as an international phenomenon, big capital's response to a profound social crisis.
jose-clemente-orozco: José Clemente Orozco was born in 1883 in Zapotlán el Grande, now Ciudad Guzmán, in Jalisco, the oldest of his siblings. His interest in art began after the family moved to Mexico City in 1890, partly through watching the satirical illustrator José Guadalupe Posada at work in a shop window on his way to school. Orozco later called this his awakening to the art of painting. He studied art at the Academy of San Carlos from 1906 to 1914. At the age of 21 he lost his left hand in an accident while making fireworks with gunpowder.

He worked as an illustrator for Mexico City newspapers and for one of the Constitutionalist armies under Venustiano Carranza. Influenced by the Symbolism of Dr. Atl, he followed him to Orizaba in 1914. When the revolutionary factions split, he sided with Carranza and Álvaro Obregón against Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata. The violence he saw marked his life and art.

In 1916 Orozco went to the United States, disappointed by the reception of his work in Mexico, and returned four years later to work as a cartoonist. His first mural project began in 1923 with the help of José Vasconcelos, at the National Preparatory School in Mexico City. His early panels caused political conflict and he stopped work; some he destroyed himself, others were vandalized by conservative students, and he repainted many after returning in 1926.

From 1927 to 1934 he lived in the United States. In 1930 he painted Prometheus at Pomona College. Between 1932 and 1934 he painted The Epic of American Civilization at Dartmouth College, covering almost 300 square metres across 24 panels. Back in Mexico he painted The Catharsis at the Palacio de Bellas Artes in 1934, then frescoes at the Hospicio Cabañas in Guadalajara, which are considered his masterpiece, and later at the Hospital de Jesús. He died in his sleep in Mexico City on 7 September 1949, aged 65, of heart failure.

Orozco was the most complex of the Mexican muralists. His work has a leftist bent, but less than that of the Marxists Rivera and Siqueiros, and he was influenced mostly by Symbolism. Where Rivera praised the glory of the revolution, Orozco was uneasy at its bloody toll. In The Trench, three anonymous men sacrifice themselves before a barricade whose beams recall a cross. In The Trinity a revolutionary leader threatens the very peasants he claims to fight for, while The Banquet of the Rich uses distortion and caricature to attack the decadence of the rich.
jose-de-alencar: José Martiniano de Alencar was born on 1 May 1829 in Messejana, Fortaleza, Ceará, the son of the politician José Martiniano Pereira de Alencar and his cousin Ana Josefina de Alencar. His family was a rich and influential clan of north-eastern Brazil, and his grandmother, the landowner Barbara Pereira de Alencar, was a heroine of the Pernambucan Revolution. He moved to São Paulo in 1844, graduated in law there in 1850 and began a legal career in Rio de Janeiro. He wrote chronicles for newspapers in Rio, which he collected in 1874 as Ao Correr da Pena.

Alencar became well known in 1856, when he wrote the Cartas sobre A Confederação dos Tamoios in the Diário do Rio de Janeiro under the pseudonym Ig. In them he bitterly criticised a poem by Gonçalves de Magalhães. He belonged to the Conservative Party and was elected a general deputy for Ceará. He was Minister of Justice from 1868 to 1870 and is noted for having opposed the abolition of slavery. He hoped to become a senator, but Pedro II never appointed him. He died of tuberculosis in Rio de Janeiro on 12 December 1877.

His breakthrough came in 1857 with the novel O Guarani. It was the first of what is informally called his Indianist trilogy, three unrelated novels on the foundations of the Brazilian nation and on its indigenous peoples and culture, continued by Iracema in 1865 and Ubirajara in 1874. He is regarded as a major exponent of the literary tradition known as Indianism. His friend Machado de Assis praised Iracema in 1866 and called Alencar in prose what Gonçalves Dias was in poetry. He also wrote plays and an autobiographical work of 1873, Como e Por Que sou Romancista.
jose-de-anchieta: Anchieta was born on 19 March 1534 in San Cristóbal de La Laguna, Tenerife, to a wealthy family. His father had come from the Basque Country, escaping to Tenerife in 1525 after an unsuccessful rebellion against Emperor Charles V, and his mother belonged to a noble family descended from Castilian conquerors of the island. At 14 he went to study at the Royal College of Arts in Coimbra, and the Jesuits admitted him on 1 May 1551. As a novice he nearly ruined his health by excessive austerity and suffered a spinal injury that left him almost a hunchback.

In 1553 the Jesuits sent Anchieta to Brazil, believing the climate would help his health. After a shipwreck he reached São Vicente. In late 1553 Manuel da Nóbrega sent him with twelve other Jesuits up the Serra do Mar to a plateau called Piratininga, where they held a first Mass on 25 January 1554, the date now called the founding of São Paulo. He learned Old Tupi and began a grammar and dictionary.

Anchieta and Nóbrega opposed the colonists' treatment of the Indigenous population, yet the Jesuits supported the Portuguese against the French, whom they saw as Protestants. Anchieta later praised Governor-General Mem de Sá for ending cannibalism, though by killing large numbers of Amerindians. Coastal peoples, attacked and enslaved, formed the Tamoyo Confederation and allied with the French settled in Guanabara Bay. Anchieta and Nóbrega negotiated peace at Iperoig, where Anchieta's command of Tupi was crucial. In 1565 he went with Estácio de Sá to expel the French, acting as surgeon and interpreter. He succeeded Nóbrega on his death in 1570 and became provincial superior in 1577. He died at Reritiba on 9 June 1597.

Anchieta wrote reports to his superiors that serve as ethnography, including accounts of cannibalism, marriage and sorcerers. His Arte de gramática da língua mais usada na costa do Brasil, written in 1555 and published in 1595, was the first work on Old Tupi. He also composed the epic De Gestis Mendi de Saa on Mem de Sá and a Latin poem to the Virgin Mary, which tradition says he composed in captivity at Iperoig in 1563 by writing verses in the sand. His devotional plays, in a mixture of Tupi, Portuguese, Spanish and Latin, were performed by local amateurs. He is called the father of Brazilian literature. He was beatified in 1980 and canonised by Pope Francis on 3 April 2014.
jose-de-san-martin: José Francisco de San Martín y Matorras was born in Yapeyú, Corrientes, an Indian reduction of the Guaraní people, where his father Juan de San Martín was governor of the Yapeyú Department. The exact year of his birth is disputed, since there are no baptismal records, and documents point to either 1777 or 1778. The family moved to Spain in 1783, settling in Málaga. In 1789 he enrolled in the Regiment of Murcia as a cadet.
He fought in North Africa from 1791 and in the Peninsular War of 1808, and for his part in the Spanish victory at Bailén on 19 July 1808 he received a gold medal and promotion to lieutenant colonel.

In 1812 San Martín sailed for Buenos Aires and offered his services to the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata. The First Triumvirate made him a lieutenant colonel of cavalry and asked him to form the Regiment of Mounted Grenadiers. His plan to defeat the Spanish forces menacing from the north by an alternative route through the Viceroyalty of Peru required a new army, the Army of the Andes, raised in Cuyo Province. He led it across the Andes into Chile.

At Chacabuco on 12 February the army won in a pincer movement; about 600 royalists were killed and 500 taken prisoner, against 12 dead in the Army of the Andes. San Martín declined the post of Supreme Director of Chile and proposed Bernardo O'Higgins, and he won at Maipú in 1818. He then sailed from Chile with a fleet on 20 August 1820 and landed at Paracas on 7 September. He was appointed Protector of Peru on 12 July 1821, and independence was declared on 28 July.

On 26 July 1822 San Martín met Simón Bolívar in two private meetings at Guayaquil. With no witnesses or minutes, their content can only be inferred from later actions and letters. San Martín then left Peru, resigned his command and moved to France in 1824. He settled in Brussels and died at Boulogne-sur-Mer on 17 August 1850. His remains were brought to Buenos Aires on 29 May 1880 and placed in a mausoleum in the Metropolitan Cathedral.

He was first acclaimed as a national hero by the Federals, while the unitarians resented his refusal to aid the Supreme Directors with the Army of the Andes. Bartolomé Mitre's biography made him universally acclaimed as Liberator of Argentina, though later historians corrected inaccuracies in it. His statues stand in most cities of Argentina and in Santiago and Lima, and the Order of the Liberator General San Martín is the highest decoration of the Argentine government.
jose-figueres-ferrer: José Figueres Ferrer was born on 25 September 1906 in San Ramón, the eldest of four children of a doctor and a teacher who had recently come from Catalonia, and his first language was Catalan. In 1924 he went to Boston and studied hydroelectric engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Back in Costa Rica in 1928 he bought a remote mountain farm which he named La Lucha Sin Fin, the Endless Struggle, and which remained his home until his death. He became a coffee grower and rope manufacturer employing more than 1,000 sharecroppers and factory workers, and called himself a farmer-socialist.

Figueres returned from two years of exile in 1944, having criticised President Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia, and founded a Democratic Action current that became the Social Democratic Party. The 1 March 1948 presidential election, in which Otilio Ulate had apparently defeated Calderón, was annulled by Calderón's supporters. Protests grew into armed conflict, and Figueres defeated the Costa Rican Army and communist-led guerrillas who had joined President Teodoro Picado. The 44-day civil war killed more than 2,000 people and was the bloodiest event of twentieth-century Costa Rican history.

Figueres then headed a provisional junta, the Founding Council, for eighteen months. It abolished the army, nationalised the banks, enabled women and illiterates to vote, gave citizenship to the children of Black immigrants, outlawed the Communist Party, set up a civil service and directed the writing of a new constitution. Figueres later said it had decreed 834 reforms. He then handed power to Ulate. In 1953 he created the National Liberation Party and was elected president.

During his presidency from 1953 to 1958 Figueres promoted private industry and the national industrial sector and helped build the Pan-American Highway. Implicated in an invasion of Nicaragua by exiles in April 1954, he faced an invasion led by Calderón in January 1955 and promised the Nicaraguan ruler to sever links with the exiles. He survived an assassination attempt in 1957. Elected again, he served from 1970 to 1974; in 1972 he sold 30,000 tons of coffee to the Soviet Union, and Costa Rica established diplomatic relations with Moscow.

His administrations created the Costa Rica Institute of Technology, the National University and the Costa Rican Electricity Institute as an autonomous body. He died on 8 June 1990 in San José at the age of 83 and was given a state funeral. His son José María Figueres was president from 1994 to 1998.
jose-gaspar-rodriguez-de-francia: José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia was born on 6 January 1766 at Yaguarón, in what is now the department of Paraguarí. His father was a tobacco planter from São Paulo and his mother a Paraguayan descended from Spanish colonists. He studied at the monastery school of San Francisco in Asunción, intended for the priesthood but never ordained, and earned a degree in theology and philosophy at the National University of Córdoba in 1785. He read Voltaire, Rousseau and the Encyclopédistes, taught theology in Asunción from 1790, and then turned to law. He joined the cabildo of Asunción in 1807 and headed it by August 1809.

After Paraguay declared independence on 15 May 1811 Francia became secretary of the ruling junta, but resigned on 1 August because the army dominated Congress. From his farm near Asunción he told ordinary citizens that the revolution had only replaced a Spanish-born elite with a criollo one. On 1 October 1814 Congress named him sole consul with absolute powers for three years, and on 1 June 1816 another Congress voted him control of the country for life. He was known as El Supremo. In March 1814 he had forbidden Spaniards to marry other Spaniards, to weaken the old elite.

In February 1820 his political police uncovered a plot against him, and almost 200 prominent Paraguayans were arrested, most of whom he executed. He outlawed opposition, kept a secret police and banished prisoners to the camp at Tevego. He closed trade with the outside world but encouraged internal agriculture and industry, nationalised about half the land in four stages, leased it to peasants, took over clerical lands and monasteries, and ended the cabildo in 1825. He made state education compulsory for males in 1828 and opened the first public library in 1836.

Francia died on 20 September 1840. He lived simply, and the treasury held at least twice as much money as when he took office. Abroad his reputation was negative: Charles Darwin hoped he would be overthrown, while Thomas Carlyle found something to admire. Paraguayans regard him as a national hero, and a museum in Yaguarón is dedicated to him. His rule left a tradition of autocracy that lasted, with few breaks, until 1989.
jose-gervasio-artigas: José Gervasio Artigas was born in Montevideo on 19 June 1764 to Martín José Artigas and Francisca Antonia Arnal, who came from a wealthy family. His parents enrolled him in the Colegio de San Bernardino for religious studies, but he refused its strict discipline. At 12 he moved to the countryside to work on the family's farms, where contact with gauchos and Indians made a great impression on him.

He later took part in cattle smuggling and was wanted by the hacienda owners and the government in Montevideo. When the Anglo-Spanish War raised the threat of British invasion, the viceroy negotiated a pardon on condition that he join the Corps of Blandengues, and his military career began in 1797. He was promoted to captain in 1809.

In February 1811 the viceroy Francisco Javier de Elío declared war on Buenos Aires, and the independence movement of the Banda Oriental began. Artigas's forces defeated a Montevidean army at Las Piedras and surrounded Montevideo. When Elío called in Portuguese forces and Buenos Aires signed a truce recognising him, Artigas felt it to be treason, broke with the city and led his followers to Entre Ríos in the Oriental exodus. He insisted on a national organisation on federalist principles.

In 1814 he organised the League of the Free Peoples and was declared its Protector, and in 1815 he took Montevideo from the centralist faction of Buenos Aires. At the Congress of Oriente in 1815 the Oriental Province, Córdoba, Corrientes, Entre Ríos, Misiones and Santa Fe declared themselves independent from Spain and formed the Federal League. In August 1816 Portugal invaded the Eastern Province, with tacit complicity from Buenos Aires, because the League alarmed Buenos Aires by its federalism and Portugal by its republicanism.

The Portuguese under Carlos Frederico Lecor occupied Montevideo on 20 January 1817, and the struggle continued in the countryside for three years. His subordinates Francisco Ramírez and Estanislao López made agreements with Buenos Aires against his principles and turned on him. Without men or resources he withdrew to Paraguay in September 1820, where the dictator Francia banished him to Candelaria. He died in Paraguay on 23 September 1850, aged 86. His remains were taken to the Artigas Mausoleum in Montevideo in 1977.

Artigas was a staunch democrat and federalist, opposed to monarchism and centralism, and drew on Thomas Paine and Rousseau. In Uruguay he is a national hero, and his birthday on 19 June is a national holiday.
jose-lopez-portillo: José Guillermo Abel López Portillo y Pacheco was born in Mexico City on 16 June 1920, the son of José López Portillo y Weber, an engineer, historian and academic, and Refugio Pacheco y Villa-Gordoa. His grandfather José López Portillo y Rojas was a lawyer, politician and man of letters. He studied law at the National Autonomous University of Mexico and began his political career with the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in 1959. After holding several posts under his two predecessors, he served as finance minister under Luis Echeverría, a friend from childhood, between 1973 and 1975. He described himself as neither of the right nor of the left.

Echeverría chose him as the PRI's candidate, which assured his victory, and in 1976 López Portillo was elected without an opponent. Mexico was then in an economic crisis. He undertook a programme of development paid for by oil revenue after Pemex, the publicly owned oil company, found new reserves in Veracruz and Tabasco. In 1980 Mexico joined Venezuela in the Pact of San José, which sold oil at preferential rates to countries of Central America and the Caribbean. Public spending rose from 32 per cent to 46 per cent of GDP during his term.

An electoral reform of 1977 raised the Chamber of Deputies to 400 members, with 100 elected by proportional representation, and opened the process to small opposition parties. Critics accused his government of corruption and nepotism, since relatives held public posts.

Oil prices fell in the summer of 1981, and by 1982 Mexico had declared a sovereign default. The peso was devalued in February 1982, and in his last state of the nation address on 1 September 1982 he ordered the nationalisation of the banking system and condemned those responsible for capital flight. In foreign policy Mexico supported the Sandinista National Liberation Front in Nicaragua, hosted the Cancun Summit of 1981, and in 1979 gave asylum to the deposed Shah of Iran, who spent some months in Cuernavaca. Pope John Paul II also visited Mexico for the first time that year.

López Portillo chose Miguel de la Madrid as his successor and left office on 1 December 1982, as Mexico entered the debt crisis of the decade that followed. He was the last of the economic nationalist presidents from the PRI, and later presidents supported free trade. He wrote books including Quetzalcóatl (1965) and the memoirs Mis tiempos (1988). He died of complications of pneumonia at his home in Mexico City on 17 February 2004, aged 83, and was buried at the Mexico City Military Cemetery.
jose-manuel-balmaceda: José Manuel Balmaceda was born on 19 July 1840 at the Hacienda Bucalemu in Santo Domingo, the eldest of twelve children of a landowner and parliamentarian from the aristocratic Balmaceda family. He studied theology at the Seminario Conciliar de Santiago and considered the priesthood, but opted against it after being exposed to the ideas of the Enlightenment. In 1868 he helped found the newspaper La Libertad, and in 1869 he joined the Club de la Reforma, which became the political basis of the Liberal Party.

He was elected deputy for Carelmapu several times from 1864 and is credited with persuading Argentina in 1878 not to join the War of the Pacific. As Minister of the Interior under Domingo Santa María he carried through compulsory civil marriage and allowed people of any faith to be buried in cemeteries previously reserved for Catholics, which earned him the hostility of conservatives and the clergy. He was proclaimed a presidential candidate on 17 January 1886 and elected as sole candidate on 25 June.

Balmaceda became president on 18 September 1886. He began heavy spending on railways, schools and colleges, the navy and the fortification of Valparaíso, Talcahuano and Iquique, with contracts worth £6,000,000 let for southern railways. Corruption crept into the spending, and contracts went by favour. Opposition in Congress grew from late 1887 and by 1889 was distinctly hostile. Chilean custom held that a ministry needed a majority in the chambers, but Balmaceda held that the constitution let him keep any ministers he chose.

In 1890 Congress refused funds, and the compromise cabinet that followed soon resigned. On 1 January 1891 Balmaceda decreed that the 1890 budget would stand for 1891, an act that exceeded the authority of the executive. The vice-president of the Senate, Waldo Silva, and the president of the Chamber, Ramón Barros Luco, then appointed Captain Jorge Montt to command the navy, and on 7 January they sailed north to Tarapacá to organize armed resistance. The army stayed loyal to Balmaceda and the navy supported Congress.

After his forces were destroyed at the Battle of La Placilla, Balmaceda took refuge in the Argentine legation. General Manuel Baquedano kept order in Santiago until the congressional leaders arrived on 30 August. On 19 September 1891, the day after the term for which he had been elected ended, Balmaceda shot himself; in letters written shortly before, he said he did not believe the victors would give him an impartial trial. His death closed the most severe and bloodiest struggle Chile had witnessed. On 23 May 1891 the Times correspondent Maurice Hervey alleged that British owners of the Tarapacá nitrate deposits had financed the revolution. His children included the poet Pedro Balmaceda and the diplomat Enrique Balmaceda.
jose-maria-arguedas: José María Arguedas was born on 18 January 1911 in Andahuaylas, a province in the southern Andes, into a well-off family. His mother died when he was two. His father, a lawyer, travelled often, and the boy's relations with his stepmother and stepbrother were bad, so he found comfort among the family's Indigenous servants. From the age of 7 to 11 he lived in two Quechua households and so became fluent in Quechua.

He began studying at the National University of San Marcos in Lima in 1931 and graduated in literature, later taking a degree in ethnology in 1957 and a doctorate in 1963. In 1937 and 1938 he was held in El Sexto Prison for protesting against an envoy sent to Peru by Mussolini.

Arguedas began with short stories about the Indigenous world of his childhood, written in a Spanish strongly influenced by Quechua syntax and vocabulary. His first novel, Yawar Fiesta, appeared in 1941. It introduced the theme he followed for the rest of his career, the clash between Western civilisation and the Indigenous traditional way of life. He followed it with Los ríos profundos (Deep Rivers, 1958) and Todas las sangres (All the Bloods, 1964).

Though counted among the indigenista writers, he tried to give the Andean Indians a true voice, and he also wrote of mestizos moving between two parts of their identity and of the violence and exploitation of race relations in rural towns and haciendas. Some critics held that he portrayed Indian characters as too gentle and childlike, and in 1965 social scientists at the Instituto de Estudios Peruanos criticised Todas las sangres bluntly at a roundtable.

In 1968 Arguedas received the Inca Garcilaso de la Vega literary prize and gave the speech No soy un aculturado, 'I am not an acculturated man'. His depression reached a crisis in 1966, when he attempted suicide. The psychiatrist Lola Hoffman advised him to keep writing, and he began El zorro de arriba y el zorro de abajo, named for a Quechua myth he had translated. In 1969 he shot himself at the National Agrarian University in La Molina, leaving instructions for his funeral, a diary and the unfinished manuscript. Since 2000 Casa de las Américas has awarded the José María Arguedas Narrative Prize.
jose-maria-morelos: José María Morelos was born at Valladolid in Michoacán on 30 September 1765. His father was a carpenter and his mother came from a village near Valladolid. Although often described as having mixed or indigenous descent, he was classed as a Spaniard in his baptismal register, though his paternal ancestry included Spaniards, Africans and mestizos. He worked as a muleteer, and in 1789 he enrolled at the Colegio de San Nicolás, where Miguel Hidalgo y Costilla was rector. He became priest of Carácuaro in 1799 and fathered at least three children, among them Juan Nepomuceno Almonte.

After Hidalgo's Cry of Dolores in September 1810, Morelos met him in October and was told to recruit troops in the south and capture Acapulco. He showed military skill, and in his first nine months he is said to have won 22 victories and taken almost all of what is now Guerrero. In his second campaign his forces were besieged at Cuautla by the royalist general Félix María Calleja del Rey; on 2 May 1812, after 58 days, he broke out. In 1812 he took Orizaba and Oaxaca, and Acapulco fell on 12 April 1813.

In 1813 he called the Congress of Chilpancingo, which called itself the Congress of Anáhuac. It endorsed his Sentimientos de la Nación, which declared independence, made Catholicism the official religion, abolished slavery, racial categories, torture and tribute, and divided government into three branches. Morelos refused the title Generalissimo and asked to be called Servant of the Nation. The Congress declared independence on 6 November 1813 and promulgated the Constitution of Apatzingán on 22 October 1814.

A series of defeats followed. In November 1815, while escorting the Congress, Morelos was beaten at Temalaca and told his men to save themselves, leaving him alone to be captured. The Inquisition in Mexico City drew up 23 charges against him, including treason and sending his sons to the United States. He was sentenced to death for treason and shot at San Cristóbal Ecatepec on 22 December 1815. His lieutenant Vicente Guerrero continued the war.

Morelos is regarded as a national hero of Mexico. The state of Morelos and the city of Morelia bear his name, and his remains lie in the Monument to Independence in Mexico City with those of other insurgent heroes.
jose-maria-velasco-ibarra: José María Velasco Ibarra was born in Quito on 19 March 1893 to Delia Ibarra and Alejandrino Velasco, a civil engineer who was a political activist for the conservative party. His mother taught him at home, and his father died when he was 16. He attended the Colegio San Gabriel and took a doctorate in jurisprudence at the Central University of Ecuador. He published books, among them Conciencia y Barbarie, and wrote as a columnist for El Comercio. After a first post in Quito's municipal government he became a deputy, and in 1932 he was elected president of the Chamber of Deputies.

In the election of 1933 he received 80 percent of the votes cast, the highest share in Ecuadorian history. His first presidency began on 1 September 1934, but parliament would not support his policies, he tried to seize dictatorial powers, and a military coup ousted him in August 1935. He lost the 1940 election narrowly to Carlos Arroyo del Río, amid signs of fraud, and was exiled after plotting a coup.

In May 1944, after Ecuador's defeat by Peru, the Glorious Revolution made him Supreme Chief and then constitutional president. In March 1946 he suspended the constitution, seized dictatorial powers and shut down most leftist media, and in August 1947 three defence ministers deposed him. He won again in 1952 and served until 31 August 1956, a term in which 311 schools were built.

Elected a fourth time in 1960, he declared the Rio de Janeiro Protocol null, which fed later conflicts with Peru, and was ousted on 7 November 1961. Winning a fifth time in 1968, he suspended the constitution in 1970. On 15 February 1972 the military overthrew him and installed General Guillermo Rodríguez Lara, fearing that Assad Bucaram of the CFP would win the elections he had announced.
Velasco Ibarra governed for nearly 13 years in all. He had no formal party; his oratory drew followers, and he is quoted as saying, Give me a balcony and I will become president.

Scholars debate whether his rule was populist. Following Agustín Cueva, some argue that he rose on the votes of coastal peasants who had migrated to the cities as the cacao industry dwindled, while Rafael Quintero argues that the landowning elite was decisive in the 1930s. He did not carry out major reforms, but he built roads, hospitals and bridges and decreed a weekly day off for workers. After his wife Corina Parral died in Buenos Aires, he returned to Ecuador, saying he came to meditate and to die. He died in Quito on 30 March 1979.
jose-marti: José Julián Martí Pérez was born on 28 January 1853 in Havana, to Spanish parents: a Valencian father, Mariano Martí Navarro, and Leonor Pérez Cabrera, a native of the Canary Islands. He was the older brother of seven sisters. When he was four the family moved to Valencia, and two years later they returned to the island. In January 1871 he sailed from Havana to Cádiz and settled in Madrid, where he studied law and took part in debate on the Cuban question through the Spanish press, circulating documents that protested Spanish actions in Cuba.

Martí lived in Mexico City from 1875 and joined the editorial staff of the Revista Universal. In 1881, after a brief stay in New York, he founded the Revista Venezolana in Caracas, which angered the dictator Antonio Guzmán Blanco and forced his return to New York. There he joined General Calixto García's committee of Cuban exiles and worked as a journalist for La Nación of Buenos Aires and Central American papers. He translated novels, served as consul for Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay, and founded the newspaper Patria, which became the organ of the Cuban Revolutionary Party. In a letter to Máximo Gómez in 1882 he proposed a revolutionary party, to keep Cuba from falling back on the Home Rule Party after the Pact of Zanjón.

In 1891 he published the essay Nuestra América and, in October, the verses Versos Sencillos. In January 1895 United States authorities stopped three ships at Fernandina in Florida and confiscated weapons, ruining the Fernandina Plan. The uprising began on 24 February 1895, and a month later Martí and Gómez issued the Manifesto of Montecristi.

Martí was killed fighting Spanish troops at the Battle of Dos Ríos, near the confluence of the Contramaestre and Cauto rivers, on 19 May 1895. Gómez had judged the Spanish position strong and ordered his men to disengage, but Martí, seeing a young courier, called for a charge. He wore a black jacket and rode a white horse. He was buried at Santa Ifigenia Cemetery in Santiago de Cuba.

He wrote poems, essays, a serialized novel, lectures, letters and a children's magazine, La Edad de Oro, and is counted a major figure of the Spanish American movement known as Modernismo. His prose influenced Rubén Darío. Verses from Versos Sencillos were adapted into the song Guantanamera. Martí opposed slavery, warned of United States designs on Cuba and argued that Latin American countries should build institutions fitted to their own history and nature. His thought has been invoked in competing visions of the Cuban nation, and José Martí International Airport in Havana bears his name.
jose-mujica: José Alberto Mujica Cordano was born on 20 May 1935 in the Paso de la Arena neighbourhood of Montevideo. His father, a farmer, went bankrupt and died in 1940, when José was five. In 1956 he met the politician Enrique Erro, and he became general secretary of the National Party. In 1962 he and Erro left it to found the left-wing Unión Popular with the Socialist Party; its candidate for president received only 2.3 per cent of the vote.

In the mid-1960s Mujica joined the MLN-Tupamaros, a far-left armed group inspired by the Cuban Revolution. In 1969 he led one of six squads in the brief taking of the town of Pando, and in March 1970 he was shot six times while resisting arrest in a Montevideo bar. He was captured four times and twice escaped from Punta Carretas Prison, in September 1971 with more than 100 other Tupamaros through a tunnel, and again in April 1972. After the military coup of 1973 he was among nine Tupamaros held in squalid conditions, including more than two years confined in an emptied horse trough. He was freed in 1985 under an amnesty after democracy returned.

With other former Tupamaros he helped form the Movement of Popular Participation, which joined the Broad Front coalition. He was elected deputy in 1994 and senator in 1999, and served as minister of livestock, agriculture and fisheries from 2005 to 2008 under Tabaré Vázquez. In 2009 he won the Broad Front's primary and then the presidency, with more than 52 per cent in the runoff of 29 November, and took office on 1 March 2010.

His government legalised state-controlled sales of marijuana from 2012, saying that this would take the trade from drug traffickers, and it passed same-sex marriage and legalised abortion. Social spending rose from 60.9 to 75.5 per cent of public expenditure between 2004 and 2013, the minimum wage was raised from 4,800 to 10,000 pesos and trade unions were strengthened. In 2013 he spoke to the United Nations General Assembly, urging a return to simplicity. He gave about 90 per cent of his salary to charity, declined the presidential palace and drove a 1987 Volkswagen Beetle. The constitution barred immediate re-election, and Vázquez succeeded him on 1 March 2015. Mujica remained a senator until 2020, and he died at his farmhouse near Montevideo on 13 May 2025.
jose-p-laurel: José Paciano Laurel y García was born on 9 March 1891 at Tanauan, Batangas. His father had been an official in the revolutionary government of Emilio Aguinaldo and signed the 1899 Malolos Constitution. Laurel studied in Manila and took his law degree at the University of the Philippines in 1915, placing second in the bar examination. He earned a doctorate at Yale Law School in 1920 and returned to the Philippines in 1921. He became secretary of the interior in 1923 and resigned the same year with other cabinet members in protest at the American governor-general Leonard Wood.

Laurel was elected to the Philippine Senate in 1925 and lost his seat in 1931. He was a delegate to the 1935 Constitutional Convention, where he sponsored the Bill of Rights, and in 1936 became an associate justice of the Supreme Court. His opinions in Angara v. Electoral Commission (1936) and Ang Tibay v. CIR (1940) became leading cases on judicial review and due process.

After the Japanese invasion of December 1941, President Manuel Quezon told Laurel and other officials to stay. Laurel cooperated with the occupation authorities, in contrast to Chief Justice José Abad Santos, who was shot for refusing. He held posts under the military administration and was shot four times at a golf course on 5 June 1943; he recovered.

Under strong Japanese influence the National Assembly chose Laurel president, and he took the oath on 14 October 1943 at the head of the Second Philippine Republic. The treaty of alliance signed on 20 October 1943 foresaw no conscription. Hunger was the chief problem, with prices rising and the sugar supply gone, and Japanese demands and guerrilla fighting made government hard. In September 1944 he declared martial law and a state of war with the United States and the United Kingdom. Much of the population resisted the occupation and supported the exiled Commonwealth government.

He left for Japan in March 1945 and dissolved his regime at Nara on 17 August 1945. He was held at Sugamo Prison, returned to Manila in 1946 and was charged with 132 counts of treason, but the trial ended with President Manuel Roxas's amnesty in 1948. He lost the 1949 presidential election, won a Senate seat in 1951 and headed the mission behind the Laurel–Langley Agreement. He died on 6 November 1959.
jose-rizal: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda was born on 19 June 1861. His family took Rizal as a second surname after Governor-General Narciso Clavería decreed in 1849 that Filipinos adopt Spanish surnames from a list, and continued to use Mercado. The family's patrilineal line traced back to Lam-co, a Chinese merchant from Fujian who settled in Calamba in 1697.

In May 1882, without his parents' knowledge, but secretly supported by his brother Paciano and his uncle Antonio, he left for Spain to study. He became an ophthalmologist by profession and a key member of the Propaganda Movement of the 1880s, which advocated political reforms for the colony.

Rizal wrote mostly in Spanish. His essays include El amor patrio of 1882 and Filipinas dentro de cien años, 1889–90, and he annotated Antonio de Morga's Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas, published in 1890 after he moved from Paris to Brussels. His novels Noli Me Tángere (1887) and its sequel El filibusterismo (1891) are together taken as a national epic. His poetry includes Mi último adiós, written in 1896.

On his return to Manila in 1892 he formed La Liga Filipina, which advocated moderate social reforms through legal means but was disbanded by the governor. On 6 July 1892 he was arrested for alleged possession of a seditious document and banished to Dapitan on Mindanao. There he built a school, a hospital and a water supply system, taught, and farmed. In February 1895 he met Josephine Bracken, an Irish woman from Hong Kong, who later became his common-law wife.

With Governor General Ramón Blanco's leave to serve as a doctor in Cuba, Rizal left Dapitan on 1 August 1896. By then the Katipunan's rebellion had become a nationwide revolution. At a stopover in Barcelona he was arrested on 6 October 1896. He was executed for rebellion on 30 December 1896 by a squad of Filipino soldiers of the Spanish Army, with a backup force of regular troops ready to shoot the executioners if they refused orders. Though not involved in the revolution's planning or conduct, he ultimately approved of its goals. His last words were reported as consummatum est, it is finished.

Rizal is widely considered one of the most influential figures in the Philippines and has been recommended as a national hero by an officially empaneled National Heroes Committee. No law, executive order or proclamation has officially proclaimed any Filipino historical figure a national hero.
josef-terboven: Josef Terboven was born in Essen on 23 May 1898, the son of minor landed gentry of Dutch descent. He volunteered for military service in the First World War, served in field artillery and the new air force, won the Iron Cross and was discharged as a lieutenant in December 1918. He studied law and political science at Munich and Freiburg but left in 1922 without a degree, and worked as a bank clerk until June 1925. He joined the Nazi Party in November 1923 and took part in the Beer Hall Putsch.

From August 1925 Terboven worked full time for the party in Essen, founding its local group and editing the weekly The New Front. Named Gauleiter of Essen on 1 August 1930, he kept the post through the Nazi period. He sat in the Reichstag from September 1930, became a member of the Prussian State Council in 1933, and in 1934 married Ilse Stahl, Joseph Goebbels's former secretary; Hitler witnessed the wedding. In 1935 he became Oberpräsident of the Rhine Province, uniting party and state offices in his area.

Terboven was named Reichskommissar for Norway on 24 April 1940, before the invasion was complete, and answered only to Hitler. He saw himself as a viceroy with limitless power of command. He had authority over the small German civilian administration, not over the 400,000 army troops under Nikolaus von Falkenhorst, but he commanded a force of around 6,000 men. On 25 September 1940 he dismissed Norway's Administrative Council, appointed a Provisional State Council, declared King Haakon VII deposed and banned every party except Vidkun Quisling's Nasjonal Samling. A Quisling government followed in February 1942.

He set up concentration camps, among them Falstad and Bredtvet, and ordered the Beisfjord massacre of 18 July 1942, in which about 288 Yugoslav prisoners were shot or burned to death. SS and Police Tribunals sentenced some 150 Norwegians to death. After two Gestapo men were killed at Telavåg in 1942, he led a reprisal that burned the village; 72 were deported, and 31 of them died in captivity. About 770 Jews were deported to Germany. In October 1944 a scorched earth policy in Finnmark forced 50,000 people to leave. Dönitz dismissed him on 7 May 1945, and on 8 May he killed himself with dynamite in a bunker at Skaugum.
joseph-bonaparte: Joseph was born Giuseppe Buonaparte on 7 January 1768 at Corte, then capital of the Corsican Republic, to Carlo Buonaparte and Maria Letizia Ramolino. Corsica was invaded by France in the year of his birth. He trained as a lawyer, sat in the Council of Five Hundred and served as French ambassador to the Papal States. In 1799 he helped Napoleon overthrow the Directory, and on 30 September 1800 he signed the Treaty of Mortefontaine, a treaty of friendship and commerce between France and the United States.

After Austerlitz, Napoleon declared on 27 December 1805 that Ferdinand IV of Naples had forfeited his kingdom. Joseph nominally commanded the invading army, with Marshal Masséna in effective command. The French crossed the border on 8 February 1806 with little resistance, and Joseph entered Naples on 15 February. On 30 March Napoleon decreed him King of Naples and Sicily.
