He kept most Bourbon officials in post and began reforms on the French model: monastic orders were suppressed and their property nationalised, feudal privileges and taxes were abolished with compensation for the nobility, and roads and public works were begun.

Joseph was moved to Spain in August 1808, and his brother-in-law Joachim Murat succeeded him in Naples. In Spain he was extremely unpopular, and his opponents called him Pepe Botella for alleged heavy drinking, though he was abstemious. His arrival sparked a great revolt and the Peninsular War, and his command of the French forces was largely nominal. He ended the Spanish Inquisition, but his foreign birth kept most Spanish people from accepting him. He left the throne after the French defeat at Vitoria in 1813.

After 1815 Joseph went to the United States, and from 1817 to 1832 lived mainly there, at Point Breeze, an estate at Bordentown, New Jersey. He was elected to the American Philosophical Society in 1823. He moved to London in 1832 and died in Florence on 28 July 1844. His body was returned to France and buried in Les Invalides. Joseph Bonaparte Gulf in Australia is named after him.
joseph-conrad: Conrad was born on 3 December 1857 in Berdychiv, in what was then the Russian Empire, in a region that had once belonged to the Crown of the Kingdom of Poland. He was the only child of Apollo Korzeniowski, a writer, translator, political activist and would-be revolutionary, and his wife Ewa Bobrowska. Almost all the countryside around was owned by the Polish nobility, to which his family belonged, and Polish patriotic literature was held in high esteem there. He was officially a Russian subject until his naturalisation as a British subject.

Conrad spoke Polish and French fluently from childhood and acquired English only in his twenties, always speaking it with a strong foreign accent. He served in the French and British merchant navies, and a Corsican seaman he befriended in Marseille, Dominique Cervoni, inspired some of his characters, such as the title character of Nostromo in 1904. In the autumn of 1889 he began his first novel, Almayer's Folly, published in 1895. His later novels include Heart of Darkness in 1899, Lord Jim in 1900, The Secret Agent in 1907 and Under Western Eyes in 1911.

Many of his novels and stories have nautical settings and depict crises of human individuality in what he saw as an indifferent, inscrutable and amoral world. He is considered a literary impressionist by some and an early modernist by others. Writing near the peak of the British Empire, he drew on the experience of Poland, divided among three empires, to explore imperialism and colonialism. In 1975 the Nigerian writer Chinua Achebe called him a thoroughgoing racist, a charge that most later criticism of Conrad has addressed.

Conrad was in Poland with his family when the First World War broke out in 1914, and they took refuge in the mountain resort of Zakopane. He died on 3 August 1924 at his house in Bishopsbourne, Kent, probably of a heart attack, and was buried at Canterbury Cemetery. His friends included Henry James, John Galsworthy, Stephen Crane and H. G. Wells. After the publication of Chance in 1913 he was the subject of more discussion and praise than any other English writer of the time, and his narrative style and anti-heroic characters have influenced numerous authors.
joseph-de-maistre: Joseph de Maistre was born on 1 April 1753 at Chambéry in the Duchy of Savoy, then part of the Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia. His family was of French and Italian origin. Maistre was the eldest of ten surviving children and was probably educated by the Jesuits. After training in law at the University of Turin, completed in 1774, he became a senator in 1787, like his father. In his early years he was a liberal and a supporter of Gallicanism,.

The passing of the August Decrees on 4 August 1789 turned him decisively against the course of events in France. When a French revolutionary army took Chambéry in 1792 he fled. He found no position at the royal court in Turin and went to Lausanne, where he discussed politics and theology in the salon of Madame de Staël and began his career as a counter-revolutionary writer, with Letters from a Savoyard Royalist in 1793. After the French took Turin in 1798 he went to Venice and then to Cagliari, where the king of Piedmont-Sardinia held his court.

In 1802 he was sent as ambassador to Tsar Alexander I in Saint Petersburg. His diplomatic duties were few, and he became a well-loved presence in aristocratic and merchant circles and wrote his most influential works. After the restoration of the House of Savoy under the Congress of Vienna he returned to Turin in 1817 and served as magistrate and minister of state until his death on 26 February 1821.

In Considerations on France of 1796 he argued that the Revolution was divine punishment for the promotion of Enlightenment thought by the Ancien Régime. He held that constitutions are not products of human reason but come from God, and that written constitutions are scraps of paper. He criticised Rousseau and the Encyclopaedists for treating people as fundamentally rational and for resting theories on abstract reasoning instead of history. His book On the Pope of 1819 set out his religious view of authority: government must rest on grounds its subjects are not allowed to question, and in Europe the final religious authority lies with the Pope.

With Edmund Burke he is commonly regarded as a founder of European conservatism. His influence reached Juan Donoso Cortés, Charles Maurras and Carl Schmitt,. Isaiah Berlin called him the most brilliant and most polemical critic of the philosophy that underlay the French Revolution.
joseph-goebbels: Paul Joseph Goebbels was born on 29 October 1897 in Rheydt, near Mönchengladbach, to Catholic parents of modest means. As a child he had a deformed right foot that an operation failed to correct. He wore a metal brace, walked with a limp and was rejected for military service in the First World War. He aspired to be an author and in 1922 obtained a doctorate in philology from the University of Heidelberg. He took an interest in Hitler during Hitler's treason trial of 1924 and joined the Nazi Party that year, drawn largely by Hitler's charisma. He worked for Gregor Strasser in northern Germany as editor and speaker.

In 1926 Goebbels accepted the post of Gauleiter of Berlin. He answered only to Hitler and controlled the local SA and SS. He deliberately provoked street brawls for publicity and used large type and red ink on posters. In the Reichstag election of 20 May 1928 he was one of the first 12 Nazi members elected, which gave him immunity from prosecution. In 1930 Hitler appointed him Reich leader of Nazi propaganda in place of Strasser.

After Hitler became Reich chancellor on 30 January 1933, Goebbels' Propaganda Ministry quickly gained control over news, media, arts and information, and he used radio and film to full effect. He was an antisemite from a young age and repeatedly urged Hitler to act against Jews. He promoted persecution through propaganda, pogroms and legislation, and in Berlin he banned Jews from public transport and required Jewish shops to be marked.

In 1943 Goebbels began to press Hitler for measures to produce total war, such as conscripting women into the labour force. Hitler appointed him Reich Plenipotentiary for Total War on 23 July 1944, but his measures were largely unsuccessful. In April 1945 his wife Magda and their children joined Hitler in Berlin. Hitler killed himself on 30 April, and under his will Goebbels succeeded him as Chancellor of Germany for one day. On 1 May 1945 Goebbels and Magda killed themselves after poisoning their six children with a cyanide compound.
joseph-haydn: Joseph Haydn was born on 31 March 1732 in Rohrau, a village then on the border with Hungary. His father Mathias was a wheelwright and an enthusiastic folk musician, and his mother Maria, née Koller, had worked as a cook in the palace of Count Harrach. Neither could read music, but the family often sang together. Around the age of six he was apprenticed to a relative, Johann Matthias Frankh, at Hainburg, and later served as a chorister at St Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna. By 1749 his voice had broken, and after he snipped off a fellow chorister's pigtail he was dismissed and sent into the streets.

Haydn made his living as a freelancer, as a teacher, a street serenader and, in 1752, valet-accompanist to the Italian composer Nicola Porpora. He taught himself counterpoint from Fux's Gradus ad Parnassum and studied Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach. As Kapellmeister to Count Morzin he wrote his first symphonies, and in 1761 Prince Paul Anton Esterházy gave him a post that put him in charge of most of the Esterházy musical establishment; he became full Kapellmeister in 1766. Isolated at the palace of Eszterháza, he was, as he put it, forced to become original.

After Prince Nikolaus died in 1790, Haydn accepted an offer from the impresario Johann Peter Salomon to conduct new symphonies in London, leaving Vienna on 15 December 1790. Returning in 1795, he again served the Esterházys part-time, and with the librettist Gottfried van Swieten composed the oratorios The Creation (1798) and The Seasons (1801). In 1797 he wrote the Emperor's Hymn after hearing audiences sing God Save the King in London.

By the end of 1803 weakness, dizziness and swollen legs left Haydn unable to compose, though musical ideas, he said, pursued him to the point of torture. He died in Vienna on 31 May 1809 at the age of 77. He composed 106 symphonies, and the scholar James Webster judged that no other composer approaches his combination of productivity, quality and historical importance in the symphony and the string quartet. Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven are sometimes called the First Viennese School. The melody of the Emperor's Hymn was used for the Deutschlandlied of 1841, whose third stanza is the national anthem of Germany.
joseph-i-holy-roman-emperor: Joseph was born in Vienna on 26 July 1678, the eldest son of Leopold I from his third wife, Eleonor Magdalene of Neuburg. He was educated strictly by Charles Theodore, Prince of Salm, and became a good linguist. Perhaps through the influence of his formerly Protestant tutor, he was a less devout Catholic than his parents and an adherent of the early Enlightenment. His two enthusiasms were music and hunting. He was crowned King of Hungary at the age of nine, in 1687, and elected King of the Romans at eleven. His only military service was at the Siege of Landau in 1702.

As emperor Joseph reduced the large number of privy councillors, tried to make the bureaucracy more efficient and had some success in stabilising the chronically poor Habsburg finances. He continued the War of the Spanish Succession in an attempt to make his younger brother Charles king of Spain. Victories won by his general Prince Eugene of Savoy established Austrian hegemony over Italy. When he laid claim to imperial rights in Italy, he risked a military conflict with the Pope over the Duchy of Mantua, and Pope Clement XI threatened him with excommunication on 16 June 1708.

In Hungary he inherited the rebellion of Francis II Rákóczi, which lasted through his whole reign. Unlike his predecessors, he refrained from executing the leaders and agreed instead to a compromise peace, which in the long term eased the integration of Hungary into the Habsburg domains. In 1706 he confirmed the religious liberties of the Orthodox Serbs and Romanians. In 1710 he extended his father's edict of outlawry against the Romani: those who returned after entering the realm were to be mutilated or branded, adult men hanged without trial, and women and boys flogged and banished. Mass killings were reported as a result.

During the smallpox epidemic of 1711 Joseph became infected and died on 17 April at the Hofburg. He was buried in the Imperial Crypt, and the Vienna district of Josefstadt is named for him. He had married Wilhelmine Amalia of Brunswick-Lüneburg in 1699, and their only son died before his first birthday. Under the Mutual Pact of Succession, his daughters were to precede those of his brother Charles, a ruling that made no provision for Charles's daughter Maria Theresa and led to the War of the Austrian Succession. Neither the Spanish war nor the Hungarian revolt was resolved in his lifetime.
joseph-ii-holy-roman-emperor: Joseph was born on 13 March 1741 in the Hofburg in Vienna, the eldest son of Maria Theresa and Emperor Francis I, and the brother of Marie Antoinette and Leopold II. He had 15 siblings. Tutors chosen by his mother gave him a structured education that included much history. In June 1760 he married Isabella of Parma, a granddaughter of Louis XV, in a match tied to the Austro-French alliance of 1756; they had a daughter, Maria Theresa. As co-ruler he sat on the State Council and wrote minutes for his mother that contain the germs of his later policy, favouring religious toleration, a weaker Church and relief of peasants from feudal burdens.

Maria Theresa's death on 29 November 1780 left Joseph free to pursue his own policy. He abolished serfdom in 1781, issued the Patent of Toleration that year giving limited freedom of worship, secularised church lands, made elementary education compulsory and, in 1784, ordered German to replace Latin as the language of instruction. He issued over 6,000 edicts and 11,000 new laws, and made German the compulsory language of official business, which especially affected Hungary. He refused to be crowned with the Holy Crown of Hungary, because he would have had to pledge to uphold its rights, and is known there as the Hat-wearing King.

In 1784 the Allgemeines Krankenhaus opened in Vienna, though centralisation worsened sanitation and caused a 20 per cent death rate in the new hospital. In foreign policy he twice tried to acquire Bavaria, in 1778 and 1785, and was thwarted by Frederick II of Prussia. He made an alliance with Catherine II of Russia in 1781, which drew Austria into the costly and largely futile Austro-Turkish War of 1787–1791.

Joseph fell ill in the autumn of 1788, probably with pulmonary tuberculosis, and died on 20 February 1790, just short of 49. He was buried in a plain copper coffin in the Kapuzinergruft in Vienna and succeeded by his brother Leopold II. His policies are known as Josephinism, and he was a patron of the arts who commissioned Mozart's Die Entführung aus dem Serail. Forged letters, the false Constantinople letters, long made him seem a more radical philosophe than he probably was.
joseph-jenkins-roberts: Joseph Jenkins Roberts was born free in Norfolk, Virginia, the second of seven children. His mother Amelia had been freed by his father, said to be a Welsh planter, before his birth. She married James Roberts, a free man of colour who owned a boating business on the James River, and the family moved to Petersburg. Joseph worked in the family business and was apprenticed in a barber shop owned by William Colson, a minister who gave him access to his library. In 1828 he married Sarah Minor.

Restrictions on free people of colour in Virginia weighed in his decision to emigrate. On 9 February 1829 the family sailed on the Harriet under the American Colonization Society, with his mother and five siblings. His first wife and their child died in Liberia, and in 1836 he married Jane Rose Waring.

In Monrovia he ran a trading firm, Roberts, Colson, & Company, exporting palm products, camwood and ivory. He became high sheriff in 1833, with the duty of leading militias into the interior to collect taxes and put down raids, and vice governor in 1839. After the death of governor Thomas Buchanan he was appointed in 1841 as the first African American governor. A referendum chose independence, which eleven delegates declared on 26 July 1847. Roberts won the first presidential election on 5 October 1847 and took office on 3 January 1848.

He was re-elected three times and served until the 1855 election, when Vice President Benson defeated him. He travelled to Europe in 1848; the United Kingdom was the first country to recognise Liberia, while the United States withheld recognition until 5 February 1862. He expanded Liberia's borders along the coast and sought to assimilate Indigenous peoples near Monrovia through education and religious conversion. After a war with the Grebo and Kru peoples in 1856, with his help, Maryland joined Liberia in 1857.

He co-founded Liberia College in 1862 and was its first president. He returned to the presidency after the deposition of Edward James Roye in 1871, serving from 1872 until 1876, and was ill from 1875. He died on 24 February 1876 and is buried in Palm Grove Cemetery in Monrovia. His birthday, 15 March, is a national holiday in Liberia.
joseph-kasavubu: Joseph Kasa-Vubu was born in the village of Kuma-Dizi in the Mayombe district of Bas-Congo, in the west of the Belgian Congo, the eighth of nine children in a family of the Yombe, a subset of the Kongo people. He was baptised Joseph in 1925 at the Scheutist Catholic mission of Kizu and studied at a minor seminary and then at the Kabwe seminary, intending to become a priest, but was expelled by the bishop in 1939. In 1941 he married Hortense Ngoma Masunda, with whom he had nine children. From 1942 he was a clerk in the finance department of the Belgian colonial administration in Léopoldville, rising to chief clerk, the highest rank open to Congolese civil servants.

Kasa-Vubu began semi-clandestine political organising while still in colonial employment. In March 1954 he was elected president of the Bakongo Association (ABAKO), which swept the first open municipal elections in Léopoldville in 1957, and he became mayor of the Dendale district. He was among the first Congolese leaders to call for independence. On 4 January 1959 an ABAKO gathering he had organised, which the colonial authorities banned, erupted into the Léopoldville riots. He was arrested for inciting the riot and released two months later.

In the 1960 elections ABAKO came third. Kasa-Vubu allied his regionalist, conservative party with Patrice Lumumba's left-wing nationalist Congolese National Movement and was elected president indirectly, with Lumumba as prime minister. He was sworn in on 27 June 1960, and independence came on 30 June. Katanga and South Kasai soon seceded and the Congo Crisis began. When Lumumba sought help from the Soviet Union, Kasa-Vubu accused him of communist sympathies and on 5 September dissolved his government. Lumumba was captured and killed by Katangese separatist forces in January 1961.

With United Nations support the secessions were put down by 1963, and the Kwilu and Simba rebellions were defeated by 1965. Kasa-Vubu named Moïse Tshombe prime minister in July 1964 and dismissed him in October 1965. On 25 November 1965 Joseph-Désiré Mobutu seized power and deposed him. Kasa-Vubu was placed under house arrest, retired to his farm in Mayombe and died in a hospital in Boma in 1969.
joseph-needham: Joseph Needham was born on 9 December 1900, the son of a Harley Street doctor and a music composer from County Meath. As a boy he heard the Sunday lectures of Ernest Barnes, to whom he later attributed his Christian faith and his openness to other religions. At Oundle School, under the headmaster Frederick William Sanderson, he gained a grounding in engineering and learned that knowledge of history was needed to build a better future. He graduated from Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, in 1921 and took his PhD in 1925, having turned from medicine to biochemistry under Frederick Hopkins.

Needham became a fellow of his college and worked in Hopkins's laboratory on embryology and morphogenesis. His three-volume Chemical Embryology of 1931 included a history of embryology, later published separately in 1934. He was elected a fellow of the Royal Society in 1941. With Julian Huxley he was one of the founders of UNESCO, where he argued that most of its support should go to countries outside the European and American centres of science. In 1936 he helped found a History of Science Committee in Cambridge, and he married the biochemist Dorothy Moyle in 1924.

In 1948 he proposed to Cambridge University Press a book on science and civilisation in China. Within weeks it had grown to seven volumes, and his first collaborator was the historian Wang Ling. The first volume appeared in 1954. Needham wrote fifteen volumes himself, and the series, of which 27 volumes have been published, continued after his death. He was Master of Gonville and Caius College from 1966.

In The Grand Titration (1969) he posed what became known as the Needham Question: why modern science took its rise only in the West, when Chinese civilisation had long been more efficient in applying natural knowledge to practical needs. His work lists Chinese inventions such as cast iron, the stirrup, gunpowder, printing and the magnetic compass. Some scholars, among them Pierre-Yves Manguin, think he tended to exaggerate Chinese achievements and assume Chinese origins. Needham was a high church Anglo-Catholic who also called himself an honorary Taoist. He died in Cambridge on 24 March 1995, aged 94.
joseph-radetzky-von-radetz: Radetzky was born on 2 November 1766 at Třebnice, near Sedlčany in Bohemia, into a noble military family of Czech origin. His father died shortly after his birth and his mother while he was still a child, so he was brought up by his grandfather and then entered the Theresa Academy in Vienna. The academy was dissolved in 1785, and he became a cadet in the Austrian army, an officer the next year and a first lieutenant of cuirassiers in 1787. He served as an adjutant in the Austro-Turkish War of 1787–1791 and was present at the Siege of Belgrade. In 1798 he married Countess Franziska von Strassoldo-Grafenberg; they had five sons and three daughters. He was a devout Roman Catholic.

In the wars against revolutionary France and Napoleon he was known for personal courage. At Valeggio sul Mincio in 1796 he rescued Johann Beaulieu with a few hussars, and at the Battle of Marengo he was hit by five bullets. He became a Knight of the Military Order of Maria Theresa in 1801. From 1809 to 1812 he was chief of the general staff and worked at reorganising the army, but resigned when the Treasury opposed his reforms. In 1813 he was chief of staff to Schwarzenberg and had a considerable share in planning the Leipzig campaign. He entered Paris with the allied sovereigns in March 1814.

He succeeded Frimont as commander of the Austrian army in Italy in 1834 and became field marshal in 1836. In 1848 he fell back to the Quadrilatero and, rebuffing one opponent after another, gained time until reinforcements arrived. He won at Novara on 23 March 1849, and his troops retook Venice after a siege that lasted from May 1848 to August 1849. From 1848 to 1857 he was viceroy of Lombardy–Venetia, the only holder not of royal Habsburg blood.

Repression in Lombardy–Venetia was severe. From 1849 Radetzky introduced public caning as a punishment, the death penalty for armed uprising and life sentences for plotting revolution; the Belfiore martyrs, Luigi Dottesio and Amatore Sciesa were among those executed for treason. He died of pneumonia in Milan on 5 January 1858 and was buried on 19 January at the Heldenberg memorial site in Lower Austria, in a crypt under an obelisk.

In military history he is highly regarded as a brilliant field marshal, while some social historians see his time as viceroy as the point of no return in the relationship between Austria and the Italian population. Johann Strauss I's Radetzky March was first performed on 31 August 1848, and several Austro-Hungarian warships were named after him.
joseph-stalin: Stalin was born Ioseb Besarionis dze Jughashvili on 18 December 1878 (6 December in the Old Style calendar) in Gori, in the Tiflis Governorate of the Russian Empire. He was the third child of Besarion Jughashvili and Ekaterine Geladze, and the only one to survive infancy. His father's shoemaking workshop declined, the family fell into poverty, and Besarion became an alcoholic who beat his wife and son. In 1894 Stalin enrolled with a scholarship at the Tiflis Theological Seminary as a trainee Orthodox priest, but he lost interest, read Marx and attended secret workers' meetings. He left in April 1899. In November 1901 he was elected to the Tiflis Committee of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party.

After the October Revolution of 1917 Stalin joined Lenin's inner circle and became People's Commissar for Nationalities. After Lenin's death in January 1924 a struggle for the succession followed, in which Stalin used his post as General Secretary to place loyalists across the party and, with Kamenev and Zinoviev, formed a triumvirate against Trotsky.

From 1928 his five-year plans brought rapid collectivisation and industrialisation. State policy contributed to a major famine in the early 1930s, with Ukraine and Kazakhstan most affected. In the Great Purge of 1936–1939 at least 700,000 people were executed and over a million imprisoned in the Gulag. In August 1939 his government signed the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact with Germany, with a secret protocol dividing Eastern Europe. Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941, and the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945.

After the war the Gulag system was expanded further, and by January 1953 three percent of the Soviet population was imprisoned or in internal exile. Stalin died on 5 March 1953 and was succeeded by Nikita Khrushchev, who denounced him and began de-Stalinisation.

Opinion of him remains divided. Most Westerners and anti-communist Russians view him as a mass murderer, significant numbers of Russians and Georgians regard him as a great statesman, and his regime has been widely condemned for mass repression, ethnic cleansing and the deaths of millions.
josephine-de-beauharnais: She was born Marie Josèphe Rose Tascher de La Pagerie on 23 June 1763 and was known as Rose until she met Napoleon, who first called her Joséphine. Her grandfather Gaspard-Joseph Tascher de La Pagerie was the first of an ancient French noble family to settle on Martinique, in 1726. Her father, Joseph-Gaspard, was a plantation owner and officer of the Troupes de marine who was almost always close to bankruptcy. Her mother's sugar plantation near Les Trois-Îlets was part of her dowry.

The name Joséphine de Beauharnais was not one she used herself. Beauharnais was the name of her first husband, Alexandre, which she gave up when she married Bonaparte, and the form arose under the restored Bourbons, who hesitated to call her by Napoleon's surname or her imperial title.

Alexandre de Beauharnais was guillotined during the Reign of Terror, and she was imprisoned in the Carmes prison until five days after his execution. In 1795 she met Napoleon Bonaparte, six years her junior, and became his mistress. They married on 9 March 1796, and on the certificate she reduced her age by four years and added eighteen months to his. In 1796 she began an affair with a Hussar lieutenant, Hippolyte Charles, and when rumours reached Napoleon his love for her changed entirely.

Napoleon became Emperor in 1804, and at the coronation at Notre-Dame on 2 December, after crowning himself, he crowned her empress. Shortly before, a quarrel at Saint-Cloud had nearly ended the marriage, for Napoleon felt pressed by his family over the lack of an heir. Her daughter Hortense reconciled them. The marriage was annulled on 10 January 1810 because she had not borne him a child, and he married Marie Louise of Austria.

After the annulment she lived at the Château de Malmaison near Paris, on good terms with Napoleon, who gave her a generous allowance and in April 1810 made her Duchess of Navarre. She died of pneumonia at Rueil-Malmaison on 29 May 1814. Napoleon, then on Elba, shut himself in his room for two days when he learned of it.

She bought Malmaison in 1799 and had it landscaped in English style, with a rose garden that she supervised closely. Napoleon ordered his warship commanders to forward plants from seized vessels, and Pierre-Joseph Redouté painted her roses for Les Roses, which was published after her death. She commissioned works from Antonio Canova. Through her children, Hortense and Eugène, she was grandmother of Napoleon III and ancestor of several European royal houses.
josephus: Josephus was born Yosef ben Mattityahu in Jerusalem, into one of the city's elite families. His father Matthias was a priest of the order of Jehoiarib, the first of the 24 orders of priests in the Temple, and his mother claimed descent from the Hasmonean dynasty. At about 26 he travelled to Rome to negotiate the release of Jewish priests imprisoned by Nero, and with help from Nero's wife Poppaea he succeeded. On his return, at the outbreak of the First Jewish–Roman War, he was appointed military governor of Galilee.

In Galilee Josephus fortified towns and contended with a rival, John of Gischala. He resisted the Roman army at the siege of Yodfat, or Jotapata, until it fell in 67. By his own account he was trapped in a cave with forty companions, who drew lots to kill one another, and he was one of two left who surrendered. He claimed to have predicted that Vespasian would become emperor, and Vespasian freed him in 69, whereupon he took the emperor's family name, Flavius. To many Jews his claims seemed self-serving.

He served Vespasian's son Titus as a translator during the siege of Jerusalem in 70, which ended in the near-total razing of the city and the destruction of the Second Temple. In 71 he went to Rome in Titus's entourage and became a Roman citizen and a client of the Flavian dynasty, with a pension. He wrote all his known works there. He read the destruction of the Temple as a sign that God had turned to the Romans because of Jewish sins.

His main works are The Jewish War, of about 75, Antiquities of the Jews, of about 94, a history of the world from a Jewish perspective, and his autobiography, the Life. Outside the Scriptures they are the chief source for Second Temple Judaea, with accounts of the Hasmonean dynasty, Herod the Great, the Sadducees, Pharisees and Essenes, and of figures such as Pontius Pilate, John the Baptist and James, the brother of Jesus. He is the first known source for the siege of Masada. Historians treat him with caution, since Carl Ritter held in the 1840s that his wish to bring his people honour among Greeks and Romans filled his history with distortions and exaggerations.

Christian readers prized him from the 4th century as an independent witness to the world of Jesus. Rabbinic writing almost never names him, and he was often seen as a traitor, until Kalman Schulman's Hebrew translation of 1863 revived Jewish interest. William Whiston's English translation of 1732 was among the books Christians most often owned after the Bible.
joshua-nkomo: Joshua Mqabuko Nyongolo Nkomo was born on 7 June 1917 at Matopos in Matabeleland, Southern Rhodesia, into a poor Ndebele family, one of eight children. His father, Thomas Nyongolo Letswansto Nkomo, was a preacher and cattle rancher who worked for the London Missionary Society. He trained as a carpenter and taught carpentry at Manyame School in Kezi. In 1942 he went to South Africa, where he attended Adams College and the Jan H. Hofmeyr School of Social Work, which awarded him a diploma in 1952.

After returning to Bulawayo in 1947 he became a trade unionist for black railway workers, rose to lead the Railway Workers Union and then headed the Southern Rhodesian branch of the African National Congress. He became chairman of its successor body in 1957, and the National Democratic Party, founded on 1 January 1960 after that body was banned, made him president. When it too was banned in December 1961 he formed ZAPU with Ndabaningi Sithole, Robert Mugabe and others; it was banned in September 1962.

ZAPU split in 1963, when Sithole and Mugabe took their supporters to form the Zimbabwe African National Union (ZANU). Ian Smith's government held Nkomo at the Gonakudzingwa Restriction Camp from 1964 to 1974, when many detainees were released under pressure from South African Prime Minister John Vorster. He then went to Zambia to pursue both armed resistance and negotiation. ZAPU's armed wing shot down two Air Rhodesia airliners, on 3 September 1978 and 12 February 1979, killing 107 people in all.

At the Lancaster House talks of September 1979, chaired by Lord Carrington, Nkomo and Mugabe shared a delegation called the Patriotic Front. In the 1980 elections ZAPU won the twenty seats of Matabeleland; Nkomo declined the ceremonial presidency and became Minister of Home Affairs. In 1982 he was accused of plotting a coup after arms were found on ZAPU farms. The Fifth Brigade's Operation Gukurahundi killed up to 20,000 Ndebele civilians, and Nkomo fled to London on 7 March 1983.

After ZAPU merged into ZANU-PF in 1987, some Ndebele accused him of selling out; he said he had acted to stop the killing of Ndebele and ZAPU organizers. He was sworn in as vice-president on 6 August 1990, a post that was in practice almost powerless. He died of prostate cancer on 1 July 1999 in Harare, aged 82, was declared a National Hero and is buried in the National Heroes' Acre.
josiah: According to the Hebrew Bible, Josiah was the 16th king of Judah. He became king at the age of eight after his father Amon was assassinated, and he reigned 31 years. His grandfather Manasseh, who turned the Temple to idolatrous worship, was among the kings blamed for turning away from the worship of YHWH, and his great-grandfather Hezekiah was a noted reformer. Josiah's reign is difficult to reconstruct. No contemporary text from Egypt or Babylon mentions him, but a seal bearing the name Nathan-melech, an official under Josiah named in 2 Kings, was found in place at a site in Jerusalem. Judah remained largely under foreign suzerainty during his reign.

When Josiah came to the throne around 641 or 640 BCE the Assyrian Empire was beginning to break up and Babylon had not yet risen, so Jerusalem could govern itself without outside interference. In his 18th year, according to both biblical accounts, he ordered repairs to the Temple. While clearing the treasure room the high priest Hilkiah is said to have found a scroll called the Book of the Law. The prophetess Huldah told the king that the evils foretold in it for disobedience would come, but not in his day.

Josiah then encouraged the exclusive worship of YHWH. Objects of the worship of Baal were removed from the Temple, local sanctuaries from Beersheba to Bethel were destroyed, and priests of other cults were executed. He also revived the celebration of Passover. Scholars hold that the book was either a copy of Deuteronomy or a text that became part of it. Some reject the historicity of these accounts entirely, while others defend a reform under Josiah.

In the spring of 609 BCE Pharaoh Necho II led an army north to aid the collapsing Assyrian empire against the Medes and Babylonians. Josiah led the Judean army to block his way at Megiddo and was killed. Why he did so is not known. The account in 2 Kings says only that Necho met and killed him, while 2 Chronicles says he was wounded by Egyptian archers and died in Jerusalem. Some scholars consider the Chronicles account unreliable, because it resembles the death of King Ahab.

His son Jehoahaz succeeded him but reigned only three months before Necho deposed him and took him to Egypt, replacing him with Jehoiakim and imposing a levy of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. The Deuteronomistic History, which many scholars see as first written in his time, holds Josiah the one king to fully carry out the book's laws.
josiah-wedgwood: Josiah Wedgwood was baptised on 12 July 1730, probably his birthday, at Burslem, then the main centre of the Staffordshire Potteries. He was the thirteenth and last child of Thomas Wedgwood and Mary Stringer, whose father was a dissenting minister. His father died in June 1739, and on 11 November 1744 Josiah was apprenticed to his eldest brother Thomas at the Churchyard Works.

Smallpox had affected his right knee, and its pain later turned him from the wheel to moulded ware. When his brother turned down his proposals for improvements, he became a partner and manager at a pot-works near Stoke and then joined Thomas Whieldon, developing an exceptionally brilliant green glaze. Knee trouble led to the amputation of his leg on 28 May 1768.

Around 1759 he expanded his business by renting the Ivy House Works at Burslem. By 1763 he received orders from the highest-ranking people, among them Queen Charlotte, who allowed him to call the creamware she bought Queen's Ware. His first order from abroad came in 1764, and he opened a warehouse in Mayfair in 1765. With Thomas Bentley he perfected a black stoneware body, basalt, which imitated Etruscan and Greek vases, and he opened the Etruria Works in June 1769. Around 1771 he began experimenting with jasperware, and his first illustrated Ornamental Catalogue appeared in 1773.

He was elected to the Royal Society in 1783 for a pyrometer working on the contraction of clay. In 1789, after three years' work, he produced a copy of the Portland Vase that he judged satisfactory. As an abolitionist he made the medallion Am I Not a Man and a Brother?, commissioned by Joseph Hooper, a founder of the Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade, which supplied the design.

Wedgwood married his distant cousin Sarah on 25 January 1764 and they had eight children. Their daughter Susannah married Robert Darwin and was the mother of Charles Darwin. Wedgwood died at home in 1795, probably of cancer of the jaw, and was buried three days later in the parish church of Stoke-upon-Trent. He is credited as a pioneer of modern marketing, including direct mail, money-back guarantees and illustrated catalogues, and is the subject of Brian Dolan's Wedgwood: The First Tycoon (2004).
josip-broz-tito: Josip Broz was born on 7 May 1892 in Kumrovec, in the Zagorje region of Croatia, then part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. His father was a Croat and his mother a Slovene; he spent much of his early childhood with his Slovene grandparents but identified as a Croat. Conscripted in May 1913, he became a sergeant major at 22, the youngest in his regiment. Wounded and captured by the Russians in the First World War, he was sent to a work camp in the Ural Mountains and took part in the Russian Revolution. He met Pelagija Belousova in Omsk in 1918 and married her the next year.

Back in Croatia in 1920 he joined the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, outlawed on 30 December 1920. He was imprisoned in 1928, and Moša Pijade became his ideological mentor in Lepoglava prison. Released on 16 March 1934, he left Yugoslavia after King Alexander's assassination in October and worked for the Comintern in Moscow. In 1937, after the party's leader Gorkić was arrested and shot in Moscow, Broz became acting general secretary and built a younger leadership around Edvard Kardelj, Aleksandar Ranković and Milovan Đilas. Tito was one of several names he used while the party was illegal.

After the Axis invasion on 6 April 1941 he formed a Military Committee, and on 27 June the Central Committee named him commander-in-chief of the Partisans. A provisional government headed by Tito was assembled in Belgrade on 7 March 1945, and his People's Front won the elections of November 1945, which monarchists boycotted.

In 1961 Tito co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement with Gamal Abdel Nasser, Jawaharlal Nehru, Sukarno and Kwame Nkrumah, and became its first Secretary-General. From the 1950s his government let Yugoslav workers go to Western Europe as guest workers, and the constitution delegated much power to the republics. After the changes of 1974 he reduced his role in daily government but kept the last word on major policy. Critics call his rule authoritarian and point to the arrest of Milovan Đilas on 19 November 1956; others call him a benevolent dictator. He received 98 foreign decorations, and died on 4 May 1980.
josip-jelacic: Josip Jelačić was born on 16 October 1801 in Petrovaradin, then part of the Slavonian Military Frontier of the Habsburg monarchy. His father, Baron Franjo Jelačić Bužimski, was a lieutenant field marshal, and his mother was Baroness Anna Portner von Höflein. He was educated at the Theresian Military Academy in Vienna and spoke all the South Slavic languages as well as German, Italian, French and Hungarian. He joined the Austrian army as a lieutenant on 11 March 1819. He led a campaign against Bosnian Ottoman troops at Velika Kladuša on 17 October 1835 and was promoted colonel in 1841.

On 22 March 1848 Jelačić was promoted major-general and the Croatian Sabor elected him Ban of Croatia. He supported Croatian autonomy from the Kingdom of Hungary and took the oath as ban on 5 June 1848. Croatia's demands included union of its provinces, separation from Hungary and the abolition of serfdom. On 19 April he proclaimed the union and separation while declaring loyalty to the Habsburg monarchy. The imperial court first declared him a rebel, then came to see Croatian forces as an ally against the Hungarian Batthyány government.

On 11 September 1848 he crossed the Drava and marched on Pest. His army was checked at Pákozd on 29 September, and he turned towards Vienna, where he joined imperial troops and helped suppress the October revolution. On 30 October at Schwechat he defeated the Hungarian army. In the winter campaign he took part in the occupation of Pest-Buda on 5 January 1849, but the army of Windisch-Grätz and Jelačić was defeated at Isaszeg on 6 April. He then fought in southern Hungary and Slavonia, and the last battle there was Hegyes on 14 July. After the revolution he implemented the new constitution of 4 March 1849 and worked under Alexander von Bach.

Jelačić died on 20 May 1859 in Zagreb after an illness and was buried in Zaprešić, near his castle. He was fairly unpopular among the Croatian political elite of his time, including Ante Starčević, but is now considered an important figure of Croatian history. His reputation differs by country: in Croatia he is a national hero, in Austria he was seen as a rebel, and in Hungary he is a very unpopular figure.

The central square of Zagreb was named Ban Jelačić Square in 1848. A statue by Anton Dominik Fernkorn was erected there in 1866, removed under Communist rule in 1947 and reinstalled in 1990. The patriotic song Ustani bane was written to glorify him, and his portrait appeared on the Croatian 20 kuna banknote.
josquin-des-prez: Little is known of Josquin's early years, and neither the year nor the place of his birth is known. He is now thought to have been born around 1450 and at the latest in 1455. Documents of 1483 found in Condé-sur-l'Escaut name him as Josquin Lebloitte dit des Prez. Nothing is known of his mother. Around 1466 his uncle and aunt named him their heir.

In 1484 he was in Milan and on 20 June entered the service of Cardinal Ascanio Sforza. He asked for a dispensation to be rector of the parish church of Saint Aubin without being ordained a priest. The motet Ave Maria... Virgo serena is dated to about 1485.

In August 1494 Josquin was in Cambrai, and he was ordained a priest at some point. In 1503 he arrived in Ferrara to serve Duke Ercole I d'Este. A courtier wrote that Josquin composed better than Heinrich Isaac but composed when he wished rather than when asked and demanded a salary of 200 ducats against Isaac's 120.

On 3 May 1504 he became provost of the collegiate church of Notre-Dame at Condé-sur-l'Escaut, where he directed a staff that included a dean, a treasurer, 25 canons, 18 chaplains, 16 vicars and 6 choirboys. In these years he composed some of his most admired works, among them the masses Missa de Beata Virgine and Missa Pange lingua, the motets Benedicta es and Inviolata and the chansons Mille regretz and Plus nulz regretz. Ottaviano Petrucci's publications spread his music across Europe, and his Misse Josquin of 1502 was the first anthology of masses by a single composer.

Josquin was a singer throughout his life, and his compositions are almost exclusively vocal: masses, motets and chansons in French. A line of musicologists credits him with moving away from long melismatic lines towards short motifs passed between voices and with an increasingly prominent imitative polyphony. His motets are his most admired works and were mostly for four voices, though he was also an innovator in five and six voices. Most of his masses are for four voices and fall into canonic, cantus firmus, paraphrase, parody and solmization types.

He died on 27 August 1521. Elders called him the first composer in the history of Western music not to have been forgotten after his death, and Martin Luther said that he was the master of the notes. After his death some publishers attributed works to him to meet demand, and a remark arose that he composed more when dead than alive.
jovenel-moise: Jovenel Moïse was born on 26 June 1968 in Trou du Nord, in the Nord-Est department. His father, Étienne Moïse, was a farmer and mechanic and his mother, Lucia Bruno, a seamstress. The family moved to Port-au-Prince in July 1974, where he went to school and later studied political science at Quisqueya University, concentrating on local governance and rural development. In 1996 he married Martine Marie Étienne Joseph, a classmate, and they settled in Port-de-Paix; they had three children. Back in rural Nord-Est he argued that Haiti should address endemic poverty in part through an agrarian economy.

In the mid-1990s Moïse founded JoMar Auto Parts, which sold automobile components, and the next year began an organic banana plantation of more than 10 hectares in the Nord-Ouest department. In 2012 he founded Agritrans SA to run the Nourribo Project, a 1,000-hectare banana plantation in the Nord-Est presented as Haiti's first agricultural free-trade zone. It aimed to export bananas to Germany, but only two containers were shipped.

In 2015 President Michel Martelly named Moïse candidate of his centre-right Haitian Tèt Kale Party. In the first round on 25 October 2015 he officially received 32.8 percent of the votes, ahead of Jude Célestin, who called the results fraudulent. Protests forced the postponement of the runoff, and the ballot was annulled in June 2016. After a new election on 20 November 2016 Moïse was declared the winner in the first round with 55.67 percent of the vote on an estimated turnout of 21 percent, and he was sworn in on 7 February 2017.

Opponents held that his five-year term should have ended five years after Martelly's term ended, while Moïse maintained that it began with his inauguration in 2017. His policies concentrated on agricultural and water infrastructure. He also built roads, rebuilt the airport at Jérémie and had power plants and asphalt plants built in several provinces. Allegations of corruption, and a falling quality of life, led to mass demonstrations demanding his resignation.

On 7 July 2021, 11 days after his 53rd birthday, Moïse was shot dead when gunmen attacked his residence in Pèlerin 5, a district of Pétion-Ville. His wife Martine was wounded and flown to Miami for treatment.
joya-de-ceren: Joya de Cerén, Spanish for Jewel of Cerén, lies in the Zapotitán Valley. Its preservation beneath volcanic ash has earned it a comparison with Pompeii. The structures are grouped in northeastern, southeastern and northwestern areas. The houses had relatively earthquake-resistant wattle-and-daub walls and adobe columns, and the surrounding plots held milpas, a kitchen garden and fruit trees. Guava, agave, cacao and manioc were among the community's major crops.

The village produced agave fibres, manos, metates and pottery, and obtained obsidian and chert cutting tools, jade from the Sierra de las Minas to the north, and fine pottery from Copán. Households exchanged surplus goods with one another and with nearby places. Each household stored about 70 vessels for cooking and for serving food and drink.

Structures 10 and 12 are interpreted as ceremonial. Structure 10, a multi-roomed building, is thought to have served community festivals; a red-painted deer and twine headdress found there is connected by archaeologists with fertility and harvest rituals, and vessels of achiote seeds beside ceremonial objects suggest that the eruption interrupted a ceremony. Structure 12, whose niche held ceramic figurines, shell fragments, beans and antlers, may have been a diviner's place for divination. Household 1 appears to have supplied masa for ceremonies in the two buildings.

The Loma Caldera erupted around 600 CE and laid 10 metres of pyroclastic debris over the site, a layer 4 to 8 metres thick blanketing the village in a few hours. Cracks in the walls suggest an earthquake of about 4.0 before the eruption, giving people time to flee. Shovels and farm tools stood near the houses, fires were lit in hearths and sleeping mats were not yet unrolled, which suggests an evacuation in the early evening. Plaster casts of plants and stored beans and mature maize point to August or September. No human remains have been found.

A bulldozer driver levelling ground for a government agricultural project found the site in 1976. Payson Sheets of the University of Colorado at Boulder explored it in depth in 1978 and 1980, and excavation resumed in 1988 and has been continuous since. The buildings uncovered include storehouses, kitchens, living quarters, workshops, a religious structure and a communal sauna. UNESCO inscribed Joya de Cerén on the World Heritage List in 1993, and it is a major tourist attraction in El Salvador.
jozef-pilsudski: Józef Klemens Piłsudski was born on 5 December 1867 into a family of nobility at Zułow, near the village of Zułowo in present-day Lithuania, then under Russian rule. He knew Lithuanian as well as Polish. The family was impoverished but cherished Polish patriotic traditions. Held at Irkutsk while being taken to Siberia, he was beaten with other political prisoners after a protest, and the cold of his first night in prison nearly killed him. In 1893 he joined the Polish Socialist Party, and in 1894 he became chief editor of its underground newspaper Robotnik. He remained a Polish nationalist and held that socialism and nationalism should be combined to win independence.

In the early 1900s almost all parties in Russian Poland sought autonomy within the empire, while Piłsudski's party was prepared to fight for independence. In 1906, with the connivance of the Austrian authorities, he founded a military school in Kraków for paramilitary units. On 3 August 1914 he formed the First Cadre Company in Kraków, and his Legions fought alongside Austria-Hungary against Russia. In 1917 he withdrew support for the Central Powers, and the Germans imprisoned him at Magdeburg.

On 11 November 1918 the Regency Council appointed him Commander-in-Chief, and that day he proclaimed an independent Polish state. As Chief of State until 1922 he faced a country with nine legal systems, five currencies and 66 types of rail system. From 1919 to 1921 he commanded forces in six wars over the borders. In August 1920 his plan, a counteroffensive led by a Reserve Army of about 20,000 men, repelled the Soviet advance at the Battle of Warsaw. On 14 December 1922 he handed his powers to President Gabriel Narutowicz.

After retiring in 1923, Piłsudski returned to power in the May Coup of 1926. The Sejm elected him president, but he refused the office and became Minister of Military Affairs, which he held until his death. His Sanation government sought to reduce the influence of parties and strengthen the army, and constitutional amendments of 2 August 1926 curtailed the Sejm. Its methods were at times authoritarian, and the imprisonment of opponents at Bereza Kartuska remains controversial. He died of liver cancer on 12 May 1935 at the Belweder Palace in Warsaw. He is widely regarded as a founder of modern Poland and a father of the Second Polish Republic.
jozef-poniatowski: Prince Józef Antoni Poniatowski was born in Vienna, the son of Andrzej Poniatowski, an Austrian field marshal and brother of the last king of Poland, Stanislaus II Augustus, and Countess Maria Theresia Kinsky. His father died when he was ten, and the king became his guardian. He began his military career in 1780 in the Imperial Army and distinguished himself in the Austro-Turkish War at the storming of Šabac in 1788, where he was seriously wounded. In October 1789, at his uncle's request, he moved to the Polish army as a major general.

Poniatowski supported the 3 May Constitution of 1791. In the Polish–Russian War of 1792 he commanded the army in Ukraine, badly outnumbered, and won the Battle of Zieleńce on 18 June, after which the king created the Virtuti Militari order. When the king acceded to the Targowica Confederation he resigned. In 1794 he fought in the Kościuszko Uprising and helped defend Warsaw. His estates were confiscated, and he later lived in private life in Warsaw.

In 1807, after the Duchy of Warsaw was created, he became its minister of war, and he was commander in chief from March 1809. At the Battle of Raszyn on 19 April 1809 his force fought an Austrian army twice its size to a standstill. He then advanced into Galicia, taking Lublin, Zamość and Lwów, and reached Kraków on 15 July. In 1812 he commanded V Corps of the Grande Armée in the invasion of Russia, and he was badly injured at Vyazma.

Poniatowski stayed loyal to Napoleon even when Tsar Alexander I offered him amnesty. On 16 October 1813, during the Battle of Leipzig, he was made a Marshal of the Empire and entrusted with covering the French retreat. He fell back on a bridge over the White Elster, which the French blew up before he reached it. Badly injured, and probably shot by allies by mistake, he drowned in the river. His remains were buried in 1817 in the cathedral on Wawel Hill in Kraków, beside Kościuszko and John III Sobieski. He became an inspiration for Polish freedom fighters, especially in the November Uprising of 1830.
jozsef-antall: József Antall was born in Budapest on 8 April 1932 into an old family of the lower nobility. His father, József Antall Sr., was a jurist and civil servant and a founding member of the Independent Smallholders' Party; his mother, Irén Szűcs, had Jewish roots. Antall studied Hungarian language and literature, history and archival science at Eötvös Loránd University and took degrees in teaching, library science and museology. He began teaching in 1955 and led his school's Revolutionary Committee during the 1956 Hungarian Uprising. After the Soviet Union crushed the revolution he was arrested and released several times, and in 1959 he was banned from teaching.

He worked as a librarian for two years and in 1963 wrote biographies of 80 doctors for the Lexicon of Hungarian Biographies. This led him to the history of medicine, and at the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History he rose from research fellow to deputy director and in 1974 to director of the institute.

The Hungarian Democratic Forum sent Antall to the National Roundtable Talks on 22 March 1989, and on 21 October 1989 he was elected its president. The party won the 1990 elections with 164 seats, just short of a majority, and on 23 May 1990 he became the first prime minister since 1948 who was neither a Communist nor a fellow traveller. He headed a centre-right coalition with the Independent Smallholders and the Christian Democratic People's Party, the first in 44 years without Communists, and made a pact with the liberal Alliance of Free Democrats.

His government set up a legal system to promote a market economy and attract foreign investment, and carried out privatization. Unemployment rose from nonexistence to 14 percent and inflation ran at 23 to 35 percent a year. Antall took part in the dissolution of the Warsaw Pact and the end of Comecon, and in the withdrawal of Russian forces in 1991. He faced a taxi drivers' blockade in 1990, conflict over powers with President Árpád Göncz, and in February 1992 the withdrawal of the Smallholders from the coalition, which forced him to restructure his cabinet.

Antall was diagnosed with non-Hodgkin lymphoma in the summer of 1990, and the cancer recurred half a year later. He died on 12 December 1993, before the end of his four-year term. Interior Minister Péter Boross, who had substituted for him in his last period, succeeded him and led the cabinet until the 1994 election, in which the Democratic Forum was defeated by the Socialist Party. Antall was buried on 18 December 1993, a day of national mourning, at Kerepesi Cemetery. In 2008 one of the buildings of the European Parliament in Brussels was named after him.
jozsef-mindszenty: József Mindszenty was born József Pehm on 29 March 1892 at Csehimindszent in Vas County, the son of a magistrate. He entered the diocesan seminary at Szombathely in 1911 and was ordained a priest on 12 June 1915. In 1919 he was arrested first by Mihály Károlyi's government and then by the communist government of Béla Kun. In 1939 he urged his followers to vote against the Arrow Cross Party, and in 1941 he adopted the Hungarian name Mindszenty. Consecrated Bishop of Veszprém on 25 March 1944, he protested to Miklós Horthy on behalf of converted Jews. The Arrow Cross government arrested him on 27 November 1944, and he was released in April 1945.

On 15 September 1945 he became primate of Hungary and archbishop of Esztergom, and on 21 February 1946 Pope Pius XII made him a cardinal. He fought the confiscation of church farmland and the state's seizure of parochial schools. Arrested on 26 December 1948 and charged with treason and conspiracy, he was beaten while in prison until he agreed to confess. His show trial began on 3 February 1949, and on 8 February he was sentenced to life imprisonment. Pius XII excommunicated all those involved in the trial.

Freed on 30 October 1956 during the Hungarian Revolution, he returned to Budapest and praised the insurgents. When the Soviet Union invaded on 4 November, he was granted asylum at the United States embassy, where he lived for fifteen years. After a compromise offered by Pope Paul VI he was allowed to leave on 28 September 1971 and lived in Vienna. In December 1973 the pope declared the see of Esztergom vacant.

Mindszenty died in exile in Vienna on 6 May 1975. His remains were brought to Esztergom in 1991 and buried in the basilica, where a museum is dedicated to him. His cause for sainthood opened in 1993, and Pope Francis declared him venerable on 12 February 2019. The Encyclopedia Britannica says that for five decades he personified uncompromising opposition to fascism and communism in Hungary. A single Western reporter, George Seldes, disputed that he had been tortured and accused him of collaboration, a charge the prosecution at his own trial did not make.
juan-gines-de-sepulveda: Sepúlveda was born at Pozoblanco in the province of Córdoba, of humble background; his parents were Ginés Sánchez Mellado, a craftsman, and María Ruiz. In 1510 he enrolled at the University of Alcalá de Henares, where he studied philosophy and Greek, and in 1513 he began theology at the College of San Antonio de Sigüenza. In February 1515 he obtained a letter of recommendation from Cardinal Cisneros to the Spanish College in Bologna, where he matriculated that September. There he studied under Pietro Pomponazzi and gained a lifelong expertise in the works of Aristotle, encouraged by his patron Alberto Pío, Prince of Carpi, and by Giulio de' Medici.

By 1523 Sepúlveda had earned doctorates in arts and theology and had taken religious vows as a Dominican priest. When Giulio de' Medici became Pope Clement VII in that year, he served at the papal curia in Rome, where he gained a reputation for scholarship and rhetorical skill. He translated several works of Aristotle from Greek into Latin, among them the Parva Naturalia in 1522 and De mundo in 1523.

He also wrote on the religious controversies of the day: De fato et libero arbitrio against Martin Luther in 1526, De ritu nuptiarum in 1531 against the divorce proceedings of Henry VIII, and the Antapologia against Erasmus in 1532. He despised Luther, but respected Erasmus and corresponded with him for many years. In 1529 he wrote Ad Carolum V, urging Emperor Charles V to unite Europe and fight the Turks.

In Democrates, of 1535, Sepúlveda defended the idea that a just war based on natural law was compatible with Christianity. His case for the conquest drew also on Saint Thomas Aquinas, on the Roman law of just war and the right of conquest, and on the Bible, which he used to justify forced conversion; his position differed from that of the School of Salamanca represented by Francisco de Vitoria. He had never been to America. He claimed that some, though not all, Amerindians were natural slaves as Aristotle defined them in Book I of the Politics, and compared them to children before parents.

Bartolomé de las Casas used the same sources in reply. He held that Christianity should be offered to the natives as an option, not imposed as an obligation, and that no Amerindians lacked the ability to rule themselves. Sepúlveda's later works include histories of the deeds of Charles V, of 1556, and of Philip II, of 1564, and De regno, of 1570. He died on 17 November 1573.
juan-jose-flores: Juan José Flores was born on 19 July 1800 at Puerto Cabello, Venezuela, the illegitimate and only son of a Spanish merchant and a Venezuelan woman, Rita Flores Bohorques. His father returned to Europe and left mother and son in poverty. Flores had little formal education, and at fifteen he enlisted as a private in the royalist army of General Pablo Morillo.

Taken prisoner as a sergeant on 31 October 1817, he joined the patriot army of Simón Bolívar. Bolívar noted his courage at the Battle of Carabobo in 1821, and at twenty-three Flores became a colonel and then commandant general of the freed city of Pasto. He was self-taught and read Rousseau and Montesquieu, and the professors of the University of Quito gave him an honorary doctorate in 1842.

On 13 May 1830, the day Ecuador broke away from Gran Colombia, Flores was named supreme chief of the new country, and on 14 August provisional president. The assembly at Riobamba elected him constitutional president, and his term began on 22 September 1830 and lasted until 10 September 1834. It was marked by turmoil: he faced a rebellion led by Luis Urdaneta, who wanted to keep Ecuador in Gran Colombia, and a threat from Vicente Rocafuerte, with whom he agreed that Rocafuerte would be president next and Flores head of the army. He also fought an invading Colombian army in 1832 and again from 1834, defeating it at Miñarica, near Ambato, on 18 January 1835.

His second term ran from 1 February 1839 to 15 January 1843. After irregularities in the elections of 1842 he had the 1835 constitution annulled, and the new constitution, nicknamed the Carta de la esclavitud, let him begin a third term on 1 April 1843. A rebellion led by Rocafuerte and Vicente Ramón Roca overthrew him on 6 March 1845.

Flores remained active in Ecuadorian military and political life. He commanded Ecuadorian forces at the Battle of Cuaspud on 6 December 1863, where a defeat weakened the army and thwarted his and Gabriel García Moreno's efforts to strengthen state centralization. In 1864 he left Quito to fight an expedition led by the former president José María Urvina in the Gulf of Guayaquil. At the Battle of Santa Rosa he received a stray shot in the lower abdomen and died on 1 October aboard the steamer Smirck, near Puná Island. He is often called the Founder of the Republic, and Floreana Island in the Galápagos Archipelago is named for him.
juan-manuel-de-rosas: Juan Manuel José Domingo Ortiz de Rozas was born on 30 March 1793 in Buenos Aires, then the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, the first child of León Ortiz de Rozas, an army officer, and Agustina López de Osornio, of a wealthy criollo family. His mother's father, a landowner, had died defending his estate from an attack in 1783. After the British invasions were repelled the family moved to their ranch, where Rosas worked among peons, most of them gauchos, who were drafted as a private defence force. He was suspicious of the May Revolution of 1810, which he saw as a movement of merchants and officials in the city, and he felt nostalgic for the stability of colonial times.

By 1826 Rosas had a power base of relatives, friends and clients and had joined the Federalist Party, though he cared chiefly for his native province. In 1827 he drove the Federalist takeover of Buenos Aires and became commander of the rural militias on 14 July. In December 1829 he became governor of Buenos Aires Province. The capture of the Unitarian leader José María Paz in March 1831 ended the Unitarian-Federalist civil war, and Rosas recognised provincial autonomy in the Federal Pact.

His term ended in 1832 and he left to wage the Desert Campaign. In October 1833 his supporters besieged Buenos Aires in the Revolution of the Restorers, and on 7 March 1835 the House of Representatives re-elected him governor with the sum of public power.

His rule used purges, banishments, censorship and terror; the armed Mazorca killed thousands, and he presented himself in a cult of personality. He declared war on the Peru-Bolivian Confederation on 19 March 1837, and France blockaded Buenos Aires from 28 March 1838. By about 1845 he held dominance over the region, and his army under Manuel Oribe besieged Montevideo from 1843. Britain and France blockaded Buenos Aires for most of the late 1840s but could not halt him.

When the Empire of Brazil began aiding Uruguay, Rosas declared war in August 1851, beginning the Platine War, and he was defeated. He arrived at Plymouth on 26 April 1852, where the British gave him asylum, and he lived his last years as a tenant farmer at Southampton until his death in 1877. His daughter Manuela followed him into exile. Efforts to reassess his reputation began in the 1880s with works by Adolfo Saldías and Ernesto Quesada, and a revisionist movement later idealised him. His remains were brought back to Argentina in 1989, and he remains a controversial figure.
juan-negrin: Juan Negrín was born on 3 February 1892 in Las Palmas in the Canary Islands, into a deeply Catholic middle-class family; his father was a prosperous merchant. Having shown interest in medicine, he was sent at 15 to study in Germany, at Kiel and then at Leipzig. In 1912, aged twenty, he took a doctorate in medicine and became an assistant at the Institute of Physiology in Leipzig.

Returning to Spain at the end of 1915, he became a professor of physiology at the Complutense University of Madrid in 1922, and his laboratory became an internationally known research centre. Among his students was Severo Ochoa, later a Nobel laureate. Close to German social democracy, he joined the Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) in 1929, sided with the moderate faction of Indalecio Prieto, and was elected deputy for Las Palmas in 1931, 1933 and 1936.

After the military uprising of 17 July 1936 he helped many people escape the revolutionary checas in Madrid and was nearly killed by anarchists. In September 1936 he became minister of finance under Francisco Largo Caballero. In October 1936, with the approval of President Manuel Azaña and other ministers, he sent Spain's gold reserves to the Soviet Union in return for arms; critics argued that this put the government under Stalin's control.

After the Barcelona May Days forced Largo Caballero to resign, Azaña named Negrín prime minister on 17 May 1937. His cabinet included Prieto at War, the communists Jesús Hernández Tomás and Vicente Uribe, and the republican José Giral. Under the slogan 'Resistir es vencer', 'To resist is to win', he sought to keep the Republic alive until a wider war brought it allies in Western Europe. He remained in Spain until the Republican front collapsed in March 1939.

Negrín lived in Paris until the fall of France in June 1940 and then in London, heading the Republican government in exile until August 1945, when he resigned and José Giral succeeded him. Franco's courts stripped him of his chair and fined him 100 million pesetas. The PSOE expelled him in April 1946 and rehabilitated him in 2008. He died of a heart attack in Paris on 12 November 1956, aged 64. Historians differ about him: later scholarship has portrayed him as a pragmatic social democrat who had no choice but to ally with the Soviets, because Britain and France would not support the Republic.
juan-peron: Juan Domingo Perón was born in Lobos, Buenos Aires Province, on 8 October 1895, the son of Juana Sosa Toledo and Mario Tomás Perón. His father's family was originally Spanish but had settled in Sardinia, and his great-grandfather emigrated to Argentina in the 1830s.

Perón entered military college in 1911 and rose through the ranks. He supported the 1930 coup against President Hipólito Yrigoyen, a decision he later regretted. Between 1939 and 1941 he served as a military attaché in Mussolini's Italy, where he developed many of his ideas.

Perón took part in the 1943 revolution and became Minister of Labor, then Minister of War and Vice President, gaining a name for labour reforms. Political disputes forced him to resign in October 1945, and he was arrested. On 17 October workers gathered in the Plaza de Mayo to demand his release. He won the presidential election of 24 February 1946 by about 11% against an alliance of the Radical Civic Union and other parties, after he turned the United States ambassador's accusation of fascist ties into a choice between Perón and Braden.

His first term brought industrialisation, expanded social rights, tuition-free universities and, in 1947, votes for women, a measure tied to the work of his wife Eva Duarte. The government nationalised the Central Bank. It also fired dissidents, controlled the press and dismissed over 2,000 university professors. Several Nazi war criminals found refuge in Argentina. Perón was re-elected in 1951, but his second term began amid drought and a trade deficit. After conflict with the Catholic Church, pro-Church elements of the armed forces bombed the Plaza de Mayo in June 1955, killing about 300 civilians, and a coup deposed him.

Perón lived in exile in Paraguay, Venezuela, Panama and Spain while the Peronist party was outlawed. When the Peronist Héctor Cámpora won the 1973 election, Perón returned on 20 June 1973 amid the Ezeiza massacre and was himself elected president in October. Violence between left- and right-wing Peronists continued, and he could not resolve it. He died on 1 July 1974 and his third wife, Isabel Perón, succeeded him as vice president.

Supporters praise the Peróns for efforts to reduce poverty and dignify labour; detractors consider them demagogues and dictators. The movement continues mainly as the Justicialist Party. Perón was buried in La Chacarita Cemetery; in 1987 his tomb was desecrated and his hands stolen, a crime that remains unresolved.
juan-ponce-de-leon: Juan Ponce de León was born in the village of Santervás de Campos, in what is now the Spanish province of Valladolid. Early historians placed his birth in 1460, but more recent evidence shows he was likely born in 1474. The identity of his parents is still conjecture, but the historian Aurelio Tió argued that he came from a distinguished noble family, with Rodrigo Ponce de León, Duke of Cádiz, as his first cousin. In September 1493, aged nineteen, he sailed as one of 200 gentleman volunteers on Christopher Columbus's second voyage, which anchored off the island the Taíno called Borikén, later Puerto Rico.

In 1502 Nicolás de Ovando arrived as governor of Hispaniola. When the Taíno overran a Spanish garrison at Higüey in 1504, Ovando sent Ponce de León to crush the rebellion. He took part in the Higüey massacre, about which the friar Bartolomé de las Casas tried to inform the Spanish authorities. Ovando rewarded him by making him frontier governor of the province, with a land grant and an encomienda of Indian labour, and in 1505 he founded the town of Salvaleón.

In 1508 Ferdinand II of Aragon gave him permission for the first official expedition to Puerto Rico, which left Hispaniola on 12 July 1508 with about 50 men and found placer gold in the west of the island. He founded settlements near the mines at San Germán and Caparra, where local people were compelled to work under the encomienda system. The Crown named him the island's first governor in 1509. A long legal dispute with Diego Colón, Columbus's son, ended in 1511 with Colón replacing him.

King Ferdinand then urged him to seek new lands outside Colón's authority. A royal contract of February 1512 gave him the right to search for the islands of Beniny, and in March 1513 he set out from Puerto Rico with three ships at his own expense and sixty-five people. He named La Florida, charted the Atlantic coast to the Keys and north along the Gulf coast. The story that he sought a Fountain of Youth has no contemporary evidence, and most modern historians consider it a myth.

In 1514 Ferdinand knighted him and reinstated him as governor of Puerto Rico. In March 1521 he returned to south-west Florida with about 200 men, priests, farmers and artisans and fifty horses, the first large attempt to found a Spanish colony in what is now the continental United States. The Calusa attacked, and an arrow struck his thigh. The colonists abandoned the settlement and sailed to Havana, where he died in July 1521. He was buried in Puerto Rico, and his remains lie in the Cathedral of San Juan Bautista in San Juan.
juan-prim: Juan Prim y Prats was born in Reus on 6 December 1814, the son of Lieutenant Colonel Pablo Prim. He joined the free corps known as the tiradores de Isabel II and had his baptism of fire on 7 August 1834 during the First Carlist War. After the pacification of 1839, as a progressist opposed to the dictatorship of General Espartero, he was sent into exile. In 1843 he was elected deputy for Tarragona, and after defeating Espartero at Bruch he entered Madrid in triumph with General Serrano. The regent Maria Christina made him a major general, Count of Reus and Viscount of Bruch.

General Narváez, the prime minister, sentenced Prim to six years' imprisonment in the Philippine Islands after he showed signs of opposition, but the sentence was not carried out, and he remained in exile in England and France until the amnesty of 1847. He later served as captain general of Puerto Rico and, elected to the Cortes in 1854, supported General O'Donnell. His service in the war with Morocco in 1860 earned him the title Marquis of los Castillejos and the rank of Grandee of Spain.

Prim commanded the Spanish expeditionary army in Mexico in 1862. A sympathiser with the Mexican liberal cause, he refused to approve Napoleon III's ambitions and withdrew the Spanish forces after meeting Manuel Doblado. Back in Spain he led pronunciamentos against Narváez and O'Donnell, all unsuccessful until Narváez died in April 1868. In September 1868 Serrano and Prim returned and Brigadier Topete, commanding the fleet, raised the standard of revolt at Cádiz. In July 1869 Serrano became regent, and Prim became president of the council and a marshal.

Prim searched the courts of Europe for a monarch willing to be democratically elected. France rejected Leopold of Hohenzollern for fear that Prussia would grow more powerful, and Amadeo, Duke of Aosta, who consented, was elected king on 6 November 1870. On 28 December, leaving the Cortes, Prim was shot by unknown assassins and died two days later. His assassination destabilised the reign of Amadeo I, who lost an important figure to legitimise his rule. The workshop of Plácido Zuloaga made a monumental sarcophagus for him, finished in 1875 in Eibar and now in the cemetery at Reus.
juan-rulfo: Juan Nepomuceno Carlos Pérez Rulfo Vizcaíno was born in 1917 in Apulco, Jalisco, though some dispute whether the place was San Gabriel. His father was killed in 1923 and his mother died in 1927, and his grandmother raised him in Guadalajara. His extended family were landowners whose fortunes were ruined by the Mexican Revolution and the Cristero War of 1926-1928.

He studied at the Luis Silva School from 1928 to 1932 and graduated as a bookkeeper, though he never practised, and attended a seminary from 1932 to 1934. The University of Guadalajara was closed by a strike, so he moved to Mexico City and left the National Military Academy after three months. In 1936 he obtained a job as an immigration file clerk and could audit literature courses at the national university.

At the university Rulfo began writing under the guidance of a coworker, Efrén Hernández, and in 1944 he co-founded the literary journal Pan. He later worked as an immigration agent and a travelling sales agent. A fellowship at the Centro Mexicano de Escritores, supported by the Rockefeller Foundation, let him write two books between 1952 and 1954.

The first, El Llano en llamas (1953), is a collection of harshly realistic stories of rural Mexico around the time of the Revolution and the Cristero War. The second, Pedro Páramo (1955), follows Juan Preciado to his dead mother's hometown, Comala, which he finds deserted and filled with spectral figures who reveal the cruel strongman Pedro Páramo. It sold only two thousand copies in its first four years, then became highly acclaimed. It has been translated into more than 30 languages. From 1954 to 1957 Rulfo worked with the Río Papaloapan Commission, and from 1962 until his death in 1986 he edited for the National Institute for Indigenous People.

Rulfo's spare style and colloquial dialogue lift regional Mexican fiction to a universal level. His former friend Antonio Alatorre noted the influence of William Faulkner on passages of the novel. Gabriel García Márquez said that discovering Pedro Páramo in 1961 opened the way to One Hundred Years of Solitude, and that Rulfo's published work, under 300 pages, is as durable as the pages that have come down from Sophocles. Jorge Luis Borges rated the novel among the best texts in any language. Rulfo was also a photographer, and the Juan Rulfo Foundation holds more than 6,000 of his negatives.
juan-velasco-alvarado: Juan Velasco was born in Castilla, a city near Piura on Peru's north coast, the son of Manuel José Velasco, a medical assistant, and Clara Luz Alvarado, who had 11 children. He described his youth as one of "dignified poverty", working as a shoeshine boy in Piura. In 1929 he stowed away on a ship to Lima, falsified his age and joined the army as a private on 5 April 1929. A year later he scored highest of all applicants in the entrance exam of the Escuela Militar de Chorrillos, and in 1934 he graduated at the head of his class.

During Fernando Belaúnde's administration (1963–1968) Congress censured several cabinets, and political instability was widely perceived. Officers who had put down two guerrilla uprisings inspired by the Cuban Revolution came to regard social inequality as a danger to national security. A dispute with the International Petroleum Company over the La Brea y Pariñas oil fields became a scandal when a key page of a contract was found missing.
