Velasco seized power on 3 October 1968 in a bloodless coup, closed Congress and sent Belaúnde into exile. The army took over the disputed oil fields on 8 October. The new Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces pursued a programme known as Peruanismo, nationalising industries from fisheries to mining and telecommunications. In its first ten years the government expropriated 15,000 properties, some nine million hectares, benefiting about 300,000 families, in what was the second-largest land reform in Latin American history after Cuba's.

The education reform of 1972 provided for bilingual schooling for indigenous peoples, and in 1975 a law made Quechua an official language equal to Spanish, though it was never enforced. In foreign policy Velasco was hostile to the United States, tightened relations with Cuba and the Soviet bloc and bought large quantities of Soviet arms. On 29 August 1975 military commanders began a coup in Tacna, known as the Tacnazo, and appointed Prime Minister Francisco Morales Bermúdez president. Velasco, seriously ill for at least a year, announced that he would not resist, saying that Peruvians cannot fight against each other.

Velasco kept a low profile until his death in 1977, and a large crowd of sympathisers attended his funeral. The success of his economic policies is still debated. After the agrarian reform people moved to Lima and other coastal cities, where the failure to manage the influx contributed to slums.
juan-vicente-gomez: Juan Vicente Gómez Chacón was born on 24 July 1857, the firstborn son of Pedro Cornelio Gómez and Hermenegilda Chacón Alarcón, in a prominent family of Andean landowners at La Mulera. In 1899 he joined the private army of Cipriano Castro, a friend since Castro's exile in Colombia, which swept down on Caracas that year and seized control of the country. He became Castro's second vice president in 1901 and first vice president in 1904, and in 1902 head of the military, responsible for putting down several major revolts, among them the battle of Ciudad Bolívar on 21 July 1903. He seized power from Castro in a coup on 19 December 1908, while Castro was in Europe for medical treatment.

Gómez reduced Venezuela's heavy debt by granting concessions to foreign oil companies after petroleum was found in Lake Maracaibo in 1914. This won him the support of the United States and Europe and brought economic stability. He launched a large public works programme that included the Transandean Highway, 1,539 km long, and founded the country's first airline and the Venezuelan Air Force, while the army was reorganized on a modern basis. He also received generous kickbacks and became by far the richest man in the country. Congress gave him the title El Benemérito, the Meritorious One; opponents called him El Bagre, the Catfish, and the Tyrant of the Andes.

He officially held the presidency on only three occasions. Re-elected in 1914, he declined to take office, and Victorino Márquez served as provisional president while Gómez ruled from Maracay. He returned to office in 1922 and ruled until 22 April 1929, when Juan Bautista Pérez became president with Gómez as the final authority. On 13 June 1931 Congress forced Pérez to resign and elected Gómez again, and this time he resumed office, holding it until his death.

Students of the Generation of 1928, among them Rómulo Betancourt and Jóvito Villalba, led protests against him in Caracas. His secret police were ubiquitous: Time magazine wrote that he kept twelve spies on his payroll for every policeman in Caracas. Gómez held basic civil liberties in disdain and did little for public education.

Supporters credit him with ending the civil wars and the power of regional caudillos, repaying all foreign and internal debt, and, through roads and oil-industry jobs, spreading a sense of national unity. Critics, including Betancourt, called him an instrument of foreign control of the Venezuelan economy, since Royal Dutch Shell and Standard Oil gained exploration rights under him. Juan Vicente Gómez International Airport was named for him in 1993.
juba-i: Juba I was an Amazigh prince of Numidia, in present-day Algeria, born at Hippo, modern Annaba, and son and successor of Hiempsal II. In 81 BCE Hiempsal had been driven from his throne, and Sulla sent Pompey to Africa to restore him. For that reason Hiempsal and later Juba were allies of Pompey. The alliance was strengthened when Juba visited Rome and Julius Caesar, defending a client against Juba's father, insulted him by pulling his beard, and again in 50 BCE when the tribune Gaius Scribonius Curio openly proposed that Numidia should be sold privately.

In August 49 BCE Caesar sent Curio to take Africa from the Republicans. Curio held the governor Publius Attius Varus in low esteem and took fewer legions than he had been given. At the Battle of the Bagradas he routed Varus's army with an uphill attack, then acted on faulty intelligence and attacked what he took for a detachment of Juba's army. The bulk of the king's forces were there, and Juba's commander Saburra ambushed and virtually destroyed the Roman force. Curio died in the fighting on a hilltop, few escaped by ship, and Juba took several senators captive back to Numidia for display and execution.

When Caesar came to Africa, Juba first planned to join Quintus Caecilius Metellus Pius Scipio Nasica, but his kingdom was invaded from the west by Bocchus II, an ally of Caesar, and the adventurer Publius Sittius, and he marched home. Scipio then appealed for help, and Juba joined him with three legions, about 15,000 light infantry, 1,000 cavalry and 30 elephants for the Battle of Thapsus, camping apart from Scipio's main lines.

Seeing Scipio's defeat to be certain, Juba took no part in the battle and fled with his 30,000 men. He and the Roman general Marcus Petreius found their retreat cut off and made a suicide pact, fighting one against the other so that one would die honourably. Accounts of their deaths differ; in the most likely version one killed the other, and the survivor, failing to stab himself, had a slave kill him. Juba was the father of Juba II, later king of Numidia and then Mauretania, whose wives were Cleopatra Selene II and Glaphyra, and the grandfather of King Ptolemy of Mauretania.
juba-ii: Juba II was an Amazigh prince of Numidia, born at Hippone (modern Annaba), the only child and heir of King Juba I. His mother is unknown, though he claimed descent from Hannibal. His father had been an ally of Pompey, and in 46 BCE Julius Caesar defeated him at Thapsus. The infant Juba was taken to Rome and walked in Caesar's triumphal procession. His biographer Duane Roller argues that he was born in early 48 BCE, though the usual estimates run from 52 to 50 BCE.

In Rome he learned Latin and Greek, became a Roman citizen and is said to have become one of the best educated men there. He was raised by Caesar and later by Octavian, the future Augustus, whom he accompanied on campaigns and beside whom he fought at Actium in 31 BCE. By the age of 20 he had written Roman Archaeology.

In 30 BCE Octavian restored Juba as king of Numidia. About 25 BCE Augustus gave him Mauretania instead, enlarged with western Numidia, perhaps as a reward for service in a campaign in Hispania, while eastern Numidia was annexed to the province of Africa Proconsularis. His marriage to Cleopatra Selene II, daughter of Cleopatra VII and Mark Antony, probably took place in 25 BCE. They made their capital at Caesarea, modern Cherchell, in honour of Augustus. Building at Caesarea and Volubilis mixed Egyptian, Greek and Roman styles.

Mauretania traded across the Mediterranean, particularly with Spain and Italy, exporting fish, grapes, pearls, figs, grain, furniture and purple dye from shellfish. Juba sent a party to the Purple Islands to revive the old Phoenician dye industry, and Tingis (modern Tangier) became a major trading centre. He supported the performing arts, the sciences and natural history. In 21 CE he made his son Ptolemy co-ruler and he died in 23 CE, to be buried with Cleopatra Selene in the Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania.

Juba wrote in Greek on history, natural history, geography, grammar, painting and theatre. His works include Resemblances, a comparison of Greek and Roman institutions, Libyka, On Arabia, and a Theatrical History in at least seventeen books. Only fragments survive, known from about a hundred quotations, around half in Pliny the Elder's Natural History. He collected a large library, and a monument to his writings stood in the Gymnasium of Ptolemy at Athens. Plutarch described him as one of the most gifted rulers of his time.
jubaland: Jubaland lies in southern Somalia, west of the Jubba River, and its largest city is the port of Kismayo. Bardhere, Luuq and Beled Haawo are other principal settlements. Its area is about 110,293 square kilometres, and in the colonial period part of the same territory was carved out as the North Eastern Province of Kenya. Most of its people are Somali. The region stretches from Dolow to the Indian Ocean and borders Kenya and Ethiopia.

In the Middle Ages the Ajuran Sultanate held sway over the territory, followed in the early modern period by the Geledi Sultanate. From 1836 to 1861 parts of Jubaland were nominally claimed by the Sultanate of Muscat. In 1819–23 Sheikh Ibrahim Hassan and his companions founded the fortified town of Bardheere, whose sheikh later led a campaign against the Oromo.

After the First World War Britain ceded Jubaland to Italy as a reward for Italy's joining the Allies in the First World War. It briefly formed the Italian colony of Trans-Juba, or Oltre Giuba, under the governor Corrado Zoli, and Italy issued its first stamps for the territory on 29 July 1925. Britain had wanted to exchange it for the return of the Aegean islands to Greece, but Benito Mussolini's government rejected that. After the Corfu incident the British prime minister Ramsay MacDonald decided to cede it unconditionally. Jubaland was incorporated into Italian Somaliland on 30 June 1926, and Britain kept the southern half, later the Northern Frontier District.

On 1 July 1960 the region, with the rest of Italian Somaliland and British Somaliland, became part of the independent Somali Republic. In 1974–1975 the Soviet Union airlifted some 90,000 people from drought-stricken northern regions to new settlements in Lower and Middle Jubba, where they were introduced to farming and fishing. After the Somali Civil War, a conference at Kismayo in 2013 approved a provisional constitution, and Jubaland became an autonomous federal member state of Somalia.
jubba-river: The Jubba River, also spelled Juba, begins at the border with Ethiopia, where the Dawa and Ganale Dorya rivers meet. It flows directly south to the Somali Sea, which it reaches at the Goobweyn juncture, and drains a basin of 749,000 square kilometres. The basin is primarily savanna and is the ecologically richest part of Somalia because of its fertile farmland. Its wildlife includes giraffes, cheetahs, lions, leopards, hyenas, buffalos, hippopotamus, crocodiles, oryx, gazelles, ostriches and Somali wild asses.

In the Middle Ages the river lay within the Ajuran Empire, which rose in the 13th century and monopolised the water of the Jubba and the Shebelle, making it the only hydraulic empire in Africa. It built limestone wells and cisterns, some still in use, and its rulers developed systems of agriculture and taxation that lasted in parts of the Horn of Africa into the 19th century.

Irrigation ditches known as Kelliyo carried water from both rivers to plantations of sorghum, maize, beans, grain and cotton. Farms at Afgooye, Bardhere and elsewhere in the valleys became more productive, and their crops went to coastal ports such as Mogadishu, Merca, Barawa, Kismayo and Hobyo, whose merchants traded with Arabia, Persia, India, Venice, Egypt, Portugal, Java and China.

In 1863 the German explorer Baron Karl Klaus von der Decken ascended the lower river on the small steamship Welf. He wrecked it in the rapids above Bardhere, and he and three of his party were killed when local Somalis attacked them. The Italian explorer Vittorio Bottego, who sailed 640 kilometres of the river in 1891, was the first European to explore it widely and complete its course. He renamed the Ganale after the Italian naturalist Giacomo Doria, calling it the Ganale Doria.

The river gives its name to the Somali administrative regions of Upper Juba, which comprises Gedo, Bay and Bakool, Middle Juba and Lower Juba, and to the wider historical region of Jubaland. Towns along its course include Dolow, Luuq, Burdhubo, Beled'hawo, Bardhere, Buale and Goobweyn near Kismaayo.
judaea: Judea is a mountainous region of the Levant, part of which is desert, traditionally dominated by Jerusalem. It rises to 1,020 metres at the Hebron Hills, 30 km southwest of Jerusalem, and descends to as much as 400 metres below sea level in the east. Rainfall falls from about 600 millimetres around western Jerusalem to about 100 millimetres in the eastern parts, which form the Judaean Desert. Geographers divide it into the Hebron hills, the Jerusalem saddle, the Bethel hills and the desert east of Jerusalem. The main north-south route ran along the top of the central ridge.

The name is a Greek and Roman adaptation of the Hebrew Yehudah, the name of one of the Twelve Tribes of Israel and later of the Kingdom of Judah. The earliest known extra-biblical record of the name Judah is Nimrud Tablet K.3751, dated about 733 BCE. Under the Hasmoneans, the Herodians and the Romans the term covered a larger area than before. Josephus described Judea as lying between Anuath on the north and a village on the border of Arabia in the south, extending from the Jordan to Joppa, with Jerusalem in the middle.

According to the biblical account, a united monarchy under Saul, David and Solomon followed the settlement of the Israelite tribes, and scholarship is divided on the historical extent of such a kingdom. The northern kingdom fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire in 720 BCE. Judah paid tribute to Assyria from 715, later to Egypt and, after 601 BCE, to the Neo-Babylonian Empire, until Babylonia conquered it in 586 BCE, destroyed the temple in Jerusalem and exiled many of the inhabitants. Cyrus the Great took Babylon in 539 BCE. Judea stayed under Persian rule until Alexander the Great's conquest in 332 BCE and later fell to the Seleucid Empire, until the revolt of Judas Maccabeus brought the Hasmonean dynasty, which ruled for over a century.

Under the Hasmoneans Jerusalem grew greatly, and the number of farming villages around it nearly doubled. Pompey besieged Jerusalem in 63 BCE during a civil war between Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II, and political rule passed to the Herodian dynasty as client kings. Judea came under direct Roman rule in 6 CE. A revolt began in 66 CE, and in 70 CE Jerusalem was besieged and razed and the Second Temple destroyed. After the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 136 CE most of the Jews in Judea were killed or displaced, and Hadrian renamed the province Syria Palaestina.

Judea's decline ended in the fifth century CE, when it became a monastic centre and Jerusalem a major Christian pilgrimage site. The Byzantines grouped it with Samaria and other districts as Palaestina Prima. The First Crusade took Jerusalem from the Seljuks in 1099.
judaism: The term Judaism derives from the Greek Ioudaismos, which first appears in the second century BCE in the book of 2 Maccabees. It meant forming part of a cultural entity, the opposite of Hellenismos, and the conflict between the two lay behind the Maccabean Revolt. According to the Hebrew Bible, God established a covenant with Abraham, who is presented as the ancestor of the Israelites. The Bible tells of a United Kingdom of Israel under Saul, David and Solomon, which split into the Kingdom of Israel and the Kingdom of Judah. Israel fell to the Neo-Assyrian Empire around 720 BCE, and Judah to Nebuchadnezzar II in 586–87 BCE. After the Achaemenid Empire took Babylon, many Israelites returned, and the Second Temple stood until 70 CE.

Judaism is an Abrahamic, monotheistic, ethnic religion. Religious Jews regard it as their means of observing the Mosaic covenant between God and the Jewish people. Its core texts are the Torah, the Nevi'im and the Ketuvim, which together make up the Hebrew Bible, or Tanakh. Alongside this Written Torah stands the Oral Torah, which includes the Mishnah and the Talmud. Rabbinic Judaism holds that God revealed his laws to Moses on Mount Sinai in both forms, and has been the mainstream form since the 6th century CE. The faith begins with ethical monotheism, the belief that God is one, which religious Jews express by reciting the Shema Yisrael twice daily.

Christianity was originally a sect of Second Temple Judaism, and the two religions diverged in the first century, at first over whether Jesus was the Jewish Messiah. Judaism's texts, traditions and values strongly influenced Christianity and Islam, and through Christianity it has had an indirect but significant role in Western culture. The Jewish Enlightenment of the late 18th century divided Western Jewry into the Orthodox, Conservative and Reform movements. Daniel Boyarin argues that Judaism does not fit conventional Western categories such as religion, ethnicity or culture.
judas-maccabeus: Judah was the third son of Mattathias, a priest from the village of Modi'in. In 167 BCE Mattathias and his sons Judah, Eleazar, Simon, John and Jonathan began a revolt against the Seleucid ruler Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who had issued decrees forbidding Jewish religious practices. After Mattathias died in 166 BCE, Judah took over the leadership in accordance with his father's deathbed wish, and the First Book of Maccabees praises his valour and military talent.

Judah received the surname Maccabee in the early days of the revolt. Its origin is unknown. One suggestion derives it from the Aramaic maqqaba, a hammer, in recognition of his ferocity in battle. The name came to signify all the Hasmoneans who fought in the revolt.

Facing superior Seleucid forces, Judah avoided their regular army at first and used guerrilla warfare. He defeated a small force under Apollonius, governor of Samaria, at Nahal el-Haramiah, killed Apollonius and kept his sword until his death. He then routed a larger army under Seron near Beth-Horon and, at the Battle of Emmaus, defeated the forces of Nicanor and Gorgias, sent by the regent Lysias, after a forced night march that eluded Gorgias.

Judah drove his enemies from Jerusalem except for the garrison in the citadel of Acra, purified the Temple and restored its service on 25 Kislev, which is 14 December 164 BCE. The reconsecration became the holiday of Hanukkah. At Beth-zechariah the Seleucids won their first major victory over the Maccabees, but a peace at the end of 163 BCE restored religious freedom and the Temple to the Jews. In 161 BCE his army destroyed a Seleucid force near Adasa and killed Nicanor, and Judah made an agreement with the Roman Republic, the first recorded contract between the Jewish people and the Romans.

The agreement with Rome did not change the policy of King Demetrius I Soter, who sent a new army under Bacchides. Of its 20,000 men, so many outnumbered Judah's force that most of his men left the field and urged him to do the same, but he stood his ground. At the Battle of Elasa he and those who stayed with him were killed. His brothers took his body and buried it in the family tomb at Modiin.

His death stirred the Jews to renewed resistance, and under his brothers Jonathan and Simon the Jews eventually won independence and the freedom to worship. Judah inspired writers, painters and composers. George Frideric Handel wrote the oratorio Judas Maccabaeus in 1746.
jugurtha: Numidia lay in North Africa roughly within what is now eastern Algeria, parts of western Tunisia and western Libya. Masinissa, chief of the Massyli near Cirta, used Roman support in the Second Punic War to found a kingdom, and on his death in 148 BCE his son Micipsa succeeded him. Jugurtha, whose name probably means he exceeded them in Libyco-Berber, was Micipsa's adopted son and the illegitimate son of Mastanabal, which made him an illegitimate grandson of Masinissa.

Jugurtha was so popular among the Numidians that Micipsa sent him to Hispania to assist Scipio Aemilianus. At the siege of Numantia, in 134 and 133 BCE, he served alongside Gaius Marius and learned that Romans could be bribed. Sallust has him call Rome a city for sale and doomed to quick destruction, if it should find a buyer.

When Micipsa died in 118 BCE, Jugurtha shared the succession with Micipsa's sons Hiempsal and Adherbal. Jugurtha quarrelled with Hiempsal at once and had him killed, which led to open war with Adherbal. Adherbal fled to Rome after being defeated, and Roman officials divided Numidia, probably in 116, giving Jugurtha the western half, though accusations arose that they had taken bribes.

By 112 BCE Jugurtha again attacked Adherbal and penned him in Cirta. Roman residents there urged Adherbal to hold out, but the Senate, with its troops busy in the Cimbrian War, only sent embassies. When Cirta fell, Jugurtha's troops massacred many of its inhabitants, including Romans, and Rome sent the consul Lucius Calpurnius Bestia. A favourable peace again raised suspicions of bribery. Jugurtha was summoned to Rome to give evidence, but a tribune's veto prevented it.

War resumed under the consul Quintus Caecilius Metellus Numidicus. In 110 BCE Jugurtha forced the capitulation of an entire army under Aulus Postumius Albinus. Metellus won several battles in 109 BCE without ending the war, and Marius, once elected consul for 107 BCE, took command against Jugurtha's guerrilla warfare.

Jugurtha was allied by marriage with Bocchus I of Mauretania, who was his father-in-law and joined the fighting against Marius in 107 BCE. In 105 BCE Marius sent his quaestor Sulla to Mauretania. Bocchus agreed to hand Jugurtha over in exchange for land in western Numidia as far as the Mulucha River. Jugurtha was brought to Rome in chains and paraded in Marius's triumph, where his robes were removed and an earring was torn off, costing him part of an ear. He was thrown into the Tullianum prison and died there in 104 BCE, most likely by strangulation, though he may have been starved.
jugurthine-war: Numidia was a kingdom of North Africa, roughly corresponding to the north of present-day Algeria, next to what had been Carthage. Its king Masinissa, a steadfast Roman ally in the Third Punic War, died in 149 BCE and was succeeded by his son Micipsa. Micipsa's nephew Jugurtha had fought under Scipio Aemilianus at Numantia and learned Roman manners and tactics there. Micipsa adopted him and left the kingdom jointly to him and his own sons Adherbal and Hiempsal. After his death Jugurtha had Hiempsal assassinated and defeated Adherbal, who fled to Rome. A Roman commission led by Lucius Opimius divided Numidia from 116 BCE, but Jugurtha bribed its members and received the better western half.

In 113 BCE Jugurtha again attacked Adherbal and besieged him in Cirta. A delegation under Marcus Scaurus failed to force him to a commitment, Adherbal surrendered, and Jugurtha had him executed along with the Romans who had joined the defence. The deaths of Roman citizens caused fury at home, and the Senate, threatened by the tribune Gaius Memmius, declared war with reluctance. The consul Lucius Calpurnius Bestia granted Jugurtha lenient terms, and Jugurtha bribed two tribunes to prevent his testimony in Rome. In 110 BCE the consul Spurius Postumius Albinus achieved little, and his brother Aulus Postumius Albinus was lured into the Sahara, lost half his army and agreed to a treaty, which the Senate refused to honour.

In 109 BCE Quintus Metellus, chosen for integrity, retrained the army and won the Battle of the Muthul, though Jugurtha escaped and turned to guerrilla warfare. Metellus took the fortress of Thala after forty days, but Jugurtha again escaped and took refuge with his father-in-law Bocchus I of Mauretania. The Tribal Assembly gave the command to Gaius Marius, elected consul in 107 BCE. Marius took Capsa and fought the Second Battle of Cirta against both kings. Through negotiations Lucius Cornelius Sulla, his quaestor, received Jugurtha in chains from Bocchus.

Bocchus annexed the western part of Jugurtha's kingdom and was made a friend of the Roman people. Jugurtha was held in the Tullianum in Rome and executed after appearing in Marius's triumph in 104 BCE. Numidia did not become a Roman province until 46 BCE. The war revealed the effect of corruption on Roman politics, and Marius's rise, with a command given by the Assembly against the Senate's usual practice, was followed by his later rivalry with Sulla. According to Plutarch the rivalry began over Sulla's role in the capture, which Sulla commemorated on a ring. The historian Sallust wrote a monograph on the war, which with Plutarch's lives of Sulla and Marius is a main source.
juho-kusti-paasikivi: Paasikivi was born Johan Gustaf Hellsten on 27 November 1870 in Hämeenkoski, in southern Finland, to a travelling merchant from Tampere. His mother died when he was four, and his father died in debt when he was 14. He took the Finnish name Paasikivi in 1885, entered the University of Helsinki in 1890 and received a doctorate in law in 1902. He was Director-in-Chief of the Treasury of the Grand Duchy of Finland until 1914, and he sat in Parliament for the Finnish Party, which supported greater autonomy but opposed steps the Russians might perceive as aggressive.

After 1914 Paasikivi became chief general manager of the Kansallis-Osake-Pankki bank. After the Bolshevik October Revolution he championed full independence in the form of a constitutional monarchy. In the Finnish Civil War he stood on the side of the White government, and as prime minister from May to November 1918 he sought a German prince, Frederick Charles of Hesse, as king. With Germany's defeat the monarchy was dropped for a republic and his Senate resigned. In 1934 he became chairman of the National Coalition Party.

From 1936 to 1939 he was envoy in Stockholm, seeking Swedish defence guarantees, which did not come. Before the Winter War he represented Finland in the negotiations in Moscow and supported compliance with some of the demands. He led the armistice and peace talks, and resigned as envoy in Moscow when he learned that thoughts in Helsinki ran towards retaking lost territory with German aid. By 1943 he had concluded that Germany would lose the war.

Paasikivi became prime minister in 1944, and Parliament chose him president in 1946, at the age of 75, when Mannerheim resigned. His policy was realistic: he held that Finland must adapt to superpower politics and sign treaties with the Soviet Union, and he aimed to prove that Finland posed no threat to it. In spring 1948 he ordered army and navy units to Helsinki against a possible communist coup, and after the elections of that year he kept the communists out of government. His approach, called the Paasikivi doctrine, was named Finlandization in the 1970s.

He was re-elected in 1950 and opened the 1952 Summer Olympics in Helsinki. By the end of his second term the Karelian refugees had been resettled, the war reparations paid and rationing ended, and in January 1956 the Soviet Union removed its troops from the Porkkala naval base. He died on 14 December 1956.
jules-ferry: Jules François Camille Ferry was born on 5 April 1832 in the Vosges department, the son of Charles-Édouard Ferry, a lawyer from a family of bellmakers established at Saint-Dié, and Adélaïde Jamelet. His grandfather had been mayor of Saint-Dié through the Consulate and the First Empire. He studied law and was called to the bar at Paris in 1854, but turned to politics and wrote for newspapers, especially Le Temps, attacking the Second Empire and above all Baron Haussmann; his articles were republished in 1868 as The Fantastic Tales of Haussmann.

Elected republican deputy for Paris in 1869, he protested against the declaration of war on Germany, and on 6 September 1870 the Government of National Defence made him prefect of the Seine. He administered Paris during the siege and resigned on 5 June 1871 after the Paris Commune. After a spell as minister at Athens he returned as deputy for the Vosges and became a leader of the Opportunist Republicans. He sat in ministries from 4 February 1879 and was prime minister in 1880–1881 and 1883–1885.

Ferry sought a non-clerical public education. After a law of 27 February 1880 reorganised the committee of public education, he passed his laws of 16 June 1881 and 28 March 1882, which made primary education free, secular and mandatory; the professors called the Republic's black hussars doubled in number under his ministry. He also formed the idea after 1870 of a great colonial empire, chiefly for economic exploitation. He directed the negotiations for the protectorate over Tunis in 1881, prepared a treaty on Madagascar and organised the conquest of Annam and Tonkin. On 28 March 1884 he told the Chamber that the superior races had a right, because they had a duty, to civilise the inferior races.

The war with Qing China over Tonkin ended his premiership. The sudden retreat of French troops from Lạng Sơn caused uproar in Paris, the Tonkin Affair, with violent denunciation by Georges Clemenceau and other radicals, and he fell on 30 March 1885. The peace treaty of 9 June 1885, by which the Qing ceded suzerainty over Annam and Tonkin, was the work of his ministry, but he never served as premier again.

After the resignation of Jules Grévy in December 1887 he stood for the presidency but withdrew in favour of Sadi Carnot when the radicals refused support. On 10 December 1887 a man named Aubertin tried to assassinate him, and he died on 17 March 1893 of complications attributed to the wound. The Chamber of Deputies gave him a state funeral.
jules-mazarin: Giulio Mazzarino was born on 14 July 1602 in Pescina in the Abruzzo region of Italy, the eldest of six children. His father, Pietro Mazzarino, had moved to Rome from Sicily in 1590 to serve as a chamberlain in the household of Filippo I Colonna, the Grand Constable of Naples. His mother, Ortensia Bufalini, came from a Roman family of noble origin. In 1628 he took a doctorate in both civil and canon law, and Pope Urban VIII, who forgave him for leaving his post in a papal regiment without permission, made him a papal emissary.

Mazarin offered his services to Cardinal Richelieu and moved to Paris in 1640. He advised Richelieu on political and cultural matters and carried out a diplomatic mission to Savoy, where he secured the position of the regent Christine, Duchess of Savoy, and arranged an alliance with France. He was made a cardinal on 16 December 1641. Richelieu did not name him as successor, though according to Mazarin he advised Louis XIII to employ him. After Louis XIII named three advisers, Mazarin and Léon Bouthillier, comte de Chavigny, had François Sublet de Noyers forced out in April 1643.

The long war against the Habsburgs cost a great deal, and Mazarin raised money by fines on Parisians living outside the old city limits, a tax on goods entering Paris and a levy on nobles who sat on royal courts and councils. Resentment of him and of the regent Anne of Austria led to the Fronde, which lasted from 1648 to 1653. The Parlement of Paris issued a charter forbidding new taxes without its approval. When the nobles' revolt led by Louis, Grand Condé, followed, Mazarin withdrew for a time to Brühl near Cologne, and returned to Paris in 1653 after Turenne had defeated Condé.

Between 1657 and 1660 Mazarin made an alliance with England, formed the League of the Rhine in 1658 and saw Turenne defeat Condé at the Battle of the Dunes. The Treaty of the Pyrenees, signed on 7 November 1659, added three provinces to France, and in 1660 he arranged the marriage of Louis XIV to Maria Theresa of Spain. He had also overseen the king's education from the king's eighth birthday and wrote guidance for him on government. He died on 9 March 1661.

Mazarin was a major patron of the arts. He founded the Royal Academy of Painting and Sculpture in 1648, introduced Italian opera to Paris and assembled a collection recorded after his death as 858 paintings and 128 statues, much of it now in the Louvre. He founded the Bibliothèque Mazarine, the first public library in France, and left funds for the Collège des Quatre-Nations, now the Institut de France.
julia-domna: Julia Domna was born at Emesa, modern Homs in Syria, around 160, into a wealthy Arab family that had provided priest-kings of the temple of the god Elagabalus and had entered the senatorial aristocracy. She was the youngest daughter of the high priest Julius Bassianus and the sister of Julia Maesa. Her name Domna is said to be an archaic Arabic word meaning black, referring to the black stone in which the god appeared.

After losing his first wife about 186, the politician Septimius Severus sought her as his wife; the Historia Augusta says he had heard a prophecy of a woman in Syria who would marry a king. They married in the summer of 187 at Lugdunum (Lyon), where he was governor. The marriage is described as a happy one, and she won a reputation for letters and philosophy. Their sons were Lucius Septimius Bassianus, later Caracalla, born in 188, and Publius Septimius Geta, born the following year.

When the emperor Commodus was murdered in 192, Pertinax and Didius Julianus held the throne briefly before Severus claimed it in 193. He defeated Pescennius Niger at Issus in 194 and Clodius Albinus at Lugdunum in 197, and Domna became empress. Unusually for an imperial wife, she accompanied her husband on campaign and stayed in camp with the army. She received many titles, among them Mother of the Invincible Camps and Mother of Augustus, and appeared on coins as Julia Augusta.

When Severus died at Eboracum (York) in 211, his sons were to rule jointly, and Domna acted as mediator between them. In December Caracalla's soldiers murdered Geta, and his name was removed from inscriptions. She received the title Pia Felix Augusta, perhaps implying that she continued her husband's attributes. She accompanied Caracalla to Nicomedia and later lived at Antioch.

In 217 Caracalla began a war against Parthia, and Domna stayed at Antioch to help with his correspondence. When he was assassinated by a soldier she killed herself, perhaps hastened by breast cancer and by reluctance to return to private life. Her sister Julia Maesa restored the family's rule in 218, and her nieces Julia Soaemias and Julia Mamaea were the mothers of the emperors Elagabalus and Severus Alexander.
Her body was brought to Rome, and was later moved with Geta's remains to the Mausoleum of Hadrian. She is thought to have encouraged Philostratus to write the Life of Apollonius of Tyana.
julia-ward-howe: Julia Ward was born in New York City on 27 May 1819, the fourth of seven children. Her father, Samuel Ward III, was a Wall Street banker and a strict Calvinist Episcopalian; her mother, the poet Julia Rush Cutler Ward, died in childbirth when Julia was five. She was educated by private tutors and at schools for young ladies until sixteen, and read widely in her eldest brother's private library, which held many books at odds with the Calvinistic view. She became a Unitarian by 1841.

In 1843 she married Samuel Gridley Howe, a physician and reformer who had founded the Perkins School for the Blind, despite an age difference of eighteen years. They had six children. The marriage was troubled: her husband disapproved of her writing and took control of her estate income, and they separated in 1852. After his death in 1876 she found that most of her money had been lost in his bad investments.

Before her marriage Howe had published essays on Goethe, Schiller and Lamartine. Her first volume of poetry, Passion-Flowers, appeared anonymously, as did her second, Words for the Hour, in 1857. She also wrote plays, among them Leonora, The World's Own and Hippolytus, and published A Trip to Cuba in 1860. Her poems often criticized women's roles as wives and the position of women in society.

From 1868 she became active in reform. She helped found the New England Women's Club and the New England Woman Suffrage Association, and became president of the club in 1870. She supported the final version of the Fifteenth Amendment, which gave the vote to African American men without barring discrimination against women, because she viewed Black men's suffrage as the priority. In 1871 the Massachusetts Supreme Court nullified her nomination as justice of the peace, ruling that women could not hold judicial office without the legislature's authorization. From 1872 she edited the Woman's Journal for twenty years, and in 1890 she helped found the General Federation of Women's Clubs.

On 28 January 1908 Howe became the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Letters. She died of pneumonia on 17 October 1910 at her home, Oak Glen, in Portsmouth, Rhode Island, aged 91, and is buried at Mount Auburn Cemetery in Cambridge, Massachusetts. About 4,000 people sang the Battle Hymn of the Republic at her memorial service, as it had been the custom to sing it at each of her speaking engagements.

Her children wrote a biography, published in 1916, which won the Pulitzer Prize for Biography. She entered the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1970 and the National Women's Hall of Fame in 1998, and the U.S. Postal Service issued a 14-cent stamp in her honour in 1987.
julian-calendar: The Julian calendar was proposed in 46 BCE by Julius Caesar, from whom it takes its name, as a reform of the earlier Roman calendar, which was largely lunisolar. That calendar had 12 months and 355 days, with a 27- or 28-day intercalary month inserted between February and March in some years. The reform took effect on 1 January 45 BCE by Caesar's edict. To realign the year with the seasons, 46 BCE was made 445 days long: it already had 378 days through the regular intercalary month, and Caesar added 67 more by inserting two extraordinary intercalary months between November and December.

The calendar has normal years of 365 days and leap years of 366, in a cycle of three normal years and one leap year that repeats without exception, giving an average year of 365.25 days. The months were formed by adding ten days to the 355-day year: two extra days went to January, Sextilis and December, and one each to April, June, September and November. February stayed at 28 days, so the ordinary month lengths are those still used today.

The old intercalary month was abolished and replaced by a single leap day at the same point, dated the sixth doubled day before the Kalends of March, which gave English the word bissextile. The pontifices at first added a leap day every three years instead of every four, an error recorded by several ancient writers.

Caesar's reform applied only to the Roman calendar, but in the following decades many civic and provincial calendars of the empire were aligned to it, and it became the predominant calendar of the Western world for more than 1,600 years. Because the Julian year is longer than the solar year, the calendar gains one day every 128 years. By 1582, 21 March was ten days out of alignment with the equinox, and Pope Gregory XIII promulgated a revised calendar.

Most Catholic countries adopted it at once and Protestant countries over the following two centuries; Greece was the last to adopt it as its civil calendar, in 1923. Most Eastern Orthodox churches still base their liturgical year on the Julian calendar, as does the Berber calendar of the Maghreb.
julian-emperor: Julian, whose full name was Flavius Claudius Julianus, was born at Constantinople, probably in 331, into the family of the reigning emperor, Constantine I. His father was Julius Constantius, Constantine's younger half-brother, and his mother was Basilina, a Bithynian noble who died shortly after his birth. As the nephew of Rome's first Christian emperor, he was brought up a Christian. He was one of few in the imperial family to survive the purges and civil wars under his cousin Constantius II. His father was executed in 337, and he lived much of his life under Constantius's close supervision, though he was allowed to pursue an education in the Greek-speaking east.

On 6 November 355 Constantius appointed Julian Caesar of the West and married him to his sister Helena. Constantius meant him to be a figurehead, but Julian learned to lead an army in campaigns against the Germanic tribes on both sides of the Rhine. In 356 he recovered towns held by the Franks, including Colonia Agrippina, now Cologne.

In February 360 Constantius ordered more than half of Julian's Gallic troops east, which provoked an insurrection, and the soldiers proclaimed Julian emperor at Lutetia, now Paris. A civil war loomed, but Constantius died before the two met in battle, having named Julian as his successor. On 11 December 361 Julian entered Constantinople as sole emperor, and his first act was to preside over the Christian burial of Constantius.

Julian purged the top-heavy bureaucracy, openly promoted pagans to high office and tried to revive traditional Roman religion at the expense of Christianity. He expelled Christians from the military and forbade them to teach or study the classical texts. His efforts to build a Third Temple in Jerusalem were probably meant to harm Christianity rather than please Jews. The Christian tradition remembers him as Julian the Apostate. His reign saw a brief resurgence of paganism, but his policies had no lasting effect on its decline.

In March 363 he launched a campaign against the Sasanian Empire with the largest Roman army ever to face the Persians. After a victory outside Ctesiphon he moved into Persia's heartland instead of besieging the city, ran short of supplies and had to retreat while Persian skirmishers harassed him. He was mortally wounded at the Battle of Samarra and died on 26 June 363. His successor Jovian had to cede territory, including Nisibis, to save the trapped army.
juliana-of-the-netherlands: Juliana was born on 30 April 1909 at Noordeinde Palace in The Hague, the only child of Queen Wilhelmina and Duke Henry of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Her birth removed the prospect of a succession crisis. She was educated at a small school class formed at the palace, then by private tutors, and in 1927 she came of age and entered the Council of State. She studied at the University of Leiden.

She met Prince Bernhard of Lippe-Biesterfeld at the 1936 Winter Olympics, and they married in The Hague on 7 January 1937. They had four daughters: Beatrix, Irene, Margriet and Christina. After the German invasion of May 1940 the family went to Britain, and Juliana took her children to Canada, returning to the Netherlands on 2 May 1945.

She served as regent from 14 October to 1 December 1947 and was sworn in as queen on 6 September 1948, two days after her mother's abdication. On 27 December 1949 she signed the documents recognising Indonesian sovereignty and became head of the Netherlands-Indonesian Union, which lasted until 1956. In 1954 she announced that the Netherlands Antilles and Suriname would become constituent countries of the Kingdom, and Suriname became independent on 25 November 1975.

During the North Sea flood of 31 January 1953, which drowned more than 1,800 people, she waded through water and mud to visit the stricken areas. Her reign saw several crises, among them the influence of the faith healer Greet Hofmans at court in 1956, Princess Irene's conversion to Roman Catholicism and marriage in 1964, and the engagement of Princess Beatrix to Claus von Amsberg in 1965. In 1976 Prince Bernhard was found to have accepted a bribe from Lockheed, and he resigned his positions.

Juliana abdicated on 30 April 1980, her seventy-first birthday, in favour of Beatrix. From the mid-1990s she suffered dementia and did not appear in public. She died at Soestdijk Palace in Baarn on 20 March 2004, aged 94, and was interred beside her mother in the royal vault under the Nieuwe Kerk in Delft. Julianadorp near Den Helder and Princess Juliana International Airport in St Maarten are named after her.
julio-argentino-roca: Julio Argentino Roca was born on 17 July 1843 in San Miguel de Tucumán into a prominent local family and studied at the National College in Concepción del Uruguay. Before he was fifteen he joined the army of the Argentine Confederation and fought in the struggle between Buenos Aires and the interior provinces. He fought in the War of the Triple Alliance against Paraguay from 1865, in which his father and two of his brothers died. Later he rose to colonel in the war against the revolt of Ricardo López Jordán, and President Nicolás Avellaneda promoted him to general after his victory at Santa Rosa.

In 1878 Roca became minister of war under Avellaneda. Frontier groups defended their traditional territories and raided settlements. His predecessor Adolfo Alsina had ordered a ditch and a line of small forts across Buenos Aires Province, but Roca saw no way to end the raids except by bringing all land up to the Río Negro under government control, in a campaign that would extinguish, subdue or expel the Indians living there. This Conquest of the Desert began against the Ranqueles in 1878–1879. Roca commanded it in the field, and it is sometimes considered a genocide.
The campaigns went on after 1880 in Neuquén and Río Negro, in the Andes and in a final phase to 1885, and Argentina completed the occupation of what are now Neuquén, Chubut and southern Río Negro.

Elected in 1880 as the candidate of the National Autonomist Party, Roca was inaugurated amid a revolution in Buenos Aires that cost 3,000 lives and ended on 25 June with an agreement. Congress federalised the city of Buenos Aires. His first term (1880–1886) saw large public works, secular reforms including a civil registry and Law 1420 on compulsory, free and secular primary education. A treaty of 1881 fixed the boundary with Chile along the Andes to the 52nd parallel.

He returned to the presidency on 12 October 1898. His second term saw the founding in 1901 of the first Argentine trade union federation and a first general strike in 1902, to which he responded with the Residence Law, which allowed the expulsion of immigrants without trial. He died in Buenos Aires on 19 October 1914 and is buried in La Recoleta Cemetery. Some currents of opinion criticise him as genocidal, and his name has been removed from several streets and schools.
julio-cortazar: Julio Florencio Cortázar was born on 26 August 1914 in Ixelles, a municipality of Brussels, where his Argentine father was attached to the diplomatic service. The family spent two years in Switzerland and settled outside Buenos Aires by the end of 1919.

His father left when Julio was six. He grew up in Banfield, a suburb south of Buenos Aires, with his mother and younger sister, and was a sickly child who spent much of his childhood in bed reading. He qualified as an elementary school teacher at 18 and studied philosophy and languages at the University of Buenos Aires, leaving for financial reasons without a degree. In 1944 he became professor of French literature at the National University of Cuyo, but resigned in June 1946 under pressure from Peronists.

His play Los Reyes, based on the myth of Theseus and the Minotaur, appeared in 1949 and passed almost unnoticed. His short stories began to attract interest in the late forties, especially Casa Tomada, published in a magazine edited by Jorge Luis Borges. In 1951 he moved to France, where he lived for the rest of his life, and from 1952 he worked intermittently as a translator for UNESCO. He wrote most of his major works in Paris or in Saignon in the south of France.

His story collections Bestiario (1951), Final del juego (1956) and Las armas secretas (1959) established his reputation. His stories often place protagonists in ordinary situations that turn strange or horrific. He published four novels in his lifetime: Los premios (1960), Hopscotch (1963), 62: A Model Kit (1968) and Libro de Manuel (1973). Cortázar drew on Surrealism and the improvisation of jazz, reflected in Hopscotch and in El perseguidor, based on the life of the saxophonist Charlie Parker.

Cortázar became increasingly engaged in opposing human rights abuses in Latin America and supported the Sandinista revolution in Nicaragua, the Cuban revolution and Salvador Allende's government in Chile. His first visit to Cuba came in 1963. In 1981 he married the Canadian writer Carol Dunlop and received French nationality from President François Mitterrand. After the restoration of democracy he made a last trip to Argentina in 1983. He died in Paris on 12 February 1984 and is buried in the cimetière du Montparnasse. Leukemia was reported as the cause, though some sources say AIDS following a blood transfusion.

Michelangelo Antonioni's film Blowup (1966) was inspired by his story Las babas del diablo, and Cortázar appears in it briefly. His story La autopista del sur influenced Jean-Luc Godard's Week End (1967). Roberto Bolaño cited Cortázar and Borges as permanent debts. A school, a public library and a square in the Palermo district of Buenos Aires bear his name.
julius-caesar: Gaius Julius Caesar was born into a patrician family, the gens Julia, on 12 or 13 July 100 BCE. The family claimed descent from Julus, the son of Aeneas, and so from Venus. There is no evidence that Caesar was born by Caesarian section, since such operations entailed the mother's death and his mother lived for decades afterwards. The Julii Caesares were not especially influential in the middle republic; their first consul held office in 157 BCE. Caesar's father, of the same name, married Aurelia, and his sister married the influential Gaius Marius.

Caesar won the consulship of 59 BCE with the support of Crassus. He reconciled Pompey and Crassus in a three-way alliance, termed the First Triumvirate in modern times. His victories in the Gallic Wars, completed by 51 BCE, greatly expanded Roman territory; during them he invaded Britain and built a bridge across the Rhine. From 52 to 49 BCE trust between Caesar and Pompey disintegrated. On 7 January 49 BCE the Senate declared Caesar an enemy, and in early January he crossed the Rubicon and marched towards Rome, beginning the civil war.

He was appointed dictator some four times from 49 BCE and annually from April 46 BCE. The Senate gave him honours, among them his portrait on coins, as the first living Roman so shown, and the renaming of Quintilis as Julius. He created the Julian calendar, settled veterans in overseas colonies and extended citizenship to communities in Spain and northern Italy. He took the title dictator perpetuo in February 44 BCE.

A group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius, fearful of his power and of the possibility that he might make himself king, assassinated Caesar on the Ides of March, 15 March 44 BCE. New civil wars followed and the Republic's constitutional government was never fully restored. His great-nephew and adoptive heir Octavian, later Augustus, rose to sole power thirteen years later and became the first emperor. Much of Caesar's life is known from his own commentaries, the Gallic Wars and the Civil War, which he wrote with his political career in mind. His name became a title, giving rise to Kaiser and Tsar.
julius-nyerere: Julius Kambarage Nyerere was born on 13 April 1922 in Mwitongo, part of the village of Butiama in Tanganyika's Mara Region. He was one of 25 surviving children of Nyerere Burito, chief of the Zanaki people. The colonial administration encouraged the education of chiefs' sons, and at his father's prompting Nyerere began school in February 1934 at the Native Administration School in Mwisenge, Musoma.

In January 1943 he arrived at Makerere College in Kampala on a bursary for teacher training. After teaching at the mission-run St Mary's in Tabora, he went to the University of Edinburgh in April 1949 and took an Ordinary Master of Arts. He later said he had evolved the whole of his political philosophy there. He returned in October 1952, married Maria Gabriel in January 1953 and taught history at St Francis' College.

In April 1953 Nyerere became president of the Tanganyika African Association, which under him turned to the pursuit of independence, and in 1954 he helped found TANU. Influenced by Gandhi, he preached non-violence and said that TANU was fighting colonialism, not the whites. Tanganyika gained independence on 9 December 1961, and six weeks later he resigned as prime minister to restructure TANU. It became a republic on 9 December 1962, with Nyerere as president.

After the Zanzibar Revolution Tanganyika united with Zanzibar as Tanzania in 1964. In January 1967 Nyerere presented the Arusha Declaration, committing the government to democratic socialism and self-reliance. Banks and major industries were nationalised and education and health care expanded. In the early 1970s villagisation moved about 13 million people into around 7,000 villages, and forced moves disrupted rural production; none of the villages had met productivity targets by 1978, and many depended on famine relief. His government also trained and aided movements fighting white-minority rule in southern Africa, and Tanzania's 1978–1979 war with Uganda overthrew Idi Amin.

Nyerere stepped down as president in 1985, succeeded by Ali Hassan Mwinyi, who reversed many of his policies. He remained chair of Chama Cha Mapinduzi until 1990. He died on 14 October 1999. Within Tanzania he is called the Father of the Nation.

Admirers praise him as an anti-colonialist and for keeping Tanzania stable and unified; critics point to his one-party state and detention without trial, and blame him for economic mismanagement. In the late 1990s he said he had made mistakes, particularly in pursuing nationalisation too early, but stood by the Arusha Declaration. In 2005 the Diocese of Musoma opened the cause for his canonisation, with the title Servant of God.
july-crisis: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 Austria-Hungary was given the right to occupy and administer Ottoman Bosnia and Herzegovina, and thirty years later it formally annexed the territory, upsetting the balance of power in the Balkans. On 28 June 1914 Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir presumptive to the throne, toured Sarajevo with his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, after attending military exercises in Bosnia. Six armed irredentists, coordinated by Danilo Ilić, waited along the route, and Gavrilo Princip, a Bosnian Serb nationalist, shot them both.

Austria-Hungary's leaders wanted to inflict a military blow on Serbia, which they saw as a threat to the unity of their multi-national empire. Wary of Russia, Vienna sought a guarantee from Germany, and Count Hoyos travelled to Berlin on 5 July. Germany gave its support, later called the blank cheque, but urged a quick attack. On 7 July the Council of Joint Ministers agreed, with the Hungarian prime minister István Tisza alone opposing war, to present an ultimatum designed to be rejected. Meanwhile France and Russia met in St Petersburg between 20 and 23 July and reaffirmed their alliance.

The ultimatum was delivered on 23 July and gave Serbia only 48 hours. It demanded that Serbia condemn propaganda against Austria-Hungary, suppress hostile publications and dissolve the nationalist society Narodna Odbrana. Serbia mobilised on 24 July, Russia began a partial mobilisation, and Britain's foreign secretary Edward Grey offered mediation. After reading Serbia's reply, Emperor Wilhelm II remarked that every reason for war had disappeared, but Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia at 11:00 on 28 July. Russia ordered general mobilisation on 30 July.

Germany mobilised between 1 and 3 August, and most of the major European states were at war by early August. Britain, fearing that Germany might overrun France, declared war on 4 August and used the German invasion of Belgium to win popular support. By then the assassination had become a side-note to a larger European war. Historians debate the responsibility of each government. Samuel R. Williamson Jr. has emphasised the role of Austria-Hungary, which hoped for a limited war and expected German support to keep Russia out.
july-revolution: After the defeat of Napoleonic France in 1814, the Congress of Vienna restored the House of Bourbon in the person of Louis XVIII, and forced him to grant a constitution, the Charter of 1814. His brother Charles X, who succeeded him on 16 September 1824, was known for more reactionary politics. His popularity in Paris fell within months, over a law imposing the death penalty for profaning the Eucharist and over indemnities for property confiscated in the 1789 Revolution. On 17 March 1830 the Chamber of Deputies passed a motion of no confidence, the Address of the 221, against the ministry of Jules de Polignac. Elections held in July gave the liberal opposition a majority of 274 to 143.

The ordinances were published in Le Moniteur on 26 July. Members of the Paris Bourse refused to lend money, factory owners shut their workshops, and nearly 50 journalists met at the offices of Le National and signed a protest. On 27 July fighting began in the evening, when paving stones and roof tiles were thrown at soldiers; twenty-one civilians were killed before night.

On 28 July Charles X, remaining at Saint-Cloud, ordered Marshal Auguste Marmont to put down the unrest. Marmont's troops were too few and some line units were deserting. An opposition committee, including the banker Jacques Laffitte, petitioned for the withdrawal of the ordinances, but Polignac refused to see them. Marmont wrote to the King that it was no longer a riot but a revolution; Polignac advised resistance. By 29 July over 4,000 barricades had been built. The Louvre fell, the Tuileries Palace was sacked, and the Hôtel de Ville was taken by mid-afternoon. Looting was small, and the crowd protected the paintings of the Louvre.

Charles X and his son the Dauphin abdicated on 2 August. Charles had intended that his grandson, the Duke of Bordeaux, should reign as Henry V, but the provisional government placed Louis Philippe of the House of Orléans on the throne as a constitutional monarch. Supporters of the exiled senior Bourbon line became known as Legitimists. The July Column on the Place de la Bastille commemorates the revolution.

The example set off an uprising in Brussels in August that led to the Kingdom of Belgium. Revolutions in Italy and the November Uprising in Poland, inspired by it, failed. In 1832 Parisian republicans, disappointed with the outcome, rose in the June Rebellion, which was crushed within a week.
jupiter-god: The name Iuppiter began as a vocative compound of an Old Latin form Iou and pater, father, and descends from a Proto-Italic phrase meaning sky father. Jupiter is thought to have originated as a sky god, and his Etruscan counterpart is usually taken to be Tinia. The Romans equated him with the Greek Zeus, and Latin literature and art adapted the myths of Zeus under his name. Georg Wissowa stressed that Jupiter is the one case among Indo-European religions in which the original sky god kept his name, identity and prerogatives.

His emblem was the thunderbolt and his main sacred animal the eagle, which became one of the commonest symbols of the Roman army; his sacred tree was the oak. As the sky god he was a divine witness to oaths, and the Romans saw in him the source of the auspices on which the relationship between the city and the gods rested. They believed that he granted them supremacy because they had honoured him more than any other people. The fetials, the college devoted to the religious side of foreign affairs, invoked Jupiter Lapis when a treaty was concluded.

He was served by the Flamen Dialis, the highest-ranking of fifteen flamines, and the augurs were considered the only official interpreters of his will. On the Ides of each month a white lamb was led along the Sacred Way to the Capitoline citadel and sacrificed to him, and more fixed holidays of the Republican calendar were devoted to Jupiter than to any other deity.

The Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill was supposedly begun by Tarquinius Priscus, completed by the last king, Tarquinius Superbus, and inaugurated on 13 September 509 BCE, in the early days of the Republic. It was topped with a quadriga, a four-horse chariot, driven by Jupiter, and inside stood a large statue whose face was painted red on festival days. There Jupiter was worshipped with Juno and Minerva as the Capitoline Triad. The cult of Iuppiter Latiaris, practised on the Alban Mount, is the oldest known cult of the god.
jura-mountains: The Jura range proper, the folded Jura, lies in France and Switzerland and mainly marks a long part of their border. To the northeast it continues as the Table Jura, which is not folded, through northern Switzerland and into the German states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria, and is crossed by the High Rhine. In France the range covers most of the Franche-Comté region and reaches its highest point at the Crêt de la Neige, at 1,720 metres, in the department of Ain. About 1,600 square kilometres of it are protected as the Jura Mountains Regional Natural Park.

The range is built of a sequence of geological folds, formed as the Alpine mountain building pushed northwards. Three bands date from the Lias, Dogger and Malm, the Early, Middle and Late Jurassic. The folds are young enough to show little erosion. The range separates the basins of the Rhine and the Rhône: the north and east drain to the Rhine through the Aare and the Ill, the west and south to the Rhône through the Doubs, the Saône and the Ain.

The name is first recorded as mons Iura in Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and the geographer Strabo gives a Greek form of it. Early Celtic scholars proposed that it was a Celtic word for mountains, but there are no clear cognates in the surviving Celtic languages, and its origin remains unclear. The range gave its name to the French department of Jura, the Swiss canton of Jura, the Jurassic period of the geological timescale and the Montes Jura on the Moon.

Much of the Swiss Jura had no historical association with early modern Switzerland and was incorporated into the Swiss Confederacy only in the 19th century. In the 20th century a separatist movement developed there, which led to the creation of the Canton of Jura in 1979. The Swiss Jura has been industrialised since the 18th century and became a major centre of watchmaking. High-lying towns such as La Chaux-de-Fonds, Le Locle and Sainte-Croix, known for its musical boxes, grew up there. In the French Jura the 11th-century Fort de Joux, near Pontarlier, was remodelled and strengthened by Vauban in 1690.

The range offers hiking, cycling and skiing, with signposted trails such as the 310-kilometre Jura ridgeway. Swiss attractions include the Creux du Van, the Chasseral, the Grottes de Vallorbe and the Taubenloch gorge. Le Locle and La Chaux-de-Fonds are together a UNESCO World Heritage Site for their watchmaking heritage.
jurchens: The Jurchens were a number of Tungusic-speaking peoples who lived in the part of north-eastern China known as Manchuria. They first entered Chinese records in 748, in the forests and river valleys of what is now divided between Heilongjiang Province and Russia's Primorsky Krai. Scholarship since the Qing period has traced their origin to the Mohe tribes, among them the Heishui or Blackwater Mohe, but this remains conjectural. They were culturally diverse, with groups living as hunter-gatherers, semi-nomadic pastoralists or settled farmers, and they generally lacked a central authority.

By the 11th century the Jurchens were vassals of the Khitan rulers of the Liao dynasty. Those near the Yalu River had been tributaries of Goryeo since the reign of Taejo of Goryeo, and they switched allegiance between Liao and Goryeo as it suited them, offering tribute to both courts for the material rewards it brought.

In 1115 Wanyan Aguda, chief of the Wanyan tribe, united the Jurchen tribes and declared himself emperor. The dynasty took the name Jin, meaning gold, after the Gold River of the Jurchen homeland. In 1120 he seized Shangjing, the northern capital of Liao. In the Jin–Song Wars the Jurchens overran most of northern China, captured the Northern Song capital Bianjing in 1127 and settled on a border with the Southern Song along the Huai River. Jurchens who settled in towns intermarried with other peoples, and the Jin rulers came to follow Confucian norms.

Under the Ming, Chinese officials sorted the Jurchens into three groups: the Jianzhou, the Haixi and the so-called Wild Jurchens. The Yongle Emperor found allies among them against the Mongols and set up 178 commanderies in Manchuria. From 1586 Nurhaci, a chieftain of the Jianzhou Jurchens, united the tribes over some 30 years. In 1635 his son Hong Taiji renamed his people the Manchus, a break from their past as Chinese vassals, and the dynasty founded the next year became the Qing.

Like the Khitans and Mongols, the Jurchens prized horsemanship, archery and hunting, and they used the title khan and the term beile for a powerful chief. Unlike the Mongols, most were sedentary farmers of grain and millet who also kept oxen, pigs, sheep and horses. They did not observe primogeniture, so any capable son or nephew could become leader. They practised shamanic rituals and revered a sky goddess, and under the Jin many turned to Buddhism. Wanyan Xiyin devised a Jurchen script in 1120, based on the Khitan script, but it died out soon after the Jin fell. Nurhaci's followers were organised into the Eight Banners and adopted a script based on Mongolian.
jurji-zaydan: Jurji Zaydan was born in Beirut on 14 December 1861 to an Eastern Orthodox Christian family of limited means, which had probably come from the Hauran. His father owned a restaurant and, being illiterate, placed little value on schooling, so Zaydan left school after elementary education to help in the business.

He studied English at night classes and in 1881 was admitted to the Syrian Protestant College as a medical student. Samuel Smiles's Self-Help and the teaching of Cornelius Van Dyck shaped his belief that education was the key to a people's progress. In 1882 the dismissal of Professor E. Lewis for praising Charles Darwin brought student protests, and Zaydan was among those who left for Cairo.

In Egypt he spent a short time at the medical school and went with a British army expedition to the Sudan before turning to writing. He worked briefly as assistant editor of al-Muqtataf and travelled to London to research Arabic history in the British Museum. In 1890 he published a History of the World, cited as one of the first non-Islamic histories written in Arabic. He opened the publishing house Dar al-Hilal. In 1891 he married Maryam Matar and published his first historical novel, al-Mamluk al-Shariid, whose success let him give up teaching. In 1892 he began the magazine al-Hilal, which carried history, articles, news and serialised novels.

Zaydan wrote roughly a novel a year, usually in the summer, for serial publication in the autumn. Each began with a historical topic in Islamic history, which he read up thoroughly, and an outline built on fact, around which he placed a love story and a mystery between invented characters. His aim was to give ordinary Arabs an accurate sense of their own history in an accessible form, and he put accuracy before plot. He wrote 23 novels in all.

In 1910 the newly opened Egyptian University offered him a chair in Islamic history. He accepted reluctantly, aware of his unpopularity among conservative Muslims, and was dismissed before beginning after public outcry over his Christian origins and secular leanings. His secular History of the Islamic Civilization, published from 1901 to 1906, had been especially controversial. The episode embittered him, and he died unexpectedly on 21 July 1914.

Al-Hilal circulated in places as distant as Persia, India, Japan, Zanzibar and North and South America. His influence is traced in Taha Hussein, Naguib Mahfouz and Fadwa Tuqan, and he is considered one of the first thinkers to help formulate the theory of Arab nationalism. Several of his novels were translated into English in 2011 and 2012.
juscelino-kubitschek: Kubitschek was born on 12 September 1902 in Diamantina, Minas Gerais, into a poor family. His father, a travelling salesman, died when he was two, and his mother Júlia, a schoolteacher, raised him. He graduated in medicine in 1927 and later specialised in urology in Paris. He was elected a federal deputy in 1934 but lost the seat when the Estado Novo began in 1937. In 1940 he became mayor of Belo Horizonte, where he began his working relationship with the architect Oscar Niemeyer, and in 1950 he became governor of Minas Gerais.

Kubitschek campaigned in 1955 with the slogan of fifty years of progress in five and won the October election with 35.6 per cent of the vote, with João Goulart as his running mate. Opponents pressed to annul the result, and General Henrique Teixeira Lott led a military countercoup to secure his inauguration on 31 January 1956. His Goals Plan had 31 goals in six groups, with the construction of Brasília as the main one. Imported machinery was exempted from taxes where foreign capital was associated with national capital, and the motor industry grew. By the end of his term foreign debt had risen from 87 million to 297 million dollars, industrial production had grown by 80 per cent and inflation stood at 43 per cent.

Brasília had been envisaged in earlier constitutions, but planning began only in 1956. Lúcio Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and Roberto Burle Marx led the work, which started in February 1957 and brought some 30,000 workers to the savanna. The city was inaugurated by the target date of 21 April 1960. His government was often accused of corruption, particularly over the construction.

Kubitschek was elected senator for Goiás in 1961. After the military coup of 1964 he was accused of corruption and of communist support, his mandate was revoked and his political rights were suspended for ten years. He lived in voluntary exile in the United States and Europe, and returned to Brazil in March 1967. He died on 22 August 1976 in a car crash near Resende, and some 350,000 mourners attended his burial in Brasília, where he lies in the JK Memorial.
justicialist-party: Peronism took shape between November 1943 and October 1945, from an alliance of unions and two soldiers, Juan Domingo Perón and Domingo Mercante, who ran the National Labor Department, later raised to the level of Secretary of Labor and Social Security. Argentina was then governed by the military regime of the Revolution of 1943. In 1945 the American ambassador Spruille Braden helped organise an anti-Peronist movement against Perón and the labour laws. Perón resigned on 8 October 1945 after losing the support of officers at Campo de Mayo and was detained. Nine days later a large workers' mobilisation, Loyalty Day, forced the government to prepare his release and call elections, and that day is most often cited as the birth of Peronism.

The party was created in November 1946, ten months after Perón's election as president, under the name Single Revolutionary Party, later called the Peronist Party. It fused three parties formed in 1945 to support his candidacy: the Labor Party, the Radical Renovating Civic Union and the Independent Party. A Female Peronist Party led by Eva Perón followed the enactment of women's suffrage.

Perón nationalised public services, strategic industries and the farm export sector, enacted labour laws and social reforms, and increased public works. He raised taxes on the agrarian sector and promoted urbanisation, which won much of the working and lower classes but alienated the upper and middle classes. Censorship and repression grew, and after losing the support of the Catholic Church he was deposed by the Revolución Libertadora in 1955. All Peronist entities were then banned from elections, and civilian attempts to lift the ban from legislative and local elections in 1962 and 1965 ended in military coups.

In exile Perón chose the activist John William Cooke in 1956 to represent the movement, and Peronism moved gradually left under the influence of the Cuban Revolution and liberation theology. With Perón's encouragement Peronist youth formed revolutionary organisations such as the Montoneros and the People's Revolutionary Army. Perón governed again from 1973 to 1974, and his wife Isabel succeeded him. From the 1990s the party was divided, until 2020, between Kirchnerism, its left-wing populist main faction, and Federal Peronism, which lay on the centre and centre-right.

Until 1955 the party was, in the account of Lewinsky, created from above by agents of the State and extremely personalist. Its statutes of 1954 declared Perón the Supreme Leader, with authority to intervene in and replace local leaders, and banned party offices from displaying any photographs but his and Eva Perón's. Its main base has historically been the General Confederation of Labor. The historian Daniel James wrote that Perón was more a creature of the trade unions than they of him.
justin-ahomadegbe-tometin: Justin Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin was born on 16 January 1917 in Abomey, a direct descendant of the kings of Abomey. He attended the École William Ponty and the French West Africa School of Medicine in Dakar, served briefly in the French Army, reaching the rank of sergeant, and then took up dentistry, opening an office in Porto-Novo. Originally a member of the Dahomeyan Progressive Union, he founded the African People's Bloc in 1946 and was elected to the General Council soon afterwards. He criticised French rule and gained influence by allying with the trade unions, and in November 1956 he was elected mayor of Abomey.

In the territorial elections of 1959 his Dahomeyan Democratic Union won 162,179 votes but only 11 seats, against 37 for Sourou-Migan Apithy's party and 22 for Hubert Maga's. His supporters rioted so severely that French soldiers were called in, and Maga was chosen as a compromise prime minister on 22 May 1959.

After independence on 1 August 1960 Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin broke with the united front of the three parties and incited strikes and demonstrations. He was sentenced to five years for a plot to assassinate Maga, and the party was banned. Maga released the prisoners in November 1962. Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin served as president of the National Assembly from April 1959 to November 1960, and as prime minister and vice president from 1964 to 1965.

After a series of coups, the election of 28 March 1970 gave Maga 252,551 votes, Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin 200,091 and Apithy 186,332, with each winning his own region. The military leader Paul-Émile de Souza annulled the results from Atakora, and on 7 May 1970 the three leaders agreed on a Presidential Council whose chair rotated every two years. Maga chaired it first, and on 7 May 1972 handed power to Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin, the first non-military transfer of power in twelve years.

The council lost support over the expulsion of the Togolese opposition leader Noe Kutuklui in 1971 and the closing of a radical student union. On 26 October 1972 a coup led by Major Mathieu Kérékou overthrew it. The three men were held until 1981. Ahomadégbé-Tomêtin sat in parliament from 1991 to 1995, led his party until his death on 8 March 2002, and was given a state funeral.
justin-i: Justin was born to a peasant family in the hamlet of Bederiana near Naissus (modern Niš, Serbia), in the province of Dardania. He was of Thraco-Roman or Illyro-Roman descent and spoke Latin and only rudimentary Greek. According to legend he was a swineherd. As a young man he left Dardania with two companions to escape poverty and took refuge in Constantinople. Illiterate on arrival, he joined the newly formed palace guard, the excubitors, campaigned against the Isaurians and the Sassanian Persians, and rose to be comes excubitorum, commander of the palace guard, under Anastasius I Dicorus. He married Lupicina, whom Procopius described as a barbarian slave.

Anastasius died childless on the night of 8-9 July 518. Amantius, the chamberlain, backed Theocritus as successor and is said to have given Justin money to buy his support, but Justin used it for himself. He controlled a smaller but better group of soldiers and was proclaimed emperor in the Hippodrome. Amantius and Theocritus were executed nine days later. His wife took the name Euphemia, a sign of the couple's fervent Chalcedonian faith.

Justin was seen as an illiterate soldier with little knowledge of statecraft, and relied on advisers, above all his nephew Justinian, whom he adopted. Because Justin could not read or write, the palace made a wooden stencil spelling the Latin word LEGI, "I have read". On 28 March 519 Patriarch John II accepted the formula of Pope Hormisdas, ending the Acacian schism between Rome and Constantinople. Justin persecuted Miaphysites for his first three years, and in 523 issued a strict edict against Arianism.

He cultivated client states on the borders and avoided serious warfare until late in his reign. King Tzath of Lazica came to Constantinople in 521 or 522 to receive royal robes from him and to be baptised. In 526 an earthquake destroyed Antioch, with an estimated 250,000 deaths, and Justin sent money for relief and rebuilding.

Procopius wrote that Justin's mental faculties declined in old age. Justinian, consul in 521 and caesar in 525, took over more of policy, and Justin named him co-emperor and, on 1 April 527, his successor. Justin died on 1 August 527. His reign founded the Justinian dynasty, which included Justinian I and three later emperors. The Cilician city of Caesarea was renamed Justinopolis in his honour in 525.
justin-ii: Justin was a son of Vigilantia, the sister of Justinian I, and of Dulcidio. He married Sophia, the niece of Justinian's wife Theodora, possibly in the 540s. His early years are obscure, but under Justinian he served as curopalates at court. He is first attested in 552 and 553 as part of an embassy to Pope Vigilius, and in 562 and 563 he dealt with riots of the Blues and Greens in Constantinople. He built a network of supporters, and early on he was seen as an energetic and even well-liked man.

Justinian died childless on 14 November 565. Callinicus, the praepositus sacri cubiculi, claimed that Justinian had named Justin as heir on his deathbed, and modern historians suspect he may have invented it. The Excubitors blocked the palace entrances overnight, and the Patriarch John Scholasticus crowned Justin before the death of Justinian was announced. Justin repaid the treasury's debts, burned its bonds and remitted tax arrears back to 560, and he became consul on 1 January 566. In 569 he let provincial elites nominate their own governors. A rival, also named Justin, a son of Germanus, was assassinated in Alexandria soon after the accession.

Justin ended Justinian's practice of buying off potential enemies. Halting subsidies to the Avars upset the balance of power in the Pannonian Basin, and after the Avars and Lombards destroyed the Gepids, the Lombards moved west and invaded Italy in 568 under Alboin.
